item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
item.description:
While walking alongside Victoria Harbour or riding the Star Ferry, luck might have allowed you a glimpse of Way Foong motoring by. Its old-fashioned appearance is a sign that the boat is obviously from an era long past but, because it is not a traditional junk, you may not have realised you were looking at an authentic piece of Hong Kong history: a wooden motoryacht constructed locally almost 100 years ago.

Commissioned by the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (now HSBC) – “Way Foong” being a transliteration of the bank’s name in Cantonese – and built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, the vessel was used by the bank as a ferry, a tugboat and a pleasure craft for employees for more than seven decades before passing into private ownership. In the late 2010s, it was acquired by a patron of the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF) – an organisation officially founded earlier this year by individuals passionate about preserving the city’s maritime legacy.

When hired for parties or other events, Way Foong can often be seen cruising side by side with Java, another 1930s-era wooden vessel built by the same shipyard. Java entered service in 1935 and served for decades in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1. It transported VIPs and port officials, conducted anti-piracy patrols, towed and positioned mooring buoys and even corralled the odd swimming water buffalo. Its Burmese-teak construction, with deck planks measuring almost 4.5cm thick, earned the boat a reputation for being “almost unsinkable” and invulnerable to typhoons.
item.content:encoded:
While walking alongside Victoria Harbour or riding the Star Ferry, luck might have allowed you a glimpse of Way Foong motoring by. Its old-fashioned appearance is a sign that the boat is obviously from an era long past but, because it is not a traditional junk, you may not have realised you were looking at an authentic piece of Hong Kong history: a wooden motoryacht constructed locally almost 100 years ago.

Commissioned by the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (now HSBC) – “Way Foong” being a transliteration of the bank’s name in Cantonese – and built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, the vessel was used by the bank as a ferry, a tugboat and a pleasure craft for employees for more than seven decades before passing into private ownership. In the late 2010s, it was acquired by a patron of the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF) – an organisation officially founded earlier this year by individuals passionate about preserving the city’s maritime legacy.

When hired for parties or other events, Way Foong can often be seen cruising side by side with Java, another 1930s-era wooden vessel built by the same shipyard. Java entered service in 1935 and served for decades in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1. It transported VIPs and port officials, conducted anti-piracy patrols, towed and positioned mooring buoys and even corralled the odd swimming water buffalo. Its Burmese-teak construction, with deck planks measuring almost 4.5cm thick, earned the boat a reputation for being “almost unsinkable” and invulnerable to typhoons.

Way Foong and Java are two of five vessels now owned and maintained by the HKHVF. “By restoring and preserving such examples of the world-class craftsmanship that Hong Kong shipyards were capable of, we aim not only to encourage Hongkongers to discover the city’s commercial, governmental and recreational maritime heritage, but also to nurture the region’s next generation of boaters and ocean-lovers,” says CEO Philip Giannecchini.

Java, the first vessel in the collection, was found by chance. One of the avid sailors who would later establish the HKHVF noticed Java moored in Tai Tam Harbour, on the south side of Hong Kong Island, when taking out his own boat, and wanted to learn more about the 56-foot wooden launch. He ended up meeting the then-owner, and bought Java in the early 2000s. At the time, the rationale behind the purchase was simply to have such a historical pleasure craft in one’s possession. Eventually, the desire to safeguard Hong Kong’s maritime history took hold, setting in motion other acquisitions and the founding of the HKHVF.

A years-long search for extant, pre-50s boats built in the city followed. Nine, in various states of repair, have been identified by the organisation’s historians – some now in the HKHVF collection, others happily and privately owned, and one, Mon Lei, whose whereabouts are unknown.

Given Hong Kong’s coastal geography, boats have, and will always be, an integral part of the city. Yet, while today’s harbours and inlets are teeming with craft of various shapes and sizes, most are built elsewhere, the city’s shipbuilding days having long passed.

However, in the early 20th century, two giants of the industry, the Taikoo Dockyard and the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, were firmly in their prime, and a number of small and medium-sized shipbuilders, such as Hung Hom’s Hop Kee Shipyard, Ah King Slipway and Cheoy Lee Shipyard, also produced wooden vessels for global clients.

Teresa Mak Hiu-see, one of the in-house researchers at the HKHVF, notes that “the 30s were one of the high points in Hong Kong’s shipbuilding tradition for all types of vessels, from cargo liners to pleasure craft, and the industry steamed ahead until Japan invaded Hong Kong in December 1941. Until the end of World War II, all dockyards were under Japanese control”.

Rare survivors such as Way Foong and Java escaped the scrapyard, but many other Hong Kong-built vessels from the 20s and 40s were not so lucky. Says Mak, “With the 40s being a time of war and post-war recovery, that might be a factor in the small number of surviving pleasure craft from that decade.”

In 1972, the Taikoo Dockyard and the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company were merged to form the Hongkong United Dockyards. In 1980, the Whampoa site was shut down and the land was redeveloped into the Whampoa Garden housing estate, now easily identified by its superyacht-shaped shopping centre, a 110-metre-long concrete landmark “moored” amid the residential blocks.

When the Cheoy Lee Shipyard at Penny’s Bay was reclaimed by the Hong Kong government in 1999 to provide a location for Hong Kong Disneyland, it signalled the end of an era: shipbuilding operations in the city were coming to an end. But the final straw came when Ah King’s Causeway Bay shipyard closed, in 2002.

With shipbuilding essentially a thing of the past, the preservation of Hong Kong-made boats has become ever more important, Giannecchini explains, as these examples are “more than just beautiful old vessels – they tell the story of Hong Kong’s craftsmanship, ingenuity and connection to the sea, and that’s a story we want future generations to be able to experience”.

James Barker, captain of the HKHVF fleet, who coordinates the repairs, maintenance and operation of the boats and can often be seen piloting them, adds, “Caring for nearly century-old boats is not easy. Every project you take on turns out to be much larger, more complicated and more expensive than you first envision. For example, the Gardner engine on Way Foong needed to be replaced, but that [British] company went out of business in the 90s, so we had to source everything we needed from other places.”

It is not just hardware that is difficult to secure. Experts who have the technical knowledge to carry out such repairs are dwindling in number as well, he says. “Everyone who used to do these specialised jobs has either retired or passed away. In the absence of all other options, we are forced to research, plan and take on the task ourselves,” says Barker.

“We recently had to pull the propeller shaft from So Fong and replace the rotten timber around the stern, which meant drilling a new hole through the replacement wood,” he continues. “We’re looking at the bones of these boats, not just making sure they look beautiful on the surface. Significant work is needed to ensure these vessels can last for another 100 years.”

As Giannecchini notes, preservation in its finest form means not only maintaining the physical aspect, but also the histories of these vessels. In an effort to share the stories behind the fleet, the HKHVF website has detailed introductions to each boat.

Some have lived lives rich with adventure and drama. Way Foong transported gold and silver bullion to and from ships anchored in Victoria Harbour, as well as chests of banknotes to HSBC branches on Hong Kong’s outlying islands. It was even used for “burning picnics”: junior staff from the bank’s note-cancellation department would burn sacks of old bills in the boiler room, back when Way Foong had its original steam engine, converting the to-be-disposed-of cash into fuel.

According to one account, Way Foong was taken up the Pearl River at the outbreak of World War II and scuppered to prevent it from falling into Japanese hands. After the war, its skipper reportedly returned to the bank to ask for his job back. He was told that it was his if he could find the missing launch. He did – Way Foong was recovered in 1945 and returned to service after a major refit.

Another HKHVF vessel, Tai Mo Shan, served as a film prop in Mamma Mia! (2008), appearing as the sailing boat that transports the three male co-leads – Pierce Brosnan, Colin Firth and Stellan Skarsgård – to the fictional Greek island of Kalokairi, where the wedding in the plot takes place. Tai Mo Shan had been domiciled in Athens at the time of filming and a broker linked the producers to its owner. While the boat was not in great condition, this suited the filmmakers, who wanted to show the fictional owner, played by Skarsgård, as a “scruffy” character; they even exaggerated its run-down look to drive the point home.

Tai Mo Shan was undergoing restoration work at a shipyard in Greece when the HKHVF became aware of it, in the summer of 2025, through a yacht broker’s flier. Arrangements were made to buy the boat, and it was delivered in October 2025.

Tai Mo Shan was built by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, in 1933, and left the city on a 16,000-plus-mile transpacific and then transatlantic voyage to Dartmouth, in Britain, which, by some accounts, included an attempt to spy on Japanese naval installations in the Kuril Islands.

Another vessel, Typhoon, was discovered by the HKHVF through research on Facebook. Built in 1934 at the Hop Kee Shipyard to a design by Harold S. Rouse, for the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, the boat enjoyed a successful racing career up until the relocation of its owner, back to his native Britain. Typhoon was in Scotland when it was acquired, also in 2025.

Late last year, Tracy Van Buskirk, a retired banker who enjoys exploring coastal Maine, in the United States, aboard a 30-foot retrofitted lobster boat, shared her recollections with the HKHVF after having googled the name “So Fong” out of curiosity and found out that the schooner, on which she had sailed in the 70s, from Stamford, Connecticut, to Singapore, was still afloat.

So Fong, a gaff-rigged schooner measuring 82 feet, was built on an Ah King slipway, on commission for American yachtsman A. Thornton Baker. It took around 250 artisans more than seven months to complete the boat. Following its launch in March 1937, So Fong sailed for about 30,000 miles, travelling through the Philippines, the South Seas, the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean and the South Atlantic before reaching San Juan, Puerto Rico, in April 1938. During World War II, the US Coast Guard requisitioned So Fong, according to a commemorative plaque aboard the vessel. After the war, it returned to the Pacific and was used for racing.

Van Buskirk recalls that, at the age of 21, in 1978, she had recently graduated from university after spending a year studying Mandarin in Taiwan.

“I had every intention of returning to Asia, but decided to spend the summer in my hometown of Fairfield to get a job. By early October, I had started planning my flights back to Taipei. One weekend, my mother invited me to go sailing with a family friend, on his 28-foot sloop. He asked me about my plans and volunteered that his son had been hired as first mate for a delivery job of a large schooner that was scheduled to leave Stamford soon and sail to Singapore. William Mathers, the new owner, had bought So Fong earlier that year and hired the captain, Don Kuhn, to take her on this 14,000-mile journey.

“I was intrigued and immediately drove to the Stamford Yacht Club to introduce myself and see about a berth. Kuhn was busy with last-minute arrangements but took a moment for a brief interview. After determining that I was healthy, held a current passport and had some savings, he said I was hired. We left two days later [on October 18, 1978].”

Van Buskirk and So Fong would reach Singapore on March 21 of the following year.

In 1984, Vietnamese authorities seized the vessel in the Pacific Ocean, on suspicion that its sophisticated navigation equipment was being used for espionage, and its owner was placed in solitary confinement. He was released the following year, having paid his way to freedom, but So Fong remained confiscated.

It would spend the next few years abandoned at anchor until yacht enthusiast Robert Verschoyle located the vessel in 1989.

Following an intensive 11-month restoration in Ho Chi Minh City, Verschoyle executed a nighttime escape with So Fong in the early 90s. Under cover of darkness, he smuggled the boat out, and the vessel eventually reappeared in Hong Kong in 1993. After a few decades, during which the boat passed through private hands, Giannecchini was alerted to So Fong’s existence in February 2025, by a friend who had read about it in an article about vintage sailing vessels available for charter in Spain. So Fong finally returned home last October, after being acquired by the HKHVF.

Earlier this year, the HKHVF learned of another Hong Kong-built wooden yacht from the 30s that was still sailing in local waters. Ariki III was constructed in 1939 at the Ah King shipyard, to a design by American naval architect Ralph E. Winslow. Completed just before the outbreak of World War II, she was meant to be shipped to the US, but those plans were foiled by the Japanese occupation of Hong Kong. After years of neglect, she sank in 1946.

New Zealander Hector Forsyth raised the boat, restored it and named it after the Maori word for “leader”. Ariki III became part of the city’s sailing scene, eventually coming into the ownership of long-time sailor Graeme Large, who restored it anew, together with Stanley-based wooden-boat specialist Fan Kwei-sum.

Current owner Peter Lau Man-pong, a businessman and the chairman of the Hong Kong Arts Centre, developed a passion for the sea at an early age, having grown up sailing in the waters around Hong Kong with his father.

“My father was the founding chairman of the Hong Kong Sea Cadet Corps. Now, as its deputy chairman, I also have a deep connection with the sea and related youth activities,” says Lau.

He believes that the HKHVF’s mission to educate the public about Hong Kong’s maritime heritage is important; the team “has a noble vision and noble hearts, in addition to their love of boats”.

Although he used to paddle his wooden kayak from Hong Kong to Macau for leisure, “unfortunately, I am getting old and don’t have the time nor energy to take my boats out as much as I used to. As the HKHVF continues to mature, I am planning on gifting them Ariki III, but the details are still being worked out”.

As its collection grows, the HKHVF has begun making its vessels accessible to the public, through collaborations with people and organisations involved in history, conservation and education, such as the Hong Kong Maritime Museum and the Royal Geographical Society. Additionally, the vessels can be chartered for business and recreational use.

As early as next year, the HKHVF plans to open a small museum at its floating headquarters – a structure made of two connected industrial barges, in the Kwun Tong Typhoon Shelter – to provide a permanent home for its fleet.

“Our vision is to keep researching Hong Kong’s maritime history, preserve significant vessels whenever we have the opportunity and find new ways to share their stories,” says Giannecchini. “We don’t want these boats sitting in a museum as artefacts. We want them to remain active, accessible and connected to the people of Hong Kong.”

As Way Foong and its restored kin continue to glide through Hong Kong’s waters, they do much more than offer a glimpse of a bygone era – they keep part of the city’s history afloat.

item.title: [SCMP] Taipei’s dilemma over history deepens with Xi-Trump praise of WWII Flying Tigers
item.description:
Taipei’s dilemma over its history during World War II appeared to deepen as Beijing and Washington looked to the Flying Tigers as a source of connection and goodwill during last month’s Xi–Trump summit.

US President Donald Trump’s description of China as an American ally during the war has raised concerns in Taiwan that what could have been a valuable historical connection with the United States ended up benefiting Beijing’s ties with Washington.

The dilemma resurfaced after Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping repeatedly invoked wartime Sino-US cooperation during Xi’s visit to Washington last week.
item.content:encoded:
Taipei’s dilemma over its history during World War II appeared to deepen as Beijing and Washington looked to the Flying Tigers as a source of connection and goodwill during last month’s Xi–Trump summit.

US President Donald Trump’s description of China as an American ally during the war has raised concerns in Taiwan that what could have been a valuable historical connection with the United States ended up benefiting Beijing’s ties with Washington.

The dilemma resurfaced after Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping repeatedly invoked wartime Sino-US cooperation during Xi’s visit to Washington last week.

Trump described China and the US as World War II allies and praised the Flying Tigers – a unit of American military personnel who helped defend mainland China against Japanese air attacks – while Xi recalled the two countries fighting “side by side” against Japanese militarism.

A White House fact sheet later said the two leaders recalled that the US and China “were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war”.

The episode has put Taiwan’s independence-leaning ruling Democratic Progressive Party in an awkward position.

Some argue that the island’s long-running efforts to emphasise a distinct Taiwanese identity over the pre-1949 history of the Republic of China (ROC) – Taiwan’s official name – have inadvertently created space for Beijing to claim that legacy.

When China fought Japan alongside the Allies, it was represented by the ROC government, which was overthrown in 1949 on the mainland when Communist forces won the civil war and established the People’s Republic of China (PRC).

Taipei objected to the wartime reference during the Xi-Trump summit, with Deputy Foreign Minister Wu Chih-chung accusing Beijing of trying to replace the ROC’s wartime role and describing the effort as part of Beijing’s “narrative diplomacy”.

The dispute has in fact exposed a dilemma for the DPP, which is now invoking the ROC’s wartime legacy internationally after years of seeking to distinguish Taiwan’s history and identity from that of mainland China.

Taiwan’s main opposition party, the Kuomintang, which ruled the ROC during the war, accused the William Lai Ching-te administration of invoking the pre-1949 republic only when politically useful.

The KMT government retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, and the island retains ROC as its formal name.

KMT communications director Chen I-hsin said Lai had emphasised the “end of the second world war” – a term Japan uses for its defeat – during last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations rather than “victory in the war of resistance against Japan”.

Chen accused the DPP of deliberately distancing itself from the ROC’s mainland-era history.

However, Chuang Jui-hsiung, the DPP’s legislative caucus chief executive, said the “China” that fought alongside the US was indeed the ROC and that “diplomatic language between major powers is often deliberately vague and should not be overinterpreted”.

The controversy has nevertheless highlighted a broader contest between Taipei and Beijing over who inherits the international historical identity of wartime China.

According to Wang Hsin-hsien, director of the National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations in Taipei, while Beijing has long maintained this wartime narrative, what sets this instance apart is that the American account also referred simply to “China” in the context of World War II.

“Trump wants something in the short term, while Xi wants a long-term discourse and narrative,” Wang said.

Washington appeared interested in invoking wartime cooperation to help stabilise Sino-US relations, he added, and Beijing was pursuing a broader historical argument involving the second world war, Taiwan and the post-war international order.

Together with Beijing’s commemorations of what it has called Taiwan’s “restoration” to China following Japan’s surrender in 1945, such arguments were gradually forming a “legal chain”, Wang continued.

If Washington increasingly accepted the same historical framework, the ROC’s role could be “taken away wholesale”, he said.

Yen Chen-sheng, a researcher at the same institute, added that the DPP’s distancing Taiwan from ROC history risked abandoning a valuable historical connection with the US.

That relationship stretched from wartime cooperation and the ROC’s status as a founding member of the United Nations to close political and security ties between Taipei and Washington after the Chinese civil war, Yen said.

The ROC was a founding member of the UN before the global body voted in 1971 to recognise the PRC as the only lawful representative of China at the United Nations.

The debate has also spread online, where critics have accused the DPP of protesting against Beijing’s “erasure” of the ROC while playing down the same name itself.

“On the one hand, they’re quietly pushing Taiwan independence and de-Sinicisation,” one critic said. “On the other, they pretend to be deeply upset and aggrieved. It’s really ugly.”

Beijing has rejected Taipei’s objections. Its Taiwan Affairs Office said victory in the war belonged to the entire Chinese nation while acknowledging that Communist and Nationalist or KMT forces fought on different battlefronts.

It also said the establishment of the PRC in 1949 represented a change of government rather than a change in China’s international legal identity, underpinning Beijing’s status as the inheritor of the historical role of the wartime Chinese state.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The historical dispute could become more consequential if Washington increasingly adopted the same terminology, analysts said.

Wang said repeated American references simply to “China” – without distinguishing the wartime ROC from today’s PRC – could gradually strengthen Beijing’s ability to define that history internationally.

“At least on the issue of the second world war, we really need to be careful.”

item.title: [SCMP] Elon Musk’s Starlink row in India exposes Asia’s deeper battle over satellite power
item.description:
Elon Musk’s accusation that powerful Indian business interests are blocking Starlink’s entry into India has sparked a political row, but analysts say the dispute also highlights security concerns, regulatory hurdles and strategic calculations shaping the satellite service’s expansion across Asia.

In a post on social media, Musk said Starlink was licensed in more than 165 countries and had spent five years complying with Indian laws and regulations.

“So why still no licence? Is Ambani the real boss of India?” he wrote, suggesting Reliance Group chairman Mukesh Ambani – one of India’s wealthiest tycoons whose sprawling conglomerate has a major footprint across the economy – might wield undue influence over the licensing process.
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk’s accusation that powerful Indian business interests are blocking Starlink’s entry into India has sparked a political row, but analysts say the dispute also highlights security concerns, regulatory hurdles and strategic calculations shaping the satellite service’s expansion across Asia.

In a post on social media, Musk said Starlink was licensed in more than 165 countries and had spent five years complying with Indian laws and regulations.

“So why still no licence? Is Ambani the real boss of India?” he wrote, suggesting Reliance Group chairman Mukesh Ambani – one of India’s wealthiest tycoons whose sprawling conglomerate has a major footprint across the economy – might wield undue influence over the licensing process.

The post drew a sharp response from Rahul Gandhi, leader of India’s main opposition party. “Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy,” Gandhi said, apparently referring to Gautam Adani, another prominent Indian billionaire whose infrastructure and energy empire has expanded rapidly in recent years.

Gandhi has frequently accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and its ruling Bharatiya Janata Party of favouring Ambani and Adani.

The Indian government said its regulatory framework for satellite communication services was fair and non-discriminatory.

Raj Kapoor, president of the India Blockchain Alliance, said Musk’s accusation overlooked the intense scrutiny Starlink was likely to face from security regulators across Asia.

“It is a foreign-controlled satellite network with the ability to provide connectivity across political borders and potentially bypass conventional terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure,” Kapoor said, adding that Indian security agencies had been scrutinising infrastructure localisation and whether user traffic could be routed outside domestic jurisdiction.

“Calling this an oligarch conspiracy is good politics on X but a poor reading of what is actually happening,” Kapoor said, pointing to past seizures of Starlink terminals from separatist militants in India’s Manipur state and from a drug-smuggling vessel off the coast. “That tells a security agency that the network can be reached by people the state cannot see.”

Starlink’s regional expansion has run into regulatory hurdles, security concerns and geopolitical resistance in several Asian countries, including Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Nepal.

Kapoor said the regulatory concerns differed across jurisdictions and should not be generalised.

Starlink’s launch in Sri Lanka faced delays over regulatory assessments, data monitoring processes and national security vetting before receiving approval in mid-2025. In Vietnam, it launched nationwide operations in August under a tightly controlled five-year pilot programme.

Globally, Starlink has expanded rapidly across more than 160 countries, serving millions of customers.

“One of the reasons for the rapid expansion of Starlink has been how quickly countries have licensed it,” said Simon Baker, a UK-based senior research director for satellite and non-terrestrial connectivity at market research firm IDC.

“The service offers productivity gains to many services with poor telecoms infrastructure and this has encouraged them to overlook security issues for the time being. However, as Starlink use grows, the conditions imposed on it could increase in many places,” Baker added.

Anndy Lian, a Singapore-based technology policy adviser to governments, said security concerns among Asian countries were “entirely genuine” because satellite networks bypass land-based infrastructure, raising questions over data sovereignty, surveillance and national defence.

“States require concrete guarantees that domestic user data remains localised and that authorities retain crisis management capabilities,” Lian said. “These regional delays are not anti-innovation roadblocks; they are standard sovereign prerogatives. India’s methodical approach reflects a sovereign state establishing equitable telecommunications rules.”

The delays facing Starlink’s application in India stemmed mainly from complex regulatory requirements, Lian added.

India’s telecommunications market is currently dominated by Reliance Jio Infocomm and Bharti Airtel, which together control more than 80 per cent of the market. Reliance is expanding its own satellite ambitions through Jio Satellite Communications and a joint venture with Luxembourg-based satellite operator SES.

While OneWeb and Starlink are among the providers granted preliminary satellite communications licences in India, none has yet received spectrum allocation or launched full commercial services.

The government said that all applicants must undergo mandatory security assessments before spectrum allocation.

An uneven landscape

Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, said that India’s market structure was heavily concentrated among a small group of large companies.

“Under such an industrial organisation, it is not unusual for foreign entrants to find the competitive conditions less than ideal,” Lim said, noting that entering a market dominated by established players was always difficult, regardless of an entrant’s technological advantage.

The dispute between Musk and New Delhi also reflects growing geopolitical overlay in economic policymaking.

“It does not help that the Indian government has had its own share of friction with the United States,” Lim said.

India has indicated that trade negotiations with the United States have largely stalled, with its willingness to make further concessions to Washington reaching a limit. US lawmakers have also enacted sanctions legislation authorising discretionary tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil, a move aimed partly at India’s continued energy trade with Moscow.

Lim noted that while Musk’s companies had “deep pockets” they should “expect no favours from Indian policymakers”.

Despite regulatory hurdles, proponents argue that Starlink offers significant benefits to Asian economies by delivering high-speed digital connectivity to remote and disaster-prone regions.

But Lian said that Starlink’s Asia-wide roll-out “will be a marathon, not a sprint”.

Kapoor predicted a segmented roll-out across the region: while some Asian countries would adopt Starlink rapidly, others would impose strict localisation rules, and a third group would pursue domestic or allied satellite alternatives.

“India does not want to exchange dependence on one set of telecoms gatekeepers for dependence on a foreign satellite network,” Kapoor said. “It wants the benefits of Starlink without surrendering strategic autonomy.”

Satya Gupta, president of the VLSI Society of India and a veteran telecoms industry executive, said the controversy highlighted the need for India to develop its own satellite service.

“We should aim to have this over the next five to seven years. This is the future of the internet for a range of services,” Gupta said. “We have all the ingredients and we need to put it together.”

India has already emerged as a major global hub for low-cost small satellite manufacturing and cost-effective space projects. Gupta said India could develop its own satellite services and offer them to regional neighbours, including Sri Lanka and Nepal.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Asian parents are trapped in a private tuition arms race
item.description:
Grace often hears other Singapore mothers debating how much private tuition their children need. Some rush to enrol their offspring in multiple classes before they turn five, while others try to resist the pressure to add lessons outside school.

She enrolled her two children, now aged four and seven, in Chinese tuition when they were three to give them greater exposure to their ancestral tongue.

“Neither of their parents speaks fluent Mandarin at home … I guess there is some degree of pressure involved too,” said Grace, 38, the founder of a creative agency.
item.content:encoded:
Grace often hears other Singapore mothers debating how much private tuition their children need. Some rush to enrol their offspring in multiple classes before they turn five, while others try to resist the pressure to add lessons outside school.

She enrolled her two children, now aged four and seven, in Chinese tuition when they were three to give them greater exposure to their ancestral tongue.

“Neither of their parents speaks fluent Mandarin at home … I guess there is some degree of pressure involved too,” said Grace, 38, the founder of a creative agency.

Her dilemma reflects a wider tension across Asia, where parents continue to invest in private tuition to give their children an academic edge, despite growing concerns over the stress placed on young learners and the widening gap between families who can afford extra classes and those who cannot.

In Singapore, a recent survey found that parents were spending more on tuition and enrichment classes than ever before, despite widespread concerns that children are already devoting too much time to them.

The survey of 1,500 primary school parents by the Institute of Policy Studies found that nearly nine in 10 agreed children in the city state were spending too much time on private classes, even as overall expenditure on extracurricular activities had increased.

Seven in 10 parents said they would spend more on such classes if they had the resources, while around half admitted feeling pressure because other parents did so.

The report, published last month, noted that parents were increasingly seeking both academic success and holistic development for their children, creating tension when one was perceived to come at the expense of the other.

“Concerns about school placement, future pathways, wider social comparisons and their own desire to safeguard their children’s opportunities can make it difficult for parents to act fully on their holistic preferences,” the report stated.

The dilemma is not unique to Singapore. Across Asia, in education systems where families compete for limited opportunities, parents can find themselves paying for tuition even when they believe the collective pressure damages children’s well-being.

Ong Ee Cheng, an associate professor of economics at the National University of Singapore, described the situation as a “thorny” paradox as everyone would be “better off” if no one sent their children to private tuition.

“But if I send my kid to tuition and you don’t, my kid will do better than yours, and vice versa,” she said. “Ironically, when we both send our kids to tuition, we’re worse off than if neither of us had done so.”

The competition has fuelled demand for private education in Singapore, where parents spent an average of S$677 (US$529) a month on tuition this year – an increase from S$318 a decade ago.

House of Hows, a tuition centre offering classes for primary, secondary and junior college students, has more than 1,000 prospective students on its waiting list.

Founder and lead tutor Laura Oh warned against viewing all tuition spending simply as a fear of missing out. While some parents viewed extra classes as a way to secure an advantage, she said many were increasingly prioritising stress management and helping children find enjoyment in learning.

Other than Chinese lessons, Grace has enrolled her children in swimming, netball and art classes to develop their interests outside the classroom.

“It’s important for parents like us to recognise their interests early in life and provide them with as much help as possible early on,” she said.

Educational arms race

Across the region, the private tuition industry continues to expand as parents try to give their children a head start. But observers warn that these advantages extend beyond the classroom, reinforcing socio-economic divides as academic perks translate into better access to further education and, potentially, the job market.

Students whose parents can afford private classes are more likely to do well in entrance examinations, experts say, with those advantages potentially creating inequalities that continue into employment.

Nathan Peng, an assistant professor of political science at Singapore Management University, said countries that sorted students through high-stakes national examinations at a young age were particularly vulnerable to widening social divides.

“Even if all schools were equally good, the earlier you test a child, the more the results reflect family background rather than schooling, because the child has spent less time in the formal education system,” he said.

“And the more a society believes credentials reflect someone’s ‘true’ potential, the less likely it is to ask how much adversity different candidates overcame to reach the same point.”

The pressure to secure an advantage can begin long before formal schooling starts. Ong said well-off parents in Singapore, China and South Korea often engaged in what she termed an educational arms race well before primary school.

The effects of private tuition on social mobility could be more pronounced in countries with high levels of inequality, she added. “Unfortunately, many countries in Southeast Asia and Asia fit the bill.”

In Malaysia, gaps in the quality of public education could leave children reliant on extra help to keep up, said M Niaz Asadullah, an economics professor at the University of Dhaka.

Learning gaps caused by under-resourced public schools disproportionately affected poorer families, who were less able to pay for private lessons, he said.

“Tuition markets can expand both because schools leave learning gaps and because families compete for limited opportunities,” Asadullah said. “The risk of widening inequality depends on how unequally families can participate in that competition.”

Can policy curb the trend?

The challenge for governments across the region is addressing both sides of the problem: fixing shortfalls in public education while curbing intense competition for scarce educational opportunities.

In South Korea, households spent about 29.2 trillion won (US$21.8 billion) on private education in 2024 – a 60 per cent increase from a decade earlier. In April, authorities announced measures banning private tutoring academies or cram schools, known locally as hagwons, for children under three and capping preschoolers’ time spent in such lessons at three hours a day.

Singapore has also attempted to reduce academic pressures. In 2021, the government replaced aggregate scoring for the Primary School Leaving Examination with wider scoring bands, allowing students to be graded on their individual learning mastery rather than relative to their peers. In 2024, full subject-based banding replaced streaming scores to reduce academic labelling.

Asadullah urged regional governments to provide free, targeted tutoring through state schools, prioritising disadvantaged students, while ensuring classroom instruction was good enough to make private tutoring unnecessary.

Peng said early support was crucial as children often started school from very different academic baselines.

“Governments should help narrow gaps in family resources from pregnancy through early childhood, including nutrition, learning materials and parents’ knowledge of child development,” he said.

Other observers acknowledged that policy fixes alone could not dismantle the culture of tutoring without a wider shift in how families and societies defined success.

“If there were more emphasis on overall well-being – including mental and emotional – and less on material wealth, perspectives may start to shift to ensuring children are happy, resilient and confident,” Ong said.

“But of course, that’s more likely if parents know that even if their children fall, there’s only so far that they can fall.”

item.title: [SCMP] Russia lifts plague lab-related measures. Should China – and the world – be relieved?
item.description:
While Russian authorities have denied the death of a woman who worked in a laboratory at an anti-plague institute in Siberia was connected with the pathogen, the incident has sparked global concern – including in China – over a potential spread of the disease and a lack of transparency.

US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he planned to speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin after it emerged late last week that the 28-year-old female lab technician had been admitted to hospital with severe pneumonia and died.

Initial unconfirmed reports linked the death to pneumonic plague – a severe lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis – following a laboratory exposure at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
item.content:encoded:
While Russian authorities have denied the death of a woman who worked in a laboratory at an anti-plague institute in Siberia was connected with the pathogen, the incident has sparked global concern – including in China – over a potential spread of the disease and a lack of transparency.

US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he planned to speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin after it emerged late last week that the 28-year-old female lab technician had been admitted to hospital with severe pneumonia and died.

Initial unconfirmed reports linked the death to pneumonic plague – a severe lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis – following a laboratory exposure at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.

On Thursday, Igor Kobzev, the governor of Irkutsk, said the region had completed quarantine measures and monitoring of close contacts of the technician, who had a case of “community-acquired pneumonia”.

“No health issues related to infectious disease were detected. Laboratory analysis of nearly 5,000 samples revealed no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms,” Kobzev added. He did not indicate the cause of the lab worker’s pneumonia.

Experts stressed that even if plague had been involved as initially suspected, the risk of a broader outbreak would have remained low.

However, suspicions about the incident have continued to be aired across social media platforms, including in China, even after Russian authorities denied the pathogen’s involvement.

Russian consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said over the weekend that the worker died of a “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, according to Russian state news agency Tass.

The watchdog said samples taken from the patient found no microorganisms associated with the technician’s professional activities. It has yet to confirm the causative agent behind the pneumonia.

Kobzev said the employee “had been vaccinated and possessed immunity against the dangerous pathogens she worked with”.

Rospotrebnadzor also said no emergency incidents involving pathogenic microorganisms were identified at the institute, which was founded in 1934 to study the plague and now also works with anthrax and other infectious diseases.

Yuen Kwok-Yung, chairman of infectious diseases at the University of Hong Kong’s department of microbiology, noted that there was still little microbiological, epidemiological or clinical information available regarding the incident.

Based on a general understanding of infectious diseases, Yuen assessed that as long as the bacterial strain involved was not “bioengineered” to possess multidrug resistance or increased transmissibility, there should be no concerns about any effect on Hong Kong.

If the pneumonia was caused by the “natural” Yersinia pestis bacterium – denied by Russian authorities, Yuen noted – the outbreak would be contained if all lab, family and hospital contacts were properly quarantined and given antibiotics, he stressed.

“If the contact tracing, isolation of cases and quarantine of contacts are correctly done in this Siberian incident, there should not be any crossover into the Chinese mainland,” Yuen told the South China Morning Post in an email on Thursday.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization (WHO), said on Wednesday that the agency had been in touch with Russia, which responded that no case of plague had been reported in the Irkutsk region.

According to the WHO chief, the Russian authorities also said they had placed about 200 contacts of the woman in quarantine.

Tedros said the agency had requested further information and more detail on what prompted the public health measures as well as the health status of the contacts.

“As we don’t yet have the full picture of this event, we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” he added.

Trump told US broadcaster NBC that he did not believe the incident was the result of biological weapons research.

According to several popular bloggers in China, suspicions over the incident and the official narrative may not be unfounded.

The concerns over bioweapons stem in part from a Telegram post by Siberian journalist and blogger Pavel Stepanov on October 2, which alleged that the infection potentially involved “military-grade strains”.

Stepanov’s post also speculated that the cause of the infection was the pneumonic plague and that the incident had occurred in a laboratory.

When asked about the outbreak on Tuesday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said “China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation on the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including plague”.

Animals frequently move across the border between Russia and China, with the two countries establishing wildlife corridors to help the movement of species such as the endangered Siberian tiger.

According to the WHO, Yersinia pestis – the bacterium behind the infamous Black Death that swept through Europe in the 14th century – naturally occurs in wild animals, typically small mammals like rats, as well as their fleas, in Siberia and much of the world.

The form that began the outbreak that caused more than 50 million deaths in Europe was bubonic plague, which came about when the pathogen was transmitted from animals and fleas to humans.

Pneumonic plague is an especially contagious form that occurs when the bacteria infect the lungs. This can spread from human to human through respiratory droplets or contact with infected materials and is often fatal if left untreated.

However, pneumonic plague can be easily treated using antibiotics if administered early, according to the WHO.

Yuen said that since the advent of effective antibiotics along with improved hygiene and sanitation measures against rats and rat fleas, the risk of a plague epidemic or pandemic was “rather low”.

Brendan Wren, a professor with the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told the Science Media Centre that while Yersinia pestis was “fairly transmissible”, it was not as transmissible as Covid-19.

In a statement posted by the centre on Monday, Wren said the plague remained endemic across the world. There were around 2,000 cases per year that could be treated with standard antibiotics, he added.

Tedros said the Russian side had confirmed that an epidemiological investigation was conducted following the incident.

“However, [the] WHO has requested further information on the laboratory tests conducted on the individual who died and the contacts, more detail on what prompted the public health measures, and details about the health status of the contacts,” he said.

“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”

According to Tass, monitoring of the close contacts of the deceased researcher identified two cases of Covid-19 and two of rhinovirus, which causes the common cold.

Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia budget: healthcare boost, Malay businesses to get more public projects
item.description:
Malaysia’s government will boost spending on social welfare while maintaining subsidies to rein in the cost of living under its 2027 Budget unveiled on Friday, as Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim seeks to shore up public support while under pressure to call for an early general election.

Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) has suffered bruising defeats in a series of state elections since December, as voters expressed disapproval of his administration’s failure to deliver on promises of reforms, which had helped the ruling coalition to secure the largest share of parliamentary seats in the 2022 polls. Malaysia’s next general election is due by February 2028.

He faces the prospect of presenting possibly the last budget of his term, as his federal partner but state electoral rival Umno demands immediate snap polls, emboldened by its decisive victories over PH in the recent Johor and Negeri Sembilan elections.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s government will boost spending on social welfare while maintaining subsidies to rein in the cost of living under its 2027 Budget unveiled on Friday, as Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim seeks to shore up public support while under pressure to call for an early general election.

Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) has suffered bruising defeats in a series of state elections since December, as voters expressed disapproval of his administration’s failure to deliver on promises of reforms, which had helped the ruling coalition to secure the largest share of parliamentary seats in the 2022 polls. Malaysia’s next general election is due by February 2028.

He faces the prospect of presenting possibly the last budget of his term, as his federal partner but state electoral rival Umno demands immediate snap polls, emboldened by its decisive victories over PH in the recent Johor and Negeri Sembilan elections.

Anwar, who is also finance minister, presented an expansionary budget of 460 billion ringgit (US$112.6 billion), with increased spending on education, healthcare and infrastructure along with higher wages and aid for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

“It must be stressed that the national budget is a moral statement of a responsible government. Malay traditional intelligentsia has long placed justice and trust as the core of governance,” Anwar said when presenting his budget in parliament.

He said the government expected to spend at least 80 billion ringgit (US$19 billion) on subsidies next year. This includes an estimated 40 billion ringgit to sustain fuel subsidies at pump stations and a 6.7 per cent increase in cash handouts to 16 billion ringgit.

The higher subsidy bill takes into account expectations of a prolonged energy crisis caused by the US-Israel war on Iran, which has already forced Malaysia to revise its 2026 budget estimates higher to 444.1 billion ringgit, Anwar said, from the initial target of about 419 billion ringgit.

“We have to remember that the cost-of-living issue is already there even before the Iran war started in February this year,” Irwan Shah Zainal Abidin, a senior associate fellow at Universiti Utara Malaysia’s Economic and Financial Policy Institute, told This Week in Asia.

“Maintaining the fuel subsidies is more about not making things worse rather than addressing the issue of living costs pressure.”

Middle-class Malaysians will benefit from a 1 per cent reduction to their 2027 income tax assessment and there will be a new tax relief ceiling of 12,000 ringgit to accommodate additional categories including maternity care and elderly care for grandparents, AI subscriptions and vaccination for pets.

The government will also raise the minimum wage for unskilled workers to 2,000 ringgit from 1,700 ringgit currently from June next year, while the wage floor for semi-skilled workers will be set at 2,500 ringgit for the first time.

Anwar said the government, supported by government-linked firms and major corporations in primary sectors such as banking and oil and gas, had paved the way for more reasonable wages in the country.

“Hence, I urge all private employers to do the same,” he said, adding that companies could only claim tax breaks on salaries paid through bank accounts to close loopholes that had long enabled the hiring of undocumented workers.

To win over the country’s Malay-Muslim majority, the government will expand their business access to nearly 70 billion ringgit worth of small-scale public projects, funding and investments, besides procurement opportunities with national energy giant Petronas and government-linked companies.

The country’s Malays account for 60 per cent of Malaysia’s 34 million population and whose support is vital for political parties to secure legitimacy to rule.

The government will also cut the cost of elderly care, allowing full service tax exemption for annual care centre fees of up to 96,000 ringgit. The government will also allocate 1.3 billion ringgit for cash aid targeted at elderly citizens.

The budget will allocate 1.5 billion ringgit for welfare aid for the disabled, including raising the wage floor by 300 ringgit to 2,000 ringgit for companies claiming benefits for their disabled employees and a 600 ringgit monthly payout for families and caregivers of disabled and bedridden individuals.

“The continued move towards more targeted assistance should help improve the efficiency of government support while reducing leakages. Subsidy reform continues to protect vulnerable households without unduly increasing the cost of living,” said Arshad Mohamed Ismail, group chief executive at local ratings firm Malaysian Rating Corporation.

To boost healthcare, the government will spend 47.7 billion ringgit in 2027 to build and upgrade facilities and improve access to primary and outpatient care and recruit at least 9,000 doctors on a full-time basis in the public health sector.

Education will get a combined budget of nearly 100 billion ringgit, to cover the construction of new schools and food aid for students at primary, secondary and university levels, besides lower repayment requirements for government student loans and tax breaks for companies that help their workers with government-back study loan repayments.

For local businesses, income taxes for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) will be brought down by 1 per cent to help cushion the blow from rising operating costs, while factories can claim sales tax refunds for machinery, spare parts and equipment sourced from local traders or distributors.

The Malaysian central bank will also offer an additional 5 billion ringgit in funding in 2027 for SMEs affected by the Iran war, adding to the 5 billion ringgit set aside for this year.

A total of 6 billion ringgit will be set aside to develop tech capabilities among Malaysians, which includes providing 100,000 free subscriptions to new AI applications on the market.

In an uncharacteristically blunt assessment of its own performance, the government said in its 2027 Economic Outlook Report that it had fallen short of delivering on promises to keep prices low, narrow the wage gap and improve healthcare access.

The report, released ahead of Friday’s budget, cited limited welfare coverage for self-employed and informal workers, fragmented delivery of targeted cash aid, substandard student performance, a chronic shortage of specialist doctors and escalating medical costs.

“Despite significant progress, Malaysia’s social protection landscape continues to face challenges in providing adequate and comprehensive protection across different forms of employment and household circumstances amid the rising cost of living,” the report said.

The government said it was on track to narrow the country’s deficit to 3.3 per cent next year through more efficient subsidy mechanisms, improving on the revised target of 3.6 per cent for 2026.

Inflation is expected to range between 1.8 and 2.8 per cent in 2027, likely tracking higher in the first half of the year due to carry-over effects from higher energy, food and other input costs before easing as the year progresses.

The economy is forecast to grow by 4.8-5.3 per cent this year before moderating slightly to 4.2-5.2 per cent in 2027, buoyed by resilient domestic demand and sustained global demand for Malaysia’s semiconductors and AI-related products.

item.title: [SCMP] Why a ‘confrontational posture’ won’t help China in the Arctic
item.description:
China should avoid taking a “confrontational posture” over a new security pact between the United States, Denmark and Greenland as it might end up being excluded from engagement on the emerging Arctic order.

That was the warning from Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies (NISS), a Chinese think tank, in a report released on Wednesday.

It also said the US was unlikely to turn the northern polar region into its “exclusive strategic backyard”. The report noted that Russia as well as America’s Nato allies including Canada and European nations could constrain how far a “northward Monroe Doctrine” would go.
item.content:encoded:
China should avoid taking a “confrontational posture” over a new security pact between the United States, Denmark and Greenland as it might end up being excluded from engagement on the emerging Arctic order.

That was the warning from Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies (NISS), a Chinese think tank, in a report released on Wednesday.

It also said the US was unlikely to turn the northern polar region into its “exclusive strategic backyard”. The report noted that Russia as well as America’s Nato allies including Canada and European nations could constrain how far a “northward Monroe Doctrine” would go.

The new pact signed by the US, Denmark and Greenland on September 22 allows America to establish two new military bases in Greenland and gives it a formal say in vetting foreign investment in “sensitive” sectors on the world’s largest island, an autonomous Danish territory. Those sectors include but are not limited to critical infrastructure and resource extraction.

The deal also bans states outside the Nato transatlantic security alliance from establishing military installations or deploying troops in Greenland without the consent of all three parties.

Observers have said the agreement could have an impact on Beijing’s engagement in the Arctic because its activities in the region could face more scrutiny, while its efforts to develop polar shipping routes could be challenged.

The NISS report echoed those views, saying that the deal would raise the political bar for Chinese capital, research and infrastructure projects to enter parts of the Arctic.

“But China still has considerable policy space,” the institute said in the report, which was posted on social media.

It noted that the Greenland agreement would not alter the rights of countries outside the region to take part in scientific research, navigation and global governance in the Arctic under international law. It said the pact also did not empower the US to close off the Arctic Ocean’s high seas or legitimate international shipping lanes.

But the institute did caution against two “misjudgments” when assessing the impact of American policy on Chinese interests in the Arctic.

“First, overestimating the speed of ice melt and the commercial value of shipping routes, leading to duplicated investment,” the report said.

“Second, treating all Western restrictions as a denial of China’s legitimate rights and interests, thereby reinforcing the other side’s security concerns through a confrontational posture.”

Still, the report said China remained the extra-regional force that the US was “most explicitly” seeking to guard against in the Arctic.

The Donald Trump administration has designated the western hemisphere as Washington’s top foreign policy priority.

That approach was framed in the 2025 National Security Strategy as the “Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine”, invoking a policy from more than 200 years ago that warned European powers against interfering in the affairs of the Americas.

Before the agreement was reached with Greenland and Denmark last month, Trump had repeatedly threatened to annex Greenland, citing national security concerns and the need to counter potential influence from Beijing and Moscow in the melting Arctic.

Unlike the US and Russia, China is not an Arctic littoral state. Beijing described itself in a 2018 white paper as an “important stakeholder” in the region and a “near-Arctic state”.

The NISS report said the Greenland security deal was a sign that the Monroe Doctrine’s scope – which traditionally focused on Latin America – was extending further north.

“[Washington] is taking the Arctic as an extension of North America’s homeland security perimeter, using military denial, investment screening and alliance rules to restrict foreign activities at the northern end of the Americas,” the institute said.

“Greenland’s particular value lies precisely in the convergence there of minerals, infrastructure and Arctic-North Atlantic routes, making it the most direct intersection of resource security and military security in the US ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’.”

But the report also noted that the Arctic was not a no man’s land that the US could unilaterally carve up, and most of the land and offshore resources in the region were already subject to clearly defined sovereignty and jurisdiction.

“The ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’ also has clear limits,” it said.

The report was released a day before the Arctic Circle Assembly – the biggest annual international gathering on Arctic affairs – began in Reykjavik, Iceland on Thursday.

American activities in the Arctic and China’s role in the region’s affairs are both on the agenda at the conference, which runs until Saturday.

The Arctic has become a new flashpoint for great-power rivalry in recent years, as climate warming and record-low sea ice open the region to shipping and resource extraction.

In its report, the NISS said the Greenland deal was unlikely to change Russia’s established presence in the region, but it could help the US to restrict rival powers’ access to strategic space in the northern reaches of North America.

Russia has the world’s densest network of Arctic ports and the largest icebreaker fleet, while the Arctic shipping corridor known as the Northern Sea Route runs along its coast.

The report also pointed to Canada’s long-standing claim that another sea lane – the Northwest Passage – lies within its territorial waters, noting that Ottawa could be wary of Washington trying to dominate the Arctic.

In addition, the NISS noted that Finland, Sweden and Norway all had their own resource, shipping, local governance and security interests in the Arctic, and that they could seek to retain a degree of policy autonomy while maintaining security cooperation with the US under the Nato framework.

It also argued that, given the European Union’s increased investment in recent years in Greenland’s communications, energy, mining and infrastructure, it might be hard for the US to “unilaterally securitise” those areas in future.

“Russia’s coastal advantages, Canada’s sovereignty claims, the autonomous interests of the Nordics and the EU and China’s continued participation all limit the expansion space of the ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’,” the NISS said.

“The US can strengthen its influence on specific areas, but it will find it difficult to turn the entire Arctic into an exclusive strategic backyard.”

It said the key to China’s future policy on the Arctic would be improving scientific research and shipping, expanding industrial cooperation, taking part in multilateral rule-making and continuing Arctic engagement.

“[China should] avoid being excluded from the process of shaping the future Arctic order while respecting Arctic states’ sovereignty and local community interests,” the report concluded.

It said China should continue investing in areas including polar science, sea-ice forecasting and ecological monitoring, improve the foundations for its involvement in Arctic shipping, and increase the transparency of commercial projects.

The institute also called on Beijing to remain involved in setting international rules on Arctic shipping, fisheries, environmental protection and ocean governance.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea struggles to curb sexual exploitation sites 10 years after Soranet scandal
item.description:
A decade after the shutdown of Soranet – a sprawling online hub for secretly filmed and non-consensual sexual videos that became a symbol of South Korea’s digital sex-crime crisis – the country is still struggling to stamp out similar networks and copycat sites that have emerged in its wake.

Their prevalence reflects the difficulties of deterring such illegal activities, policing the online space and changing societal attitudes towards women.

Last month, a man was detained over an alleged Soranet offshoot that investigators said shared more than 2,000 sexually explicit videos, illegally filmed material and deepfakes.
item.content:encoded:
A decade after the shutdown of Soranet – a sprawling online hub for secretly filmed and non-consensual sexual videos that became a symbol of South Korea’s digital sex-crime crisis – the country is still struggling to stamp out similar networks and copycat sites that have emerged in its wake.

Their prevalence reflects the difficulties of deterring such illegal activities, policing the online space and changing societal attitudes towards women.

Last month, a man was detained over an alleged Soranet offshoot that investigators said shared more than 2,000 sexually explicit videos, illegally filmed material and deepfakes.

The site also allegedly recruited participants for partner-swapping sessions that were later filmed and uploaded, while members shared photographs of family members and acquaintances so users could rate their bodies.

The case highlights the challenge South Korea faces in tackling the darker side of the online space despite tougher laws and more aggressive police investigations.

Soranet was home to thousands of illegal pornographic videos viewed and shared by more than a million users in South Korea. The site featured videos secretly filmed in toilets and changing rooms, as well as intimate footage posted by former partners without the consent of the women recorded. Some victims who appeared in the videos later took their own lives.

A public outcry, including large street protests organised by women’s groups, put pressure on the government. Authorities later arrested Soranet’s operators and shut down the site in 2016.

But the closure did not prevent similar sites from emerging, particularly small networks that have eluded the scrutiny of authorities.

Tougher laws

In May, police shut down a Soranet-inspired site known as the “Honours Club” after discovering that about 6,300 members had shared and watched photographs and videos of group sex and orgies facilitated through the platform.

Another infamous site, Yadong Korea, resurfaced last month under the same name after it was shut down in August, prompting the country’s feminist political group, the Women’s Party, to urge the police to reopen investigations into illegal pornography networks.

A police officer in Seoul was recently detained on suspicion of creating and distributing hundreds of AI-generated sexually explicit deepfakes and possessing about 5,600 illegal sexual images and videos.

The officer was caught following an undercover investigation by the Busan Metropolitan Police Agency into a Telegram chat room where such images were circulated. He was also suspected of possessing child sexual exploitation material and creating more than 400 AI-generated images and videos depicting acquaintances as nude.

During the molka, or spycam, crisis of the 2010s, the government strengthened laws against non-consensual distribution of intimate images, regardless of who originally recorded them.

In 2020, the Nth Room case further exposed how online platforms could be used to produce, sell and blackmail victims with sexually exploitative material. It led to the so-called “Anti-Nth Room Act”, which expanded criminal liability beyond creators and distributors to buyers and viewers.

Purchasing, downloading or knowingly viewing illegally filmed sexual exploitation material carries a sentence of up to three years in prison or a fine of 30 million won (US$22,440).

South Korea subsequently overhauled its laws on deepfakes following public outrage over Telegram-based sex crime rings that distributed doctored images of women and girls.

Creating sexually explicit deepfakes carries up to seven years in prison or a fine of 50 million won, while possessing, purchasing, storing or knowingly viewing such material can also result in criminal penalties.

An Gab-chul, a lawyer at Gammyung Law Firm who specialises in sexual crimes, said the law was now clearer on such offences.

“There are cases where the footage was originally recorded with the person’s consent. But if that material is later distributed without the person’s consent, that in itself constitutes a violation of the law,” An said.

But tougher laws have not eliminated the need for improved investigative tactics as perpetrators are often caught only following reports by victims, according to An.

Undercover investigations, once uncommon in South Korea, were authorised in 2021 for crimes involving minors and expanded last year to cover digital sexual offences involving adult victims.

A representative of the National Police Agency told This Week in Asia that a team of 20 investigators across four regional police agencies was established this month to investigate illegal websites promoting sexual exploitation.

“The more actively we investigate these cases, the more criminals try to evade detection, whether by using overseas servers or adopting other methods to prevent their activities from being traced,” the representative said.

“These cases are becoming increasingly difficult to investigate, but we are also working hard to keep pace with those changes.”

Eluding police crackdown

However, An is not optimistic that the underground networks will disappear any time soon.

“What I found through my research is that whenever one of these sites is shut down, another one keeps appearing,” he said. “They disappear, and then they are created again.”

“There are people who demand these services, and there are people who see an opportunity to make money from them. As long as that structure remains in place, these sites will continue to be created.”

An said the problem extended beyond dedicated pornography sites, with online communities and open chat rooms becoming gateways to sexual exploitation and prostitution.

“Some of our most popular chat services seem to have essentially turned into platforms for prostitution,” he said.

Joohee Kim, an assistant professor of women’s studies at Duksung Women’s University in Seoul, said online sexual exploitation cases in South Korea had exposed the limitations of its legal understanding of sexual violence.

“The legal understanding of sexual violence has historically focused more on whether an act was forced through violence or threats than on whether the woman consented.”

Kim cited choehyeobui-seol, the legal interpretation under which rape or indecent assault was established only when a perpetrator’s violence or threats were serious enough to make it impossible or extremely difficult for the victim to resist.

The interpretation dominated South Korea’s criminal justice practice and legal scholarship for decades, and its influence remains despite a 2023 Supreme Court ruling that lowered the threshold for establishing indecent assault.

“Online sexual exploitation can be understood as a problem in which this disregard for consent is repeatedly amplified through digital technology,” Kim said.

Kim Yeo-jin, director of the Korea Cyber Sexual Violence Response Centre, linked the problem to the country’s online culture, particularly how technology had been used to sexualise women.

Male-dominated online forums, such as DCinside and FMkorea, have helped spread misogynistic language and a culture of sexualising women through lewd images and videos shared in open chats, according to Kim Yeo-jin.

“The biggest underlying problem is that attitudes towards sexually objectifying women without their consent have not fundamentally changed,” Kim said

“Ordinary members of the public need to change how they perceive and treat victims of sexual exploitation. Only then can we truly understand the magnitude of these crimes and have deeper discussions on how we can change for the better.”

item.title: [SCMP] How expanded Japan-US military exercises could complicate PLA planning over Taiwan
item.description:
Japan and the United States will rehearse moving anti-ship missiles, air defences and communications networks onto islands near Taiwan this month in an expanded military exercise that analysts say could complicate Beijing’s planning for a Taiwan or East China Sea conflict.

Keen Sword 27, which runs from October 19 to 29, will involve about 45,000 Japanese personnel, 6,100 vehicles, 40 ships and 260 aircraft, up from about 33,000 personnel, 30 ships and 250 aircraft in 2024.

About 12,000 US troops are reportedly expected to take part. France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines, which were observers in 2024, are listed as participants this year alongside Australia and Canada.
item.content:encoded:
Japan and the United States will rehearse moving anti-ship missiles, air defences and communications networks onto islands near Taiwan this month in an expanded military exercise that analysts say could complicate Beijing’s planning for a Taiwan or East China Sea conflict.

Keen Sword 27, which runs from October 19 to 29, will involve about 45,000 Japanese personnel, 6,100 vehicles, 40 ships and 260 aircraft, up from about 33,000 personnel, 30 ships and 250 aircraft in 2024.

About 12,000 US troops are reportedly expected to take part. France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines, which were observers in 2024, are listed as participants this year alongside Australia and Canada.

Christopher Hughes, a professor of international politics and Japanese studies at the University of Warwick, said Japan and the US were “building out their ‘wall’ strategy in the East China Sea”.

He said that meant reinforcing and “fortifying” Japan’s southwest islands and rapidly moving forces and anti-ship weapons there to hinder the movement of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) through nearby straits during a Taiwan contingency.

“The operational problem Keen Sword is built around is clearly the one the PLA poses,” said Masashi Murano, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute.

He said that meant “holding the southwest islands, defending them against missile and air attack” and keeping Chinese surface ships at risk along the first island chain.

Japan does not present Keen Sword as preparation for war with China; its Joint Staff says the exercise trains responses to “various contingencies”. Tokyo’s latest defence white paper, however, describes China’s military activities as its “greatest strategic challenge”.

The exercise’s clearest link to a potential Taiwan contingency is the activity planned for Yonaguni Island, just over 100km (62 miles) from Taiwan.

Japan will temporarily deploy Type 88 surface-to-ship missiles and Type 03 medium-range air-defence systems, while the US Marine Corps will bring its Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (Nmesis) anti-ship missile platform and its Marine Air Defence Integrated System (Madis).

They will move equipment through Yonaguni Airport and Kubura fishing port. Communications training will connect Yonaguni with Ishigaki and Miyako islands.

Murano described the Type 88 deployment alongside Nmesis as “something like a test of a Japanese version of EABO”, referring to the US Marine Corps’ concept of Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations – operating mobile forces from dispersed temporary bases in contested maritime areas.

In a conflict, Murano said, Nmesis deployed on Yonaguni could cover waters between the Japanese island and Taiwan, as well as areas to Taiwan’s north and east, including approaches the PLA Navy could use to operate east of Taiwan or enforce a blockade.

Even then, the Taiwan Strait itself would remain “largely out of range”, with Nmesis at most able to reach its northern entrance, he added.

Murano noted that to engage ships beyond the horizon, Nmesis would rely on targeting data from other sensors and platforms.

Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, said the significance of the Yonaguni deployment lay less in exactly which waters the missiles could cover than in showing that US anti-ship capabilities could be “rapidly deployed to an island close to Taiwan”.

Tokyo has said it has no current plan to permanently station anti-ship missiles on Yonaguni. Matsuoka said that made the temporary deployment significant as a test of whether such systems could be moved there quickly during a crisis.

She described the drills as both an “operational rehearsal” and a “political signal”, stressing the “important distinction” between testing an option and committing to it.

Repeated rehearsals, however, could “lower the practical and political barriers” to deploying the systems in a future crisis, she added.

Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo, was more sceptical of the deployments’ military weight.

Given China’s growing missile and naval capabilities, he said, such Japanese and US military assets were “likely irrelevant in halting a Chinese military operation”, but could still affect Beijing’s calculations by raising the risk of drawing Japanese and US troops into any such operation.

The wider international participation in Keen Sword could further complicate Beijing’s calculations.

Hughes said the Philippines’ involvement was particularly significant, as it suggested Japan and the US were extending their “wall strategy” farther south along the first island chain.

Maslow said the wider participation was evidence of an Indo-Pacific security architecture that had “moved beyond symbolism”.

Matsuoka noted that repeated participation in exercises such as Keen Sword could build familiarity among the forces involved without obliging their governments to intervene over Taiwan. For Beijing, she added, it could reinforce perceptions that “a wider group of states is becoming integrated” into a US-Japan-centred regional security network.

Beyond the widening foreign participation, Keen Sword 27 will also be the first iteration of the exercise since Japan established its permanent Joint Operations Command in March last year.
