The programme has expanded from 10 training areas in 2024 to 15 this year, including separate cyber, information, space, electromagnetic and distributed-operations components.

Murano said closer coordination between the new command and US forces was likely to concern the PLA because it could allow Japanese and US anti-ship and air-defence capabilities to be employed together “from early in a crisis”.

A distributed posture also meant the PLA “cannot simply concentrate on Taiwan”, he said, but would have to “find, track and suppress many small, mobile targets”, diverting surveillance assets and munitions while stretching its timeline.

However, the measures designed to complicate PLA planning could also deepen strategic mistrust.

Matsuoka warned they could be interpreted in Beijing as preparations for conflict, feeding a cycle of mainland Chinese countermeasures and Japanese and US responses.

Maslow argued that this cycle could also make repeated military deployments to Japan’s southwest islands increasingly routine, embedding them further in Tokyo’s regional contingency planning.

With any further deployments in the area, he said, “security tensions with China are bound to intensify”.

Hughes said that despite concerns in Tokyo over Washington’s security commitments under US President Donald Trump, the military side of the alliance told a different story.

“The substance of US-Japan alliance planning and interoperability is only further tightening and integrating,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] From kitchen waste to sky-high costs: inside Hong Kong’s quest for green jet fuel
item.description:
China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold.

The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area.

EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity.
item.content:encoded:
China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold.

The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area.

EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity.

“I can recall that the gutter oil we collected was basically free 10 years ago, and authorities even offered subsidies [to collectors], but now the unit cost is even more expensive than fuel,” he said.

Gutter oil is among a selection of feedstocks, such as animal fat and agricultural waste, that can be used to produce renewable jet fuel, an alternative that will reduce life-cycle carbon emissions by up to 80 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel.

SAF, a “drop-in” substitute, can be safely blended with jet fuel and used in aircraft engines without modification, but the challenge is the price.

The Hong Kong government has set a 2030 target for the use of SAF, but has yet to clarify who will pay for it.

“Producers need confidence that demand will be there. Airlines need fuel that is available and affordable. Investors need clarity on the direction of policy. A well-designed policy can connect these needs,” the CEO of Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways, Ronald Lam Siu-por, said at a clean jet fuel conference in September.

A ‘cautious’ target

The city government initially set a goal for SAF to account for between 1 and 2 per cent of all fuel consumed by flights departing from Hong Kong International Airport by 2030.

But in the city’s first five-year plan released in September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu revised the target to 1 to 3 per cent. He also said the city would aim to develop an internationally competitive SAF value chain in the bay area.

Niki Wang Yangwen, Asia-Pacific associate director of biofuels at S&P Global Energy, said Hong Kong’s aim was considered achievable, with Asian economies generally setting targets of 1 to 5 per cent for 2030.

“From our conversations with the market, the general feeling is that 1 to 3 per cent is a fairly cautious target, and people do not have much concern about it,” she said of the city’s goal.

Some industry players expected the city to be a trial site for mainland China to gauge market reactions and, if things worked out, gradually roll out similar measures, she explained.

Hong Kong, like Singapore, is a key aviation hub in Asia, with a dominant home carrier and mostly international traffic, Wang said.

Hong Kong’s airport is one of the busiest in the world, last year recording 61 million passenger trips and a sector-leading 5.07 million tonnes of cargo throughput.

According to the Civil Aviation Department, the number of flights departing from Hong Kong, including cargo and passenger services, jumped by 8.6 per cent to 197,374 in 2025 from a year earlier, while the number in 2024 was 181,663, up by 31.6 per cent from 138,056 in 2023.

In addition, 197,325 flights arrived in 2025, representing an 8.7 per cent increase from the previous year.

Hong Kong is not alone in setting green fuel targets. Elsewhere, demand for SAF is being driven more by mandates than pledges by airlines.

The International Civil Aviation Organisation has adopted a collective goal to cut global aviation emissions by 5 per cent by 2030 on the path to net zero by 2050.

The European Union requires fuel suppliers at its airports to use SAF, starting at 2 per cent of overall fuel in 2025, rising to 6 per cent in 2030 and to 70 per cent by 2050.

Singapore has confirmed a goal of SAF accounting for 1 per cent of overall fuel by 2027 and 3 to 5 per cent by 2030, subject to global developments and SAF availability, while other Asian countries, including Thailand, Japan and South Korea, have also set targets.

How can Hong Kong achieve its goal?

In its latest policy address, the government committed to studying a mandatory consumption mechanism, and launching targeted publicity and educational campaigns by 2028. It will also develop a local blending facility to mix neat SAF with conventional jet fuel into a ready-to-use supply to support uptake.

Separately, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing’s Core Climate carbon marketplace will explore offering green energy and other environmental equity products to the market, including SAF certificates and green hydrogen certificates.

In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the Transport and Logistics Bureau and the Environment and Ecology Bureau said the local blending facility was expected to begin operations by 2030.

“This will complete an end-to-end regional value chain, streamline logistics and enhance SAF price competitiveness,” the bureaus said.

As part of the broader value chain in the bay area, the government has also spearheaded the establishment of EcoCeres’ SAF production base in Dongguan, which will begin production by 2030, producing 450,000 tonnes of SAF and renewable diesel per year at full capacity.

EcoCeres’ Chan said the company’s current production of about 770,000 to 800,000 tonnes, well above the 3 per cent requirement of around 200,000 tonnes, was manageable.

“I also believe we will not be the sole supplier. There will be other suppliers in a fair market, so I don’t think there will be any pressure on the overall supply, even at 3 per cent or up to 10 per cent,” he said.

EcoCeres, a clean energy unicorn backed by the family office of Henderson Land Development co-chairman Peter Lee Ka-kit, is the world’s second-biggest producer of SAF, after Finland’s Neste.

Chan said the supply chain was end-to-end, with Dongguan as its starting point. Used cooking oil is collected from nearby bay area cities and pre-processed in the area, while Hong Kong handles blending, research and development, and financing.

Who pays the extra cost?

Chan said the government should have a longer-term plan beyond 2030 and provide details of its mandatory mechanism, noting that the EU had set goals for 2050.

Merlin Lao Man-chi, the head of policy and research at the Business Environment Council, said the government’s mandatory mechanism was crucial, as it would determine market confidence and who would ultimately bear the cost.

“It is important to determine the cost allocation and who will be in charge of the cost as it could scale up the whole industry,” he said.

According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), global SAF production is expected to reach 2.4 million tonnes in 2026, representing just 0.8 per cent of aviation fuel use, at a cost of US$4.3 billion to airlines.

The South China Morning Post contacted four Hong Kong-based airlines – Cathay, its budget arm HK Express, Hong Kong Airlines and Greater Bay Airlines – but none offered any comment.

Singapore introduced the world’s first green levy, with passengers bearing the cost, while the EU holds suppliers responsible through penalties.

Lao said the government should offer short-term subsidies, but it would also need to determine how to allocate costs in the longer run.

He said the levy mechanism in Singapore helped encourage acceptance among consumers, but such a move would be “a long shot” in Hong Kong and the government would need to work to garner broad public support.

Lao used Hong Kong’s ill-fated waste-charging scheme in 2024 as an example. Officials and lawmakers initially had good thoughts initially and all agreed on the proposal. But when it came to implementation, residents opposed the measure and the scheme was eventually scrapped.

Asked whether imposing a levy would threaten the city’s status as an international aviation hub, Lao said the fee could be imposed only on passengers or cargo departing from Hong Kong, not those in transit.

Hong Kong’s airport currently charges a HK$200 (US$25) departure tax. In the past few months, airlines have added fuel surcharges on the back of price hikes caused by the Middle East war.

“The mechanism will ensure that we do it first and decide the transshipment and transition later, as they are very price sensitive,” Lao said, noting that a green levy would also hedge against future price volatility.

Lawmaker Chan Siu-hung said he was not worried that the aviation industry would lose customers, as the city’s airport should fight for its own “target customers”.

“Everyone has to understand that protecting the environment comes at a cost. If we do not pay it today, our children and grandchildren will have to pay it in the future,” he said.

However, Chan argued that the government should not offer subsidies because Hong Kong relied on both local and international airlines. Subsidising local airlines could be regarded as unfair competition, while taxpayers’ money should not be used to fund foreign airlines, he said.

Alan Chan of EcoCeres said the extra cost of SAF should be seen as “green value” rather than a “green premium” as each tonne of its fuel would cut life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by up to 94.4 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel depending on feedstock composition. This was a benefit that everyone would enjoy, he argued.

“If you do not realise it is a value, the product itself will have no value,” he said. “Why would you pay more for the same thing?”

How to lower the price of SAF?

The IATA estimated that the price of SAF would surge to US$2,872 per tonne in 2026, about 2.5 times the price of jet fuel, while S&P Global Energy’s data showed that the SAF price in China was US$2,340 per tonne on October 6.

Lawmaker Chan said scaling operations was essential to bringing down SAF costs.

“Hong Kong is a small market without the scale or critical mass, but the Greater Bay Area has many airports, and their combined demand can reach critical mass,” he said.

If there was a clear demand for SAF, the region’s many facilities and suppliers would naturally be willing to invest in scaling, he added.

The legislator said the next step was developing a carbon trading market that could help bring down costs as the industry scaled up.

One example, he said, was the SAF certificate mentioned in the policy address: airlines could trade the certificates in the market, while companies short of carbon credits could buy them.

Samuel Wong, Asia-Pacific vice-president for sales at PAC LP, a technology supplier in the United States, said used cooking oil alone would not be sufficient to produce SAF on the scale the aviation industry would eventually require.

“Used cooking oil can be turned into SAF, but it can also be used to produce biodiesel and other renewable fuels, so different sectors are competing for the same limited supply,” Wong said. “That competition has pushed prices above US$1,000 per tonne in some markets.”

He said the supply of used cooking oil was inherently limited, meaning the industry would have to develop alternative feedstocks and production technologies as SAF demand increased.

“There are fundamental constraints on both supply and cost,” Wong said. “The amount of used cooking oil that can be sustainably collected is finite, so used cooking oil alone cannot provide all the feedstock needed to scale SAF globally.”

HEFA, or hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids, is currently the main commercial pathway used for producing SAF and uses feedstocks including used cooking oil, vegetable oils and animal fats.

But Wong said achieving much larger SAF volumes would require the industry to diversify beyond HEFA.

“HEFA is essential for scaling SAF today, but it cannot be the only solution,” he said. “The industry needs a portfolio of pathways.”

Lawmaker Chan said Hong Kong needed a detailed action plan beyond 2030.

“[The government] needs a mandatory target by 2030, and then have a clear direction in 2035 to raise the target along the way,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] In Indonesia, will VP Gibran’s ‘diploma-gate’ haunt his future after court ruling?
item.description:
A legal challenge to the vice-presidency of Indonesia’s Gibran Rakabuming Raka could haunt his political future even though he has survived damning court findings on his educational qualifications.

The Constitutional Court on Tuesday dismissed a petition to unseat the son of former president Joko Widodo, ruling that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing. But it also found no convincing evidence that Gibran’s overseas education met the minimum high-school qualification required for presidential candidates.

Legal experts say the ruling has shifted the battleground to parliament and law enforcement agencies, potentially opening a Pandora’s box for Gibran.
item.content:encoded:
A legal challenge to the vice-presidency of Indonesia’s Gibran Rakabuming Raka could haunt his political future even though he has survived damning court findings on his educational qualifications.

The Constitutional Court on Tuesday dismissed a petition to unseat the son of former president Joko Widodo, ruling that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing. But it also found no convincing evidence that Gibran’s overseas education met the minimum high-school qualification required for presidential candidates.

Legal experts say the ruling has shifted the battleground to parliament and law enforcement agencies, potentially opening a Pandora’s box for Gibran.

Political observers, however, doubt President Prabowo Subianto would risk a confrontation that could destabilise his government. Gibran, who ran on the 2024 ticket alongside Prabowo – capturing 58.59 per cent of the vote – is likely to retain his office for now, but analysts say he will be dogged by questions over his future political career.

Delivering the judgment on Tuesday, Chief Justice Suhartoyo argued that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing to dispute the presidential election result because they were not contestants in the race.

“Consequently, the court rules that their petition be declared inadmissible,” he said.

Although the court unequivocally stated it was in no position to disqualify the vice-president, it noted there was “no convincing evidence” to confirm that Gibran had completed an education equivalent to Indonesian senior high school.

In a news conference after the ruling, lawyer Refly Harun, one of the plaintiffs, quipped to reporters that it was unprecedented in Constitutional Court history for a ruling to bring celebration to both sides of a trial.

“The defendant is happy because he still gets to keep his vice-presidency, for now. But we are also happy because we’ve satisfactorily proved that he doesn’t have a high school diploma,” Refly said, adding that the ruling should shame Gibran into resigning.

Known locally as “Gibran’s diploma-gate”, the saga erupted on September 10 when 12 plaintiffs, led by constitutional law expert and former deputy minister of law and human rights Denny Indrayana, filed a petition with the court.

In their complaint, they accused Gibran of manipulating his secondary school degree equivalency certification. Under Indonesian election law passed in 2003, presidential and vice-presidential candidates must have completed senior high school or its equivalent.

According to his educational record, Gibran attended Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore, where he completed his O-Levels, before taking a pathway programme at UTS Insearch in Sydney, Australia. He subsequently attained his bachelor’s degree in marketing from the UK’s University of Bradford via the Management Development Institute of Singapore in 2010.

The petitioners asked the court to nullify his vice-presidency on grounds of fraud.

Herlambang P. Wiratraman, an associate professor and director of the Research Centre for Law and Social Justice at Gadjah Mada University in Indonesia, told This Week in Asia that the Constitutional Court had delivered a sound ruling that had gone as far as its legal remit allowed.

“I see it as a vigorous nudge at getting the other state institutions to act on the verdict and do their jobs under the constitution,” Herlambang said.

State administrative law scholar Bivitri Susanti, who testified as an expert witness for the plaintiffs during the court’s two-week proceedings, agreed that the ruling opened up other legal avenues for Gibran’s removal.

“The House of Representatives can now legally start a process of impeachment against the vice-president,” she said, adding that law enforcement agencies should also initiate an investigation into Gibran for alleged forgery to strengthen the impeachment case.

“So the ball is in the politicians’ court now.”

On Wednesday, a group calling itself Advocators For Upholding National Ethics, Morals and Integrity filed a police report against Gibran for falsifying his educational record.

“But I suspect the police will stop short of conducting an actual investigation,” said Made Supriatma, a political analyst and visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

Made said Prabowo would want to prevent the issue from escalating into a full-blown political crisis. “The ramifications for an impeachment process would be too volatile and unpredictable for his administration.”

Prabowo has so far steered clear of the controversy, offering no public comment.

However, Syahganda Nainggolan, recently appointed head of the Government Communications Agency, said in a podcast on Monday that the president had “long been aware of Gibran’s fake diploma, but saw it as a non-priority for the government to tackle”.

Saidiman Ahmad, a researcher and programme manager at Jakarta-based pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting, pointed to another aspect of the debate he believed was being overlooked.

“As a guardian of democracy, the court should’ve borne in mind that limiting elected office to people of certain educational backgrounds is elitist, if not non-inclusive,” Saidiman said. He questioned using formal qualifications as a benchmark for public officials, pointing out that most Western democracies did not impose educational prerequisites on elected political leaders.

He also questioned the plaintiffs’ motives in targeting Gibran’s overseas education as a legal loophole. “It’s obvious they had a target on his back with this manoeuvre, with the end game being his political demise – either through removal from office or by barring him from future elections on technicalities.”

But Made said that what Gibran did with his education documents was essentially illegal. “He sought to circumvent existing regulations through falsification, and that is always wrong.”

Analysts are divided on whether the court’s findings automatically bar Gibran from running again for vice-president or president in the future.

“This constitutional blight on his persona should strongly dissuade political parties from nominating him as a candidate,” Bivitri said.

In contrast, Saidiman saw the ruling as no impediment to Gibran’s future candidacy, provided a proper degree equivalency certificate could be obtained from the Ministry of Education.

Gibran has publicly denied not having completed his secondary education.

“If I hadn’t graduated from high school, I wouldn’t have been able to enrol at a university. Please bear in mind I finished my tertiary education in Singapore,” he told reporters on Wednesday.

Made said that Gibran might retain his current post but would likely not emerge unscathed.

“His political legitimacy will greatly suffer as a result,” Made said. “And this will come back to haunt him again and again.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s new air force base in Laos could rattle Vietnam
item.description:
A newly opened China-backed air force training centre in Laos could unsettle Vietnam, even as it aims to modernise Vientiane’s military and balance defence ties among Beijing, Moscow and Hanoi, observers say.

China’s National Defence Ministry said last Tuesday that the joint support and training facility at Ban Keun Airport in the Laotian capital would strengthen the expertise of local air force pilots and was “not directed against any third party”.

“The establishment and operation of the two institutions reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, aligning with domestic laws of both countries, as well as international law and common practices,” the ministry said in a statement.
item.content:encoded:
A newly opened China-backed air force training centre in Laos could unsettle Vietnam, even as it aims to modernise Vientiane’s military and balance defence ties among Beijing, Moscow and Hanoi, observers say.

China’s National Defence Ministry said last Tuesday that the joint support and training facility at Ban Keun Airport in the Laotian capital would strengthen the expertise of local air force pilots and was “not directed against any third party”.

“The establishment and operation of the two institutions reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, aligning with domestic laws of both countries, as well as international law and common practices,” the ministry said in a statement.

It added that the installation, widely described as China’s third overseas defence base, “contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation, as well as promoting regional peace and stability”.

China’s other two military facilities are in East Africa’s Djibouti and Ream Naval Base in Cambodia.

Operational activities have already begun at Ban Keun, with satellite images taken on September 30 by Vantor showing what security analysts believe are eight K-8 light attack jets ‌and more than two dozen support vehicles on a runway that is still being built.

Abdul Rahman Yaacob, a research fellow at the Rabdan Security and Defence Institute in the United Arab Emirates, said the facility indicated that Laos was looking to juggle defence relations between China, Russia and Vietnam.

“As Vietnam continues to maintain close defence partnerships with Russia, Laos could look to China as a counter balance,” Rahman said.

Modernising its air force and roping in China as a potential supplier and partner were also high on Vientiane’s agenda, but the move has another dimension: “a competition between Vietnam and China for influence in Laos”, he said.

Given Vietnam’s long history of exercising political, military and strategic sway in Laos, Rahman said Hanoi may see the latest development as “China encroaching into its area of influence”.

He added that Beijing could also monitor military activities in southern Vietnam by developing Cambodian naval and air defence facilities.

“Vietnam could be surrounded by China from the north and China-friendly regimes in Laos from the west and Cambodia from the south,” Rahman said.

‘Chosen partner’

Beyond keeping an eye on Vietnam, the Laos facility signalled China’s deepening competition with the United States for influence in mainland Southeast Asia, he said.

Hanoi and Beijing maintain a quietly tense relationship driven by a complex strategy of balancing intense economic interdependence against maritime territorial disputes in the South China Sea.

Rahman noted that China has the ability to monitor air activities deep into Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam if it decides to install the 700km (434 miles) YLC-8B long-range radar system.

Security analyst Olli Pekka Suorsa said from Vientiane’s perspective, Beijing appeared as an ideal partner to help develop the country’s small, capacity-constrained air force, which has sent its pilots to China for training.

“The [facility] is of great importance to the [Laos air force] and its future development road map,” Suorsa said.

The assistant professor of security at the Rabdan Academy in Abu Dhabi said “China has become the chosen partner” for the modernisation of Laos’ air force, whose SAIC LE500 and Hongdu K-8 jets are also Chinese-made.

He added that Chinese flight instructors would be sent to the new facility in the future, allowing local pilots to complete their military flight training syllabus entirely in Laos.

Vientiane could also seek to acquire budget-friendly Chinese combat jets, including the JF-17 and FTC-2000, Suorsa said.

Describing reports that the airfield would be occupied by Chinese combat aircraft as implausible, Suorsa said the facility had limited infrastructure and runway to support a large Chinese air force contingent.

With a single 2,000-metre runway, Suorsa said it was relatively short for military operations as Chinese airbases under the Southern Theatre Command generally had runways of about 2,500 metres.

In addition, China already had a significant airbase network close to Laos and Vietnam across Yunnan and Guangxi provinces, as well as on Hainan Island, under the Southern Theatre Command, he noted.

“For operations in mainland Southeast Asia, the PLA Air Force has a broad network of bases that provide it with significant reach,” Suorsa said, adding that China’s growing fleet of aerial refuelling aircraft could further extend the reach of its tactical and strategic aircraft without the need to base them in Laos.

“Taken together, the fear of China using the new facility as a forward base is likely overblown,” he said, adding that China’s military and civilian aid to Laos had been extensive over the past two decades, including in the Kingdom’s aviation sector.

Simon Creak, an associate history professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore and modern Southeast Asia historian, said the training, equipment and infrastructure benefits for Laos were clear.

“A joint facility like this delivers something Laos cannot develop by itself,” Creak said.

Though Laos has similar arrangements with China in other areas of development and infrastructure, it was the first time the country used this model to strengthen its military capacity, he said.

“It is unprecedented in this sense.”

Laos and China have long-standing defence ties that include holding the “Friendship Shield” drills and providing modern military equipment, maintenance support and training to Vientiane.

Keith Barney, an associate professor at the Australian National University and country expert on Laos, said there was a broader connection between the Ban Keun air facility and the US$6 billion Laos-China Railway, both built with Chinese support.

During the 2024 exercise near Vientiane, the rail link was used to move personnel and military equipment. Vehicles were unloaded at a station some 25km from Ban Keun.

Ban Keun’s under-construction runway could potentially be extended from 2,000 metres to 3,000 metres (9,842 feet), enabling longer-range aircraft to operate from there, Barney said.

“Infrastructure can have both civilian and military uses and infrastructure can become strategic,” he said, adding that the facility could potentially acquire wider logistical or operational functions over time.

Barney said Laos’ need for Chinese financial support might constrain its room for manoeuvre in negotiations with Beijing, including over military cooperation and access to infrastructure.

“I would not assume that this means China has imposed particular terms on Laos in the case of Ban Keun, but the wider debt relationship is relevant to understanding the context in which such agreements are made.”

Laos faces a severe debt crisis with public and external debt exceeding up to 118 per cent of its gross domestic product, struggling to meet its financing and repayment obligations.

Massive financial losses in the state-run energy sector and heavy infrastructure overborrowing from Chinese banks have largely contributed to the situation.

item.title: [SCMP] Data centre opposition is growing in Australia. Is there a middle ground?
item.description:
Australia may have vast tracts of land and political will to support the growth of the artificial intelligence industry, but the development of data centres to power the technology is proving more challenging.

Last month, property developer Goodman Group withdrew its application for a 90-megawatt data centre in Lane Cove, on Sydney’s lower north shore, after months of opposition from residents about the potential impact on their electricity and water supplies, noise pollution and other concerns.

In a press statement, Goodman said it had considered changes in the policy and regulatory environment, as well as feedback from residents.
item.content:encoded:
Australia may have vast tracts of land and political will to support the growth of the artificial intelligence industry, but the development of data centres to power the technology is proving more challenging.

Last month, property developer Goodman Group withdrew its application for a 90-megawatt data centre in Lane Cove, on Sydney’s lower north shore, after months of opposition from residents about the potential impact on their electricity and water supplies, noise pollution and other concerns.

In a press statement, Goodman said it had considered changes in the policy and regulatory environment, as well as feedback from residents.

It is not the first time that a developer has pulled the plug on a proposed data centre in Australia this year.

In May, GreenSquareDC shelved its plan for a 120MW data centre in Hazelmere, in Perth’s eastern suburbs. A much smaller proposed data centre in Katoomba, in New South Wales’ Blue Mountains, was also withdrawn by MAK Urban Group in June.

Although the projects were in two different states, residents had raised similar concerns – that the large resource-hungry facilities would be located too close to their homes and schools, and could cause environmental damage.

Rob Nicholls, a senior research associate at the University of Sydney, who recently gave evidence to a New South Wales legislative inquiry on the development of data centres, said these facilities had run ahead of current land-use categories.

Developers typically looked for sites with convenient access to high-capacity electricity networks, fibre-optic connections, water and sewerage, Nicholls said, adding that these requirements favoured established industrial estates.

Yet he said such sites had often been designated for warehouses and lighter industrial uses, located near residential neighbourhoods, schools and waterways.

Existing telecommunications infrastructure could fit into the plans of data centre developers if they were scaled down, Nicholls added.

“I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see lots of Telstra telephone exchange buildings hosting small inference-level data centres.”

Residents push back

Sasha Titchkosky, from the Lane Cove Responsible Planning group, explained to This Week In Asia why residents were up in arms over the data centre plan, saying it would be built just 20 metres (66 feet) away from the nearest house, close to a nursery and conservation bushland.

Residents were concerned about the constant noise and fire hazards created by diesel backup generators, air pollution and water use, Titchkosky said.

While the community was not totally opposed to having a data centre, the scale of the Goodman plan meant it was not suitable for Lane Cove, she added.

“We would say that data centres fit into the heavy-industry kind of classification because of their impact.”

In Hazelmere, community members and Trillion Trees Australia objected to GreenSquareDC’s planned facility, which would have been located near a school, residential areas and Helena River, a major environmental and cultural landmark.

Kate Herren of Trillion Trees Australia said the conservation charity was not wholly against the development of data centres.

“We understand the need for it, but there needs to be very careful consideration of the impact of these developments on the environment and the local community,” she said.

Herren said planning staff from the City of Swan, the local government area in Perth, had recommended rejecting the GreenSquareDC plan, as operating diesel backup generators overnight could exceed the residential noise limit. The developer withdrew the proposal before local authorities could assess the data centre’s feasibility.

Titchkosky and Herren said the communities they served were part of the Australian Community Alliance for Responsible Data Centres, an informal network sharing information and strategies on proposals for such facilities.

The alliance has called for a moratorium on new approvals while local governments develop stronger safeguards for communities and the environment.

Nicholls and his University of Sydney colleague Deanna D’Alessandro have proposed a “dual-gate” approval process for data centres that sets a threshold for power usage. Under their proposal, conditional planning permission and breaking ground on construction would hinge on electricity and water companies guaranteeing adequate supplies for data centre operators.

In addition, the researchers have proposed using recycled water and restricting drinking water supplies if levels drop too low.

Guidelines for development

Australia’s federal and state governments have been taking steps to address community concerns.

In March, the federal government’s Department of Industry, Science and Resources published a document stating that data centre expansion must meet certain national expectations for operators to retain their “social licence to operate”.

The document also states that new facilities should enhance clean-energy generation or storage, minimise water use, engage communities and indigenous groups early in site selection and pay their share of infrastructure upgrades.

“New data centres and AI infrastructure should not place upward pressure on energy prices and should make a positive contribution to Australia’s energy transition,” it said.

New South Wales state has introduced a separate policy framework requiring developers seeking approval for energy and water infrastructure to meet environmental and efficiency standards and avoid shifting costs to households and small businesses.

Data Centres Australia, an industry association and lobby group, has said the sector is already subject to extensive regulation.

Belinda Dennett, the association’s CEO, has rejected claims that data-centre construction and operation are unregulated, citing existing planning, building, environmental, water, electricity and critical-infrastructure laws.

“What is disappointing is that some continue to perpetuate the myth that this sector is unregulated,” she wrote in a social media post in September.

That same month, the association issued a media statement welcoming the federal government’s consultation on nationally consistent standards for AI infrastructure.

Calling for one set of rules at the national level, Dennett said in the statement that “a clear and certain framework is better for communities and better for investment than a patchwork of different rules across the country”.

The association also said its members had adopted voluntary commitments on energy, water, community consultation and transparency. These include pledges to engage communities before and during approvals on land use, noise, traffic and amenities, minimise water use, choose recycled or non-potable water where available, and fund their own energy and water connections.

Opposition in the US

Several industry players, including Data Centres Australia, have noted that objections against data centres in Australia appear to mirror the backlash in the United States.

In July, Blackstone-owned QTS terminated its Digital Gateway project in Virginia after years of planning and regulatory review. A month later, developer Stillwater withdrew its permit application for a proposed US$1 billion facility in Georgia.

The US also saw multiple protests against data centres across 42 states on July 18, as opponents expressed concerns over water and energy use, and transparency in approvals.

Despite differences over how the data centre issue has evolved in the two countries, the communities’ concerns are the same, according to Titchkosky.

“It’s the same impact in terms of diesel generators, the pollution, light, the heat impact, and the water and noise issues,” she said.

“What the US situation showed us was what the future could look like if you just allowed unfettered data-centre development.”

item.title: [SCMP] After cordial Xi-Trump summit, could China’s US dollar pivot cause tremors?
item.description:
As President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump talked tariffs, agricultural quotas and critical minerals at last month’s closely watched summit in Washington, an “elephant in the room” loomed over the discussion: China’s efforts to gradually diversify away from US dollar assets.

Beijing has gradually been cutting its holdings of US Treasuries while pushing to expand the yuan’s global use and developing alternative financial architecture. While these issues may not have featured in the summit’s official communique, they have not gone unnoticed by economists and investors – or by policymakers on both sides of the Pacific.

Charles Chang, a finance professor at Fudan University, said topics such as China’s holdings of US debt were likely to have been raised during the talks, although he added they were unlikely to result in a formal agreement similar to those covering trade.
item.content:encoded:
As President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump talked tariffs, agricultural quotas and critical minerals at last month’s closely watched summit in Washington, an “elephant in the room” loomed over the discussion: China’s efforts to gradually diversify away from US dollar assets.

Beijing has gradually been cutting its holdings of US Treasuries while pushing to expand the yuan’s global use and developing alternative financial architecture. While these issues may not have featured in the summit’s official communique, they have not gone unnoticed by economists and investors – or by policymakers on both sides of the Pacific.

Charles Chang, a finance professor at Fudan University, said topics such as China’s holdings of US debt were likely to have been raised during the talks, although he added they were unlikely to result in a formal agreement similar to those covering trade.

“Unlike tariffs, which can be set out as part of a policy framework, sovereign debt management involves actual capital allocation and is highly sensitive, making it unlikely to be formally addressed in official statements,” Chang noted.

“However, from a strategic perspective, Beijing’s ongoing reserve diversification does serve as an important piece of leverage in these high-stakes bilateral negotiations.”

These moves, together with Beijing’s push to internationalise its currency and develop alternative payment infrastructure, are viewed by some analysts as largely defensive measures rather than an attempt to displace the US dollar.

But they cautioned that any efforts to protect China against potential US financial pressure could themselves become a long-term source of friction between the two countries, particularly if Washington sees them as weakening its currency’s international role.

Beijing still has significant dollar exposure, so a sharp Treasury sell-off would hurt China as well

Matteo Giovannini, Centre for China and Globalisation

The Treasury retreat

Long regarded as one of the safest assets in global markets, US Treasuries have come under increasing pressure as investors grapple with the more than US$40 trillion federal debt burden and the prospect of interest rates continuing to remain high amid stubborn inflation.

A global sell-off in government bonds in recent months has pushed long-term Treasury yields to multi-decade highs, with both the 10-year and 30-year yields recently rising to their highest levels since 2002. Underscoring this retreat, Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages Norway’s US$2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund, recently proposed a significant reduction in its exposure to US government bonds.

Short-term market factors have played a role, but the latest unease about American government debt has also fed into a broader debate over “de-dollarisation”.

Barry Eichengreen, a professor of economics and political science at the University of California, Berkeley, described this latest wave as different from previous episodes, as questions mount over the strength of American political institutions and the durability of its geopolitical alliances.

Japan, one of Washington’s long-standing allies, cut its US Treasury holdings for three consecutive months to US$1.1 trillion in July, according to the latest data from the US Treasury Department.

Once Washington’s largest foreign creditor, China continues to diversify its foreign reserves away from US Treasuries as uncertainties in the bilateral relationship persist. The shift has also coincided with growing concern among Chinese officials and academics over the risks of relying too heavily on the American currency.

China dropped to third place among foreign holders of US Treasuries in March last year, and its holdings fell to an 18-year low of US$618 billion this July, according to the US Treasury Department – though questions remain over whether headline figures tell the full story.

Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote last month that China’s state-owned banks held substantial dollar assets offshore that were not included in the country’s official reserves.

At the same time, Chang said China’s massive US Treasury holdings might give Beijing some potential leverage because a deliberate sell-off could destabilise markets.

“Beijing can also use modest, short-term increases in its holdings to send a friendly signal, particularly when the Treasury market is under pressure,” Chang said. “It is a reciprocal diplomatic dynamic – if China shows goodwill, it would naturally expect certain concessions from the US in exchange.”

Some analysts argued that China also had an interest in preventing a disorderly crisis in the US Treasury market, even as it continued to gradually reduce its stockpiles.

“Beijing still has significant dollar exposure, so a sharp Treasury sell-off would hurt China as well,” said Matteo Giovannini, a non-resident associate fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation. “I would therefore distinguish between gradual diversification and actively destabilising the market.”

China’s continued trimming of Treasury holdings was nevertheless part of a broader shift in the market’s investor base, Giovannini noted, making it “more sensitive to supply-demand pressures.”

Wiring a safety net

Alongside China’s diversification away from US dollar-denominated assets, Beijing is building financial infrastructure that could give it more options for cross-border payments and trade. That includes efforts to expand the international use of the yuan and systems such as the Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) and Project mBridge.

CIPS provides an alternative channel for cross-border payments to Western-dominated networks such as the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, commonly known as Swift. Project mBridge, meanwhile, is a multilateral platform designed to ease direct settlements using digital currencies issued by central banks.

Both initiatives have made headway, though the pace of growth has varied. The value of transactions processed through CIPS grew at a double-digit pace for several years before rising by just 2.7 per cent last year, official data showed. Transaction value then rose 11.9 per cent year on year to 100.9 trillion yuan (US$14.9 trillion) in the first half of this year, according to the People’s Bank of China’s annual yuan internationalisation report released last month.

By the end of June, CIPS had 210 direct participants and 1,619 indirect participants, with services reaching 192 countries and regions, the report said.

Analysts said Beijing’s main objective was to make China’s financial system more resilient and reduce its vulnerability to potential sanctions or other restrictions.

“I would see this as building a safety net, consolidating global financial influence and even laying the groundwork for the future – but not as an effort to replace the US dollar, which is not something that could be achieved in the foreseeable future,” said Chang of Fudan University.

He added that meaningfully challenging the US dollar would require China to fully open its capital account – the rules governing how freely money can move in and out of the country. Any such move would require Beijing to surrender greater control over the exchange rate and could undermine its export-driven economic model, he said.

Data also underscores how far the yuan remains behind the US dollar as a reserve currency. The yuan accounted for 2.11 per cent of global central bank reserves in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 56.7 per cent for the US dollar, according to the International Monetary Fund.

The purpose of projects such as mBridge, Chang argued, should be understood primarily in terms of making cross-border trade and payments easier in regions that had often been underserved by the US financial system.

“Once you establish payment infrastructure, you can build trust and facilitate capital flows, which also opens the door to broader financial services,” Chang said.

Project mBridge has brought together the central banks of mainland China, Hong Kong, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates, as well as Macau, which joined in June. Saudi Arabia joined the project in 2024 but ceased taking part in May of last year.

Even if replacing the US dollar is not Beijing’s intention, analysts cautioned that a larger global role for the yuan could still be viewed in Washington as a challenge to the dollar-based financial system.

“Parts of Washington will treat even a regional yuan system as a strategic threat, because payments infrastructure is dual-use: trade convenience plus sanctions resilience,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis.

These concerns could lead to greater scrutiny of CIPS links and correspondent banks, she added.

Washington has also shown sensitivity to potential challenges to the US dollar’s dominant role, including Trump threatening to impose 100 per cent tariffs on Brics countries if they move to create a new currency or replace the dollar.

Brics, a grouping of major emerging economies, currently counts Brazil, Russia, India, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates among its members.

Garcia-Herrero forecast a future of “managed coexistence”, with the US dollar retaining its role as the global reserve and invoicing currency while the yuan expands across Asia, energy markets and China-centric trade. She also expected “occasional political flare-ups when either side talks [about] ‘weaponisation.’”

Giovannini, also an AsiaGlobal Fellow at the University of Hong Kong, expressed a similar view, saying concerns in Washington could become more pronounced if the yuan expands its role in trade and financial infrastructure across the Global South.

“This could also create a feedback loop, with US financial leverage encouraging China to build alternatives, and those alternatives in turn increasing US concerns about dollar primacy,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Abby Choi called ex-father-in-law ‘old crook’ amid HK$72m flat row, court hears
item.description:
Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her former father-in-law an “old crook” as she accused her ex-relatives of turning her children against her when she tried sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat, a court has heard.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, on Tuesday said her daughter had become hostile towards her former parents-in-law, Kwong Kau and Jenny Li Sui-heung, in the months before the influencer’s death in February 2023.

Cheung wept in the witness box as she watched footage of her late daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat, prompting the judge to temporarily halt the trial.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her former father-in-law an “old crook” as she accused her ex-relatives of turning her children against her when she tried sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat, a court has heard.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, on Tuesday said her daughter had become hostile towards her former parents-in-law, Kwong Kau and Jenny Li Sui-heung, in the months before the influencer’s death in February 2023.

Cheung wept in the witness box as she watched footage of her late daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat, prompting the judge to temporarily halt the trial.

“My daughter was a really good daughter, a really filial daughter,” Cheung said tearfully. “She trusted and gave her heart to the wrong people. This family, this family really bit the hand that fed them.”

Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial at the High Court after pleading not guilty to murdering the model on February 21, 2023.

Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body between February 21 and 23. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial.

The killing allegedly stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of the HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s attempts to sell it and enlisted his two sons to help kill her so he could keep it for himself.

Cheung said on Monday that her daughter had bought the property in 2019 for her children and partly as a personal investment, but she registered it in her former father-in-law’s name to avoid double stamp duty. She stressed that Choi had never intended to give the flat to her former in-laws.

Giving evidence for a second day, Cheung said Kwong Kau became furious when her daughter first told him in June 2022 that she intended to sell the flat. He threatened to kill her entire family if she went ahead, Cheung said.

The elder Kwong signed a power of attorney authorising Choi to negotiate the sale only five months later, after Cheung threatened to sue him.

Choi aired her grievances in a series of audio messages to her mother in October and November 2022, saying her former in-laws were ungrateful despite her having supported their lavish lifestyle for years.

“She does not cherish her blessings at all,” Choi said in an apparent reference to Li, who is not a defendant in the case. “[They are] not grateful to me even while leading such a lifestyle.”

The influencer also expressed regret at having registered a property in Hainan province and a Rolls-Royce in Kwong Kau’s name.

Cheung said Kwong Kau and his wife also disparaged her daughter in front of the two children she had with Alex Kwong and told them not to listen to their mother.

The court heard that Choi and her mother had further discussions in November 2022 about how to get Kwong Kau to sign legal documents authorising her to negotiate the sale.

Choi suggested that the elder Kwong, whom she called an “old crook”, “scum” and a “stinking bastard”, was deliberately delaying the process and would play tricks on them unless the matter was settled quickly, the court heard

Cheung said her daughter wanted to sell the property as soon as possible and was willing to lower her asking price by a few million dollars because Kwong Kau could revoke the power of attorney at any time.

The model also complained that the Kwong family had prevented her from speaking to her two children by phone while she was attending a fashion event in France during the Lunar New Year holiday in January 2023.

Cheung told the court she received her final message from her daughter at around 2pm on February 21, saying she would pick up her daughter from school.

Fear for the model’s safety grew that night when Choi’s husband, Chris Tam Fong-chun, informed Cheung that she had gone missing.

Cheung said she called Anthony Kwong, who was working as Choi’s temporary chauffeur at the time, but he appeared impatient and insisted the influencer had got out of her car after an argument over the phone.

She said her former relative gave conflicting answers when pressed to explain Choi’s whereabouts. He also allegedly suggested that she might have got drunk and become lost, even though she normally avoided alcohol.

Cheung said she and Tam reported the case to police shortly before midnight, much to Alex Kwong’s dismay.

“He said: ‘Damn you! Why didn’t you alert me when you called police?’” she said.

“I said to him: “Damn you! I reported my daughter’s disappearance to police. What does it have to do with you?”

When Cheung suggested that Alex Kwong and his father must have taken Choi somewhere, her former son-in-law replied with a question: “Why did you say so?”

“I called the whole [Kwong] family but nobody cared,” the witness added.

Defence counsel Trevor Beel, representing Anthony Kwong, argued the elder Kwong was reluctant to sell the flat during the economic slump linked to the Covid-19 pandemic.

“I suggest, madam, that it would be understandable that Kwong Kau would not be keen to sell the property at that time, because the property price was low,” he said in cross-examination.

Cheung disagreed.

“The money wasn’t his. What did he stand to gain? We were entitled to reclaim [the flat]. He had no say on it,” she said.

Some members of the public burst into laughter when Cheung recalled her exchange with Alex Kwong, drawing a stern warning from lead prosecutor Charlotte Draycott SC.

“It’s important for the public to remember that this is a woman who has lost her daughter,” she said. “If you want to laugh, you go outside.”

The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] Beyond the summit: how US-China relations could still unravel
item.description:
This year’s Chinese National Day reception in Washington felt noticeably jollier than those I have attended in recent years. The mood was more relaxed and Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng’s opening speech was upbeat. He even joked about the panda ambassadors at his own expense.

The cheerful tone followed President Xi Jinping’s short but successful state visit to the US, during which his counterpart, President Donald Trump, gave him an unprecedented high-level reception that would have flattered even the most fastidious of guests.

Yet the mood outside the embassy was decidedly different. The opposition Democrats criticised Trump’s cosying up to “communist” China as another example of his misguided foreign policy, a betrayal of American allies and even a sell-out of national interests.
item.content:encoded:
This year’s Chinese National Day reception in Washington felt noticeably jollier than those I have attended in recent years. The mood was more relaxed and Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng’s opening speech was upbeat. He even joked about the panda ambassadors at his own expense.

The cheerful tone followed President Xi Jinping’s short but successful state visit to the US, during which his counterpart, President Donald Trump, gave him an unprecedented high-level reception that would have flattered even the most fastidious of guests.

Yet the mood outside the embassy was decidedly different. The opposition Democrats criticised Trump’s cosying up to “communist” China as another example of his misguided foreign policy, a betrayal of American allies and even a sell-out of national interests.

The mainstream media, locked in a feud with Trump over his ban on media access to the White House, either downplayed the visit or focused on its lack of tangible progress. Even the president’s allies admitted in private that the timing “was not right” to expect a major breakthrough.

With the midterm elections just weeks away, the polarisation of American politics can only deepen. Even among Trump’s supporters and the business community, there is little agreement on what deals to seek with Beijing. Americans certainly want China to lift its rare earth export controls, but there is no consensus on what to offer in return.

Relaxing the US ban on advanced chips to China meets strong opposition. At the risk of oversimplification, there are two camps. One argues that the restrictions will only push Beijing to accelerate its own chip development, and that it is in American interests to allow a controlled flow of advanced chips to China to maintain its “chip dependency”.

The other believes that China will pursue an alternative chip industry regardless, and that selling advanced chips would merely buy Beijing time. This camp holds that the US should double down on the restrictions, particularly as nobody can be sure whether China, or any other country, can really build an alternative system independent of American-controlled components.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su sat at the head table at the state dinner Trump hosted for Xi, but the South China Morning Post was told that chip controls were never on the negotiating table. That suggests the hawks on this issue are in the driver’s seat.

There is similarly no consensus among Americans on regulating artificial intelligence, or “superintelligence” as the White House calls it. Some see regulation as a power grab by a handful of tech giants. Advocates of the open-source approach want to know how standards would be set, who would be responsible for verification, and how, even if a common set of standards could be agreed. The Chinese proposal to include chip controls in the bilateral AI dialogue only complicates matters.

The same is true of allowing more Chinese investment, or Chinese-owned electric vehicle and battery factories, in the United States. As the SCMP reported, some Chinese company executives travelled to Washington in the hope of a last-minute agreement that might open the door to US investment, but it proved futile.

It is telling that just a few days after Xi’s visit, Ford CEO Jim Farley warned that the US must carefully consider whether to admit Chinese carmakers to the American market, lest it become another Europe – a reference to the explosive growth of Chinese cars there. Farley wants to work with the Chinese only in areas where America can acquire technologies it lacks, which is hardly something Beijing will be excited about.

Beyond business, matters are even more complicated. It is widely known that Taiwan is Beijing’s absolute red line. Trump showed remarkable restraint on this sensitive issue throughout Xi’s visit, but even for him, the Chinese request that he openly oppose Taiwan independence was a bridge too far.

There is considerable pushback on the issue, even among Trump’s supporters. The president has delayed the latest round of arms sales to Taiwan, partly helped by supply shortages for more urgent needs elsewhere, but how long the administration can keep the lid on is an open question.

In his speech, Ambassador Xie highlighted the good rapport between Xi and Trump, which has become the most critical ballast stabilising the bilateral relationship. Western media wrote about how Trump caged the China hawks. Yet it is always risky to predict the American president’s behaviour.

He has been careful to maintain his relationship with Xi, but his China policy can change course drastically at any time. Those who accuse Trump of going soft on China would do well to remember that he launched an unprecedented trade war against Beijing just 18 months ago.

Trump has still to make a historic trip to Shenzhen, home of Huawei, BYD and DJI, and Xi will visit Miami. But the focus of these meetings will be more on international affairs, compared with their summit in September. The whispers in Washington are that, besides the lack of American consensus, US allies alarmed at the unprecedented reception Xi received are also working hard to lobby Washington to push back.

Japan is the most obvious example, but it is hardly the only country that feels this way. If there is no significant progress between Beijing and Washington by the time of the G20 summit, it will give the US, the European Union, Japan and others an opportunity to press China on issues such as the trade imbalance and rare earth controls.

Added to this is uncertainty over the impact of the midterm elections, which many predict will go badly for Trump. How will the president react? Will he shift his focus to domestic issues, take a more conciliatory approach, or double down? Dabbling in the arcane art of Trumpology is a career hazard.

None of this is to gainsay the positive results of Xi’s state visit, about which Beijing has plenty of reasons to feel pleased. But it would be dangerous to assume smooth sailing for China-US ties from here on. The next three months will determine whether strategic stability can truly emerge, or the relationship could go off the rails again.

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing’s policy advisers map out how post-reunification Taiwan could be governed
item.description:
In 2019, President Xi Jinping became the first Chinese leader to publicly call for the exploration of detailed proposals for governing Taiwan after reunification.

Seven years later, the first proposals from a handful of the mainland’s leading research institutes have either been finalised or are nearing completion, the South China Morning Post has learned.

Rather than setting out a single fixed model, scholars involved in those studies told the SCMP there should be different scenarios based on how reunification was achieved, with peaceful reunification granting Taiwan the largest scope of autonomy under Beijing’s “one country, two systems” framework for post-reunification governance.
item.content:encoded:
In 2019, President Xi Jinping became the first Chinese leader to publicly call for the exploration of detailed proposals for governing Taiwan after reunification.

Seven years later, the first proposals from a handful of the mainland’s leading research institutes have either been finalised or are nearing completion, the South China Morning Post has learned.

Rather than setting out a single fixed model, scholars involved in those studies told the SCMP there should be different scenarios based on how reunification was achieved, with peaceful reunification granting Taiwan the largest scope of autonomy under Beijing’s “one country, two systems” framework for post-reunification governance.

“The earlier Taiwan engages in talks with the mainland, the more bargaining power it would have, and therefore the greater the space it would have to shape the terms. That is almost inevitable,” said Chen Xiancai, a Taiwan affairs professor at Xiamen University.

Chen said that, given the state of cross-strait relations, one scenario he considered “highly viable” would be forcing Taiwan into reunification talks by applying pressure across the political, military and international arenas.

While this does not represent Beijing’s official policy, Chen said he believed some of the measures had already been employed in recent years, and that a blockade of the island could not be ruled out if deemed necessary in the future.

The sooner they talk, the better the terms

The study led by Chen, the director of the university’s Centre for Taiwan Studies, is among the research projects undertaken by mainland Chinese scholars since Xi’s landmark speech to explore a “two systems” Taiwan.

These projects have not yet been published.

Xi’s call built on the “one country, two systems” model, which was first formulated by former Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping in the late 1970s as a possible solution to the Taiwan question. It has already been implemented in Hong Kong and Macau.

Under the formula, which holds that there is only one China, the island could retain its existing economic and social systems and enjoy a high degree of autonomy after reunification.

In that 2019 speech, Xi reiterated Beijing’s long-standing position that peaceful reunification remained “the best approach”, saying the “one country, two systems” formula was designed “precisely to accommodate Taiwan’s actual conditions”.

Seven years after the speech, Beijing has said little publicly about how it would seek to govern Taiwan following reunification.

However, Tsinghua University and Xiamen University have finalised their studies on the subject this year, with another one conducted by Peking University close to completion, according to academic sources.

The studies do not represent Beijing’s official policy, but serve as a reference for policymaking and offer a rare glimpse into academic discussions about the possible terms of a future settlement across the Taiwan Strait.

A recurring theme discussed by scholars involved in the studies is that the circumstances under which reunification took place would determine the extent of autonomy granted to Taiwan.

“If reunification were achieved entirely through peaceful means, with the two sides negotiating now, Taiwan’s room to manoeuvre – or the powers and status it might retain – could potentially be greater than those of Hong Kong and Macau,” Chen said.

But if reunification were achieved through what Chen described as “compelled reunification”, Taiwan could be offered a Hong Kong- or Macau-style model, or possibly “even less autonomy” than the two special administrative regions, he said.

“Compelled reunification” – or bitong – is a term coined by mainland scholars to describe an approach between complete peaceful reunification and a full-scale attack.

This approach, they argue, means reunification is compelled after Beijing deploys a range of political, economic, military and diplomatic measures.

“However, if Taiwan does not accept the goodwill offered by the mainland or its policy of peaceful reunification, and instead forces the mainland to resort to military means, Taiwan will have fewer bargaining chips, and its room to manoeuvre will be severely curtailed,” Chen said.

Other heavyweight policy advisers have echoed this point, including Li Yihu, a lawmaker and Taiwan specialist at Peking University, who warned last year that if Taiwan left Beijing no choice but to reunify by force, the island’s autonomy would be the same as an average province.

Discussions among scholars about a detailed plan for Beijing to govern Taiwan have grown in the past month. On September 12, more than 20 mainland scholars, led by Wang Jianmin of Minnan Normal University in Fujian province, reached a 12-point consensus on a plan for Taiwan at a seminar in Beijing.

Their proposal included maintaining a People’s Liberation Army presence on the island and introducing patriotic education.

However, another scholar, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Taiwan-related academic research on the mainland was far more diverse than the 12-point proposal, which did not represent the full range of views among mainland academics.

The discussion was joined by Li Ci-ze, an associate professor at Taiwan’s National Changhua University of Education. In a proposal published in August, Li argued that after peaceful reunification, Taiwan should be able to retain its direct elections for the island’s top executive official and legislature while “fully retaining” its opposition parties.

Beijing said it was pleased to see the proposal, without hinting at whether it agreed with the details.

Chang Ya-chung, head of the Taiwan-based Sun Yat-sen School advocacy group, said the two sides should take gradual steps towards signing a peace deal before discussing the details of post-reunification governance.

He made the comments during his trip to Beijing to attend last month’s Xiangshan Forum security conference, and later elaborated on them in an article.

When asked about Chang’s remarks, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office said it welcomed suggestions from Taiwan’s people, and “the sooner and more extensively” the Taiwanese held such discussions, the more benefits they would see.

‘Compelled reunification’

The strategy of “compelled reunification” is highly feasible under current cross-strait conditions, according to Chen, though Beijing authorities have never publicly acknowledged the idea.

“What we mean by ‘compelled reunification’ is essentially the use of certain measures to shape, guide or pressure the Taiwan authorities towards reunification,” Chen said.

He argued that this was a special form of “peaceful reunification”.

“It is carried out within the broader policy of peaceful reunification, but its distinctive feature is the use of pressure,” he said, adding that it could encompass military, diplomatic, economic and legal measures.

“Compelled reunification does not necessarily mean a military conflict. It would not necessarily be like the Russia-Ukraine war, where the PLA would have to enter Taiwan or launch a landing operation on the island.”

A blockade could also be one possible form of pressure under such a scenario, he added.

In recent years, Beijing has conducted large-scale military exercises around Taiwan, including drills that have simulated elements of a blockade and involved coordination between the PLA and mainland China’s coastguard.

Chen said the approach also had historical precedents in the Communist Party’s handling of the civil war against the Nationalists before 1949. He cited the case of the “Beiping model”, referring to the peaceful takeover of Beiping, now Beijing, by the Communist Party in 1949.

The Communist forces’ military advantage in north China, including the seizure of Tianjin and the siege of Beijing, forced the Nationalist defenders to agree to a peaceful takeover by the PLA in Beijing.

Although Chen said the approach did not represent an official policy of Beijing, he believed that elements of such a strategy had already been put into practice, with pressure extended across military and international arenas.

In the military domain, PLA exercises in recent years have pushed beyond the Taiwan Strait median line, an unofficial boundary that has long served as a de facto buffer between the two sides.

After then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in August 2022, Beijing intensified military exercises around the island, and PLA aircraft have increasingly crossed the median line.

Diplomatically, Beijing has stepped up efforts to restrict Taiwan’s international space. A total of 10 countries have cut off diplomatic ties with Taipei since 2016, when the island’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party came to power.

In April, Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te was forced to postpone his visit to eSwatini, the island’s only remaining diplomatic ally in Africa, because three countries along the flight route – Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar – revoked flight permits for Lai’s aircraft, according to Taipei.

Integration push

The idea of “one country, two systems” appears to be highly unpopular in Taiwan. More than 80 per cent of people in Taiwan oppose the “one country, two systems” formula, according to a poll in August conducted by Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council.

However, mainland scholar Chen argued that peaceful reunification remained possible, saying Beijing was seeking to integrate Taiwan with the mainland and gradually shape public opinion in favour of reunification.

“It’s not that the prospect of peaceful reunification has disappeared. That’s why both the government and academia are still discussing it – the prospects for peaceful reunification remain strong,” he said.

He argued that Beijing’s growing power was one factor, and “internationally, the situation is also moving in the mainland’s favour”.

He added that the stability of Sino-American relations as well as Washington’s stance on Taiwan were things Beijing could work on to create a more favourable environment for its reunification goals.

It’s like dating. If a man wants to pursue a woman, shouldn’t he take the initiative and buy her a coffee?

Chen Xiancai, Taiwan affairs expert

After meeting Xi in May, US President Donald Trump said of Taiwan: “I’m not looking to have somebody go independent.” The American leader also described a US$14 billion arms sale to the island as “a good negotiation chip”.

Chen said Beijing could not rely on any single political party in Taiwan to support reunification, and that Beijing sought to work with pro-reunification forces across the island and use cross-strait integration to influence public opinion.

“Our approach to reunification is to win people’s support. We are not simply trying to work through individual political parties,” he said.

He added that public opinion in Taiwan could ultimately change policy, though it would take time.

Wang Huning, Beijing’s fourth-ranked official and its top official overseeing Taiwan affairs, last year outlined what he described as “seven betters” that Taiwan could enjoy through reunification, covering areas including infrastructure, the economy, energy and disaster relief.

The remarks marked a rare effort by a senior Chinese leader to explicitly spell out the potential benefits of reunification for people in Taiwan.

Beijing has in recent years promoted greater cross-strait “integration”, particularly through pilot projects in the coastal province of Fujian.

These initiatives have been presented as potential models for future cross-strait arrangements while also serving as a means of increasing pressure on Taipei, according to Chen.

For example, construction of the mainland section of a bridge between the Fujian city of Xiamen and the Taiwan-controlled island of Quemoy is nearing completion. The necessary connecting infrastructure is already in place for it to eventually link up with Quemoy, also known as Kinmen.

Chen said Beijing had taken the initiative in showing the potential benefits of reunification while maintaining pressure on Taiwan’s authorities.

“It’s like dating. If a man wants to pursue a woman, shouldn’t he take the initiative and buy her a coffee?” he said.

“We have the financial resources and the machinery. We can get these projects built, continually putting pressure on Taiwan while making people in Kinmen feel that they stand to benefit.”

item.title: [SCMP] PAS wants urban Malaysia’s vote. Can it win over urban Malays?
item.description:
A string of electoral victories in recent years has inspired the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) to go for more urbanised and developed states in the run-up to Malaysia’s next general election. PAS’ strategy is straightforward: besides leveraging its religious credentials, it also seeks to underscore its ability to govern well. The problem here, however, is that PAS might not have a solid technocratic record to sell to voters.

PAS was established by the ulama (religious scholars) wing of the United Malays National Organisation. As part of an Islamic resurgent wave starting in the 1980s, the ulama leadership began to shape PAS into a movement that represented the “authentic Islam”, as opposed to the more “Westernised” and “secular” Umno.

PAS became synonymous with the image of a party that exclusively focuses on matters of faith and whose solutions to real-world problems can only be found in religious texts. Consequently, the general public perceives PAS’ ulama leadership to be ill-equipped to deal with the complex challenges of modern life.
item.content:encoded:
A string of electoral victories in recent years has inspired the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) to go for more urbanised and developed states in the run-up to Malaysia’s next general election. PAS’ strategy is straightforward: besides leveraging its religious credentials, it also seeks to underscore its ability to govern well. The problem here, however, is that PAS might not have a solid technocratic record to sell to voters.

PAS was established by the ulama (religious scholars) wing of the United Malays National Organisation. As part of an Islamic resurgent wave starting in the 1980s, the ulama leadership began to shape PAS into a movement that represented the “authentic Islam”, as opposed to the more “Westernised” and “secular” Umno.

PAS became synonymous with the image of a party that exclusively focuses on matters of faith and whose solutions to real-world problems can only be found in religious texts. Consequently, the general public perceives PAS’ ulama leadership to be ill-equipped to deal with the complex challenges of modern life.

Currently, PAS controls the state governments of Kedah, Kelantan, Perlis and Terengganu. In the 2022 general election and various state polls the following year, PAS made inroads into states previously controlled by Umno, such as Perak, Pahang and Selangor. These states, however, are more urbanised, economically developed and demographically diverse, and campaigning on a platform of Islamic credibility to govern was not enough to attract Malay voters there. They may be religiously conservative but will not blindly vote based on faith alone.

The results of the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state elections this year show that the more urbanised west coast and southern states pose a challenge for PAS. The only way for PAS to expand its presence is by allying with Malay nationalist parties such as Umno and the newly formed Wawasan.
