A nationwide poll in April by the Merdeka Centre showed that 81 per cent of Muslim Malays listed economic concerns as the country’s main challenge. About 53 per cent of Malays feel the country is going in the wrong direction. Most of those making less than 4,000 ringgit per month (US$980), many of whom are Malays, feel the same. PAS is targeting these voters, and it is clear that their top priority is the economy. PAS’ aim is to show them it has a sound and feasible economic agenda and, more importantly, the technocratic chops to carry it out.

At its annual congress, or muktamar, last month, PAS sought to convince the Malaysian public of its ability to govern. The party put forth reformist-like motions, such as the creation of a Royal Commission of Inquiry on the so-called corporate mafia; increasing protection of healthcare workers and ramping up rice production to augment food security. Whether PAS can convince voters of this reformist, welfare-focused vision remains a challenge in the months leading up to the general election.

PAS has some ground to cover from its posturing of the past decade. After purging the “professional” faction in 2015, PAS has since adopted a more ethno-religious stance. It has fused Islamism and Malay nationalism and coalesced around its hardline president, Abdul Hadi Awang. The image turns off many Malays who are pious but do not buy into PAS’ divisive rhetoric. Hence the appeal of technocrats in PAS who are seen as the party’s moderate face.

Since 2018, PAS has been showcasing technocratic leaders such as Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar, the chief minister of Terengganu, and Syahir Sulaiman, MP of Bachok in Kelantan. Ahmad Samsuri holds a PhD in aerospace engineering from the University of Leeds and is a protege of Abdul Hadi. Syahir has a private sector background, having worked with the Sime Darby Group before becoming a full-time politician in 2018.

PAS regularly uses the Samsuri administration in Terengganu as an example of the party’s governing achievements. But PAS might be overstating its case. As an oil-producing state, Terengganu is highly dependent on oil royalties from the federal government, which make up about 80 to 90 per cent of its budget. Such royalties played a big role in the Samsuri administration’s ability to fulfil its populist agenda in its first term from 2018 to 2023. This was primarily due to the unimpeded flow of revenue from the then Perikatan Nasional federal government, of which PAS was part.

The dynamic changed after 2022 when the current Madani federal government took over. These royalty payments are now subjected to onerous conditions set by Putrajaya. This affects the Samsuri administration’s visibility significantly, as the federal government can now claim credit for the payments. The federal government has also opted to develop the state directly by funding myriad projects such as a new hospital in Dungun and a 60 million ringgit (US$14.7 million) poverty eradication programme.

But are the technocrats in PAS actually more religiously moderate compared with the hardline ulamas in the party? Given that PAS seeks to propel an ideologically driven movement, party members must go through a regimented indoctrination process, such as regularly attending usrah (guided study sessions). In short, a PAS technocrat can be as dogmatic as a religious scholar; the only difference is that one wears a suit and a tie while the other wears a robe and a turban. Authority over matters of faith and ideological underpinnings still resides with the ulama council. Economic policies formulated by the party’s technocrats have to get a religious imprimatur from the ulamas.

As Malaysia heads into the 16th general election, PAS needs to make a case for its governing ability to hesitant Malay voters in urban and semi-urban areas. This is especially so when development in PAS strongholds still lags behind Pakatan Harapan-governed areas like Selangor and Penang.

Working with Umno would help PAS leverage the former’s vast experience and proven track record in government. In the 2022 general election and various 2023 state polls, PAS combined forces with Bersatu, allowing it to penetrate Malay-majority areas outside its strongholds. As a result, PAS increased its parliamentary seats from 18 to 43 and made inroads in Perak, Selangor and Pahang.

There is a similar dynamic now with Umno, but a key difference is that Umno is stronger than Bersatu and would not want to play second fiddle to PAS in this partnership. The tussle for dominance will be a key dynamic as the general election looms closer. If PAS decides not to ally itself with Umno, it would face a tough challenge in persuading the sceptical Malay electorate to put their trust in its mixed technocratic record.

Dr Azmil Tayeb is a Visiting Senior Fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is an Associate Professor at the School of Social Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia. This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder?
item.description:
In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot.

“Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig.

The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience.
item.content:encoded:
In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot.

“Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig.

The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience.

That expense paid off: Temu’s downloads jumped 45 per cent on the day of the Super Bowl campaign compared with a day earlier, according to a report by trade outlet ModernRetail, citing Sensor Tower data.

The platform’s breakneck rise continued to gain momentum from there, bringing Chinese-style e-commerce to markets around the world.

However, three years on, Temu’s initial business proposition is being rewritten amid a wave of global regulation, with rising customs barriers eroding some of the advantages that made its cut-to-the-bone prices possible.

At the heart of the change is a simple issue: shipping a dress directly from a warehouse in China to doorsteps in America or Europe is no longer as simple – or cheap – as it was a couple of years ago.

Temu’s ability to offer such ultra-low prices was built on two main factors: its vast, well-oiled Chinese supply chain and a clever distribution strategy that allowed the firm to avoid paying hefty import tariffs.

[PDD] has operated in China for so many years and built a very mature ... and reusable supply chain system

Chen Tao, Analysys International

On the supply side, Temu could draw on parent company PDD Holdings’ years of expertise operating Pinduoduo – one of China’s largest e-commerce platforms, which has built a sprawling supply chain with deep roots in the Chinese manufacturing sector.

PDD “has operated in China for so many years and built a very mature … and reusable supply chain system”, said Chen Tao, an e-commerce analyst at consultancy Analysys International.

Temu had effectively copied Pinduoduo’s business model and rolled it out globally, Chen added.

The model allows Temu to draw on China’s sprawling network of factories, suppliers and cross-border merchants, which is able to produce and ship goods at a scale and cost unmatched anywhere else in the world.

Since China began opening its economy in the late 1970s, specialised clusters for producing particular products have formed across the country, concentrating factories, suppliers, logistics firms and skilled workers into dense, tightly woven ecosystems.

In southern China’s Guangdong province, for example, the city of Dongguan is known for electronics and toys, while Shenzhen is a hub for electronics. Foshan specialises in furniture, and Zhongshan is a major centre for lighting products.

Vast trading and logistics networks have formed alongside these manufacturing clusters, helping factories reach buyers around the world.

Yiwu, a city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, has developed a gargantuan wholesale market where hundreds of thousands of vendors sell almost any small product imaginable to overseas buyers – from toy cars to Christmas decorations.

The city is home to well over 260,000 cross-border e-commerce businesses, according to non-exhaustive local government data. Temu estimates that about 40 per cent of its merchants are based in the city.

Another critical piece that made the economics work for Temu was the once-permissive trade policy in some of its largest overseas markets including the US, according to Chen.

In the US, the long-standing “de minimis” exemption allowed individual shipments worth less than US$800 to enter the country without the duties normally imposed on larger commercial imports, helping make it economical for Temu to ship low-cost goods directly from Chinese suppliers to American doorsteps.

It had become a major conduit for Chinese cross-border commercial parcels entering the US. About 60 per cent of the more than 1 billion packages that entered the US under the de minimis exemption in fiscal 2023 came from China, according to US Customs and Border Protection data.

Temu paired that trade advantage with its fully managed model, under which Chinese merchants supplied the goods while the platform handled much of the overseas sales process, from pricing and marketing to cross-border logistics.

“For a small merchant, the cost of shipping a small batch is very high,” Chen said. “But with a platform like Temu, many small batches of goods can be consolidated,” significantly reducing logistics costs.

At Temu’s scale, analysts said, orders from different merchants could be gathered in China and transported together across the Pacific, spreading freight costs across huge volumes of parcels while retaining their identities as individual consumer shipments for US customs and qualifying separately for de minimis treatment.

China’s low-cost supply base, Temu’s fully managed model and duty-free treatment of small parcels allowed the platform to sell to consumers an ocean away while keeping inventory in China until they ordered.

However, that formula was attracting scrutiny almost as quickly as Temu was attracting shoppers.

In April 2023, just two months after Temu’s first Super Bowl appearance, research staff at the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a congressional advisory body, identified the de minimis exemption as one of the regulatory advantages helping Chinese e-commerce platforms expand in the US.

The report said the huge volume of low-value packages made it harder for US authorities to inspect shipments and enforce trade rules, while also pointing to accusations against Temu over product quality and copyright infringement.

The commission said Chinese e-commerce platforms were particularly well positioned to benefit from de minimis because their goods were typically shipped as individual low-value parcels.

Temu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The formula that once worked like magic began to quickly unravel in the US in May 2025 – four months after Trump was sworn into office – when the Trump administration ended de minimis treatment for low-value shipments from mainland China and Hong Kong. The exemption was later removed for shipments from all countries in August.

The change struck at one of the central advantages of Temu’s original model: goods could still be made cheaply in China, but getting them into the hands of American consumers suddenly became more expensive.

The impact was swift. Temu’s daily US users fell 48 per cent in May compared with March, according to Sensor Tower data cited by Reuters.

Analysts said the policy change threatened to weaken Temu’s low-price proposition by raising the cost of the direct-shipping model that had powered its expansion.

The new taxes would significantly increase the cost of shipping low-priced goods directly to overseas consumers and potentially push up retail prices, Chen said. That posed a particular challenge for Temu because many of its customers were price-sensitive, meaning higher prices risked driving some away, he added.

Zhang Zhouping, executive director at Ben Se Think Tank, a cross-border commerce consultancy, echoed Chen’s view.

“Taxes on small parcels erode the low-price advantage, while tax, logistics and compliance costs pile up,” Zhang said. “If those higher costs are reflected in final prices, price-sensitive consumers could be affected.”

In response, Temu began moving goods closer to American shoppers.

The company had already started recruiting US-based sellers and rolling out what it called a “semi-managed” model in 2024, under which merchants took greater responsibility for moving and stocking their goods overseas.

Under the semi-managed model, merchants take on more responsibility for overseas logistics and warehousing, shifting inventory closer to consumers and reducing reliance on individual parcels shipped directly from China.

The change makes Temu less dependent on the cross-border shipping model vulnerable to changing tariff rules, but introduces more inventory, warehousing and local fulfilment costs into the supply chain.

By early 2025, about 20 per cent of Temu’s US sales were being shipped by local sellers, according to Marketplace Pulse, cited by Reuters. The end of de minimis accelerated that transition.

The pressure is not confined to the US.

The European Union has also tightened rules on low-value e-commerce imports. Since July, goods worth less than €150 (US$177) entering the bloc have been subject to an interim €3 customs duty for each different category of goods contained in a parcel, ending the previous duty-free treatment ahead of a broader overhaul of the EU customs system.

The change has particular implications for Chinese e-commerce platforms, as some 4.6 billion low-value parcels entered the EU in 2024, with 91 per cent coming from China, according to the European Commission.

Other markets have moved in the same direction. Thailand began imposing a 10 per cent customs duty in January on imported goods worth 1,500 baht (US$46) or less, which had previously been exempt from customs duties. South Africa has also tightened tax treatment of low-value e-commerce parcels.

Together, the changes point to a broader erosion of the favourable treatment for low-value parcels that helped Chinese cross-border e-commerce platforms expand internationally, increasing the pressure to rethink a model built heavily around shipping inexpensive goods directly from China to overseas consumers.

PDD has acknowledged the consequences.

At the company’s latest earnings call, Zhao Jiazhen, PDD’s co-chairman and co-chief executive, said cross-border orders in affected markets would face “lower fulfilment efficiency and higher costs”, which would have a “considerable impact” on parts of its business.

For the past decade, we sold the cheapest products in the world … In the next decade, we need our own brands to have bargaining power and pricing power

Wang Xin, Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association

In the longer term, Zhao said Temu would bring in more local merchants and accelerate investment in local warehousing and fulfilment infrastructure to “integrate more deeply into every market we serve”.

That marks a significant pivot for a platform whose original appeal rested partly on reaching overseas consumers without building out the extensive local infrastructure associated with established global e-commerce businesses such as Amazon.

Another response could be geographic diversification, with Chinese platforms accelerating expansion into markets beyond the US and Europe where regulatory conditions differ, Ben Se’s Zhang said.

Analysys International’s Chen said Temu was unlikely to abandon its original model altogether. Instead, he expected it to combine direct shipping where it remained economical with overseas warehouses and locally held inventory elsewhere.

But the transition may ultimately involve more than changing how Temu gets goods to consumers. It could also change what it sells.

If the low-price strategy becomes less effective, Temu could increasingly turn towards branded products carrying higher margins and more moderate prices, Chen said.

PDD has already taken a significant step in that direction.

In March, the group announced Xinpinmu, a strategic project to develop and operate its own brands by combining the supply chain resources accumulated by Pinduoduo in China with Temu’s overseas reach.

The group has injected 15 billion yuan (US$2.2 billion) into the project and plans to invest a total of 100 billion yuan over three years, with the venture developing brands across different product categories and markets for global consumers.

“Temu’s rapid growth over the past three years was a key leap made possible by the strength of China’s supply chain, and has also created a new opportunity to upgrade and reshape the domestic supply chain,” Zhao said when announcing the initiative.

Three years after Temu promised Americans they could “shop like a billionaire”, the factories capable of producing a US$8.99 dress cheaply have not disappeared, nor has the vast Chinese manufacturing ecosystem behind them.

What has changed is the economics of getting that dress from China to consumers thousands of kilometres away, and, increasingly, the kind of goods PDD wants those factories to sell.

Those economics could shift again as Washington and Beijing continue to negotiate the terms of their trading relationship.

During President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month, tariffs and other trade issues were high on the agenda as the world’s two largest economies seek to manage a fragile detente.

For Temu and other Chinese cross-border e-commerce companies, the stakes of that meeting are high, as their low-price model is particularly sensitive to tariffs and trade rules that raise the cost of moving goods from Chinese factories to US consumers.

For some in the industry, however, the changing environment is accelerating a broader push to upgrade China’s cross-border e-commerce sector beyond its reliance on low prices.

“For the past decade, we sold the cheapest products in the world,” said Wang Xin, president of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, in an interview with state broadcaster CCTV earlier this year.

“In the next decade, we need our own brands to have bargaining power and pricing power,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
item.description:
When the time came to renew his certificate of entitlement (COE), Andrew Tan hit the brakes on coughing up an eye-watering S$112,000 (US$87,400) to keep his car on Singapore’s roads for another 10 years.

Instead, the 49-year-old business consultant decided in May to go without a car for the first time in two decades.

High COE prices, rising running costs and the hassle of parking and congestion are prompting more Singaporeans to reconsider car ownership, as the land-scarce city state expands public transport, cycling infrastructure and other alternatives in a push for a more “car-lite” society.
item.content:encoded:
When the time came to renew his certificate of entitlement (COE), Andrew Tan hit the brakes on coughing up an eye-watering S$112,000 (US$87,400) to keep his car on Singapore’s roads for another 10 years.

Instead, the 49-year-old business consultant decided in May to go without a car for the first time in two decades.

High COE prices, rising running costs and the hassle of parking and congestion are prompting more Singaporeans to reconsider car ownership, as the land-scarce city state expands public transport, cycling infrastructure and other alternatives in a push for a more “car-lite” society.

Quarterly figures released by the government’s Land Transport Authority in July showed there were 516,237 privately owned cars in Singapore, the lowest number since 2019, even as the share of rental, ride-hailing and corporate cars had increased. Privately owned cars still accounted for 79 per cent of all those on the roads, however.

When Tan bought his first car in May 2006, he said the COE cost S$10,000. A decade later it had climbed to S$50,000 and renewing again this summer would have cost more than double that amount.

Other reasons to give up driving included rising road tax, fuel, maintenance and insurance costs, he said, as well as the city state’s congestion-charging system, known as electronic road pricing (ERP).

An automated system that charges drivers a fee for using busy roads during peak hours, ERP dates back to 1998, though there were other paper-based systems in place beforehand.

At the start of last month, ERP charges returned to the Orchard Road shopping district for the first time since the start of the pandemic in 2020.

Singapore has been actively encouraging people to walk, cycle and use more public transport under the Land Transport Authority’s “Move Lite” campaign, first launched in 2022.

In its early days, the campaign mostly focused on the positives of public transport and not owning a car, but the strategy has since moved towards spotlighting the downsides of driving such as being stuck in traffic and wasting time hunting for parking.

Still, its main aim was to promote more sustainable ways of travelling, not deter people from driving, through its use of “relatable, everyday scenarios”, a spokesman for the authority said.

“The campaign seeks to help commuters make informed travel choices while raising awareness of the increasingly convenient and accessible alternatives to driving,” he said, adding that planning and managing Singapore’s transport network meant balancing the needs of different road users while making the best use of limited land.

To achieve this, the spokesman said Singapore was investing in public transport and “active mobility” infrastructure while managing vehicle ownership and road usage to keep transport efficient and sustainable.

“Our objective is not to prioritise one group of commuters over another, but to provide Singaporeans with more mobility options that are safe, reliable and sustainable for different journeys and needs.”

Singapore only has 744.3 sq km (287.4 square miles) of land and roads take up about 12 per cent of it, which is why authorities have been working to make walking, cycling and public transport more accessible and convenient.

The COE system, launched in May 1990, controls how many vehicles are allowed on the roads by requiring motorists to bid for a certificate in online open auctions. Each COE confers the right to own a vehicle for 10 years.

Singapore has maintained a zero-growth policy for private cars and motorcycles since February 2018 and the Land Transport Authority aims to keep this cap in place until January 31, 2028, while allowing for a small expansion of commercial vehicle and bus fleets.

With the cost of living on the rise, Tan said owning a car was a poor coping strategy for uncertain times, especially considering he had to “set aside contingency funds for young children and aged parents as well”.

Rising costs have also prompted other car owners to think twice about renewing their COEs.

Retired engineer Ricky Quek, 63, recently decided to stop driving after 28 years, citing high COE and petrol prices. Renewing his COE would have cost him S$130,000, he said.

“Public transport is reasonably cheap and no hassle compared to owning a car,” Quek said. “Having a car is definitely convenient but drives up the expenses.”

Small annoyances

Mounting expenses are only part of the picture, however. Other factors discouraging driving include efforts to lower speed limits with stricter enforcement and penalties, and extensive road works linked to major construction projects.

Work on a new multilayered expressway known as the North-South Corridor, the multimodal Changi Northern Corridor project near the airport and a new subway called the Cross Island Line is affecting a number of major arterial roads and highways.

Tech entrepreneur Davidson Chua, 27, says he has noticed more of these roadworks recently, especially during the off-peak times when he likes to commute.

“I do often feel a small annoyance when I am expecting less traffic but end up [encountering] lane closures because of road works or pruning,” said the self-proclaimed motoring enthusiast, adding that he typically preferred covered parking spaces though those could be harder to come by.

Chua said he would only drive two or three days some weeks, “because I don’t see a point in driving down to areas like the CBD [central business district]. It costs more time and money.”

His car is now on its second 10-year COE cycle, with the next renewal due in three years’ time.

“I would love to renew,” he said. “But the COE price will definitely play a huge role in the decision-making process.”

Gopinath Menon, a former chief transport engineer at the Land Transport Authority who led the ERP’s roll-out, told This Week in Asia that measures to limit car ownership had been a part of Singapore’s overall transport strategy since the mid-1970s.

“Realising that the small island cannot keep building more roads to tackle traffic congestion, the strategy called for reasonable demand management for private vehicle travel and for public transport to be the main mode of travel,” said Menon, who is now an independent transport engineering consultant.

Higher parking charges were first to be introduced, alongside an analogue predecessor to the ERP known as the Area Licensing Scheme in 1975. The COE bidding framework followed in 1990, with ERP being rolled out later that same decade.

“Higher driving costs have pushed more people to switch from cars to vastly improved public transport and other public modes such as private-hire vehicles and active mobility,” Menon said, referring to walking and cycling. “This is called the push-pull strategy.”

Speed bumps on the road to a “car-lite” concept included “ambition and attitudes towards car ownership”, he said.

But infrastructure can help lead the way. Menon pointed to the increasing number of pedestrianised zones and bus lanes as ways to reclaim road space for non-car traffic.

Some districts and towns are also car-lite by design, with amenities placed close together, public transport prioritised and access to cycle paths and footpaths improved.

Given the high costs of car ownership, Singapore’s government needs to make the case that cars are a luxury, not a necessity, for the vast majority of citizens, according to public policy expert Terence Ho, an adjunct associate professor in practice at the National University of Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

“There will naturally be some unhappiness about the high COE and ERP charges, particularly when certain roads are still congested at peak hours despite the charges,” Ho said. “But by and large, the vehicle control measures have been effective.”

The number of private cars, excluding private-hire vehicles, had grown just 1 per cent over the past five years, he said, while the share of resident households owning a car had fallen from as high as 42 per cent in 2012/13 to 36 per cent in 2023.

This was despite the fact that many households included young children or elderly family members, Ho said.

For Derek Wong, 35, a car is a non-negotiable for ferrying around his two young children and ageing parents. He bought a second-hand Honda Freed in December, with a COE that expires in September 2035.

“I just felt we had to bite the bullet and this will probably be our last car since we won’t need it when the children are older,” said Wong, a writer whose children are aged two and seven.

“The benefits of the convenience still outweigh the drawbacks. It is a hefty investment but given the time it saves, we feel it is worth it.”

Whether COE subsidies should be granted to large families or to those with elderly members, young children or people with disabilities has repeatedly been raised in parliament.

In a reply on the government portal AskGov in November, the Transport Ministry said the difficulty lay in deciding which groups should receive preferential treatment. A COE subsidy for families would have to be substantial, it said, and lower-income families unable to own a car would be unlikely to benefit.

“COE revenues go towards funding public transport,” the ministry said, adding that its approach was to provide high-quality public transport, complemented by taxis and private-hire cars.

On the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), Singapore’s main underground and elevated railway system, reliability hit a record in August, the Land Transport Authority said in a report released last month. The network’s mean kilometres between failures, a measure of the average distance a train travels before a delay of more than five minutes, rose to 2.88 million km (1.79 million miles) from 2.37 million km in July.

About seven in 10 resident households are already within a 10-minute walk from an MRT station and the government aims to raise that proportion to 80 per cent by the 2030s.

Yet the overall decline in private car ownership had as much to do with the cap on total vehicle numbers as improving public transport links, said Walter Theseira, an associate professor of economics at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

This restriction tended to push car usage towards private-hire models whereby higher utilisation rates made the expensive COE premiums easier to justify, Theseira said.

“The high willingness to pay for COEs suggests that the underlying private demand for cars continues to be strong,” he said.

“The policy objective can’t be to help Singaporeans achieve car ownership ambitions, as it’s a zero-sum game, but … to help Singaporeans stop needing a car.”

Alternative paths

For those ready to ditch the car, Singapore’s expanding cycling network offers a ready alternative. The city state currently has more than 730km (454 miles) of cycling paths and dedicated traffic-free green corridors known as “park connectors”, with work under way to expand the network to about 1,300km by 2030.

Bicycles have been allowed to share pavements with pedestrians since around 2010, according to Menon, with many walkways later widened to ease congestion and improve safety.

Even so, he said cycling was still mainly used for recreation, running errands and so-called first- and last-mile trips to railway stations and bus interchanges. It was unlikely to become the No 1 choice for most commuters given the high quality of public transport, Menon said.

Theseira agreed, pointing to Singapore’s hot climate and the relatively long distance of an average commute as limiting factors – though he saw potential in electric bikes and other motorised devices.

“In many places, very quickly, when people get access to electrified modes of cycling, they usually take that up,” he said, while noting the city state’s current restrictions on such devices, imposed for pedestrian safety, and lack of suitable infrastructure.

Jason Slaughter, an Amsterdam-based content creator who runs the YouTube channel Not Just Bikes, published a video late last month arguing that rules forcing riders to frequently slow down, give way to cars or dismount and push would limit the take-up of cycling in Singapore.

He also critiqued the city state’s cycling infrastructure, highlighting what he called “questionable choices” such as 90-degree turns and lanes that end abruptly, adding he suspected it was “designed by people who never ride a bicycle”.

His video, titled “Cycling Made Difficult (but it’s getting better!)”, had been watched almost half a million times as of Friday.

For Tan, who now relies on public transport and bicycle paths to get around after giving up on car ownership, the trade-offs are worth it.

“I grew up without a car, so I do not have much difficulty adjusting,” he said. “For my Japanese wife, my two young kids and business needs, the adjustments are not as easy. Yet for the amount saved, it’s worth the inconvenience.”

item.title: [SCMP] From Hong Kong to Guangdong, exploring the rich tapestry of Cantonese culinary traditions
item.description:
The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine?

Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer.

Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms.
item.content:encoded:
The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine?

Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer.

Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms.

From Guangdong’s northern coast, the traditional Chiu Chow or Chaoshan dish of poached saltwater chicken sees the meat steeped in a heavily seasoned salt brine or master stock, cooled and served at room temperature with a pounded garlic vinegar dip.

Hakka culinary heritage, founded in the hills of the province’s interior, takes an entirely different approach, wrapping the chicken tightly in paper and burying it completely in a pot of blazing hot, coarse sea salt.

Four distinct takes, four very different culinary approaches. Yet all of these dishes developed in the historic Guangdong province, an area roughly a third the size of France or Spain. Despite their common origin, should these different culinary traditions all be considered Cantonese?

Yes and no, says Silas Li, chef at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983. “I look at this almost like a family tree,” he says. “Technically, they represent distinct cultural traditions, but practically – and especially here in Hong Kong – they live under the same big roof.”

Historically, geography is a key determinant of a cuisine’s evolution. Li calls it the “true mother of recipe development”.

Shunde, sitting within the fertile Pearl River Delta surrounded by streams and fish ponds, supported a cuisine based on freshwater fish, mud carp, milk-yielding water buffalo, and tender river vegetables. For Li, this is the “cradle of classical Cantonese cooking”, the place where the region’s core standards for knife skills, slow-braising, seafood precision, and controlling the wok were established.

Elsewhere, along Guangdong’s Chaoshan coast, Chiu Chow communities had direct access to the ocean, inspiring a cuisine centred on deep-sea catches, saltwater poaching, and marine preserves, such as home-made fish sauces.

Hakka communities, however, were historically migratory and lived up in landlocked, rugged hills that offered no easy access to the coast or rivers. Consequently, they relied on calorie-dense pork, preserved salted vegetables and heavy salt-baking.

In Hong Kong, however, the different traditions have lived together for so long that the lines have naturally blurred.

“For me, Shun Tak is Cantonese core, while Chiu Chow and Hakka are sibling traditions that make our local food scene so much richer,” says Li, who draws inspiration for modern and classic dishes from all three culinary traditions at his restaurant in Happy Valley.

Chef and restaurateur Du Jianqing from Puning in Chaoshan is behind Shanghai’s two-Michelin-starred Amazing Chinese Cuisine and Selection by Du.

Du says he prefers not to view the question of whether Chiu Chow is part of Cantonese cuisine as a “battle over belonging”. Instead, he casts a wider, more inclusive net, thinking of both traditions as integral parts of the cuisine of Lingnan, a geographical area below the Nanling mountains that encompasses Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan, Hong Kong, Macau and northern Vietnam, once occupied by the ancient Baiyue people.

“From the perspective of Chinese culinary culture, Lingnan cuisine has always been a rich and open system. Cantonese (Guangfu), Chiu Chow and Hakka cuisines together form the essential components of Lingnan culinary culture,” he says.

Cantonese and Chiu Chow cooking both place great emphasis on seasonality, ingredient quality, natural flavours and a high level of craftsmanship. But for Du, the main defining feature of Chiu Chow cuisine is not a specific classic dish or set of dishes, but an obsessive pursuit of xian, or freshness/umami.

“This freshness is not just about flavour, but an overall respect for seasonality, origin, firepower, knife skills, and the state of the ingredients. People in Chaoshan often talk about ‘eating fresh’ (shi xian), which means savouring the best possible state of today, this season and this exact moment,” he says.

If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience

Silas Li, Hong Kong Cuisine 1983

Chef Huang Jinghui, better known as Chef Fei, was born and raised in Chaoshan. He runs a small empire of celebrated restaurants, all of which specialise in Cantonese and Chiu Chow dishes.

Chef Fei also highlights how porous boundaries between culinary traditions can be. “I see Chiu Chow cuisine and Cantonese cuisine as deeply interconnected culinary traditions, rather than two that need to be clearly separated,” he says.

He points to the considerable overlap in ingredients, techniques and culinary traditions – from delicacies such as abalone, sea cucumber and fish maw to Chiu Chow-style braised dishes, Cantonese barbecue and traditional slow-cooked soups, each with its own expression across the two cuisines.

However, he says that at the same time, Chiu Chow cuisine has its own distinctive regional character and culinary traditions.

“For me, rather than focusing too much on how Chiu Chow cuisine should be categorised, what matters more is the flavour, craftsmanship and traditions it represents, and the richness and diversity it brings to the dining experience,” he says.

While Du and Chef Fei are less fussy about a fluid, inclusive view of Cantonese cooking, Li at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983 argues that maintaining distinct categories remains essential for the dining experience itself.

“If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience,” he says. “If we just call it generic Chinese food, it dilutes the respect these ancient subcultures deserve.”

While he finds diners from the communities whose cuisine he cooks to be his toughest critics, Li notes that the average local guest has become far more sophisticated.

“The modern Hong Kong diner – and even international guests – is way more educated now,” Li says. “They aren’t just looking for a vague ‘Chinese meal’; they want provenance, they ask about techniques, and they appreciate the subtle regional nuances.”

At Yan Garden in Beijing – a restaurant conceptualised by Chef Fei and led day-to-day by executive Chinese chef Peter Chen at the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen – Chen sees this curiosity playing out among broader audiences. He notes that around 10 to 15 per cent of guests are international, while the remainder are local Chinese consumers, with the dining experience itself serving as an educational bridge.

“Dishes such as our traditional marinated specialities, seafood preparations and seasonal Chiu Chow delicacies often spark conversations about the cuisine’s heritage and techniques,” Chen says.

Du observes a similar dynamic at Selection by Du in Shanghai. “Guests from Europe and the Americas tend to view us as ‘Chinese cuisine’, hoping to discover Chinese food through this meal,” he says. “Guests from Southeast Asia, Hong Kong and Macau – owing to the deep Chiu Chow or Nanyang cultural roots in their home regions – more easily recognise the delicate nature and emphasis on original flavours in Chiu Chow cuisine.”

This evolving awareness reflects a broader transformation across Chinese gastronomy. Over the last 10 years, Du notes that diners’ knowledge has expanded rapidly, moving regional cooking into a dynamic new phase.

“More regional cuisines are establishing their own brand identities – Yunnan, Guizhou, Jiangxi, Taizhou, Shunde and Zhejiang cuisines are all receiving increasing attention,” he says. “This does not mean Cantonese cuisine’s influence is waning, but rather that Chinese dining as a whole is becoming richer and more specialised.”

item.title: [SCMP] Antwerp: a well-seasoned melting pot of Rubens, diamonds and Belgium’s only Chinatown
item.description:
Tourists visiting the Belgian city of Antwerp are usually drawn by its reputation as the cradle of Flemish culture.

This was home to the Baroque painter Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), whose masterpieces decorate churches across the city, including St Charles Borromeo Church and the soaring Cathedral of Our Lady. Grand squares and marketplaces are lined with flamboyant Renaissance guild-houses and palatial merchants’ mansions dating back to a golden age, at the beginning of the 16th century, when Antwerp’s port was the undisputed capital of world trade. And then there is the Royal Museum of Fine Arts, which showcases an unparalleled collection of Low Countries old masters, from Rubens, Jan Brueghel the Elder (1568-1625) and Jan van Eyck (1390-1441) to modern artists such as René Magritte (1898-1967), Rik Wouters (1882-1916) and James Ensor (1860-1949). But Flemish heritage is just one face of this city of 568,000 people.

On closer inspection, the city reveals itself to be a colourful melting pot of cultures, cuisines and religions, those of generations of immigrants who have chosen to make their home in Antwerp.
item.content:encoded:
Tourists visiting the Belgian city of Antwerp are usually drawn by its reputation as the cradle of Flemish culture.

This was home to the Baroque painter Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), whose masterpieces decorate churches across the city, including St Charles Borromeo Church and the soaring Cathedral of Our Lady. Grand squares and marketplaces are lined with flamboyant Renaissance guild-houses and palatial merchants’ mansions dating back to a golden age, at the beginning of the 16th century, when Antwerp’s port was the undisputed capital of world trade. And then there is the Royal Museum of Fine Arts, which showcases an unparalleled collection of Low Countries old masters, from Rubens, Jan Brueghel the Elder (1568-1625) and Jan van Eyck (1390-1441) to modern artists such as René Magritte (1898-1967), Rik Wouters (1882-1916) and James Ensor (1860-1949). But Flemish heritage is just one face of this city of 568,000 people.

On closer inspection, the city reveals itself to be a colourful melting pot of cultures, cuisines and religions, those of generations of immigrants who have chosen to make their home in Antwerp.

Jews began to settle in the city after their expulsion from Spain in the late 15th century, and their descendants transformed it into a global centre of the diamond trade. Belgium’s 19th century empire resulted in immigration from the Maghreb and Central Africa, and after World War II, a wave of settlers from Hong Kong and mainland China arrived, creating what is today the only official Chinatown in the country. The latest additions to the city’s cosmopolitan character have been refugees fleeing conflict in countries such as Afghanistan, Syria, Iraq, Somalia and Ukraine.

Just 40 minutes north by train from the Belgian capital, Brussels, Antwerp’s late-19th century Central Station has a lavish dome, a sweeping marble staircase, frescoes and stained-glass windows that periodically win the building awards for “World’s Most Beautiful Station” in travel magazines.

Walk out of what locals call their “railway cathedral” and you plunge into a harmonious clash of cultures: on one side, the ornamental pagoda gate at the entrance to Van Wesenbekestraat that marks the beginning of Chinatown; on the other, Pelikaanstraat, home to a tight-knit Orthodox Jewish community and its diamond stores.

One-hundred-and-twenty boutiques full of glittering, dazzling diamonds and gold jewellery are crammed into this single square mile, though it is a wonder how they all survive when they seem to be selling the same items.

“I came to Antwerp 35 years ago, from Israel, though my family is originally from Georgia,” says Yosef Degan, standing proudly next to a replica of a gold bullion bar in his temptingly named store, Be Very Rich. “I am one of the last authentic goldsmiths here, because apart from dealing diamonds, I specialise in buying old gold, melting it down and creating my own unique jewellery designs.”

Although Yiddish is the lingua franca for the hundreds of Jewish dealers, brokers, cutters and jewellers working here, and the kippah skullcap and tzitzit trouser tassels can be seen everywhere, Degan insists that his community remains discreet.

I take his recommendation to have lunch nearby, at Hoffy’s, a kosher diner filled with noisy diamond dealers, whose owners, three Hoffman brothers, explain their Hasidic Ashkenazi culture to customers through their unique cuisine: in my case, a slow-cooked cholent of baked beef and vegetables, kugel potato pancakes, veal schnitzel, poached gefilte fish and salt-beef pastrami.

Another world awaits through the jewel-toned archway that stands at the entrance of Van Wesenbekestraat, ablaze in radiant reds and brilliant golds and proudly flanked by two sculpted stone lions.

Attracted by the city’s port, Chinese sailors and dock workers began settling in Antwerp from the early 20th century. They were followed in the late 1940s by larger numbers of mainly Cantonese-speaking immigrants from Hong Kong (particularly the New Territories) and southern China, who were escaping political turmoil and a lack of jobs, and were drawn by a post-war European revival and what was known as the “chop-suey boom”.

As with all Chinatowns, the restaurant business was the obvious line of work for most of these new immigrants, and from the 70s, the closeness to Antwerp’s railway station helped solidify Van Wesenbekestraat and the surrounding area as a genuine community.

Recognised as Belgium’s sole official Chinatown in 2001, the neighbourhood’s culinary scene has mushroomed from the early Cantonese restaurants to an eclectic kaleidoscope of Thai, Philippine, Malaysian and Nepalese eateries. A dozen bustling Asian supermarkets rub shoulders with two martial-arts schools, traditional-medicine establishments, a lion-dance school and the Fo Guang Shan Belgique Temple, located not in an ornate pagoda but in a simple Flemish house on a terraced row, painted a distinctive yellow, with a wrought-iron-framed window in the front door.

Much of the fare on offer in Chinatown is cheap and cheerful street food – hand-pulled noodles, char siu pork, wonton soup, even the classic sweet and sour chicken – but two addresses stand out, both just off the main drag of Van Wesenbekestraat.

Fong Mei opened more than 30 years ago and its classic Cantonese cuisine – more than 50 handmade varieties of dim sum alongside steamed fish with ginger and coriander, lacquered roast duck, beef-tripe soup and duck tongue – has been recognised by Belgium’s Michelin Guide. The decor is delightfully kitsch, with red lanterns, giant photos of Hong Kong, even a poster depicting a dragon boat powering through a village scene and celebrating Chinese-Belgian friendship.

The proprietor at the hole-in-the-wall Ni Shifu Sichuan Cuisine & Fondue, “Master Ni”, as the chef-owner describes himself, came to Antwerp 25 years ago, from Chengdu, and still does not speak a word of Flemish or English, but he certainly cooks up a storm in his tiny kitchen, dressed in shorts and a T-shirt, bent over his smoky wok. His dan dan noodles are wickedly spicy, the best I have eaten outside Asia, with the small dining room packed with a mix of Flemish locals, Antwerp Chinese and savvy visiting foodies. Ni Shifu has been singled out for Michelin praise for its authentic Sichuan cuisine and booking in advance is recommended.

Antwerp’s crucial bridge to the world, the docks – alongside the Scheldt river – are still among the busiest in Europe, but much of the surrounding Het Eilandje neighbourhood has been redeveloped. Its cutting-edge architecture includes the abstract pile of towering red-sandstone blocks that is the MAS maritime, history and cultural museum and Zaha Hadid’s metallic Port House, which resembles the shimmering prow of a floating ship.

Less conspicuous is the old red-brick warehouse that houses the Red Star Line Museum, a memorial to the millions of emigrants who passed through Antwerp on their way to a new life in North America. This intensely personal collection graphically illustrates the stories of some of the two million people who transited through Antwerp between 1873 and 1924, often after a long, tortuous journey from Central or Eastern Europe. Here, they endured medical examinations, disinfection and exhaustive immigration checks before finally being allowed to board a Red Star Line ship bound, in most cases, for New York. Most were fleeing poverty and persecution, little different from today’s migrants, and the anonymous tales are just as moving as those of the more famous émigrés who set sail on the Red Star Line: theoretical physicist Albert Einstein, composer Irving Berlin and future Israeli prime minister Golda Meir.

Just around the corner, in the Montevideo area – Antwerp’s quays are named after the exotic ports that produce was exported to and imported from – celebrity chef Nick Bril has just relocated his two-Michelin-star restaurant, The Jane, into a minimalist dining room, a striking departure from its original location, in a deconsecrated chapel downtown.

“Choosing Het Eilandje felt like a very logical step,” explains Bril, who has appeared on television in Belgian reality show Special Forces: Who Dares Wins, has served as a judge on Celebrity MasterChef Vlaanderen and is a renowned DJ. “It is an area where Antwerp’s history and future come together in a very natural way. The city has always drawn its strength from its openness to the world, and though our cuisine is firmly rooted in Belgium and in the products that surround us, it has always been influenced by experiences beyond our own borders.”

Gert de Mangeleer is present for every service in his kitchen at the two-Michelin-star Hertog Jan at Botanic, overseeing a tasting menu that is his own interpretation of a Japanese omakase experience.

“When I decided to open my restaurant in Antwerp, it was the perfect inspiration for my cuisine: this cosmopolitan harbour city that is an entrepôt for spices and exotic produce from around the globe,” says de Mangeleer, who gained prominence as part of the Flanders Kitchen Rebels campaign, a movement of young, talented chefs who brought a modern, rebellious attitude to traditional Belgian gastronomy.

His diners are tempted with dishes such as Japanese binchotan-grilled Wagyu beef served with locally smoked eel sauce, crispy veal sweetbreads, steamed dumplings of spinach dim sum and a sauce of Zeeland oysters.

One of Belgium’s two three-Michelin-star restaurants, Zilte, stands in the old docks area of Antwerp, but a favourite haunt of local chefs and sommeliers – evidenced by the fact that it’s open on Mondays, a traditional day off for restaurant staff – is the casual bistro Invincible. Here, animatedly supervising a brigade of cooks, Kenny Burssens interprets traditional Flemish cuisine, sautéing crunchy Brussels sprouts with bone marrow, and pairing tiny girolle mushrooms with tender chunks of milky cows’ udder, or line-caught cod with the salty sea-vegetable salicorne. The wine list includes vintages from little-known Belgian vineyards.

A little different is a meal at Samenloop, a restaurant that occupies the ground floor and cobbled courtyard of the Maagdenhuis, which was opened in 1552 as an orphanage for girls and also houses a museum and a chapel. The recently opened Samenloop is a social project for refugees: its waiters from Afghanistan and Palestine, and kitchen staff from Eritrea, the Maldives and Colombia are offered hospitality training so they can better integrate into society. One of a changing cast of celebrated chefs (for two months from November, it will be Karen Shu, an American-Filipino chef with a restaurant near Antwerp who is known for vegan and plant-based cuisine) collaborates by selecting recipes from the homelands of the refugees and adapting them into a tasting menu: crispy Nepalese pani puri surprisingly stuffed with chopped local asparagus; traditional Syrian falafel with fresh green peas; a light Ukrainian strawberry sernik cheesecake.

Another string to Antwerp’s bow is its reputation as a cutting-edge capital of European fashion. The Fashion Museum, known as MoMu, is a hotbed of creation, its studios and ateliers training the next generation of designers.

The city broke onto the international fashion scene in the 80s, with the rise of the Antwerp Six: revolutionary stylists who all graduated from the city’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts and colonised the pages of Vogue, Elle and Harper’s Bazaar.

“[Antwerp] is the perfect place to work,” one of the six, designer Walter Van Beirendonck, told Surface Magazine in 2016. “It’s not expensive, it’s quiet and it’s close to Paris, Milan and London. The art is great, the food is good, you can live well. There’s a real sense of possibility here.”

The visionary designs and eye-catching fashion shows of the likes of Dries Van Noten, Ann Demeulemeester and Van Beirendonck can now be seen at the MoMu exhibition “Antwerp Six”, which runs until January 17, 2027.

Another innovative temporary show can be found at the monumental Royal Museum of Fine Arts, with its colonnaded facade, neoclassical architecture, marble staircase and huge exhibition rooms. “KMSKA x Young Fashion Designers” (until November 8) gives free rein to 10 young graduates from the Antwerp Fashion Academy to create fashion sculptures influenced by pieces in the museum’s collection, inspiration having come from the dramatic flowing robes with cascading folds of fabric often depicted by Rubens and the revolutionary slashed canvases of Lucio Fontana (1899-1968).

A fitting way to end an exploration of eclectic, multi-ethnic Antwerp is to head for the Theaterplein square on a Saturday, the venue for the Exotic Market.

As Chinese immigrants were arriving after the end of World War II, migrants from countries such as Spain, Greece, Turkey and Morocco settled here, too, bringing the spices and ingredients of their native cuisines. They started selling their wares at the Theaterplein every Saturday, at what was first termed the Foreigners’ Market.

Teeming with locals and tourists from 8am to 4pm, this is more a multicultural, all-day party than a commercial centre, where the cava flows and food trucks serve customers sitting on temporary terraces a kaleidoscope of global cuisine: cheesy Turkish börek; plump Tibetan momo dumplings; Pakistani palak paneer; Peruvian panini; North African couscous and tagines; Vietnamese glass noodles. And to remind you that this is still Antwerp, there are also Flemish specialities, such as matjes (herrings), local oysters and bowls of karakol, a tasty soup of whelks and celery.

item.title: [SCMP] After losing both legs, snowboarder Neil Tsui sets his sights on the Paralympics
item.description:
I was born in 1981, in Surrey, south of Vancouver, in Canada. I’m the youngest of four – three boys and one girl. My father is Chinese, originally from Shanghai. He left during the communist revolution and moved to Macau and then Hong Kong. My mother is Brazilian, originally from just outside São Paulo. They met in Brazil and immigrated to Canada in 1970. My upbringing was very outdoors. Everywhere you go, there are mountains and ocean. I got into snowboarding when I was about 13 years old. It’s my favourite thing to do.

I went to Earl Marriott Secondary School, and didn’t go to university, much to my parents’ frustration. I loved carpentry, was a petrolhead and enjoyed fixing cars with my brothers. Then, I worked in sales. I had a great life, friends, family. But as I approached 30, I felt that if I didn’t leave, I was never going to go. I went to visit my sister, who was living in Hong Kong, and just like everyone else, I fell in love with the city. So, I got a job working in business development and marketing for professional services.

From 2011, for three years, I lived in Mid-Levels and was a recruiter and really enjoyed it. I was then approached about a technology role within recruitment. It was a start-up, an American firm, and that was a great experience. The start-up was based in San Francisco, but we launched it in Asia. I later worked for another tech company, Phaidon. In 2019, my sister and her family left Hong Kong, and I felt ready for my next move.
item.content:encoded:
I was born in 1981, in Surrey, south of Vancouver, in Canada. I’m the youngest of four – three boys and one girl. My father is Chinese, originally from Shanghai. He left during the communist revolution and moved to Macau and then Hong Kong. My mother is Brazilian, originally from just outside São Paulo. They met in Brazil and immigrated to Canada in 1970. My upbringing was very outdoors. Everywhere you go, there are mountains and ocean. I got into snowboarding when I was about 13 years old. It’s my favourite thing to do.

I went to Earl Marriott Secondary School, and didn’t go to university, much to my parents’ frustration. I loved carpentry, was a petrolhead and enjoyed fixing cars with my brothers. Then, I worked in sales. I had a great life, friends, family. But as I approached 30, I felt that if I didn’t leave, I was never going to go. I went to visit my sister, who was living in Hong Kong, and just like everyone else, I fell in love with the city. So, I got a job working in business development and marketing for professional services.

From 2011, for three years, I lived in Mid-Levels and was a recruiter and really enjoyed it. I was then approached about a technology role within recruitment. It was a start-up, an American firm, and that was a great experience. The start-up was based in San Francisco, but we launched it in Asia. I later worked for another tech company, Phaidon. In 2019, my sister and her family left Hong Kong, and I felt ready for my next move.

I moved with the company to Singapore in September 2020. I’d met my (future) wife, Sarah, on a dating app in 2019. We finally met in person in May 2021 and an attraction was that she loved wakeboarding, like me. We got married in 2023. Six weeks after we arrived back from our honeymoon, I had an eczema spot on the back of my leg. My dermatologist gave me a cortisone jab but made me get a blood test as I had also been taking Olumiant, a strong drug for alopecia, for six months. I then went wakeboarding on Sentosa beach, where the water is filthy, and, in the evening, started getting chills. My fever got worse and I collapsed on the bathroom floor. We got a taxi to the hospital. My blood pressure was spiking and I passed out.

The following day, my wife told me I had developed sepsis and gone into septic shock. I had necrotising fasciitis, which is a flesh-eating disease. My whole body was shutting down. I was put into an induced coma, so that my body could fight to stay alive. My sister flew out from Amsterdam and my mother-in-law came from Britain. For three days, my wife just held my hand, staring at a heart monitor, not knowing if I was going to make it. Miraculously, after four days, I started turning around – my heart, my kidneys on dialysis, everything was starting to turn around. They woke me up 10 days later. My legs were covered in bandages. And all I could see were my feet, which had gone this kind of blue-purple colour. Three of my doctors came in and told me they had given me an inotrope drug – it’s what they give anyone who goes into serious septic shock. It redirects all the blood flow to your torso, to preserve your vital organs. As a result, your extremities – such as hands, feet, even your face, your nose – get cut off from adequate blood flow. So, they stood by the bed and explained all of this, and then said, “We’re going to give you a bilateral amputation. We’re going to amputate both your legs below the knee.”

All I could picture was my wife, who I’d been married to for six weeks, pushing me in a wheelchair. And then I thought about my dad. My parents started out as broke immigrants. And my dad’s outlook is: if you fall, it’s up to you to pick yourself up. In my head, it just clicked – “OK, you’re going to own this” – and I opened my eyes and looked at the doctors and said, “Can I still snowboard?” And they said yes. I was lucky to be alive.

I typed into Instagram: “Amputee Snowboarding”. And it came up with a Canadian athlete named Tyler Turner. He’s the first Canadian to win a gold medal for snowboarding, at the 2022 Beijing Paralympics. And he was the same as me – a double amputee below the knee. I wrote to him and then we talked for an hour and a half. He told me to harness the snowboarding as that would get me through my recovery. As a joke, he said they were always looking for double-amputee athletes for the Paralympic team. In my head, it clicked – getting on the team would be my North Star.

Four days later, I had the first leg amputated. (Tsui has undergone 17 surgeries in total.) A couple of months later, I got my first set of prosthetics. I felt so tall! I had an incredible physiotherapist, who worked with me on my core, and knew about my snowboarding goal. I just kept building up my strength and balance, and started playing tennis again and riding a bike. I met Tyler in the summer of 2024 and we went surfing together in Tofino, on Vancouver Island; it was an instant bond.

He asked me if I wanted to go to the Netherlands in November 2024, to get my classification for the Paralympics and, since I was living in Singapore, I hadn’t even been on a snowboard yet. I went to Trifecta Singapore, a sports facility with an indoor Snow Arena for practising snowboarding and skiing using hi-tech simulators. I couldn’t even balance. I was there for an hour and I couldn’t let go of the bar long enough. When I got home, I ripped my legs off and was on the floor, absolutely broken. Sarah encouraged me to go and meet Tyler and get the classification.

Two weeks later, I was in the Netherlands, at SnowWorld Landgraaf, an indoor ski resort. I strapped my snowboard on and we went up in the chairlift and Tyler filmed. As soon as I started going, it just clicked. I did a big carve right, a big carve left, and then I just ripped all the way to the bottom without falling. I was screaming and hooting. The video is quite ridiculous; I’m literally whooping the whole way. And I’m crying. I was so elated and, all the way down, I was saying, “We did it!” I was just thinking about Sarah and how this was for us – this is what had got us through a hellish year, to get to this moment. It was 366 days after my right leg was cut off. I did two runs and went to get my classification.

We now have a son, he’s nine months old, and we are moving back to Canada next year. Canadian Olympic snowboarder Mark Fawcett said I need to spend as much time on snow as I can. I’m still aiming for the Paralympics in 2030. We bought a house on Vancouver Island. By the time of the next Winter Paralympics, in 2030, in the French Alps, I’m going to be 49. Three years ago, I was getting my legs amputated and I’m now snowboarding with Mark, one of the godfathers of snowboarding.

I now do public speaking at corporations and at schools. I’m not trying to be some sort of inspirational person. I am just trying to be the old Neil, who just loves activity. But, obviously, I know there is a lesson in there. The irony is that it took me losing both of my legs to feel limitless. I won’t know until literally a month or two before the actual Games if I’m on the team. It’s a lofty goal and a total gamble, but you need to stay the course.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Tsui Ao-lung’s journey from airport worker to Hong Kong fashion champion
item.description:
Tsui Ao-lung did not walk a conventional path to becoming Hong Kong’s newest fashion-design champion. He has no formal training in garment design and he spent three years away from the industry altogether, earning an income moving cargo at the Hong Kong International Airport and waiting restaurant tables to pay off debts from a T-shirt brand he had co-founded. When he finally returned to the craft last year, it was almost by accident: a stylist had asked him to create stage outfits for a concert, so he taught himself how to design for the stage.

It was a circuitous route that led him, on September 5, to claim the top prize at the Hong Kong Young Fashion Designers’ Contest 2026 (YDC), a highlight of the annual Centrestage showcase, itself a flagship event of the third Hong Kong Fashion Fest, organised by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. Competing against nine other finalists under the theme “You”, the 29-year-old took home the HK$60,000 cash prize, champion title and an overseas internship opportunity sponsored by knitwear manufacturing firm Fang Brothers Knitting.

His winning collection, “The Tide”, draws its name and mood from “Kuang Chao”, a 1970s Cantopop hit by Hong Kong singer Susanna Kwan Kuk-ying. Tsui used the song as a springboard to dive into the journey of a woman’s life across four seasons, capturing her highs, lows and the experience of existence in four hand-stitched pieces.
item.content:encoded:
Tsui Ao-lung did not walk a conventional path to becoming Hong Kong’s newest fashion-design champion. He has no formal training in garment design and he spent three years away from the industry altogether, earning an income moving cargo at the Hong Kong International Airport and waiting restaurant tables to pay off debts from a T-shirt brand he had co-founded. When he finally returned to the craft last year, it was almost by accident: a stylist had asked him to create stage outfits for a concert, so he taught himself how to design for the stage.

It was a circuitous route that led him, on September 5, to claim the top prize at the Hong Kong Young Fashion Designers’ Contest 2026 (YDC), a highlight of the annual Centrestage showcase, itself a flagship event of the third Hong Kong Fashion Fest, organised by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. Competing against nine other finalists under the theme “You”, the 29-year-old took home the HK$60,000 cash prize, champion title and an overseas internship opportunity sponsored by knitwear manufacturing firm Fang Brothers Knitting.

His winning collection, “The Tide”, draws its name and mood from “Kuang Chao”, a 1970s Cantopop hit by Hong Kong singer Susanna Kwan Kuk-ying. Tsui used the song as a springboard to dive into the journey of a woman’s life across four seasons, capturing her highs, lows and the experience of existence in four hand-stitched pieces.

However, what the judges and the audience could not have anticipated, when the designer’s creations strutted down the catwalk, is that Tsui had let his exacting nature take the wheel, scrapping and overhauling entire looks in the days before the show, with the final touches to his pieces added right before he had to present them. A real-life Project Runway – Hong Kong edition, that is.

We talk to Tsui about winning the competition, his three years away from design, his ambition to eventually launch his own brand again and how he thinks he can work 18 hours a day without ever feeling tired.

What motivated you to enter YDC this year?

It was to tell stories, to express things I wanted to say. I think YDC is a great opportunity. It has a good platform and a complete system that lets people from all walks of life see your work. I never thought of taking part before, because I wanted to try and rely on myself, to strive on my own. But then, at a certain point, I thought, “Since the opportunity is there, why not give it a shot?”

How did it feel to win the contest?

I felt happy, very happy, but also relieved. So many people were screaming. I worked long shifts leading up to the finale. After that, I slept for hours.

What was your biggest challenge?

I used to do casual wear – simple clothes. YDC was my first time doing fittings, organising so many outfits, shoes and so on – I felt like I couldn’t handle it all. When I finished the four designs, I was very unsatisfied. So, I kept tweaking them, completely redoing some of the looks from scratch, and I ended up remaking the pieces I wasn’t happy with after the fittings, working on them up to the last minute before I had to leave for the show.

What was your workspace like?

I actually went back and forth to Guangzhou to make the clothes. A lot of suppliers are concentrated there, so if I needed materials or components, I could buy them straight away. Because I don’t have my own studio, I worked out of a shared “central sample room” – a space used by several shops. I didn’t have a fixed area on the premises, so whenever a space opened up, I’d drag my dress dummy and tools over there to work. Most of the time, I’d wait until late at night, after everyone else had left and the lights were off, so I could spread all my stuff out and sew in peace, staying until 4am or 5am. It took a lot of patience, and I kept pricking my fingers, but that’s how I got it done. Many friends were helping me. I didn’t ask them to, and I never shared what I was making with anyone. But in the last two weeks, they came to the fittings and helped me. I am so grateful.

How did you arrive at the core theme for your winning collection?

I often refer to music and films to capture a mood or feeling. For “The Tide”, the theme came from a Cantopop song called “Kuang Chao”. I came across it and was inspired to take that mood and expand on it. Since the song is about ups and downs, I thought about leaning into a woman’s perspective to explore the cycles of her life, moving through spring, summer, autumn and winter. I also wanted to connect it to the city – you’ll find elements of Hong Kong hidden in the clothes. Whether it’s a person or a place, there will always be moments of glory, but also moments of decline. It’s just as the lyrics go, “It’s them; it is also you and me”.

What was the most important quality you wanted to showcase?

For me, it’s all about the handiwork and hand-stitched details – they really make up the core of the whole collection. Having that focus on craftsmanship gives the collection a natural, cohesive feel.

What first got you into making clothes?

It was a total accident. After secondary school, a friend – my former business partner – had a group of friends who were really passionate about making clothes and starting brands, so I tagged along to join the fun. Back then, our mindset was purely about having a good time and experimenting together. “You make one for me to wear, I make one for you to wear” – that kind of thing. Slowly, everyone else stopped making clothes and abandoned dressmaking. I’m the only one left.

You spent three years away from designing. What was that period like?

During those three years, I actually prepared a lot; I mapped out plans for the next five seasons. I specifically avoided taking on design work because I’m uncompromising – I didn’t want to enter a system of creating commercial filler to make money. I waited tables and moved goods at the airport to make ends meet. Ironically, even while trying hard to avoid seeing them, I’d still spot people wearing clothes from my previous brand on their way to work. I really want to start a brand again, but I know one thing: you have to be ready before you do it. Once you come out, you have to be confident, professional, strong. You can’t just do it half-heartedly.

Describe your creative process.

First, I think of a story. When we actually start making the clothes, we often look at the fabric first and then build on the basic concept, step by step. I write a narrative, and then build the storyline, block by block, although whether it turns out the way I originally intended is a different matter.

How does Hong Kong shape your designs?

I watch a lot of concerts; they often inspire my work. For example, the second look in my collection, the cheongsam – nobody guessed that the inspiration came from one of Eason Chan Yick-shun’s concerts, where he happened to be wearing a belt styled like a corset. I pull inspiration from plenty of other concert looks, too, though I never copy them directly; I just use them as a starting point.

What kind of designer do you want to be?

I’m open to pretty much anything. My advantage, or maybe my flaw, is that I can see the positives in any style, so I don’t mind doing whatever type. But I’m more drawn to pieces with character. I’ll mostly stick to a story-driven line. I want to tell a story naturally, with relevant clothing elements to package it, while keeping my own touch.

What’s your ideal way of working?

I hope it’s one where I don’t have to rest, because I don’t like being inactive. I did YDC and worked 18-hour days – eating just one late-night meal a day – and had absolutely no problem with it. I didn’t feel tired. I can work straight through the night. It’s not just passion – my body’s simply wired that way. It’s like an engine: once it starts, it runs non-stop. Once I start working, I can’t stop.

item.title: [SCMP] Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
item.description:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.
item.content:encoded:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.

Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of the Thai economy, from the five-star resorts of Phuket and Koh Samui to the jet-ski operators and massage parlours of Pattaya.

The industry has never been immune to external shocks, however – and Charoon, who is in his seventies, has felt each one register at the ticket office of a business his father founded nearly 90 years ago to sell crocodile leather to tourists.

Sars, bird flu and the global financial crisis of 2007-08 all took their toll on visitor numbers, interspersed with boom years as mass tourism from China, an emerging Russian middle class and increasingly affluent Southeast Asian travellers pushed up attendance.

Then came a three-year closure amid the Covid-19 pandemic and – as with so much else in this world – nothing at Charoon’s zoo has been quite the same since.

“We used to have maybe 100, 200 big tour buses a day,” he told This Week in Asia. “But they stopped and we had to close because of the lockdown.”

By the time the business was able to reopen, tourism trends had changed. “People stopped travelling as big groups and instead they came as FITs,” Charoon said, using the industry acronym for “free, independent tourists”.

The zoo’s ample car park now welcomes only a handful of buses at a time. Across from it, a turreted wall built for elaborate performances once staged for Chinese tour groups stands as a chipped and faded monument to the high-water mark of Thai tourism.

Nearly 40 million people visited Thailand in 2019, the final year before the pandemic’s onset and still a Southeast Asian record.

Last year’s total of 32.9 million fell well short of that peak, despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 to lure travellers back.

The Tourism Authority of Thailand has now trimmed its 2026 forecast to between 30 million and 34 million international visitors, as this year’s US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s 4½-year-old war with Ukraine conspire to drive up oil prices and, with them, international airfares to Southeast Asia.

Years of a strong baht, meanwhile, have nudged budget-conscious international travellers towards cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia.

Money, geopolitics and changing tastes tell only half the story, however. The rest is down to patience – and Thailand’s is wearing thin.

Misbehaving tourists

Long known as the “land of smiles”, Thailand has for years prided itself on its easy-going approach to hospitality that asks little of guests beyond good manners.

But scroll through Thai social media on any given morning nowadays and the previous night’s transgressions are laid out for all to see: unpaid bills, drunken brawls and arrests for theft or vandalism among them.
