This is the work of real social science, and it involves transparency and openness on data and a willingness to welcome the gathering of data, rather than assuming that it has to be banned for security reasons.

So, although more scholars are coming back to China, opening up more capacity to be able to do real research in China is the next barrier that needs to be overcome.

There are a lot of brilliant Chinese students in many countries in the West who are doing significant social science and humanities research. But their Western equivalents who study China can’t do that kind of work in China, so it becomes very unbalanced.

What about your own experience with the Asia studies and Chinese history students you taught at Oxford and now Harvard?

When it comes to postgraduate students doing PhDs, a significant number are Chinese. We do still have some Westerners, but the problem is that they have to be enthusiastic about China, willing to learn its language and culture, and then be able to find a meaningful project to research.

It’s harder now to assure students that they can find a pathway to doing really good social science research inside China, so a lot of students just leave China out. If people say China is a very difficult place to do research and South Korea is easy, maybe people just decide they want to learn Korean instead.

The sense among Western researchers that it’s hard to do serious research in China has transmitted to students finding it difficult to find a career path if they do study China. I think that’s a great shame.

item.title: [SCMP] Jeffrey Sachs says US sabre-rattling at China can become self-fulfilling prophecy of war
item.description:
Jeffrey Sachs is an economics professor and director of the Centre for Sustainable Development at Columbia University. He is president of the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. He was a special adviser to the UN Secretary General and has advised multiple governments on economic transition, debt crisis solutions and poverty alleviation policies. Part 1 of the Sachs interview, published in July last year, can be found here. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The tariff truce between China and the United States is set to end in August. What do you forecast will happen after that? And what will happen to trade relations between China and the US for the rest of US President Donald Trump’s second term?

The United States learned that it can’t impose its will on China. The rare earths threat by itself was enough to cause the US to reconsider. So, almost immediately after putting on the high tariffs, the US backed down. And both sides know that each has some chokeholds on the other. For that reason, we might expect the two sides to maintain certain limits on the trade frictions in the years ahead. There will be, therefore, some kind of agreement, but it won’t stick in the details, and frictions will continue to wax and wane, with neither side definitively imposing its will on the other. The basic reason is that both sides have a mutual gain from continued trade. I’m hopeful that a measure of rationality will therefore prevail.
item.content:encoded:
Jeffrey Sachs is an economics professor and director of the Centre for Sustainable Development at Columbia University. He is president of the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. He was a special adviser to the UN Secretary General and has advised multiple governments on economic transition, debt crisis solutions and poverty alleviation policies. Part 1 of the Sachs interview, published in July last year, can be found here. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The tariff truce between China and the United States is set to end in August. What do you forecast will happen after that? And what will happen to trade relations between China and the US for the rest of US President Donald Trump’s second term?

The United States learned that it can’t impose its will on China. The rare earths threat by itself was enough to cause the US to reconsider. So, almost immediately after putting on the high tariffs, the US backed down. And both sides know that each has some chokeholds on the other. For that reason, we might expect the two sides to maintain certain limits on the trade frictions in the years ahead. There will be, therefore, some kind of agreement, but it won’t stick in the details, and frictions will continue to wax and wane, with neither side definitively imposing its will on the other. The basic reason is that both sides have a mutual gain from continued trade. I’m hopeful that a measure of rationality will therefore prevail.

The biggest challenge, of course, is the behaviour of the US. The US started this trade war. This is not two sides fighting each other, but rather the US fighting China. We should remember that. The US needs to show some prudence at this point. I do suspect that there is a chastened view among many senior US officials. Trump himself is unpredictable. He has a very short attention span. Agreements with Trump don’t stick. So, I don’t foresee a quiet period, but I do foresee some limits to the competition because each side can do damage to the other and both sides have a strong reason to achieve some cooperation.

Let me add one more point. From a long-term point of view, China certainly should not regard the US as a growth market for its exports. The US is going to restrict China’s exports to the US one way or another. The relationship will not be harmonious. The US will not be friendly to China, or trustworthy. China should just take care that it’s expanding its exports to other markets, and should not be overly focused on trying to break through to the US market, or even to Europe for that matter. The rapid growth of China’s exports will be with Africa, Southeast Asia, South Asia, west Asia, Central Asia, Latin America – not with the US and western Europe.

What is your forecast for the US midterm elections, and will it be a tough battle for Trump? Can you comment on how divided the US is compared to before the election of Trump last year?

I think that the Democrats will likely regain control of one or both houses of Congress, because in midterm elections that is generally the pattern.

Even without getting deeply specific about the current context, the prevailing party that holds the White House almost always loses ground in the midterms, and the Republican majority in both houses of Congress is very small. Having said this, we should also understand that Trump is ruling mainly by executive decree, not by legislation. Even if the Democrats regain one or both houses of Congress, Trump will continue with his decrees.

The US currently does not have a functioning constitutional system in my view. It is one-person rule by declarations of emergencies by Trump. The orders generally start with the statement: “By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered”. This is a kind of soft dictatorship, not a constitutional system. The lower courts object, but the Supreme Court lets Trump have his way. The Congress is nearly moribund.

Even if the Democrats regain some control of the House or the Senate, it won’t stop a lot of what Trump is doing. I should also add that while Americans are polarised, they generally dislike both political parties. Most Americans are unhappy about the direction of the country. They’re distrustful of the politicians. Our political institutions are not functioning properly and that’s why there’s a high level of distrust.

I don’t think that China can, or should, base its policies on a return to normal trade with the US

Jeffrey Sachs

Another point that I think is important to understand is that the swings between the Democrats and the Republicans do not change US foreign policy. [Former president Barack] Obama started the anti-China policies in his term. Then came Trump’s tariffs in his first term. Biden kept those Trump tariffs and had a hostile policy towards China. Now Trump is picking up where Biden left off. The deep state drives foreign policy, not public opinion or presidents.

In sum, I don’t have much hope that some change in the midterm elections will change the direction of US politics very much. Even a change in the White House in four years is not likely to change US politics very much. Our problems are deep seated. Our institutional failings are deep. It’s going to take perhaps 20 years to work through this. This is not a Trump phenomenon by itself.

What effect will the One Big Beautiful Bill have on the US economy?

The One Big Beautiful Bill weakens the US in two ways. First, it adds to the already large budget deficits by making additional tax cuts that mainly benefit rich Americans and the corporate class. These tax cuts raise the budget deficit substantially and are partially offset by cuts in healthcare benefits for the poorest Americans. The bill, therefore, is dramatically unfair and unwise in its impacts on the deficit and inequality.

Second, the legislation phases out some of the modest earlier US efforts towards low-carbon energy and modernisation of infrastructure. So, the legislation marks a US retreat from leadership on 21st-century technologies. Basically, the Trump administration is a gift to China, with Trump’s policies saying to China, “China should lead the way on climate safety, low-carbon energy, electric vehicles and all of the green and digital technologies that the world needs, while the US will ignore the future”.

So, none of this is a big, beautiful bill. It is a mess that reflects the failures of the American political system.

What are the implications of the fallout between billionaire Elon Musk and Trump?

Trump doesn’t have long-term relations with any individual other than his immediate family. Trump falls out with everybody. Remember Steve Bannon? He was once Trump’s closest adviser. That came to an end quickly. Almost all Trump advisers get fired at one point or another. Trump is not a person with long-term loyalties to anybody.

The individual feuds don’t mean very much. Breaking with Musk does not mean breaking with Silicon Valley. Silicon Valley put Trump back into the White House with enormous financial backing for Trump’s campaign. There are still tens of billions of dollars of government contracts going also to Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and other Big Tech operators.

The basic relationship between Silicon Valley and Washington remains intact because the Pentagon believes that it needs AI and can’t pursue AI on its own. While Trump has cut support for EVs, including Tesla, the Pentagon will continue to rely on Musk’s SpaceX for many years to come. And the same is true of the Pentagon’s reliance on Big Tech’s AI capacities generally.

You have mentioned in other interviews that Trump lacked a coherent strategy in foreign policy, including his handling of China. Why do you think this? And what do you see ahead for China-US relations?

The most fundamental trend in the world economy is the rapid rise of the non-Western economies, led by China and including Russia, India, Southeast Asia and, in future decades, Africa. The US is flailing about trying to maintain its dominance in a world in which the emerging economies are rising rapidly. The US will not be able to prevent the emergence of multipolarity, but it will try. Trump will try one thing or another, but without success or coherence. Multipolarity has already arrived.

The broad pattern of economic convergence – in which the emerging economies narrow or close the income gap with the high-income countries of the West – means that Western hegemony is over. This is leading to deep frustration, not only in the US political class but in Europe as well.

China vastly outproduces the United States in advanced industrial goods, such as EVs, solar power, wind power, advanced nuclear power, batteries, low-cost 5G and many other key technologies. China incorporates AI into advanced manufacturing processes more than the US.

Many European leaders feel that if they stick with the US against China and Russia, then maybe the Western hegemony will continue. This is delusional in my view, but nonetheless creates a lot of noise, friction and risks of conflict. None of it is a coherent strategy, however.

The US has no strategy to stay ahead of China. In fact, the US can’t succeed in that. We hear a lot of US sabre-rattling against China, Russia and the Brics countries. This is all dangerous. I think the heated rhetoric by itself can become a self-fulfilling prophecy of war. There are a lot of ignorant people in the US political leadership, and I worry very much about their naivety and delusions.

This, in my view, is essentially the origin of the “trade war”. The US decided during 2010-2015 that China is now a threat to US primacy. The US has tried a lot of things to block China’s continued rise, including: a military build-up in East Asia; export restrictions on hi-tech goods, especially advanced chips; economic sanctions on key Chinese companies; investment restrictions by US companies, and ownership restrictions on Chinese companies in the US; high tariffs against China’s exports; and others. But none of this stops China’s rise. China’s development results from hard work, ingenuity, high rates of saving, high rates of investment, very effective long-term planning and a very skilled, very entrepreneurial generation of business leaders, especially young business leaders. Those fundamental strengths continue despite America’s anti-China policies.

Trump’s policies are accelerating the move of top scientists to China. My overall view is that Trump is creating a lot of noise and some real dangers, but with no real strategy and no likelihood of success in holding back China’s rise. That’s a good thing. The rest of the world benefits from China’s economic success, including the US.

In your last Open Questions interview, you talked about “the deep state”, a complex vested interest group in industry, the military and other spheres. Does the deep state want military conflict with China? And do foreign governments – such as China and Russia – believe in the existence of a deep state, which many dismiss as a conspiracy theory?

The deep state means the permanent security system of the United States and its partners in Europe and in East Asia, including Japan, Korea and other places where the US has military bases and other security institutions. It includes the military, the CIA, the military contractors and the politicians who serve the military-industrial complex.

Does such a deep state exist? Yes. The US has around 750 overseas military bases and many of them are in East Asia. The US has many major military contractors with hundreds of billions of dollars of annual business with the US government. The US fights overt and covert wars pretty much non-stop, some of which are proxy wars (in which the US arms and funds Ukraine to fight Russia), and sometimes open conflicts with heavy US involvement, as in Iraq and Afghanistan. The US has the extensive global networks of the CIA and other intelligence and covert institutions. All of this constitutes the deep state. Presidents come and go but the underlying foreign policy is consistent and set largely out of view of the public, and without any reference to public opinion.

When Obama replaced [US president George] Bush Jnr, and Trump replaced Obama, and Biden replaced Trump, and Trump replaced Biden, on the PR level there was alleged to be change, but in fact very little policy change occurred. For example, how much foreign policy change was there when Obama succeeded Bush Jnr? Very little. Obama launched many wars, just as Bush had done. Obama’s team actively participated in the coup in Ukraine in 2014 that set the path for the Ukraine war. Obama went to war against Libya. Obama gave the CIA the order to overthrow the Syrian government. All of this was a continuation of the policies of the Bush period.

Trump continued most of the same policies. Trump continued to build up the Ukraine military. The Trump administration dismissed the Minsk 2 agreement that could have prevented the escalation of the Ukraine war. There was not any major change between Obama and Trump.

When Biden came in, their claim again was that there would be a new foreign policy, but it didn’t happen. What did Biden do with China? He continued Trump’s tariffs. He continued Trump’s hardline rhetoric. Biden absurdly divided the world between the so-called democracies and autocracies, which was an incredibly naive approach, as I said from the beginning.

Biden escalated the Ukraine war. He rejected all attempts at peace negotiations, including the Istanbul process that could have ended the Ukraine war in 2022. When it came to the Middle East, Biden was complicit in Israel’s ongoing genocide. So, Biden did very little different from Bush Jnr, Obama and Trump before him.

Now, Trump has returned. What’s the real difference? Trump is different in style, in his unpredictability, nastiness, self-dealing and endless flip-flops. Yet, in terms of basic foreign policy, Trump is not very different from his predecessors.

This is the sense in which deep state means an ongoing consistency of the US security institutions that run American foreign policy. American foreign policy is not determined by public opinion, or Congress, or even the president in large part. Look instead to the CIA, the Pentagon and the other parts of the deep state.

The deep state also determines the politics of US vassal states. Many observers consider Japan to be a US-occupied country, with Japan’s foreign policy basically subservient to the US. One can say the same about many other countries. Where the US has military bases, the host countries tend to act like occupied countries, bending their own foreign policy to that of the US.

The US deep state is profoundly arrogant, thinking that it can have its way around the world. The US deep state thinks that it can dominate not only US allies, which is typically true, but also China, Russia, Iran, Brazil and others. When US arrogance becomes too strong, we face the danger of disaster. That’s what happened in Ukraine. The US thought that it could push Russia around to its will. It could not. The attempt to assert US power in Ukraine led to war.

US arrogance deeply worries me. Trump certainly is not a strategist. There’s no long-term plan. The US is playing poker, but not very well or wisely. It often bluffs. The whole approach can lead to war.

China is now drafting its economic policies for the next five years. You have advised many countries before. What is your advice to China in the face of this tension and the global tariff war?

My main advice to China is look to the non-Western world for the strongest partnerships in trade, investment and diplomacy, at least for a while. The US-led alliance (US, Canada, Britain, EU, Japan, Korea, Australia and New Zealand) is around 13 per cent of the world population. China is another 17 per cent. The remaining 70 per cent of the world – in Asia, Africa and Latin America – wants good and strong economic and diplomatic relations with China. That 70 per cent of the world population wants to modernise, and China provides the means for those countries to achieve rapid growth and modernisation. China is key to the global energy transition to zero-carbon energy, especially in the markets outside the US and Europe.

The emerging and developing economies of Asia, Africa and Latin America will be the markets for China’s rapid export growth in the years ahead. China will play a vital global role in these economies in building advanced green and digital economies, using Chinese cutting-edge technologies.

This will be a great win-win for the world because China will continue to grow rapidly while also empowering rapid growth throughout the emerging and developing nations. Sadly, in my view, the US will not play much of a role in that modernisation in the next generation. The US under Trump is withdrawing from green technologies, and from global responsibility.

The US cannot compete with China for the global renewable energy market. The US can’t compete with China for the global digital connectivity market. The US can’t compete with China in fast rail or low-carbon ocean shipping. In all these sectors, Trump is handing world trade and leadership over to China.

Regarding the US markets, China should certainly attempt to make a suitable trade deal with the US but China should not fret too much either way. The US is already a small part of China’s exports – perhaps around 10-12 per cent. That share of China’s exports will most likely decline further.

I hope that I’m wrong and that the US regains some sense and rejoins the global effort for green transformation and re-establishes normal trade with China. Yet, I don’t think that’s going to happen for many years, and I don’t think that China can, or should, base its policies on a return to normal trade with the US.

More specifically, I advocate expanding [China’s] Belt and Road Initiative. I advocate that China should deal with regional groups, including Asean, the African Union, the Arab League and the Community of Latin America and Caribbean States (CELAC). China’s relations with these regional groups can be very strategic, as the regional groups can, and should, spur the interconnectivity of infrastructure among all the members of the group. For China, it will be easier to interact with regional plans rather than one country at a time.

In fact, no individual state in Asean, or the Middle East, or Latin America can modernise on its own without strong links with its neighbours through trade, finance and infrastructure. With Asean, for example, there really is the need for an Asean-wide energy system, not separate energy systems for Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia etc. These countries need an interconnected power grid, and China will play a key role in achieving an Asean-wide grid. Therefore, China-Asean diplomacy is strongly win-win.

I also believe that Hong Kong will have a huge and indeed unique leadership role in the global transformation. Hong Kong is vital for China’s growing links with Asean, the African Union, and beyond. The Greater Bay Area (GBA) combines Hong Kong’s world-class leadership in international finance, higher education and global management, with Shenzhen’s leadership in cutting-edge technologies, and the advanced manufacturing of Dongguan, Guangzhou and other GBA cities.

Put these strengths together, and the GBA becomes the beating heart of the global green transformation, in zero-carbon energy, robotics, AI-based manufacturing, digital connectivity and much more. All of this will help to fuel China’s – and Hong Kong’s – rapid growth for the next generation.

This year marks the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. How is the post-war world order changing and what will the new world order look like?

There are three scenarios.

One is that we create a truly multilateral world. For that, we need a United Nations 2.0. We need an upgraded international system in which all the major powers agree to invest in the international rule of law and peaceful resolution of conflicts. This will require an upgrade of the UN Security Council, and UN institutions more generally.

I’d love to see a major UN campus in China, to help lead the green and digital transformation worldwide. I’d love to see China and India working together closely at the UN, including towards India’s seat in the UN Security Council. I’d like China to support the African Union to play a much larger role in global governance. I’d like to see China, Japan and Korea end the geopolitical divisions and form a strong alliance in northeast Asia. Most importantly in this scenario, the US and Europe accept the rising role of China, India and the rest of the non-Western world.

A second scenario is that the Western world hunkers down. It goes protectionist and the US tries to divide the world into camps. This is perhaps the likely US strategy, but I think it is significantly worse for the US and the rest of the world than the first scenario. I think the US absolutely should abandon the idea of building competing camps.

The third scenario is that we don’t have a global system at all, but rather increasing chaos from climate change, wars and geopolitical conflicts. This dire scenario is a real possibility.

Any of these three trajectories is possible. We should be aiming for the first. The United States and Europe should take a deep breath, sigh and welcome the non-Western world into a shared global leadership. The major powers – the US, Europe, Russia, China, India – should agree to prevent confrontations.

The US should stop Nato enlargement and should stop providing armaments to Taiwan. Such actions are provocative and lead to great-power conflicts that threaten the safety and security of the whole world.

In short, the West should stop asking “Who is Number One?” and instead ask, “How can the whole world work together for the global common good?” In my experience, China, Russia and other nations would enthusiastically back such a global, cooperative effort that is based on mutual respect and mutual security.

item.title: [SCMP] How Japan’s innovative Nakagin Capsule Tower is finding new life
item.description:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.
item.content:encoded:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.

Nakagin’s scattered course would have pleased its avant-garde architect Kisho Kurokawa (1934-2007), who conceived the design to emancipate what he called Homo movens (mobile humans). Many fans still demonstrate their unbridled enthusiasm for the building by donning zany get-ups inspired by its form – often described as a stack of front-loading washing machines.

In my mind’s eye, however, Nakagin had always been a colony of barnacles. That analogy borrows from the free movement of these crustaceans before anchoring themselves in place. But unfortunately, it was the unexpected immobility of Kurokawa’s capsules during their first phase of life that ultimately thwarted his vision that they be modular, interchangeable and recyclable.

That idea of impermanent permanence remains irresistible, however – at least in Japan. Which was one reason Metabolism captured the imagination of many during the country’s buoyant post-war expansion, making its name and ethos heard at the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo. Adaptable buildings and cities – with renewable nodes fed by circulation systems – sparked interest. Adding excitement was the promise of Expo ’70, whose theme was “progress and harmony for mankind”.

At that landmark event in Osaka, futuristic pavilions, including several by Kurokawa, allowed the forward-thinking to see for themselves the biomimetic potential of a movement whose proponents included other eminent architects, Kenzo Tange and Fumihiko Maki among them.

Nakagin, however, earned the kind of cult status accorded few other buildings in Japan. One reason was the charisma of Kurokawa, also a media personality and, towards the end of his career, a politician. His building was among the few examples of Metabolist architecture ever realised.

In late 2022, Ikko Yokoyama visited a warehouse in Chiba, near Tokyo, where salvaged Nakagin capsules, resembling pet Cyclops, awaited adoption. As lead curator of design and architecture at M+, she was there to see one of 23 pods that had been saved by the Nakagin Capsule Tower Preservation and Restoration Project, founded by former resident Tatsuyuki Maeda.

Hong Kong’s museum of contemporary visual culture was prepared for this inevitable moment, according to Yokoyama. Debate had raged for years about whether to preserve Nakagin whole, with Kurokawa himself shifting from yes to no. Ultimately, land value outweighed legacy, says Dytham, who had tried without success to persuade developers and hospitality groups to turn Nakagin into a boutique hotel. “It wasn’t sustainable to keep it there,” he says.

The decision to tear it down was made despite its uniqueness. Unlike anything the West had produced – except, perhaps, in the minds of Britain’s Archigram group of architects – Nakagin consisted of capsules “plugged” into the building’s towers, or cores, one 11 storeys high, the other two floors taller. Tight spaces between each pod impeded access and meant that repairs were difficult because “you couldn’t get in”, says Dytham. Worse, owners were unwilling to pay the high cost of detaching their capsules for upkeep every 25 years, as Kurokawa had warned they must. Decay set in, leaks appeared and damage from Japan’s frequent earthquakes saw the building’s exterior netted for safety. Additionally, the presence of asbestos complicated matters.

But M+’s capsule speaks volumes about their enduring appeal. A806 now stands beside another of the museum’s inspired acquisitions, Kiyotomo (1988), the sushi bar designed by Shiro Kuramata. Unlike that 656 sq ft restaurant – which was disassembled in Japan, shipped to Hong Kong and later put together again by the original contractors and an M+ team of restorers – Kurokawa’s capsule was purchased fully reconditioned.

The 2.78 metre x 2.69 metre x 4.21 metre capsule in the East Galleries is one of six standard units, complete with their famous round window at one end accommodating a circular blind that folds open like a hand fan. Also included within the 121.9 sq ft space are mod cons and a dinky unit bath, those tiny waterproof rooms sold as a single product in Japan.

“Like organ donation”, as Yokoyama puts it, parts for the capsule were harvested from others in the building because none of the pods survived with all of its original fittings intact. Kiyotomo’s neighbour now also boasts a new blue carpet and mattress, in addition to a fold-down desk, television and reel-to-reel tape deck, among other integrated features. Combine the service and payload modules of a spaceship and you get the idea.

Of the capsules plucked to safety by Maeda’s group, 14 have been sold to companies and museums, including M+ and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which purchased Kurokawa’s prized personal unit. Of the nine remaining, he says, four are to stay in Japan while five will head abroad.

Some have already been turned into display modules and mobile units and, next year, hotel-room conversions are expected, which should come as no surprise: in 1979, Kurokawa’s ideas also gave birth to the world’s first capsule hotel. New Japan Umeda continues to offer budget accommodation in Osaka.

Maeda’s is not the only group intent on giving the (in) famous corner building a second life. The Nakagin Capsule Tower A606 Project is named after the pod that another ex-resident helped restore several years before the building came down. This group, which owns seven units, has even more ambitious, albeit firmly parochial, aims.

“We plan to reconstruct a mini-tower using several capsules we own,” the group reveals via core member, architect Akiko Ishimaru.

“We aim to keep the reconstructed ones for 50 years [100 years after their completion] by continuing to use them ourselves. We want to utilise the capsules that were born in Japan and rebuild them in Japan.”

Crowdfunding has helped pay for the work so far. “The cost of asbestos control and investigation during the survey and dismantling, transportation and storage of seven capsules, storage of original parts, printing of a book with records, restoration of the interior of capsule A606, crowdfunding gifts [such as the aforementioned book], and fees consumed most of the total 8,673,000 yen [HK$443,000],” the group says.

Ishimaru’s efforts to keep Nakagin from history’s scrapheap underscores the passion in the project. But that’s not to say she fully enjoyed her year living in the building (and seven more working in two other capsules).

“One of my fond memories is drawing the actual survey plan for Nakagin Capsule Tower on my laptop at the original desk of Capsule A606 in August 2021,” she recalls, adding, “The 1.3-metre-diameter round window meant that the small room didn’t feel cramped.”

Having been designed as “hotel-like second homes” – or crash pads for salarymen – none of the capsules came with a kitchen. It was “very quiet”, Ishimaru recalls. The prefabricated steel modules didn’t share walls and, by 2013, when she moved in, there were only a few residents left. “Since it was so old and there was no hot water, I couldn’t even take a shower inside the capsule, so I stopped living there and used it as a shared office.”

Other assessments were bleaker. “From outside, the tower looked like a dying animal, sweating and greasy in the heat, trapped inside its wire netting,” reads an account by The Paris Review of Nakagin’s condition in 2016. “Looking up, you could see that some capsules had been half-filled with rotting garbage, a rippling line of trash drawn across their single windows. Inside, panels peel from the ceilings and mold crawls underneath; grime and seepage scorches the concrete with strange, bubbling forms.”

The reviewer added: “Kurokawa’s masterpiece was an utter, unsalvageable failure.”

And there’s the rub.

On whether Metabolism remains relevant in the 21st century, few can deny the importance of urban development that hews closely to principles of sustainability and flexibility. “The idea that buildings can change, grow and regenerate over time within a city may be increasingly needed to adapt to urban population growth and environmental issues,” the A606 group argue.

But how to label Kurokawa’s achievement remains as polarising as the fractious debates about whether the building should have been protected for posterity.

“It was an amazing success because he made it happen,” says Yokoyama, referring to how Kurokawa turned theory into reality and created a prototype. “It wasn’t just imagination.”

Dytham also believes Kurokawa got it “pretty right”, explaining that Nakagin was an early model. “If you’re building 10 of them, you get it. That was the first one.”

He adds that, for him, the building’s success had much to do with a design so simple that even a child could read and recognise it. “That would be a totally protected building if it was in the UK,” he posits. “Traditionally, here [in Japan], things are built in a temporary way.”

However, the recent wide dispersal of Nakagin capsules underscores the fact that Kurokawa’s vision has come to fruition. As Dytham says, “How many buildings have been taken apart and put all around the world?

“Taking [Nakagin] to the rest of the world is as important as just being all in one place.”

Metabolism was simply operating at its own pace.

item.title: [SCMP] Protect the middle? Why Southeast Asia should care about a vulnerable class
item.description:
As households across Southeast Asia face rising prices, higher borrowing costs and insecure jobs, analysts say governments should do more to protect a middle class that drives consumer spending but can fall between the cracks of social protection systems designed primarily for poorer households.

The issue has come into sharper focus in the Philippines, where the Asian Development Bank Institute (ADBI) urged the government in September to provide targeted support for the middle class to protect its purchasing power and avoid a drag on economic growth.

Bambang Brodjonegoro, ADBI dean and CEO, said Philippine officials should focus their efforts on the middle class, which made up the bulk of household consumption.
item.content:encoded:
As households across Southeast Asia face rising prices, higher borrowing costs and insecure jobs, analysts say governments should do more to protect a middle class that drives consumer spending but can fall between the cracks of social protection systems designed primarily for poorer households.

The issue has come into sharper focus in the Philippines, where the Asian Development Bank Institute (ADBI) urged the government in September to provide targeted support for the middle class to protect its purchasing power and avoid a drag on economic growth.

Bambang Brodjonegoro, ADBI dean and CEO, said Philippine officials should focus their efforts on the middle class, which made up the bulk of household consumption.

“For the Philippines to revive its economic growth, the attention needs to be on how to increase the purchasing power of the middle class and to not let the middle class shrink,” Brodjonegoro told local media on the sidelines of a forum on September 17.

The Philippines’ inflation rose to a four-month high of 7.2 per cent in September, adding to pressure on household finances.

“The Philippines is one of the most affected countries in the Asean region from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to its high oil import dependence that goes through the Strait and its twin energy and current account deficits,” said Maria Monica Wihardja, an economist and fellow of the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s media, technology, and society programme.

The Philippines reflected a wider regional problem, Wihardja said, as governments faced difficult trade-offs between fiscal constraints and expanding social protection.

“Recent shocks have significantly affected the middle class because they are the income class that spend a lot on fuel, take loans and work in sectors that have been affected by a series of external shocks, but at the same time they are not covered by any safety net programmes unlike the poor and the vulnerable,” she said.

The problem matters beyond household welfare because middle-class consumption is an important source of economic growth.

“When middle-class households have to cut back sharply on consumption, growth can suffer,” Jose Ramon Albert, a senior research fellow at the Philippine Institute for Development Studies, said.

Albert said the Philippines had launched a social assistance programme called Uplift to ease recent price spikes, but it was designed for poor and low-income households.

“We do not have a programme designed for the middle class as such … a middle-class family hit by a shock may obtain help, but must seek assistance and undergo assessment,” he said.

The issue is particularly visible in Indonesia, where the middle class has been shrinking, according to Wihardja.

Analysis by the Carnegie Endowment last October also pointed to protection gaps for the aspiring middle class, including exclusion from cash transfers, scholarships and subsidised health insurance. It found that households between the 50th and 80th percentiles saw real consumption fall between 2019 and 2022, while the bottom 20 per cent, supported by social protection, gained.

The experience highlights a broader question over whether assistance reaches households that are above the poverty line but remain vulnerable to shocks.

According to Albert, Indonesia and the Philippines share a basic vulnerability in that much of their middle class sits in the emerging segment, living on between US$8 and US$16 each day and remaining at risk of falling back into low income, while Vietnam’s middle class has a larger share at the higher end of the threshold.

“But income or consumption levels alone do not establish resilience. Assets, debt, insurance and job security also matter,” he said.

“The contrasts lie in the mix of exposures: how much household income comes from informal work or small enterprises, reliance on remittances, exposure to food and fuel prices, and access to insurance and other protection.”

For governments, the question is therefore not simply whether to create a new welfare category for the middle class, but how to make existing systems more responsive when households are pushed towards vulnerability.

Wihardja said protecting middle-class purchasing power through targeted means would be wise because this group was a key source of consumer demand for goods and services.

But assistance does not necessarily have to come through direct subsidies.

“It can be done by making sure that the quality, accessibility and affordability of public infrastructure and services, from transport to education, are improved so the middle-class households don’t have to opt for more expensive private services,” she said.

Vietnam offers an example of how broad-based measures can also benefit middle-income households.

The government has temporarily kept VAT at 8 per cent on most goods and services instead of 10 per cent, while public school tuition from preschool through high school became free nationwide from September 2025. Personal income tax deductions have also been raised, providing relief to eligible salaried families.

Different countries, however, face varying vulnerabilities.

“There are common global and regional patterns or causes of increasingly insecure middle class but there are also country-specific differences,” Wihardja said.

In Thailand, many middle-class households were burdened by high debt, while the Philippines remained heavily dependent on remittances from abroad, she said.

For regional governments, strengthening resilience means making access to basic services and protection against major risks available to larger groups beyond low-income households.

“When a crisis hits, governments should be able to extend temporary support quickly to those who need it, including middle-class households that are not poor in normal times but are pushed to the edge by a shock,” Albert said.

That meant broad social registries, clear eligibility rules, benefits that could expand when conditions deteriorated, and stronger social insurance for health, unemployment and old age, he said.

But short-term protection is only part of the answer.

Wihardja said governments also needed to focus on quality job creation, industrial upgrading, AI-related supply chains and the green transition, as technological change could affect jobs previously considered secure, including white-collar work in high-value services.

“At the macro level, middle-income countries need to have policies that can support structural transformation towards higher-value, higher-productivity sectors and jobs including skill- and knowledge-intensive industries,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] The ‘G2’ illusion? After Xi-Trump summit, China wants equality while the US seeks deals
item.description:
Washington and Beijing may have signed an agreement built around “reciprocity”. But a more consequential question remains unresolved: does it mean equal status for Beijing? Countries without a seat at the table are watching that ambiguity closely.

The spectacle of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington – the tarmac greeting, the flyovers, the state dinner – has been interpreted less as courtesy than as a statement of rank. Some argue that China is no longer being treated as part of the Global South, but as the US’ peer.

But “reciprocity” does not necessarily mean the same thing to both sides.
item.content:encoded:
Washington and Beijing may have signed an agreement built around “reciprocity”. But a more consequential question remains unresolved: does it mean equal status for Beijing? Countries without a seat at the table are watching that ambiguity closely.

The spectacle of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington – the tarmac greeting, the flyovers, the state dinner – has been interpreted less as courtesy than as a statement of rank. Some argue that China is no longer being treated as part of the Global South, but as the US’ peer.

But “reciprocity” does not necessarily mean the same thing to both sides.

For the United States, reciprocity is transactional: a concession matched by a concession, a deal measured by what each side gets in return.

For China, it means equal standing: the recognition that Beijing should be dealt with not as a subordinate power being managed by Washington, but as a peer.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi made that meaning explicit as the visit ended. In remarks released by state news agency Xinhua on September 26, he said reciprocity meant the two countries were “equal in sovereignty”, that neither side stood above the other, that concerns were handled “on an equal basis” and that cooperation developed “in a balanced manner”.

According to analysts, US President Donald Trump’s embrace of “G2” diplomacy and the extraordinary choreography of his reception for Xi give Beijing an opportunity to turn the language of a transaction into the image of parity.

Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said the reception showed that Washington valued Beijing’s international weight and was willing to “invest political resources into improving ties” – a signal that could “set the stage for future negotiations and inter-agency cooperation”.

But he cautioned against reading the symbolism too far. “Reception protocol alone is not enough to conclude that both sides have accepted a ‘G2’ framework,” Sun said, referring to the idea of a “Group of Two”, or a global duopoly with China and the US as the world’s leading powers.

“If ‘G2’ merely emphasises the importance of US-China coordination to global affairs, that indeed reflects reality,” he said.

“If it implies the two countries jointly dominating the world and making decisions on behalf of other nations, that goes beyond any conclusion this meeting can support.”

“China is more concerned with whether the relationship is equal, whereas the US side is more focused on whether specific trade-offs are worthwhile,” Sun added.

Trump’s warmth towards Xi appears personal rather than institutional. The White House “still stresses that the US should exercise leadership from a position of strength”, he said.

What matters, he said, was “whether the US can respect China’s right to development and core interests in concrete policies, and accept addressing differences through consultation on an equal footing”.

That gap is the “G2” illusion: the two sides can sit across the same table while attaching very different expectations to what the relationship means.

Sourabh Gupta, a senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, was blunt: a US-China “G2” is not emerging.

“Trump aside, much of his administration and the beltway political establishment seek rivalry with China. But China won’t play ball,” he said.

“Just as one cannot clap with one hand, so also the two sides are stuck between uneasy coexistence and the drift towards rivalry.”

The same logic applies to the economy. China wants interdependence; much of the US would rather decouple.

The result, Gupta said, was “a mediocre and deteriorating economic equation that might appear stable at a given moment, but which masks a deeper strategic hollowness”. In that condition, a “G2” was “a far-fetched assumption”, he added.

Xi Jinping does not want a G2 that governs the world together with the United States

Ken Moriyasu, Hudson Institute

Sarang Shidore, director of the Global South Programme at the Quincy Institute, said “a sweeping G2” was unlikely. “[But] limited G2s may emerge down the road that create bargains in certain spaces in which outright competition is too costly or risky for both. AI is such an area,” he added.

The chances of a resolution rise if neither side can prevail easily – which he noted was the present reality – and if both see mutual benefit, a condition he said had yet to be observed.

Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, argued that Beijing did not even want to be part of a duopoly. “Xi Jinping does not want a G2 that governs the world together with the United States,” he said.

According to Moriyasu, Xi wants a “new model of major-country relations” in which the two powers respect each other’s political systems, core interests and spheres of concern while avoiding confrontation.

He said Beijing’s preferred order was more multipolar than a “G2” – closer to the UN Security Council, with five major powers standing above the rest.

As the weaker power, Gupta said, Beijing “harps on sovereign equality in its dealings with Washington, much as New Delhi continually does so in its dealings with Beijing. It is a function of weakness, and strict reciprocity viewed as an equaliser.”

He added that the US had stood “head and shoulders above its peers for the past 75 years” and treated sovereign equality as “a notional concept” while leveraging its advantages for “transactional gain”.

The Global South question

These observations land on a larger question: whether China still belongs in the Global South category it has long claimed.

Shidore drew a distinction between the treatment and the label.

“Most certainly, Washington treats China very differently from any other Global South middle power,” he said. “China is being recognised as a great power, a recognition that China has itself long craved. With President Trump, it has received it without any reservations.”

Moriyasu went further. “I doubt many countries in the Global South now look at China and see a fellow Global Southerner,” he said. “If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck. China is now a full-fledged great power.”

Gupta rejected the binary. China “can be a great power and still remain very much a part of the Global South”, he said, calling it a “bundle of contradictions” that could sit at the global head table and still be “a great power within the confines of the Global South’s rise”.

If Washington deals with Beijing as a peer, however, China begins to look less like the most powerful member of that camp and more like one of the powers sitting above it. That reading has landed hardest in New Delhi.

Indian officials and commentators watched the Chinese leader’s Washington visit with a familiar dread: a US-China “G2”, long feared in private, was being staged in public. Trump was receiving Xi as a peer.

India in the audience

Ivan Lidarev, a visiting research fellow at the National University of Singapore’s Institute of South Asian Studies, said the fanfare had sparked “unease and jealousy” in India.

“New Delhi has long feared the emergence of a US-China G2 through which the two sides will manage the world and South Asia,” he said.

Trump has refrained from using the phrase “G2” in recent days, though he has framed his encounters with Xi in those terms since their summit in South Korea last autumn.

To Brahma Chellaney, a New Delhi-based strategic analyst, Trump’s language was more revealing than the pageantry.

“The writing on the wall is clear: Trump sees America and China as the world’s two pre-eminent powers that should cooperate in managing global affairs, despite their intense rivalry,” he wrote on social media.

“For America’s allies and strategic partners, especially in Asia, that signals a profound shift in Washington’s strategic world view.”

For some Indian observers, the summit pointed to “how far China is ahead of India”, Lidarev said, with the US increasingly treating China as an equal superpower. He said it also threatened the two-decade bedrock of US-India ties – which were “built on counterbalancing China” – just as those ties were strained over trade and oil sanctions.

Jabin Jacob, a professor at Shiv Nadar University, said India would not read much into the pageantry.

“It certainly understands that [the meeting] does not fundamentally alter the trajectory of US-China relations,” he said. “This is competitive more than it is cooperative.”

Lidarev noted that India’s fears about the Xi-Trump meeting included the possibility of joint Sino-American oversight of the Indo-Pacific, a technological duopoly in AI and semiconductors, and US concessions on Taiwan that could embolden Beijing.

“Fortunately for India, none of these concerns were justified,” he said.

But more frequent Trump-Xi meetings still raise the prospect of a real “G2” at India’s expense. Lidarev said he did not expect a major recalibration following the summit, but Delhi would pursue a thaw in ties with Beijing and adopt a “less US-leaning position”.

Jacob said India had to reset its policy towards both powers anyway, because its compromise-heavy stance, driven by economic strain and reliance on Russian oil, was “suboptimal”.

That need would become more urgent if US-China ties evolved into a genuine duopoly.

Shidore said that if such an arrangement emerged, even in just a few sectors or specific regions, other countries would find less room for independent policy.

“Rather than exploit the competition between Beijing and Washington, these states will have to conform to rules jointly defined by the two great powers, rules against which they will have little capacity to resist,” he said.

He added that the pressure would be less about choosing a side than “falling in line with an arrangement they had no voice in shaping”.

“We are not there yet,” he said. “It remains to be seen if we will get there.”

item.title: [SCMP] How closer China-US ties – and more Xi-Trump summits – could work in Iran’s favour
item.description:
China and the US – Iran’s key partner and its chief adversary – found firmer common ground on Tehran at the Washington summit last month, and further head-of-state diplomacy could work in Iran’s favour, according to analysts.

Iran was on the agenda when the presidents of the United States and China met in Beijing in May and again in Washington in September.

There was no direct reference to Tehran in Beijing’s statement after the May summit, but following the September meeting China was more specific, saying it and the US agreed that Iran must uphold its commitment against developing nuclear weapons.
item.content:encoded:
China and the US – Iran’s key partner and its chief adversary – found firmer common ground on Tehran at the Washington summit last month, and further head-of-state diplomacy could work in Iran’s favour, according to analysts.

Iran was on the agenda when the presidents of the United States and China met in Beijing in May and again in Washington in September.

There was no direct reference to Tehran in Beijing’s statement after the May summit, but following the September meeting China was more specific, saying it and the US agreed that Iran must uphold its commitment against developing nuclear weapons.

In an eight-point consensus, the two powers also agreed that no country or organisation should impose tolls on international waterways, according to the Chinese foreign ministry.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua also reported that Xi Jinping said in Washington that China hoped that the US and Iran would resolve their conflict through dialogue, prompting thanks in a social media post from Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Donald Trump and Xi are expected to meet twice more this year, creating opportunities for dialogue despite Iran’s fears that it could be reduced to a bargaining chip in great-power competition, observers say.

Niu Xinchun, director of the China-Arab Research Institute at Ningxia University, said the shift in China’s statements between the two summits showed that Beijing and Washington had “built greater alignment on Iran than before”.

“This demonstrates that exchanges between the two nations are increasing and their consensus is expanding,” he said.

A more stable US-China relationship was “undeniably beneficial” for Iran, because it gave Tehran an additional and “potentially far more effective” channel to communicate with and influence Washington, Niu said.

Iran has relied on regional powers such as Pakistan and Qatar to communicate with the US. Russia had also offered to mediate, but its strained ties with Washington made it a poor fit for an effective diplomatic bridge, Niu said.

“On the flip side, Iran harbours a concern typical of smaller powers – the fear of ultimately being used as a bargaining chip in major-power dealings,” he said, adding this was why Tehran sent its top diplomat to Beijing for talks just days ahead of Xi’s US trip.

During the discussions with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi reaffirmed Beijing’s support for Tehran, called for a political resolution with Washington and warned against regional tensions spilling over into Yemen.

Araghchi also visited Beijing in May shortly before Trump’s state visit to China.

Iran harbours a concern typical of smaller powers – the fear of ultimately being used as a bargaining chip in major-power dealings

Niu Xinchun, Ningxia University

Xi and Trump are expected to meet twice more this year – once at Apec in Shenzhen in November and again at the G20 in Miami in December.

With the Middle East conflict already in its seventh month and no end in sight, it is likely to be a recurring topic between Xi and Trump.

Ali Salehian, a senior researcher at the Tehran-based Governance and Policy Think Tank, said Iran did not need to panic over closer US-China engagement, citing the consistency of Beijing’s policy on the Middle East and Tehran’s resilience to withstand political shifts.

Salehian also saw “more opportunity than threat” for Iran in improved US-China diplomatic ties. “We see opportunities – similar to the mediation role China played between Iran and Saudi Arabia,” he said.

Salehian said Tehran had sought to deepen strategic ties with Beijing, a position not likely to change in the near future.

Beijing could also become an economic “anchor of stability” for the Middle East but it needed to go beyond its “wait-and-see” approach by being proactive in regional affairs and translate ideals such as “multipolarity” and “Global South solidarity” into action.

Jesse Marks, founder of Rihla Research and Advisory, a Washington-based consultancy focused on the Middle East, said Iranian authorities would be sceptical of improved Sino-American ties but there was confidence in Tehran that “Beijing will not abandon them politically”.

He noted that there was a fundamental internal clash between Iran’s diplomatic class and the country’s most powerful military branch, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

“Both sides understand that China is unlikely to help the Trump administration end the war, but the bigger issue is the internal struggle for identifying a clear, united Iranian state position on engagement with the US,” Marks said.

Diplomatic efforts between Iran and the US have stalled since Trump rejected an Iranian proposal – conveyed through Qatar – to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the conflict.

In addition, Washington is reportedly preparing to send a third aircraft carrier to the region and Trump has threatened to resume military action after the midterm elections in November.

In Tehran, Iran’s top diplomat has said the country is “ready for real diplomacy” but would remain steadfast even in an “apocalyptic war”.

According to Marks, Beijing had the “legitimacy and economic weight” crucial for Iran’s post-war reconstruction and global reintegration, a role that other powers, like Russia, could not easily replicate.

However, Marks said, while warmer ties between Xi and Trump could improve coordination on Iran’s nuclear programme, this was highly unlikely to fundamentally change regional realities as China was “not a major player in Middle East security”.

“Iranian rigidity towards a ceasefire negotiation comes at the expense of Chinese energy interests in Hormuz. So, Chinese leaders have to balance how it encourages Iran back to the negotiating table without undermining their position once at the table.”

Jodie Wen, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy who specialises in the Middle East, said China’s cautious approach to the region avoided US-style heavy-handed intervention and was a conscious strategic choice rather than a reflection of limited capability.

She said China and the US remained the decisive players on the Iran issue, as both European and regional actors had limited leverage and capacity.

“The significance of the US-China summit lies in the positive signal it sends – namely, that when Washington and Beijing build a foundation of strategic stability, regional tensions can begin to ease.”

item.title: [SCMP] China has dominated tungsten for decades. Can US cash in Central Asia loosen its grip?
item.description:
The race to loosen China’s grip on tungsten is moving to Kazakhstan, where United States-backed mining projects are attempting to compete in an industry where Chinese investment already has an operating foothold.

Global tungsten prices have surged more than 200 per cent since May 2025, according to commodity and energy information provider Argus Media, adding urgency to efforts to develop alternative supplies. The soaring costs followed Beijing’s export controls on selected tungsten products introduced in February 2025 in a market already facing tight mine supply and increased demand from the defence industry.

The supply squeeze has reached US oilfield equipment makers, which are redesigning one of their most important tools as the global shortage raises the cost of making drill bits.
item.content:encoded:
The race to loosen China’s grip on tungsten is moving to Kazakhstan, where United States-backed mining projects are attempting to compete in an industry where Chinese investment already has an operating foothold.

Global tungsten prices have surged more than 200 per cent since May 2025, according to commodity and energy information provider Argus Media, adding urgency to efforts to develop alternative supplies. The soaring costs followed Beijing’s export controls on selected tungsten products introduced in February 2025 in a market already facing tight mine supply and increased demand from the defence industry.

The supply squeeze has reached US oilfield equipment makers, which are redesigning one of their most important tools as the global shortage raises the cost of making drill bits.

According to Ulterra Drilling Technologies, the cost of manufacturing drill bits had risen by as much as 50 per cent over the past year. The company is responding by shifting production towards steel-bodied models, even as bits containing more tungsten typically last longer when cutting through hard, abrasive rock.

Rival Varel Energy Solutions has made a similar calculation. “Without any stabilisation in tungsten pricing, manufacturers will be forced to transition to steel alternatives,” chief commercial officer Jayme Sperring told Reuters in a report published in May.

China accounted for nearly 80 per cent of mined tungsten globally, producing about 3.7 times the output of the rest of the world combined, according to data from the US Geological Survey. Its dominance extends beyond mining into processing and manufacturing, making it difficult for new producers to compete simply by bringing more of the metal to market.

Prized for its hardness and heat resistance, tungsten is used in industrial tools and some military equipment, including armour-piercing ammunition and missiles, as well as in semiconductors and electronic components supporting AI hardware and data centres.

The US is a major consumer but has recorded no commercial tungsten mine production since 2015. That dependence has made overseas projects increasingly important to Washington’s efforts to secure supplies.

A new front in the race

In April, US mining investment firm Cove Capital acquired a 70 per cent stake in two deposits in Kazakhstan’s Karaganda region: Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty. Their combined estimated development cost is US$1.1 billion, though both remain at the engineering and feasibility study stage, with production targeted for around 2028.

Financing cannot automatically replicate the industrial system China has built over decades

Liu Wenjing, Elistra Advisory

That timetable contrasts with Chinese-backed investments in the country. Hong Kong-listed Jiaxin International Resources already operates the Boguty Mine in Kazakhstan’s Almaty region after the facility began trial production in November 2024 and entered commercial operations in April 2025.

Another proposed tungsten investment, involving Kunxin International Investment and Kazakhstan’s SP Saryarka Tungsten, was among more than 60 agreements signed at Hong Kong’s Belt and Road Summit in September, though few details were disclosed.

This difference in development timelines had given China an immediate advantage in the supply chain, according to Liang Yan, Kremer Chair Professor of Economics at Willamette University. Boguty was already producing, she added, while the US-backed projects still needed to complete studies, secure financing and build their facilities.

Liang argued Kazakhstan could become a “vital producer of tungsten”, citing the Central Asian nation’s more than 2 million tonnes of forecast resources and saying it could eventually supply about 15 per cent of annual global mine output.

“I don’t think US financing can neutralise China’s lead in processing capacity and commercial scale,” said Liang, who is also a non-resident senior fellow at Boston University’s Global Development Policy Centre.

The challenge goes beyond bringing new mines into production. Kazakhstan, Liang suggested, would also need to develop more local refining capacity if it wanted to build a supply chain less dependent on China. Without such capacity, new mines might still have to send concentrate to Chinese processors if alternative facilities faced delays or cost overruns, Liang said.

Liu Wenjing, a member of the Astana International Financial Centre’s Executive Council for the Mining Sector and founder and principal adviser of Elistra Advisory, acknowledged that US financing could significantly lower the barriers to building an alternative tungsten supply chain.

But, she cautioned, “financing cannot automatically replicate the industrial system China has built over decades”.

China’s advantage spanned much of the tungsten supply chain, Liu said. That includes processing mined ore into concentrate and producing ammonium paratungstate (APT), an important intermediate material used to make tungsten products, and making finished products such as cemented carbides.

Geography also matters. Kazakhstan borders China while shipments bound for Europe and North America face longer routes, including across the Caspian Sea. “The US has effectively recognised that investing in overseas mines alone will not solve the problem,” said Liu, who previously served as board secretary of Jiaxin.

That strategy is reflected in Washington’s investments in processing capacity at home, including plans to convert tungsten into APT. In mid-September, Washington announced a US$450 million investment in Elmet Group through redeemable preferred shares.

“This shows that US strategy is moving beyond securing ore towards filling the gap in midstream processing,” Liu said.

The same logic applies to transport, as Northern Katpar is being designed to reach international markets through the Trans-Caspian route. The plans, according to Liu, suggested Western-backed projects were addressing how the metal would reach buyers, not just where it would be mined.

The cost of dependence

This push to develop alternative supply routes has only intensified since China introduced export-licensing requirements in February 2025, the same day new US tariffs on Chinese goods took effect.

While Beijing said the controls were intended to safeguard national security and fulfil its non-proliferation obligations, they were widely interpreted as part of the broader trade and technology rivalry between the two superpowers.

At the same time, China has authorised only 15 companies to export tungsten under its state-trading system for 2026 and 2027. Products covered by the 2025 controls remain subject to separate export licences and end-user checks.

Chinese customs data showed that exports of tungsten products by weight fell 25 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026. Exports of sodium tungstate plunged 94.9 per cent, while shipments of ammonium paratungstate, an important intermediate material, dropped 89.3 per cent.

Exports of tungsten-related products from China to the US also fell 21 per cent by volume year on year over the same period. Shipments of unwrought tungsten and tungsten carbide stopped altogether, while exports of tungsten bars fell 42 per cent.

Kazakhstan could move from being a small producer today to a strategically important source of additional tungsten supply outside China

Liu Wenjing, Elistra Advisory

The restrictions, along with tight mine supply and rising demand, have added upwards pressure on prices.

Fastmarkets, a global price-reporting agency specialising in metals and mining, assessed global tungsten concentrate prices at US$2,500–2,800 per metric tonne unit from May 29, up from US$750–850 at the start of 2026 – an increase of about 230 per cent.

The price pressure is reaching manufacturers. MSC Industrial Supply, a major US distributor with nearly US$4 billion in annual sales, told an investor conference in New York last month that tungsten-related input costs had surged by about 500 per cent.

“They have stabilised, but the ripples through the supply chain aren’t over yet,” chief executive Martina McIsaac said during the event, adding that suppliers were continuing to raise prices at different rates depending on their inventories and access.

Higher costs are also prompting Washington to look beyond new mines for additional supply, including recycling. On August 27, it imposed a one-year ban on exports of tungsten scrap to retain material for US processors. According to materials research platform Material Insights, recycled tungsten provided about 25 to 30 per cent of global supply and was particularly important to the US because it lacks domestic mine production.

The scramble goes global

For Kazakhstan, the main question may be how quickly proposed mining and processing projects can be brought into operation. The country still accounts for less than 3 per cent of global tungsten mine output, though Liu said new projects could significantly increase its share.

“If Jiaxin International’s Boguty mine continues to expand, and Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty come into production as planned, Kazakhstan could move from being a small producer today to a strategically important source of additional tungsten supply outside China,” she said.

EarthRarest, a strategic metals research and investment platform, made a similar assessment in a report shared with the South China Morning Post. It estimated that Kazakhstan’s 2.8 per cent share of global mine production represented about one-eighth of production outside China.

“An additional reliable source can matter to buyers diversifying their purchases well before it changes China’s overall lead,” EarthRarest said, adding that the US could help finance mines, processing facilities and transport links, particularly alongside purchase commitments. But it cautioned that it remained unclear whether the projects could produce at competitive costs and deliver reliably.

“The reviewed evidence does not establish that finance alone removes a cost or scale disadvantage,” EarthRarest said.

Kazakh tungsten could potentially reach Western buyers without passing through China if the required mining, processing, transport and customer arrangements all proved workable, according to the report. For the proposed large Kazakh projects, however, “a fully independent route remains a project objective rather than an established operating fact”.

Yet Kazakhstan is not merely choosing between Chinese and American investors. Astana is also seeking to move beyond its traditional role as an exporter of raw materials and develop more of the tungsten supply chain at home.

The Kazakh government’s 2023–2027 geological development strategy called for expanded exploration, digitised geological records, improved mining infrastructure and greater investment in research and skills.

A separate government plan covering rare and rare earth metals through 2028 called for modernising existing facilities, introducing more advanced processing technologies and attracting investment from a wider range of international partners.

Kazakhstan is only part of a broader effort by governments to secure tungsten supplies and capture more value from their mineral resources.

In late August, Britain’s National Wealth Fund announced an investment of up to £71 million in Tungsten West to support the proposed restart of the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon. The project is targeting full-scale production in the first quarter of 2027.

Resource-producing countries are also tightening their grip on the metal. Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade has proposed removing tungsten from the list of minerals permitted for export. It has not specified how long the proposed restriction would last and has stressed that it would not amount to a permanent ban.

Zimbabwe went further in September, suspending exports of antimony and tungsten in all forms, including ores and concentrates, until further notice. The government said the measure was intended to encourage mining companies to refine and process more of their minerals domestically, allowing the African nation to retain more value before export.

item.title: [SCMP] The myth of brotherhood: Hong Kong’s triads evolve amid new criminal landscape
item.description:
Not long after he entered secondary school, Hong Kong youth Jason* was bullied by an older student with triad links. He was relieved when another senior stepped in to protect him. He helped Jason take revenge on the bully, then recruited him into a syndicate.

Without undergoing any initiation ritual, Jason paid his protector a red packet to become an informal triad member. Later on, he discovered that the two seniors belonged to the same gang but took orders from different bosses.

At first, Jason was just a street-corner kid, pushing people around at a housing estate. But as he drew closer to the triad’s core group, Jason began to realise that brotherhood was a myth and that business was the order of the day. In the underworld, everything was built on money.
item.content:encoded:
Not long after he entered secondary school, Hong Kong youth Jason* was bullied by an older student with triad links. He was relieved when another senior stepped in to protect him. He helped Jason take revenge on the bully, then recruited him into a syndicate.

Without undergoing any initiation ritual, Jason paid his protector a red packet to become an informal triad member. Later on, he discovered that the two seniors belonged to the same gang but took orders from different bosses.

At first, Jason was just a street-corner kid, pushing people around at a housing estate. But as he drew closer to the triad’s core group, Jason began to realise that brotherhood was a myth and that business was the order of the day. In the underworld, everything was built on money.

‘Once I got closer to the boss, I started realising how it worked. He was using the triad to make money. I felt I could actually make a living off this, so I joined the inner circle to give it a shot,’ he said.

Soon Jason was taking job orders from his boss, which were sometimes conveyed through messaging apps. His tasks ranged from property damage to procuring bank accounts for laundering fraudulent funds. Through these assignments, his illusions about brotherhood evaporated.

He saw peers chicken out during vandalism runs and scramble for excuses when the boss ordered them to engage in street fights.

To protect himself, Jason avoided direct involvement in high-risk operations by outsourcing most of his tasks to his peers, taking a cut of several hundred to several thousand dollars each time they completed a job.

“I stayed away as much as I could to avoid getting arrested,” the 26-year-old said.

Shifting focus in illicit activities

The triad Jason joined 14 years ago was Shui Fong, one of four major syndicates still operating in Hong Kong. The others are Wo Shing Wo, Sun Yee On and 14K.

According to experts in the field – including police, a retired anti-triad investigator and a youth organisation – the four triad groups have evolved over the past decade, with rituals simplified and street violence transforming into white-collar crime and cybercrime. Triad groups also often see one another less as rivals than as partners in making money.

“The violent clashes and bloody scenes are gone. Instead, there are less conspicuous crimes, involving underground banking networks, cross-border money laundering and cybercrime. They do not require a physical presence and are much more low-profile,” said Superintendent Joe Au Yeung Tak of police’s organised crime and triad bureau.

According to police, triad-related crimes rose to 2,554 cases in 2022, up 35 per cent from the previous year. Au Yeung said the spike was driven primarily by a sixfold jump in fraud, with 591 such cases accounting for nearly a quarter of all triad crime that year.

Before the surge, the city’s triad-related crimes between 2016 and 2021 hovered at around 1,700 to 1,900 cases annually.
