The number of triad-related cases dipped to 1,353 in 2019 amid a wave of social unrest in the city, with police diverting resources to manage widespread violent protests, according to Au Yeung.

As triads shifted into the digital sphere, law enforcement was adapting to keep pace. “As they transformed, we evolved,” he said.

Historically, police relied on high-profile sweeps and mass arrests to deter gangs. Now their strategy has shifted towards intelligence-led operations targeting deception and financial investigations to cut off the triads’ sources of income.

“Our focus has shifted to tracing the illicit funds, specifically the channels they use to launder the money, and figuring out how we can freeze those assets and confiscate them. Hitting them where it hurts financially is the only way to make them truly feel the pain,” Au Yeung said.

Police also cooperated with other jurisdictions and organisations such as banks and telecommunications service providers to combat triad-related deception.

This multipronged approach has yielded positive results. The number of triad-related deception cases decreased steadily to 323, 162 and 129 in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. The total number of triad-related crimes was below 2,000 last year.

Besides deception, triads also engaged in money laundering, which often involved the use of cryptocurrency, Au Yeung said. In such cases, his team relied on the expertise of colleagues from the cybersecurity and technology crime bureau.

While low-level triad members still relied on traditional crimes such as vice, gambling, drugs, extortion, illicit cigarettes and illicit fuel for survival, other businesses – selling pirated video discs, controlling red minibus routes and managing nightclubs, for instance – had grown obsolete as society evolved.

Au Yeung said different triads and factions had started cooperating in recent years, creating a “win-win situation” for themselves.

“If the pie is big enough and transnational, it’s really not surprising at all for several triad factions to team up and work on it together,” he said.

In the past, each of the 18 districts in Hong Kong was dominated by a single triad faction, a situation Au Yeung described as “strictly demarcated territoriality”.

However, over the past decade or so, territorial boundaries have become increasingly blurred.

“When everyone shares a common interest, focusing on making money rather than fighting, even different factions can collaborate. Nowadays, having multiple factions coexisting peacefully within the same region is actually not uncommon,” he said.

Tougher laws lay bare the myth of brotherhood

Gregory Lau Tat-keung, a former superintendent who retired from the police force in 2013, is another close observer of the gangs and has written a book about them. He has testified more than 40 times against gangsters in court as a triad expert.

“A lot of people have been misled into thinking that the triads are all about loyalty and brotherhood,” he said.

Despite hailing from a supposedly long tradition of ritualistic oaths, Lau recalled that many of the gangsters he had arrested had lined up to be prosecution witnesses.

“Let me be a tainted witness. I’m ratting out my boss. Otherwise, how can I get my sentence reduced?” he said, describing the detainees’ thinking.

“We shouldn’t believe in loyalty. Actual substantial interests are what matter most, including [having] fewer sentences and getting more money for informants.”

The Prisons Ordinance was amended last year to tighten restrictions on inmate visits, including prohibiting them from receiving outside food. The changes were made after the enactment of the national security law in 2020.

Lau said he believed the amendment was effective in deterring minor offenders from taking the fall for syndicate bosses because they were subject to stricter prison rules while on remand.

“Before, it was relatively easy to convince them to break the law for the mastermind, because they mistakenly believed that as long as they could receive outside food [while on remand], their boss still controlled everything,” he said.

“It wasn’t until they were convicted in court that they realised they were in trouble. They suddenly realised they were subject to strict prison regulations, no outside food, no special perks and fewer visitation rights.”

The stricter rules also made it more difficult for visitors to bring inmates cigarettes, which served as a kind of “underground currency” in prisons, Lau said.

History of political resistance

According to Lau, the triads could be traced back to around 1644 with the formation of the Hung League, a Han underground organisation dedicated to overthrowing the Manchu-led Qing dynasty. Sun Yat-sen, leader of China’s 1911 revolution, was a member of the league.

Over time, some exploited the name of the Hung League, with several developing into secret society factions, known as “huidang”, that turned to illegal activities after the fall of the Qing.

Lau said the history of local triad societies could also be traced back to Cheung Po-tsai, a notorious pirate who was granted an amnesty after giving himself up to authorities in 1810. Some of his followers who refused to do the same turned to banditry, establishing what was considered the earliest prototype of triad societies in the city.

The four main triad groups still active in Hong Kong have different origins.

The 14K triad has historical roots tied to the Kuomintang. According to Lau, its original headquarters was located at 14 Baohua Road in Guangzhou, with the “K” in its name allegedly standing for Kuomintang.

Similarly, Sun Yee On was founded by Kuomintang general Heung Chin. Originating from Chaozhou, “Yee On” was the historical name of the region. The organisation was originally registered with the Hong Kong government as the Yee On Commercial and Industrial Guild. After this registration was revoked, the members formed a new group, prefixing the name with “Sun”, meaning new in Chinese.

Many triad groups in Hong Kong traditionally carried the suffix “Wo”, meaning harmony, including Wo Shing Wo. According to Lau, the naming originated from Chung Wo Tong, a secret society formed by Yau Lit, a close ally of Sun Yat-sen, to support the revolution.

Another prominent group with the Wo suffix was Wo On Lok, commonly known as Shui Fong. It was originally established by workers of the Connaught Aerated Water Co Ltd, with “On Lok” being a Chinese transliteration of the company’s name and “Shui Fong”, meaning “water factory”, used as a shorthand for the aerated water plant.

Traditional rituals succumb to modernity

Lau’s book, From Hung League and Huidang to Modern Triads, published earlier this year, offers a rare glimpse into the triads’ traditional initiation ceremonies.

The rituals – gruelling affairs that could last for hours – centred around a sacred altar draped with command banners and ancestral tablets honouring fallen members.

New recruits were required to recite secret verses before lighting joss sticks and being covered with a sandpaper quilt. They shredded paper lotuses and chopped a chicken’s head to seal a blood oath.

They had to pledge allegiance by reciting 36 oaths and swear to abide by 21 regulations, 10 prohibitions and 10 punishments. Finally, new recruits would present their “protectors” with a red packet containing HK$3.60, a symbolic figure invoking the phrase “three times three never ends, six times six is infinite”.

According to Lau, the knowledge of traditional initiation rites has waned over time, with triads either forgoing rituals to avoid arrest or struggling to maintain them in the face of modern limitations.

“Take chopping off a chicken’s head [as an example]. Where do you even get a chicken’s head nowadays? Ever since the avian flu outbreaks, there are no chicken heads any more. So it turned into chopping an egg,” Lau said.

“And taking a blood oath? What about cross-contamination? We might as well just drink red wine.”

He added that he had seen triad members using a red plastic hosepipe or a red mop handle to symbolise the rank of “red pole” – a senior member responsible for organising fights and enforcing gang rules.

To avoid attention from law enforcement, some triads held ceremonies in the mountains, on barges or in mainland China.

More commonly, initiations were reduced to a mere verbal agreement, a practice known as “hanging the blue lantern”, Lau said.

More like rogue ‘employment agencies’

Michael Leung Siu-kei, a supervisor at the Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups’ youth crime prevention centre, said triads in the past would recruit youths loitering in public spaces such as football fields, but that practice had faded into history.

Triads nowadays were more like “employment agencies”, with syndicates using Telegram, Signal or even in-game chat rooms to advertise various “well-paying part-time jobs” to lure teenagers to work for them, he said.

“They list how much [they pay] for splashing red paint, how much for distributing illicit cigarettes, how much for criminal damage.”

He added that syndicates paid around HK$500 (US$64) for young people to distribute illicit cigarette leaflets at an entire housing estate overnight and HK$6,000 for a group to commit criminal damage against an office. They offered HK$1,000 to anyone willing to lend a physical bank card and HK$2,000 for an online bank account to launder money.

Once a person accepted a job, it effectively meant they had pledged loyalty to a specific triad boss, although these allegiances were often loose, Leung said.

“In fact, when we ask some youths about their gang ties, they’ll say: ‘I’ve never even met my boss.’ Sometimes they claim to belong to one triad faction, but after a while, we find them working on another job under a different faction.”

Leung said he had to constantly warn youths of the risks and serious consequences of accepting these jobs.

Au Yeung agreed that triads’ tactics for recruiting young people were no longer as blatant as in the past, as police deployed undercover officers to catch recruiters.

“The triads use a much softer entry point these days. ‘Want to make some quick cash?’ ‘Come out and meet some new friends.’ ‘There’s free beer’,” he said.

Police also worked closely with schools to prevent triads from infiltrating campuses and conducted cyber patrols to combat online recruitment, Au Yeung added.

For Jason, earning quick money came at a cost as he became wracked with anxiety about being followed and developed a drug habit.

“You get paranoid. You worry people or enemies might have followed you home and know where you live. Whenever I slept, even the slightest noise woke me up,” he said.

Jason was once arrested by an undercover police officer after divulging that he was a triad member, but was acquitted by the court due to lack of evidence.

At the age of 15, he began taking Ice and got involved in drug trafficking. But as his addiction grew more severe over a year, he started consuming his own supply and ended up owing the triad HK$40,000 for the drugs.

Raised primarily by his grandparents, Jason was surprised when his estranged father stepped in to help clear his debt.

“It felt like he had not given up on me,” he said.

Around that time, the death of his beloved grandfather proved a final wake-up call for Jason, prompting him to quit drugs, cut ties with the triad and return to school.

He now runs his own small delivery team.

Looking back, he said he regretted joining the triad and could see more clearly how the organisation had exploited him.

“At the end of the day, the triads are driven purely by self-interest,” he said. “Your family is always your strongest backing. No matter what happens, they will always support you.”

*Name changed at the interviewee’s request.

item.title: [SCMP] US seeks US$100 million bail each for Chinese-born couple in surrogacy child abuse case
item.description:
Los Angeles County prosecutors are seeking bail of US$100 million each for a Chinese-born couple charged on Tuesday with conspiring to abuse young children who were born through surrogacy and raised in their California mansion.

Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, allegedly directed nannies to physically punish the children, watched the beatings through an extensive surveillance system and coached children before police arrived to deny the abuse, according to a felony complaint.

At least 14 surrogate-born children, some as young as two months old, were abused, the district attorney’s office said. It said the couple were accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in the home to repeated physical abuse.
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles County prosecutors are seeking bail of US$100 million each for a Chinese-born couple charged on Tuesday with conspiring to abuse young children who were born through surrogacy and raised in their California mansion.

Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, allegedly directed nannies to physically punish the children, watched the beatings through an extensive surveillance system and coached children before police arrived to deny the abuse, according to a felony complaint.

At least 14 surrogate-born children, some as young as two months old, were abused, the district attorney’s office said. It said the couple were accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in the home to repeated physical abuse.

“The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement.

Prosecutors cited the risk that the defendants would flee and the nature and extent of the alleged crimes in recommending the bail amounts.

Both defendants are charged with felony conspiracy to commit child abuse, between April 2021 and May 2025, and with being accessories after the fact for allegedly helping a nanny avoid arrest. Xuan also faces a separate felony child abuse charge and five counts of dissuading a witness. Zhang faces four counts of dissuading a witness.

If convicted as charged, Xuan faces up to 17 years and four months in prison and Zhang up to 11 years and eight months, according to the district attorney’s office.

The South China Morning Post has sought comment from Mitchell Krems, who has represented Xuan in related child custody proceedings. It was not clear whether either defendant had a lawyer in the criminal case.

The alleged abuse came to light after police responded to a report that a two-month-old boy had suffered a head injury, the district attorney’s office said. Prosecutors allege that a nanny, Chunmei Li, struck the infant on May 4, 2025, and that Xuan and Zhang did not obtain medical treatment until two days later. Zhang allegedly told hospital staff the baby had fallen from a bed.

When detectives came to the home on May 7, Zhang and Li gave the same false account and the couple directed officers to the wrong bedroom, the complaint alleges.

Li has been charged separately with felony child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death and faces up to 12 years in prison.

According to the complaint, about 32 motion-activated cameras recorded video and audio throughout the home, with live feeds displayed on a large television beside the couple’s desks in their shared office. Prosecutors allege the system recorded nannies repeatedly striking children on each of 11 consecutive days, from April 27 to May 7, 2025.

On April 30, Xuan allegedly told a nanny who was striking a child to hit harder, then joined in, delivering open-handed blows to the child’s head and lifting him by one arm while continuing to strike him.

On May 4, Zhang and Li allegedly laughed as they watched footage of a nanny striking a child with a shoe. The next day, the couple allegedly met the nannies and discussed the importance of disciplining children without leaving visible marks.

Before police arrived on May 7, Xuan and nannies allegedly undressed several children to check them for marks, and Zhang told a nanny to put away the sticks used to strike the children. The couple also allegedly told children to deny they had been beaten.

The nannies shown in the footage are described in the complaint as uncharged co-conspirators.

The complaint also alleges that the couple ran a surrogacy agency, Mark Surrogacy Investment LLC, from the home and gave false information to women recruited across the United States to carry more children for them.

One surrogate was allegedly told Zhang was a single mother struggling to conceive and learned only during a second pregnancy for the couple that they already had about 16 children.

Zhang kept a spreadsheet that, as of May 7, 2025, listed 21 children by name and date of birth, prosecutors allege.

Xuan has told investigators that he fathered 22 children, all but two of whom were born to surrogates, according to the Los Angeles Times.

The Wall Street Journal, in an investigation published in August 2025, identified both defendants as Chinese-born. It reported that Xuan came to the United States from Xinjiang and that the couple ran a Los Angeles-area property business with partners based in China.

Zhang told the Journal that her experience of China’s one-child policy had motivated her to have a large family. She denied selling children and said the couple could provide for them. Xuan told a Chinese-language outlet that they were both US citizens, according to the Journal.

The Arcadia household had already been featured in the US debate over birthright citizenship before charges were filed.

At a congressional hearing in March titled “Protecting American Citizenship: Birthright Citizenship for Illegal Aliens and Tourists”, Peter Schweizer, president of the Government Accountability Institute, cited surrogacy arrangements with Chinese ties as part of what he described as the exploitation of birthright citizenship.

“Even more insidious is the use of surrogacy in the United States to produce children for senior CCP officials and elites,” he wrote in his testimony. He cited the Arcadia case as a “prominent example”.

“These cases highlight a largely unregulated surrogacy industry in states like California, where over 100 companies with ‘surrogacy’ in their names are owned by Chinese individuals,” he wrote.

The criminal complaint against Xuan and Zhang does not allege any link to the Chinese government.

Amanda Frost, a law professor at the University of Virginia who also testified at the hearing, challenged that argument in an interview with the SCMP in March, arguing that separate issues had been conflated.

“Nothing about President Trump’s executive order would address that,” Frost said. “If there’s a problem with abuse of surrogacy relationships, that’s a surrogacy regulation question, which is a state law matter.”

The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump vs Barbara on June 30, striking down the Trump administration’s executive order restricting automatic citizenship for children born to parents in the country unlawfully or temporarily.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Myanmar bet? Repatriations pave way for diplomacy
item.description:
Malaysia’s repatriation of Myanmar nationals ahead of a visit to Kuala Lumpur by the war-torn country’s leader appears to mirror efforts by other Asean countries seeking to mend ties with Naypyidaw.

Several members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations have stepped up engagement with Myanmar at the bilateral level recently, raising questions about whether a gradual normalisation between the bloc and the country could undermine efforts to end its civil war, according to analysts.

Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals repatriated from Malaysia arrived in southern Yangon on Sunday, regional government minister Nay Lin Tun said.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s repatriation of Myanmar nationals ahead of a visit to Kuala Lumpur by the war-torn country’s leader appears to mirror efforts by other Asean countries seeking to mend ties with Naypyidaw.

Several members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations have stepped up engagement with Myanmar at the bilateral level recently, raising questions about whether a gradual normalisation between the bloc and the country could undermine efforts to end its civil war, according to analysts.

Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals repatriated from Malaysia arrived in southern Yangon on Sunday, regional government minister Nay Lin Tun said.

Under the repatriation scheme – which has drawn criticism from human rights groups and the United Nations refugee agency – 1,479 returnees were transported from Malaysia aboard two navy warships and a hospital ship.

They are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals slated for phased repatriation from Malaysia, where more than 10,300 others remain in immigration detention centres, according to the country’s home ministry.

The repatriation coincided with preparations in Kuala Lumpur to host Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing, who arrived in Malaysia on Wednesday for a two-day trip.

Min Aung Hlaing, the former leader of Myanmar’s military junta who was elected president in April after a controversial election several months earlier dominated by an army-backed party, would be among several foreign leaders visiting Kuala Lumpur in October, state news agency Bernama quoted Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil as saying last week.

Myanmar has been embroiled in a civil war since a 2021 coup led by Min Aung Hlaing ousted the National League for Democracy government.

Rejecting accusations that Malaysia was returning the Myanmar nationals without regard for their safety, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said last month that continued engagement was necessary to resolve long-standing ⁠issues, adding that his government would hold more talks with Myanmar to facilitate additional returns.

Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor of international relations and human rights at the University of Malaya, said Malaysia’s repatriation efforts had raised concerns.

“I would be careful about calling this definitively a quid pro quo unless we know what was actually agreed between the two sides,” Khoo said. “Still, given the timing of the repatriation and Min’s upcoming visit, it is difficult not to see a connection.”

She added that the move could set a worrying precedent if the migrant issue were to become part of wider talks with Myanmar.

The UN High Commissioner for Refugees was denied access to the Myanmar nationals, preventing any assessment of whether their return was voluntary, according to media reports.

“Malaysia can pursue its national interests, but those interests should not come at the expense of basic protection safeguards,” Khoo said, noting that Thailand had repeatedly deported Myanmar nationals.

“The danger is that, as governments focus on getting people out of their own countries, much less attention is paid to whether it is actually safe for them to go back,” she added.

According to rights group Fortify Rights, Thailand worked with Myanmar to forcibly return over 3,500 Myanmar nationals via the Ranong-Kawthaung border crossing between February 2024 and late 2025, a practice that continues today.

Khoo noted that Malaysia’s former foreign minister Saifuddin Abdullah was particularly critical of the junta and pushed for the 11-member Asean to engage a wider range of actors in Myanmar’s conflict.

“But that approach also had its limits,” Khoo said, citing poor progress on Asean’s Five-Point Consensus, with Malaysia and other members of the bloc failing to translate strong language into tangible changes in Myanmar, referring to the bloc’s peace plan adopted in 2021 to tackle the crisis in Myanmar.

The Anwar administration is more inclined to resolve concerns with Myanmar at the bilateral level, such as repatriation and practical security cooperation, according to Khoo.

In recent months, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam have hosted Min Aung Hlaing, while Asean foreign ministers had initiated what officials described as a “calibrated re-engagement” with his government in July.

While maintaining open lines of communication was crucial, allowing bilateral interests to drive normalisation without progress on ending the civil war, dialogue and humanitarian access was not an ideal way to deal with the Myanmar crisis, she said.

“Taken together, they [these meetings] begin to look like a gradual normalisation of his [Min Aung Hlaing’s] government without a corresponding improvement on the ground. That weakens Asean’s collective leverage,” Khoo said.

On Monday, Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR) urged Malaysia not to confer legitimacy on Myanmar’s leadership by signing agreements or issuing joint statements.

“[Malaysia should] extend no further invitations to Min Aung Hlaing,” the advocacy group said, calling on Kuala Lumpur to suspend repatriations until the safety of the returnees could be guaranteed.

“Malaysia should not be receiving Min Aung Hlaing at all. Every red carpet rolled out for him tells the people of Myanmar, who live under air strikes and forced conscription, that the region has made its peace with what is being done to them,” said APHR chair Mercy Chriesty Barends.

Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia, said Asean and the global community had failed to take firm action to improve the Myanmar situation. He pointed out that Malaysia also sent back large numbers of Vietnamese boatpeople in the 1970s and 1980s.

“As with previous spans of military rule in Myanmar, the regime will gradually come to be accepted, or at least tolerated, by most if not all,” Oh said. “That’s just the cold, harsh fact of realpolitik.”

Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute, said Bangladesh, which shelters over 1.2 million Rohingya from Myanmar, had taken a different approach by not returning displaced Myanmar nationals to their country.

“This is more of a one-of-a-kind situation in which Anwar is seeking to bolster his domestic political credentials in response to recent setbacks at the ballot box,” Marston said.

Following the ruling Pakatan Harapan coalition’s losses in elections in Negeri Sembilan and other states, Anwar has rolled out populist policies and promised to carry out various reforms.

While Malaysia continued to focus on the Five-Point Consensus in line with Asean’s stance, Marston said the bloc and Kuala Lumpur differed in terms of their actions in dealing with Myanmar.

“[This] leaves room for ambiguity and uncertainty regarding the direction of their policies,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] US accuses mainland China of targeting Taiwan leader’s family in surveillance case
item.description:
The United States has accused mainland China of hiring an American citizen of Chinese origin to surveil the family of Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te, days after President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation on Sunday arrested 34-year-old Zhang Wanying at Los Angeles International Airport, alleging that she attempted to flee the country and charged her with acting as an unregistered agent for the Chinese government.

The FBI accused her of surveilling the Taiwanese leader’s son and his family in Seattle last year, filming their home and vehicles and sharing the footage with handlers in China.
item.content:encoded:
The United States has accused mainland China of hiring an American citizen of Chinese origin to surveil the family of Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te, days after President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation on Sunday arrested 34-year-old Zhang Wanying at Los Angeles International Airport, alleging that she attempted to flee the country and charged her with acting as an unregistered agent for the Chinese government.

The FBI accused her of surveilling the Taiwanese leader’s son and his family in Seattle last year, filming their home and vehicles and sharing the footage with handlers in China.

“The Chinese government allegedly sent an operative to surveil the family of Taiwan’s President ON AMERICAN SOIL – photos, video, license plates – then she tried to hop a flight back to Shanghai. Wrong move,” FBI Director Kash Patel wrote on social media.

Zhang appeared in the US District Court in Los Angeles on Monday for an initial hearing, with a second hearing scheduled for Wednesday to determine whether she will be released on bail or remain in custody. She has not been formally indicted yet.

On Tuesday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said that he was “not familiar” with the situation, but “opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative”.

In an affidavit filed with the US District Court in Orange County, the FBI did not identify the surveillance target, referring to him only as “a close relative of a Taiwanese government official”. The FBI later identified him on social media as Taiwanese leader Lai’s son, whose name is Ting-Yu Lai.

It alleged that Zhang, a resident of Irvine, California, travelled to Seattle in September last year with another person to conduct surveillance.

“She coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection. She never notified the attorney general she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offence,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, said on social media.

Lai’s office condemned what it called “barbaric acts” and said that “such behaviour should not be tolerated in the civilised world”.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

According to court documents, Zhang is facing charges under 18 USC section 951, a federal criminal law that forbids acting inside the United States as an undisclosed agent of a foreign government without giving prior notification to the US attorney general. A violation is a felony and usually carries a maximum penalty of up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both.

A RedNote account believed to belong to Zhang and identified by the South China Morning Post appears to place her in Seattle in early September 2025, matching the timeline in the federal complaint.

The account, named “美美哒 Heather” – the complaint gives “Heather” as Zhang’s alias – posted on September 2, 2025, with a US location tag. The Chinese-language post reads: “Seattle airport must be the least efficient international airport in the US? Security line took an hour.” The complaint does not cite the post.

According to the federal criminal complaint and affidavit, Zhang stayed in touch for years with a former classmate in Beijing whom the FBI calls “PRC Official 1”.

The US authorities believe that when Zhang met Official 1 in China in January 2025, Official 1 directed her to obtain information about an Irvine address previously associated with a Taiwanese elected official.

“Based on my training and experience and conversations with others involved in the case, it is likely that PRC Official 1 tasked ZHANG, while ZHANG was visiting China, to obtain information about this address,” FBI agent Kevin Holt wrote in the affidavit. “I know that China’s Intelligence Services often tasks individuals visiting China while they are in China in order to evade US government scrutiny.”

In June 2025, Official 1 introduced Zhang to another purported Chinese government official, whom the FBI calls “PRC Official 2.” Official 2 later met Zhang in China, according to the complaint.

In a July 7 WeChat exchange, Official 2 referred to “our thing last time” and said he had intended to provide Zhang with “some assurance”.

On September 1, 2025, while outside the Seattle home, Zhang messaged Official 2, “Saw him. Young male,” and said she was video-recording, according to the document. She sent two licence plate numbers and a video of the house. A week later, she asked her travel companion to AirDrop her the Seattle pictures rather than send them over WeChat or text.

On September 11, Official 2 asked Zhang for pictures of the house. Zhang told him that her friend had deleted the pictures.

No message in the complaint explicitly tells Zhang to surveil the house. The FBI affiant interprets Official 2’s references to “our thing” and “assurance” as referring back to their June 2025 discussion of a “US house”.

Dennis Wilder, a former senior US intelligence official and a China expert, expects that the arrest will have limited influence on the ongoing US-China talks, as the two leaders are scheduled to meet twice more this year.

“This will have minimal impact on Sino-US relations,” he posted on X. “Spy games are an accepted superpower competition and have been forever.”

Who is Zhang Wanying?

According to a LinkedIn profile under her name, Zhang has been CEO of Alphabet Investment Management since 2017. She has also worked on the Douglas Elliman sales team for Metropolis, a luxury residential development by Greenland, a Chinese company and a Fortune Global 500 firm.

A representative from Douglas Elliman confirmed her employment but said she had left the company nearly a decade ago.

“I am the only native Chinese speaking in the team,” Zhang wrote on LinkedIn, where she described herself as “detail oriented, action oriented” with “excellent negotiation and relationship management” skills.

She earned a bachelor’s degree in public administration from the University of International Relations in Beijing in 2014 and a master’s degree in public administration from the University of Southern California in 2016, with a concentration in real estate.

item.title: [SCMP] Zheng Yongnian on China-US realism and battling for the upper hand before the next summit
item.description:
Zheng Yongnian is a political scientist in China and a government adviser. His academic work is mainly about contemporary China, particularly politics, the country’s transformation and its external relations.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

Many have offered a lukewarm assessment of the Xi-Trump summit in Washington, citing the lack of a breakthrough. What is your take?
item.content:encoded:
Zheng Yongnian is a political scientist in China and a government adviser. His academic work is mainly about contemporary China, particularly politics, the country’s transformation and its external relations.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

Many have offered a lukewarm assessment of the Xi-Trump summit in Washington, citing the lack of a breakthrough. What is your take?

There are two primary views right now. One is nihilism, which holds that China and the US are ultimately bound to fight for global dominance – that the world isn’t big enough for two superpowers. The other is idealism, which expects all differences to be resolved in a single step.

We should assess China-US relations with realism. The fact that both countries have managed to get to where they are today is already no small feat. China and the US will remain somewhere between a de facto G2 and a formal G2 for a long time, navigating between being two de facto superpowers and exercising joint governance.

As two major powers, China and the US naturally have distinct national interests. We must recognise that cooperation and competition coexist.

Everyone must keep a floor in mind, acknowledging that conflict between China and the US would only bring about the destruction of the world, whereas their cooperation can lead to win-win outcomes.

China has published its list of deliverables and the United States has released its fact sheet of the event. What did the summit achieve?

The summit delivered the best outcome within the range of expectations. Although the two sides framed the results differently, that is because they have different priorities.

Two aspects stand out. The first is economic and trade relations, which I think have become more stable. That is very important. According to our assessment, about 70 per cent of the Chinese and US economies are highly complementary, while 20 to 30 per cent are competitive, such as the hi-tech sector.

The summit essentially confirmed the structural complementarity between the two economies and further consolidated the consensus that economic and trade ties are indeed the ballast of the bilateral relationship.

Even in the hi-tech field, there is common ground. As for “super intelligence” and “artificial intelligence” (AI), that is a distinction in technical wording but not a substantive one. The consensus [the establishment of the bilateral AI dialogue] is a positive trend.

The second aspect is political trust. China-US relations need to proceed in three steps: first economic and trade ties, then politics and finally security. The Chinese list of deliverables and understanding reflects such a sequence.

The Chinese statement announced eight points of consensus, but the most important element is the one that follows them – that we consider the “ninth point” even though it was not described in this way. That is about military-to-military communication and security.

Still, security issues are not ready to be addressed, as the level of bilateral political trust remains insufficient. Perceptions that the other side poses a security threat are high in both the US and China. Many so-called security threats are perceived, rather than real. Tackling this will require building a lot of political trust through frequent communication between the two countries’ leaders. Without that, it could get challenging.

President Xi [Jinping] and President [Donald] Trump are on track to meet twice more this year, which is remarkable. For the leaders of China and the US to meet four times in a single year on different occasions is unprecedented and might not happen often in the future.

Looking ahead to the next two summits, a task should be to further expand and strengthen the economic and trade ballast while making the consensus on stability bigger, stronger and deeper.

After trust has gradually built up, it would be somewhat easier for the two countries to then work on security issues. This is not an impossible mission.

Speaking of the “ninth point”, only the Chinese readout said the two militaries “agree to conclude a memorandum of understanding on crisis communication and prevention as soon as possible”. The White House’s fact sheet did not include this, although the US has long called for keeping military-to-military communication open. Instead, it mentioned Trump’s call for trilateral arms control negotiations between the US, China and Russia. How do you read those differences?

Of course, what the US highlighted were the issues of its concern, such as the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Korean peninsula and the war on Iran. The Beijing side’s emphases, though not explicitly written out, remained on Taiwan and the South China Sea, which are our most significant security concerns. From the Chinese perspective, these are issues of sovereignty that transcend security. Still, they manifest as security issues and call for more communication. There is an implicit shared understanding regarding those fields, namely, both sides need to cooperate.

To address the Taiwan question and the South China Sea, Beijing needs US cooperation. Likewise, Washington needs the Chinese side’s cooperation to resolve the major challenges on its agenda.

You said Beijing and Washington should work together to make the consensus on stability bigger, stronger and deeper. What should they do to ensure a durable, stable relationship that outlasts Trump’s presidency?

There are both certainties and uncertainties. The certainty is the minimum baseline for the stability of the bilateral relationship, which is that the two countries cannot come into conflict. This is a consensus not only between China and the US but also between the Democratic and Republican parties in America. The consensus has been even clearer [since the summit]. Such a consensus will go beyond Trump’s current term and likely endure for much longer.

This is grounded not only in the reality that the China-US relationship rests on a foundation of strength but also in the common recognition by both sides that a conflict between the two countries would not merely affect themselves; it would throw the entire world into chaos.

Today, much of the world conflates issues of sovereignty with those of geopolitical space. They are completely different.

Zheng Yongnian

Meanwhile, there is still much that can be done. First, shaping the future of China-US relations hinges on high-level summits. Communication between the heads of state should continue. This will continue even if the Democrats return to power or another Republican takes office. It is impossible for China and the US to absolutely not engage.

Second, both sides should continue to enlarge and strengthen the economic and trade ballast. For China, this is a force to help keep US capital engaged. As long as American interests are deeply embedded in China’s economy and China’s in America’s, there is a foundation to build on. Economic interdependence does not necessarily prevent war but it can encourage everyone to be more rational and continue to expand bilateral trade and investment reciprocally.

Third, it is critical for bureaucracies on both sides to earnestly materialise the consensus rather than undermine it. That involves communication and coordination between the two countries’ respective bureaucratic apparatuses as a whole, not just their diplomatic services.

Fourth, the overall media environment needs to improve. Mutual criticism is fine, but demonising each other is not. We talked about the American press’ unfriendliness towards China. Chinese media should also tone down their rhetoric about the US being finished, degraded or in decline. Both sides should practise empathy. If the Chinese press attacks the US all day while American outlets constantly attack China, it will only worsen public sentiment in both countries.

Will Trump’s high-level reception for Xi’s Washington visit put Beijing in a stronger position for their potential bilateral encounters during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting in November and the G20 gathering in December?

The summit gave both nations greater confidence to face and discuss problems directly, rather than shunning them. As for the high-level reception offered by President Trump to President Xi, this reflected reciprocity. When Trump visited China in May, Beijing also arranged warm hospitality for him.

This is a good trend. Major powers truly should show mutual respect. It is often difficult for a major power and a small nation to get along with each other due to the gap in strength. However, it is actually easier for major powers to deal with each other, as their strengths are matched, allowing for genuine equality.

From the perspective of the different civilisations they each represent, China and the US are also bound to cooperate rather than be in conflict. In the sphere of media discourse, there are overly simplistic interpretations of one another on both sides. We should see the reality of the two countries rather than solely look through the lens of ideology and moral sentiment.

How might the two further bilateral summits this year help manage or shape the China-US relationship, especially given that the US midterm elections will be held before those meetings?

Apec is about economics and trade. It grew during the heyday of globalisation and free trade. One of the largest concerns in the region has been that security issues have come to dominate the agenda, overshadowing economics and trade. When security becomes the overriding focus, it can lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy where everyone actually ends up less secure. It is not that the US no longer wants to trade now, but it is adjusting its approach.

China and the US can do a great deal not only on the bilateral dimension but also on advancing economic development across the entire Asia-Pacific. It is feasible to build on good interactions between the two countries to steer Apec back towards economic cooperation and trade facilitation, which would benefit all sides.

China is well positioned to contribute a lot in this regard, including on energy, agricultural goods and rare earths. We should think about how to use the positive momentum to take the China-US relationship into its next phase, rather than simply maintaining the current situation. After all, standing still can mean stepping back.

After the four summits this year, how can the momentum be sustained into next year? You have emphasised the importance of stable economic and trade ties. Should we be concerned that while the two-month trade truce extension would offer a window of opportunity, the outlook could again become uncertain?

First, we should recognise that Trump’s trade war is not directed exclusively at China. China is just one part of his broader trade war, which has also targeted US allies. If China has the capacity to expand economic and trade ballast, why not do so? We should not struggle for the sake of struggling. Struggle must have a purpose.

In fact, there is plenty of room for cooperation between China and the US. For instance, both countries are confronting the question of how a major power manages its borders. Many of the problems facing the US come from its immediate neighbourhood, including illegal immigration and drugs. China also faces challenges, such as telecoms fraud operations in Myanmar and Cambodia.

China-US ties are not like the US-Soviet relationship. Never before in history have two economies this large been so closely interconnected. The two countries can build consensus not only at greater depth but also across a wider range of areas. And effective policy implementation will lay the foundation for credibility and trust.

Even if there are no formal meetings next year [as there were in May and September], there will still be the annual Apec and G20 gatherings, as well as many other potential occasions. There are many ways for communication. We do not have to worry too much.

Replicating this year’s high frequency of bilateral summits may not be necessary, but head-of-state diplomacy will certainly continue. The key is not to lose the momentum, which is hard won. China and the US could mobilise the positive forces for the bilateral relationship in both countries.

Negative forces undoubtedly exist too, on both sides. For example, we see constant talk of “China is going to defeat America” or “America must defeat China” within the two societies. We need to shape a favourable media and social environment, which is crucial.

Take China’s unilateral opening-up measures in recent years to welcome more American visitors; both sides should do more of what benefits China-US relations, rather than framing the relationship in terms of who defeats whom. Neither side can defeat the other.

When the two sides agreed in May to build “constructive strategic stability”, the White House cited demands for “fairness and reciprocity”. China echoed the two points this time, and both sides added “respect”. What is your take on this development?

China certainly values respect, as the US has long been accustomed to exercising hegemony. I have argued that managing two variables is crucial to handling China-US relations properly.

First, China must manage its own rise. What we consume and do not consume and how much we consume all affect global markets, and even China-US relations. It is not that the world should applaud simply because we have risen. The way China rises matters a great deal.

It is not enough for us to feel that we are rising; other countries must also come to regard China’s rise as a positive development and welcome it. That would constitute a successful and peaceful rise. The Chinese modernisation also emphasises the path of peaceful development.

Second, the relative decline of the US must be managed too. [In a de facto Group of 2] the US has had a considerable psychological adjustment. It is no longer as arrogant or dismissive of others as it once was, and it has come to view China as a much more equal counterpart, as evidenced by speaking of “respect, fairness and reciprocity”.

That is beneficial for China. But the more this is so, the more humble China should be. Nations are like people – feelings and face matter. It is important to be mindful of the US’ psychological position. It would be unwise to show no consideration for that or adopt an attitude of kicking someone when they are down.

Narratives such as “the East is rising and the West is declining” still resurface from time to time in public discourse. Is this view still open to question?

I have said that great powers are not to be defeated. If the US were to fail, it would not be because China had defeated it, but because of problems within itself. And the same holds true for China. China and the US can only coexist. Neither can defeat the other. If one were to defeat the other, the result would be the destruction of the world.

China now should go for smart diplomacy, approaching foreign policy through reason and wisdom rather than simply acting on instinct.

Great powers must shoulder their responsibilities. Managing the two variables discussed [in the previous answer] is one example of doing so. A country does not become a great power by defeating another. No one would like such a great power, and it will end up defeating itself.

At this summit, both presidents recalled that China and the US were allies during the World War II. Shortly after the meeting, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke with Trump and exchanged views primarily on issues related to China, including security. Meanwhile, new stand-offs have emerged between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea.

With Beijing and Washington agreeing to build constructive strategic stability, how should China manage its relations with US allies in the region, particularly Japan and the Philippines? These countries are also actively strengthening security ties between themselves. Could that in turn affect China-US relations?

[The de facto G2] has implications for many so-called middle powers. Countries such as France, Germany, Canada and the United Kingdom, which have fewer geopolitical disputes with Beijing, are not choosing sides between Beijing and Washington in managing their relations with the two powers.

Meanwhile, Japan appears to be trying to play the role of an “Israel in East Asia”. It likely feels that the US is now paying less attention to protecting it, so the country seeks to take security into its own hands and, based on that, keep Washington tied to its side. But there are limits to this approach.

As long as China and the US have enough trust between them, Japan and the Philippines will have little role to play. As a relationship between major powers, China-US relations constitute a structure within which Japan and the Philippines can only make some autonomous choices. No matter what [Japan and the Philippines] do, they cannot themselves become a structure.

On Taiwan and the South China Sea, there is still considerable room to explore in future exchanges between Beijing and Washington. For Beijing, Taiwan and the South China Sea are matters of sovereignty. For the US and Japan, these are issues of geopolitical space. Today, much of the world conflates issues of sovereignty with those of geopolitical space. They are completely different.

On the basis of mutual respect and reciprocity, we can talk with the American side over how to ensure US interests in the western Pacific. Addressing the Taiwan question and South China Sea issues does not mean Beijing wants to exclude Washington from the region. Likewise, we can also talk with the US about how to assure China’s interests in the eastern Pacific, including in Latin America. These are reciprocal matters the two sides can discuss. That rests on the deeply intertwined nature of China-US relations, and the two countries not carving so-called spheres of influence.

Once the Taiwan question is resolved, we could welcome US warships and aircraft carriers making port calls at the island openly, just as we once welcomed American military vessels to dock in Hong Kong. The two sides should work together to manage the Pacific and the world as a whole instead of trying to exclude each other.

Will the dynamics of Sino-US relations and Beijing’s posture vis-a-vis Washington during this summit affect how middle powers, including Japan and the EU, approach their relations with China?

They have already begun to change. We should go back to the realistic dimension when looking at international relations.

Since the dawn of the modern era, an idea originating from Europe holds that all states are equal. This is an ideal, not a reality. As countries differ in size and strength, we cannot assume that they are fully equal at the starting point. But we can strive for equality. Every nation has its own positioning in international relations. If a country does what it ought not to do, or fails to do what it should, that is not helpful to its own national interests and is not sustainable.

Under the de facto G2 context, both China and the US are repositioning themselves. Other countries will also be doing the same. This is a structural issue that could shape international relations for decades. The boundaries of the China-US relationship may gradually become the boundaries of international relations as a whole. The bounds set by the two countries for the bilateral ties could also define red lines that other states should not cross.

Neither side’s release mentioned Taiwan. Trump said he and Xi “didn’t talk about it too much” at the summit. Should there be concern that the question has been shelved? How might Beijing and Washington approach Taiwan in future exchanges?

The fact that Taiwan was not mentioned in the documents does not mean the two sides did not consider or discuss it but only indicated they had not yet reached a broader consensus on it. Indeed, there is a concern that Taiwan could become the focal point of a conflict if it is not handled carefully, potentially undoing progress on all other work.

But as we talked about earlier, Taiwan is not a subject that cannot be discussed. Many specific issues need to be gradually untangled. If the dialogue simply consists of China accusing the US of being “a force from outside the region” while Washington levels the similar charge against Beijing, it goes nowhere and the two sides could drift towards conflict.

But adopting a more mutually inclusive mindset can make a difference. The US is still a significant actor in the western Pacific. Similarly, China’s influence in Latin America is growing. Every issue has its origins and its solutions. There are always solutions other than war. We should not underestimate human wisdom.

China made no mention of rare earths and critical minerals in its own list of summit outcomes, although the US repeated its concerns in its fact sheet. Does this signal a firm stance by Beijing on the issue, and how might it affect competition in this domain?

The US is looking to reinforce its toolkit, looking for additional means. China is doing the same, like the case of AI start-up Manus. This is reciprocity – and you can only negotiate for reciprocity when you have the strength to back it up. If political trust between China and the US gradually builds and both sides move towards the same direction, I do not think rare earths will be a problem. But if [political trust] deteriorates, more points of friction could emerge.

Rare earths serve as a countermeasure for China but the country’s purpose is rather simple - zhi ge wei wu [a Chinese idiom meaning “true martial virtue lies in stopping warfare”].

If the US weaponises something to pressure us, China has tools of its own to push back. Still, as long as the US remains rational, the Chinese side would not cut off rare earth supplies.

China and the US have agreed to establish an AI dialogue. Given their differing approaches to the technology and divisions within the US on AI slowdown, what concrete outcomes can we expect from AI discussions between the two countries?

First of all, when it comes to AI development, there is little consensus within China or the US, let alone between them. Domestically, the US is currently split into two camps on AI: one believes AI can solve many of our problems, while the other fears it could bring about doomsday. But China and the US do share a consensus on the security risks posed by AI; what remains to be mapped out is the specifics of what they should discuss.

The two countries also follow different models of AI development. Trump supports accelerated development with no regulation. China, at least theoretically, tries to balance development with security.

AI requires multilevel discussion between China and the US. Technology and capital circles essentially dominate the discourse about AI. Trump aligns himself with them, further reinforcing their power. Talk of regulation and slowing down AI development in the US has gone on for a long time but with little real progress. These issues cannot be driven by commercial companies – they can only be tackled by governments.

AI will undoubtedly serve as a major platform for future US-China discussions, much like nuclear weapons did between the US and the Soviet Union. [Former US secretary of state Henry] Kissinger’s final visit to China was also aimed at easing AI negotiations between Beijing and Washington.

Despite their different rhetoric on AI, both sides share the consensus that discussion between them is necessary. When people talk about AI today, they are effectively talking about China-US relations, as its technology and production capacity are highly concentrated in the two countries.

Trump has confirmed his intention to attend the Apec summit, further raising global expectations for the event in November. What impact do you think this could have on the host city, Shenzhen? And how do you view the frequent comparisons between Shenzhen and Hong Kong?

This is certainly a boon for Shenzhen. The entire Pearl River Delta, including Shenzhen and Hong Kong, has an export-oriented economy, for which China-US relations are paramount. Every twist in the relationship would be reflected immediately in Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Hong Kong and Shenzhen can also be key to implementing the consensus reached by the Chinese and US leaders.

If local governments and businesses do more to foster China-US friendship, it benefits not only themselves but the whole country. With the relationship enjoying such good momentum, I expect the Apec summit in Shenzhen to be a great success. It will also mark the first visit to Shenzhen by a sitting US president since the Chinese special economic zone was founded more than four decades ago.

Shenzhen can be proud in showing the world what it has achieved but should also stay humble. Although Shenzhen is a city that buys globally and sells globally, it still has things to learn from Hong Kong when it comes to institutions and mechanisms, and the internationalisation of people.

Apec is a test for Shenzhen. Although much is arranged by the central government, the local side will shape the atmosphere of the summit on the ground. I hope that, through the coming Apec summit, Shenzhen can gradually move closer to Hong Kong, though the city still has a lot to learn.

item.title: [SCMP] US sanctions forced Xinjiang cotton to adapt, but survival comes at a cost
item.description:
The fields in Xinjiang’s Awati county – a cotton hub hit by US sanctions – were nearly ready for the October harvest.

Yusup Molamaiti, a 36-year-old technician, recalled what it was like manually planting and harvesting 37 mu (about 2.5 hectares or 6 acres) of scattered plots of land.

“Planting a single mu took up to three hours with two people laying plastic film by hand,” he said. Harvesting would lock his family into year-round labour, yielding just 250-300kg (551-661lbs) per mu.
item.content:encoded:
The fields in Xinjiang’s Awati county – a cotton hub hit by US sanctions – were nearly ready for the October harvest.

Yusup Molamaiti, a 36-year-old technician, recalled what it was like manually planting and harvesting 37 mu (about 2.5 hectares or 6 acres) of scattered plots of land.

“Planting a single mu took up to three hours with two people laying plastic film by hand,” he said. Harvesting would lock his family into year-round labour, yielding just 250-300kg (551-661lbs) per mu.

Today, his 100-household village is a model for Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region’s agricultural overhaul. Region-wide, over 90 per cent of cotton is now harvested by machine, according to China’s cotton association.

Following land consolidation, seeders guided by satellite navigation can plant the entire village in two days, drones spray fields in five hours, and domestic harvesters have pushed mechanisation to nearly 100 per cent, boosting yields to 400kg per mu, according to the village leader’s collective.

For Yusup and his wife, less than five months of work as cooperative technicians yields over 30,000 yuan (US$4,200). Combined with livestock farming, their annual household income now exceeds 90,000 yuan – a 125 per cent increase from before mechanisation.

The cooperative members shared their stories with a delegation of journalists from domestic and foreign media – including the South China Morning Post – during a government-organised media tour in early September.

The tour was part of Beijing’s broader campaign to showcase Xinjiang’s development and to push back against Western allegations of forced labour.

Since the US began placing textile manufacturers on entity lists under the Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act (UFLPA), Xinjiang’s industrial players have forged a sophisticated survival model, backed by state price supports, rapid mechanisation, technological upgrades, aggressive market diversification and domestic brand substitution.

Yet, on-the-ground sociologists and global trade specialists warn that this resilience comes at a steep hidden cost, including squeezed profit margins, a chilling effect that has triggered a “domestic decoupling” and an unintended spillover into European markets.

Failed legal remedies

Signed into law in 2021, Washington’s UFLPA establishes a “rebuttable presumption” that all goods produced in whole or in part in Xinjiang involve forced labour – a charge Beijing consistently denies – and specifically bars listed companies from exporting to the US unless they can provide “clear and convincing evidence” to the contrary.

Additions to the list in August brought the total number of blacklisted companies to 187 across sectors including gold, pharmaceuticals, aluminium, clothing and food.

From early on, targeted companies tried to fight the restrictions.

A senior manager of a major yarn spinning giant, who preferred to remain anonymous, said that in May 2020, a local subsidiary in Aksu was added to the US Commerce Department’s entity list for alleged human rights abuses, followed by a broader import ban under the UFLPA in June 2022.

“They even included several subsidiaries that had been liquidated five or six years earlier,” he said.

In 2020, the textile maker invited Western clients and third-party social compliance auditors to conduct on-site inspections, where they were shown fully automated lines.

When the press delegation visited the company’s sprawling manufacturing complex in September, both Han and ethnic minority workers were seen moving side by side through the deafening roar of spinning machinery.

Cotton harvested from 5.3 hectares of local fields is fed into automated lines, where raw white fibres are dyed and spun into spools of black, grey and vibrant melange yarns.

According to the manager, foreign clients had acknowledged to him that the automated facilities operated without coercive practices but said their hands were tied by political pressure back home.

“They said: ‘I believe there is no forced labour in your factory, but this is not something we can decide,’” the manager said.

Other efforts proved similarly futile.

Hong Kong-based textile giant Esquel Group – which operated spinning mills in Xinjiang – commissioned independent third-party audits that returned scores above 85 out of 100, finding no evidence of forced labour.

When targeted by US sanctions, Esquel filed a lawsuit against the US Commerce Department in federal court in 2021.

The legal challenge stalled, and by late 2024, the US government added Esquel’s parent group and subsidiaries directly to the UFLPA entity list. Major clients including Nike, Tommy Hilfiger and Patagonia cancelled orders, forcing Esquel to shut factories in Mauritius and Malaysia and shed more than 10,000 global jobs.

Sheng Lu, a professor of fashion and apparel studies at the University of Delaware, noted that hi-tech field mechanisation had done little to ease US customs enforcement because the burden of proof under the rebuttable presumption was extraordinarily high.

“In practice, US fashion brands and retailers regard sourcing cotton from Xinjiang as extremely risky,” Lu said.

“Given plenty of alternative sourcing destinations in countries like Bangladesh and nearshoring opportunities in Mexico and Central America, incentives to challenge the ‘rebuttable presumption’ are extremely low among US fashion companies.”

Pivot and diversification

Faced with an unyielding US legal barrier, textile producers abandoned litigation and launched sweeping operational pivots.

“In 2020, when the sanctions hit, our core leadership established a strict policy: no lay-offs, no pay cuts and no production shutdowns,” the manager of the Aksu spinning giant said.

The company’s solution was a drastic shift towards China’s domestic market and non-Western trade corridors. “Otherwise, how could you keep the workers fed?” he said.

The company redirected 60 to 70 per cent of its capacity to domestic Chinese apparel powerhouses such as Anta Sports. Another 20 to 30 per cent was routed to Southeast Asia, East Asia, Central Asia and Eastern Europe.

Before 2020, overseas markets accounted for 75 per cent of the company’s total business, with the US representing 80 per cent of those export orders. Following its inclusion on the entity list, the company’s US exports dropped to zero, while its Western European share shrivelled to just 3 to 5 per cent.

After years of heavy financial losses, internal balance sheets stabilised in 2024 before returning to profitability last year, the manager said.

Today, the Aksu facility employs more than 5,000 workers and is actively building new production lines to recruit another 1,000 employees. The parent group has set a goal to double its annual revenue to 200 million yuan, according to the manager.

Other industry players have also adopted a “dual-track” sourcing model: using imported cotton sourced from Australia or Brazil in coastal factories to service export orders, while reserving Xinjiang’s cotton for domestic product lines.

This strategy has been reported by Chinese media and confirmed by Lin Fangfei, a professor of sociology at Xinjiang University who has conducted extensive fieldwork across sanctioned supply chains.

National figures back up the domestic absorption.

Data from China’s National Bureau of Statistics shows Xinjiang’s cotton output hit a record 6.17 million tonnes last year, accounting for 92.8 per cent of national production.

Meanwhile, China’s domestic cotton consumption is forecast to hit 8.91 million tonnes this year – up from 7.8 million tonnes in 2024 – with about 1.6 million tonnes of raw cotton imported.

The trajectory of China’s domestic market is critical because local consumers already absorb 50 to 60 per cent of the country’s apparel production, according to Lu.

“This means that China’s domestic market can provide an important buffer for Xinjiang cotton,” Lu said. “But it may not be sufficient to absorb unlimited additional production, particularly if domestic apparel demand weakens.”

The long-term sustainability of this strategy would “depend heavily” on China’s domestic consumption and government policies, such as subsidies, he added.

Since 2014, Xinjiang cotton’s production has been supported by a state target-price subsidy programme that has guaranteed a minimum price of 18,600 yuan per tonne for Xinjiang cotton growers.

When initial US sanctions hit, manufacturers faced existential liquidity crises as banks hesitated to lend.

The government intervened to guarantee bank credit and preserve operating cash flow, preventing large-scale shutdowns. Local authorities have also organised peer-sharing forums for sanctioned firms to exchange mitigation strategies, according to the anonymous manager.

Following an August 2024 resolution by the Xinjiang People’s Congress opposing US sanctions, regional policies now pair state cotton target-price subsidies with legal support and financing for tech upgrades to help targeted firms pivot to new markets.

Meanwhile, the companies have been moving up the value chain by upgrading technology.

Inside the modernised processing plants, contrary to Western narratives of forced labour, the manager said the main challenge was “an acute labour shortage”.

As education levels rise and demographics shift in southern Xinjiang, younger generations increasingly prefer gig-economy jobs, such as food delivery, over factory work.

Rapid industrial automation had also eliminated the demand for low-end manual labour, shifting recruitment entirely towards educated, tech-savvy technicians capable of operating digitised machinery, he said.

Esquel Group has pivoted towards direct-to-consumer retail, expanding its self-owned premium brands.

“Esquel remains focused on our ongoing transformation into a knowledge-based innovation company,” the group wrote in a reply to the SCMP.

It added that the company had also launched the Esquel Innovation and Incubation Village in Urumqi, transforming a former manufacturing facility into an incubation platform for agricultural tech and green technologies.

Chilling effect

While corporate pivots show individual resilience, field researchers stress that looking only at the surviving industrial giants paints an incomplete picture, as the impact varies across different nodes of the supply chain.

According to a forthcoming study in the peer-reviewed International Review of Financial Analysis, the sanctions inadvertently spurred asset growth and production efficiency among “smaller, younger, non-state-owned enterprises with high R&D investment”.

Those companies located in central and western China were able to capitalise on domestic brand substitution, the Chinese researchers found, according to the October study.

Some export-oriented firms in coastal provinces, however, were “dealt a huge blow”, other research shows.

“Even for firms that survived by restructuring, the forced pivot has eaten heavily into their profit margins and introduced extra compliance costs that simply would not exist without sanctions,” Lin said.

She said another major destructive effect of the sanctions was the pervasive culture of fear and the “chilling effect” generated throughout the market.

For years, Chinese officials and businesses have faced a delicate narrative balance. If the media emphasises that targeted industries have adapted, Washington will interpret it as a sign that sanctions were insufficient. But if Beijing reports severe economic fallout, Western policymakers will cite it as proof that their measures are working.

Lin said that during her research, corporate leaders expressed fear that media attention would invite “further US punishment”.

To dodge the risk of secondary sanctions and safeguard their own export revenues, some apparel brands in coastal provinces are quietly severing supply ties with sanctioned Xinjiang mills.

Lin also pointed to an unquantifiable “hidden iceberg” of lost economic activity, where foreign multinationals such as Volkswagen and Tesla have abandoned prospective investments or facilities in Xinjiang.

In the US, however, “strengthening customs enforcement has become a critical part of the Trump administration’s trade policy”, Lu said.

This was especially evident in an executive order signed by US President Donald Trump in June prioritising investigations into forced labour and illegal transshipment through heightened audit frequency, stricter disclosure mandates and rigorous supply-chain documentation requirements, he added.

“The recent US Section 301 investigation is pushing more countries not only to implement their own forced labour laws but also to adopt the US legislative framework and criteria. In other words, the Xinjiang cotton ban is expanding beyond the US to the rest of the world,” he said.

More than 24,300 shipments with a total value of almost US$1 billion have been blocked since the act came into force, according to the US Department of Homeland Security.

US Customs and Border Protection had intensified scrutiny of all major import sources, including potential transshipment routes through Southeast Asia, Lu observed.

But Western fashion companies are not fully decoupling from China.

As of July, China remained the second-largest source of US apparel imports, after Vietnam, and was “increasingly seen as a strategic sourcing destination that offers flexibility, agility, and cost-efficient apparel products, even with relatively higher tariff rates”, Lu said.

In a recent study Lu conducted with the US Fashion Industry Association, respondents indicated that sourcing from China was “somewhat stabilising” this year, and few companies planned to fully decouple from China. Beyond finished garments, China is also regarded as an indispensable supplier of textile raw materials with no easy alternative.

European spillover

According to a May study, researchers from Britain, the European Union and the World Bank found that direct Chinese exports of cotton and cotton products to the US fell by 19 per cent at the intensive margin following the restrictions.

Unlike the US, the EU has not enacted a blanket import embargo against Xinjiang cotton.

However, Jo Van Biesebroeck, co-author of the paper and an economics professor at KU Leuven in Belgium, pointed out that US trade sanctions had triggered unintended spillover effects across Europe.

“We were very surprised that the negative effect on EU imports is as large as we found,” he said.

Their research found that the European retreat from Xinjiang cotton has been driven not by official EU policy, but by voluntary risk avoidance and concerns of “reputational damage” among European importers.

While US customs enforcement heavily targets less processed raw materials and yarns at ports, the drop in European imports is sharpest in finished apparel sold directly to consumers.

He said that because Xinjiang sent very few direct exports to Europe, most European scrutiny fell on downstream manufacturers in other Chinese provinces whose supply chains extended back to the far western region. This indirect link makes traditional factory audits far less convincing to European consumer advocates.

Van Biesebroeck noted that standard compliance audits failed to reassure buyers because European consumer dissatisfaction extended beyond specific forced-labour metrics to broader scepticism towards Beijing’s official narratives.

“I have never seen any real evidence of forced labour, but the overall situation is rather murky,” he said. “It is more the general treatment of the minority population that consumers want to protest.”

Researchers caution against viewing Central Asia or the Middle East as replacements for Western markets, as these regions cannot match the high-margin markets of the US and Europe.

Van Biesebroeck’s work showed that Russia was the only major market that registered a statistically significant increase in Chinese cotton product imports following the US ban.

Over the past five years, Beijing has been building up its own legal shield by enacting the Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law alongside regulations on countering “improper extraterritorial jurisdiction”. But the practical enforcement of these countermeasures remains to be seen.

Lin argued that solution strategies must move beyond micro-level compliance to embrace macro-level institutional support. By building a formal state-corporate community of shared interest, Beijing can prevent cash-flow collapses among Xinjiang manufacturers and avert local unemployment risks.

Beyond borders, China must transition from fighting unilateral sanctions in isolation to forging a broader multilateral coalition against economic coercion, she added.

“Many nations across the Global South have long suffered under the weight of unilateral US sanctions,” she said, adding that by uniting with affected countries and neutral trade partners, China could leverage collective international pressure to gradually rebuild a more balanced global trade order.

item.title: [SCMP] Slow is beautiful: China launches war against AI drama, goes beyond algorithms
item.description:
China’s broadcasting regulator has called for greater support for live-action dramas as the government seeks to steer the booming microdrama industry towards higher-quality production and tighter rights safeguards amid the rapid rise of AI.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has created innovation and production possibilities for microdramas, while also posing challenges over content quality and rights protection, according to Wang Xiaoliang from the National Radio and Television Administration.

item.content:encoded:
China’s broadcasting regulator has called for greater support for live-action dramas as the government seeks to steer the booming microdrama industry towards higher-quality production and tighter rights safeguards amid the rapid rise of AI.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has created innovation and production possibilities for microdramas, while also posing challenges over content quality and rights protection, according to Wang Xiaoliang from the National Radio and Television Administration.

“Faced with this new challenge … our position is very clear. Live-action dramas are the mainstay of high-quality production and should be strongly supported,” said Wang, who heads the department overseeing online audiovisual content.

AI has rapidly expanded the scale and efficiency of microdrama production in China while intensifying concerns over copyright and the mounting pressure on human creators.

Wang’s remarks, made at a press conference on September 17, follow a proliferation of formulaic and derivative content as producers race to churn out more dramas in pursuit of hits and profits.

The scale of the shift is striking. Around 430,000 microdramas were released in China in the first eight months of 2026 – as much as 13 times the figure for the whole of last year – with AI dramas accounting for more than 90 per cent of new releases, Wang said.
