According to Wang, the regulator will step up its initiative to promote and distribute high-quality microdramas, guiding platforms to create dedicated sections for live-action dramas while providing financial support so that quality productions can find audiences and generate returns.

Microdramas or duanju, meaning short or mini dramas, have exploded in popularity in China in recent years.

Built for mobile screens and short attention spans, the fast-paced, scripted and often melodramatic shows are divided into dozens of episodes, usually in a vertical format, with each lasting just a few minutes.

AI is moving beyond a supporting tool and into almost every stage of production – from story adaptation and scriptwriting to character and scene generation, and onwards to post-production – upending an industry that supports more than 2 million jobs nationwide.

The change has spawned a new format known as AI microdramas – AI-generated animation and live action-style dramas featuring lifelike digital characters that reduce the need for conventional filming.

Companies can now churn out AI-generated content at a pace that was previously impossible, lowering production costs and technical barriers while allowing producers to test more titles in the hope of finding hits.

Johnny Chan, a senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, said microdrama platforms created a self-reinforcing cycle: the more you watch, the better the algorithm learns what keeps you hooked.

Creators keep refining the cliffhangers and paywalls that work, while the platforms invest more money to make the experience even stickier, he wrote in a paper published in August by the journal Systems Research and Behavioural Science.

Chan wrote that while people would usually get bored eventually by the formula, the ability of AI to rapidly generate endless fresh stories and variations meant the natural “boredom brake” might never fully kick in, causing viewers to keep scrolling for longer.

According to data from the China Netcasting Services Association, more than 275,000 AI microdramas were released online in the first half of 2026, an average of about 1,500 each day.

The explosion in numbers has created a broader regulatory challenge for Chinese authorities: how to encourage this form of cultural production while preventing speed, scale and platform-driven consumption from coming at the expense of quality, originality and rights.

The expanded use of the technology has given rise to various types of regulatory abuse, including content plagiarism and repackaging, as well as AI face-swapping and voice cloning, along with copyright infringement involving online literature.

Many high-profile actors and the general public alike have accused AI microdrama producers of using their likenesses without consent.

The speed at which AI is reshaping the industry has also exposed a growing gap between production capacity and the quality and originality of what gets made.

In the first half of 2026, only 0.48 per cent of new AI microdramas released on the social media platform Douyin surpassed 100 million views, according to industry data provider DataEye.

Lydia Chen, a 30-year-old AI microdrama writer and director producing live action-style dramas for overseas audiences, said the industry’s rush for hits had made copying almost routine.

Platforms and production companies often copied each other’s hits and were used to taking dramas that had already gone viral in China, tweaking the plot and transplanting the story to a foreign setting, she said.

For example, a Chinese tale of a ba zong – internet slang for a bossy president or a powerful, domineering businessman – and a female lead from the countryside can be repackaged as a New York billionaire falling for a woman from rural America.

“You can see the productions becoming increasingly like internet products,” said Chen, who worries that as real-world filming declines, the craft itself will stagnate while AI models will have fewer new examples of real filmmaking to learn from.

“If everyone keeps copying past hits, where will the new ideas of the future come from?”

Chen also noted that some storylines adapted for overseas audiences reproduced traditional and conservative Chinese cultural attitudes towards gender, relationships and family – as they catered to the tastes of the mass-market microdrama audience.

She pointed to the plotline of a “bossy president” falling for a rural woman whose virginity is portrayed as part of her appeal, along with plots idealising women as stay-at-home mothers with multiple children.

“Sometimes I wonder whether this is really the kind of culture we should be exporting,” she said. “To me, some of these ideas feel quite outdated.”

Beijing has responded to the challenges by tightening oversight of both the content and the systems through which it reaches audiences.

The National Radio and Television Administration launched a two-month campaign in June targeting “harmful, lowbrow and pirated” microdrama content.

The campaign focused on material harmful to children as well as sexually suggestive scenes, wealth-flaunting, “distorted” views on marriage and relationships, along with superstitions, violent revenge, sensationalist titles and copyright violations.

Everyone was working themselves to the limit just to … make money.

Shiliu, microdrama director

Wang told the press conference that since the beginning of the year, regulators had removed 68,000 microdramas that violated the rules and guided platforms to punish more than 1,200 accounts.

More than 90 per cent of the problematic content involved AI dramas, he said.

The government has also introduced rules specifically addressing the use of AI in production.

The microdrama development and management measures, which took effect on September 1, require clear labelling for every episode of AI-generated microdramas, along with “respect for original works, copyright protection, fair competition and more orderly industry development”.

Platforms must also regularly review and assess their recommendation algorithms, models and data, give priority to high-quality microdramas and prohibit suggestions that are designed to encourage user indulgence or excessive consumption.

The pressure is also being felt by people working inside the industry, with microdrama actors facing a harsh reality.

Since the beginning of the year, many have said they are struggling to find roles, with some actors taking on part-time work as AI-generated dramas increasingly replace live-action productions.

For those still working in AI microdrama production, greater efficiency has not necessarily meant an easier workload.

Shiliu, a 28-year-old AI microdrama director who joined the industry 2 ½ years ago, said his team was expected to complete five dramas a month, each running for 50 to 70 episodes.

As the team shrank, he found himself taking on multiple roles and working 14 to 16 hours a day, said Shiliu, who asked not to be identified by his real name.

“Because AI is so convenient, bosses only focus on efficiency,” he added. “Everyone was working themselves to the limit just to [fulfil demand] and make money.” The workload eventually took its toll, prompting him to quit the industry.

The state-run Economic Daily urged the industry last month to move away from scale-driven growth in favour of higher quality, more original and professionally produced content.

Familiar formulas were being repeatedly recycled while a flood of lookalike content competed for limited attention, the paper said in an article published on August 13.

“Promotion and computing costs rise, leaving producers caught in a cycle of producing more without earning more,” it noted. “Audiences’ willingness to pay is further eroded while the industry’s reputation is bound to suffer.”

DataEye estimates that the overseas market for Chinese microdramas will exceed US$6 billion in 2026, with AI-generated animated and live-action style dramas accounting for more than US$4 billion.

The netcasting services association said that China’s AI microdrama industry was reaching a turning point, shifting from rapid, loosely regulated expansion towards more disciplined and quality-driven growth.

In Chen’s view, as AI lowers the technical barriers to content creation and more people without a professional background are able to turn their ideas into original works, individually created non-formulaic projects will have a better chance of standing out.

“We must strike a balance between encouraging innovation and upholding safeguards,” Wang said.

“Ultimately, AI is a tool, while people remain the creators. The faster AI dramas develop, the more important it is to ensure content quality.”

item.title: [SCMP] 2025 was a tough year for Hong Kong’s bar industry, so how are new concepts carving a path forward?
item.description:
Despite this being the year Hong Kong hosted its first edition of World’s 50 Best Bars (with Asia’s 50 Best Bars held in nearby Macau), the scene as a whole suffers from headwinds stemming from declining interest in alcohol and dining out, combined with a significant price gap with the Greater Bay Area, to which tourists and weekend revellers are flocking, as the Post reported earlier this month.

Bars and restaurants close every year, but 2025 saw the closure of extremely recognisable venues that have been serving the city for anywhere between half of to beyond a decade. Foxglove, which celebrated a decade this year, closed its doors last week. The Daily Tot shuttered just a few weeks before that, preceded by Stockton (est. 2014) earlier in the year. Last year, Dr Fern’s Gin Parlour and Please Don’t Tell were closed to make way for major renovations at The Landmark, Mandarin Oriental. The Envoy, The Pottinger’s outdoor terrace bar, and its neighbouring speakeasy Room 309 also served their last drinks in 2024.

“I feel very sad that these bars closed down for good,” says Jo Lo, co-founder of Bar Mind, a minimalist cocktail bar in SoHo. “These are the bars [that] really opened my eyes to Asian and Hong Kong bar culture.” Before opening Bar Mind this year, Lo spent almost six years at Room 309 and The Envoy as part of Tastings Group. In 2022, she won Diageo World Class Hong Kong & Macau Bartender of the Year.
item.content:encoded:
Despite this being the year Hong Kong hosted its first edition of World’s 50 Best Bars (with Asia’s 50 Best Bars held in nearby Macau), the scene as a whole suffers from headwinds stemming from declining interest in alcohol and dining out, combined with a significant price gap with the Greater Bay Area, to which tourists and weekend revellers are flocking, as the Post reported earlier this month.

Bars and restaurants close every year, but 2025 saw the closure of extremely recognisable venues that have been serving the city for anywhere between half of to beyond a decade. Foxglove, which celebrated a decade this year, closed its doors last week. The Daily Tot shuttered just a few weeks before that, preceded by Stockton (est. 2014) earlier in the year. Last year, Dr Fern’s Gin Parlour and Please Don’t Tell were closed to make way for major renovations at The Landmark, Mandarin Oriental. The Envoy, The Pottinger’s outdoor terrace bar, and its neighbouring speakeasy Room 309 also served their last drinks in 2024.

“I feel very sad that these bars closed down for good,” says Jo Lo, co-founder of Bar Mind, a minimalist cocktail bar in SoHo. “These are the bars [that] really opened my eyes to Asian and Hong Kong bar culture.” Before opening Bar Mind this year, Lo spent almost six years at Room 309 and The Envoy as part of Tastings Group. In 2022, she won Diageo World Class Hong Kong & Macau Bartender of the Year.

“This year feels like a market correction,” says Ming Cheung, co-founder of 001. “Rents have readjusted in some areas, but not enough. Consumer spending is more cautious. It’s a perfect storm – pre-pandemic business models are colliding with post-pandemic economics and consumer behaviour. It’s a cleansing, but a painful one for the culture.” Originally founded near Gage Street Market in 2010, 001 closed in 2022 before finding a new home a year later in Tai Kwun.

Opening a successful concept in Hong Kong requires a delicate confluence of factors. Rent and operational costs have to be kept as lean as possible. Lo observes that breaking even can take anywhere from six months to two years even with significant initial investment, cost control and effective marketing. John Nugent, founder of The Diplomat and co-founder of Sugar King, emphasises the fundamentals of business planning – maintaining doomsday, middle-of-the-road and success scenarios; pivoting as needed; and knowing the product and clientele.

With costs, breaking even and engagement key to a concept’s survival, it’s easy to assume that bars must consistently predict what the drinking public will enjoy. While many recent closures were speakeasies opened in the 2010s, this year also saw an influx of neighbourhood bars. Bar Leone took home World’s Best Bar, as other “community first” concepts spread their wings: Mius, Oasis and Sugar King, to name a few, focus on simple drinks and convivial atmospheres to great success.

Nugent feels that predicting tastes is only part of the equation, however. “I think it’s a dangerous question to read into drinking preferences,” he says. “We want to make sure that every guest who walks into our venue is treated like they’re getting away from the doldrums of everyday life. Whether you’re serving a fast food item, a curated cocktail or a fine dining meal, you’re giving the best hospitality you can.

“We have to ask ourselves, ‘Is it the guest’s job to keep these places afloat or is the onus on us?’ How do we keep creating new and exciting ways for guests to come back? To take on these challenges, you really have to love the industry we’re in – otherwise, there’s no reason to get out of bed to take on these challenges.”

For Cheung, this focus on the guest makes training another key challenge. “In 2010, we needed people who could master technique,” she says. “Today, that’s the baseline. Now, we need storytellers, hosts, diplomats. They need to navigate social media, understand global trends, manage guest allergies and preferences with ease, and be ambassadors for a vast portfolio of spirits. The skill is in connection, making a guest feel uniquely seen in a 60-second interaction.”

“The challenge is sustaining interest past the two-year mark,” Cheung continues. “We need to consistently turn first-time visitors into regulars, and regulars into ambassadors. There’s no foot traffic to cushion the early months – just the steady, growing trust of people who make the effort to find you. It’s a marathon of consistent excellence, not a sprint.”

“Consistent quality in product and service leads to positive word of mouth and returning customers,” Lo notes. “The ‘hype’ window is like the honeymoon for a new establishment. It reflects the reality that initial excitement [can fade] unless sustained by quality and engagement.”

So is it due to these shifting sands, or a venue’s glaring inability to serve guests or offer something unique – to capture lightning in a half-to-two-year bottle – that causes it to close? Not necessarily. When 001’s original NoHo lease was ending, Cheung explains, the bar was not facing unmanageable financial pressures, but renewing would have locked the business into costs that Cheung and the team felt did not allow for growth or stability. The speakeasy, at its new location in Tai Kwun, celebrated its 15th anniversary last month.

Similarly, as the Post reported, Singular Concepts CEO David Sit attributed The Daily Tot’s closure to rent increases when it was attempting to renew its lease. “We hold onto the concept and the spirit of The Daily Tot, and hope to be back in the near future,” Sit stated in a press release. Reopening has come about for 001 and Dr Fern’s Gin Parlour – now The Doctor’s Residence at The Pottinger – though it is its own gamble.

“I’d say we were 80 per cent confident [we would reopen],” Cheung said. “We had the will, the brand, the team’s core and a strong reputation. But finding the right home – one that matched our ethos and made financial sense – was the 20 per cent gamble.” To reopen, a bar has to “protect its soul, not just the logo”, she advises. “Wait for the location that doesn’t just fit your budget, but fulfils your narrative. A rushed comeback can do more damage than a graceful exit.”

Some venues have indeed exited gracefully and given their mixologists room to develop something new. Nugent previously helmed the beverage programme at Lily & Bloom, a restaurant and bar in Lan Kwai Fong that closed in 2018. In 2020, he opened The Diplomat, a venue known as much for its bar bites and midnight cookies as its classics-based, martini-forward menu and one of the best Irish coffees in town. The opening of Sugar King over the summer has only added to the throngs of imbibers crowding Peel Street every weekend.

“The beauty, but also the curse of Hong Kong, is that it’s ever changing,” Nugent says. “These venues [that have closed] were incredible in their own right; they offered something that was part of the ethos of Hong Kong hospitality.

“We wish nothing but the best for anybody and everyone involved with these places. Who knows? One closure could [lead to] another opening of something even more incredible.”

Ultimately, whether it’s staving off closure, reopening or building something new, guest support and word of mouth go a long way towards keeping valued concepts alive. “One visit a month from a true regular is worth 10 one-time visits from trend chasers,” Cheung affirms. “Be a regular, come on a Tuesday, bring someone new. That’s the oxygen that lets a concept like ours live, breathe and evolve over 15 years.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Singapore’s local cafes compete with Chinese coffee giant Luckin
item.description:
When Chinese coffee giant Luckin Coffee moved into the unit next to his neighbourhood cafe in Singapore, Folk Yard owner Chew Yit Shan grew nervous.

Luckin launched with an aggressive promotional deal of S$1 (78 US cents) per cup, served in just two minutes. In the first few months following its arrival, Chew saw sales at his independent cafe drop by 15 per cent.

But once the initial hype had died down and the promotions ended, Chew said regular patrons returned and coffee sales bounced back.
item.content:encoded:
When Chinese coffee giant Luckin Coffee moved into the unit next to his neighbourhood cafe in Singapore, Folk Yard owner Chew Yit Shan grew nervous.

Luckin launched with an aggressive promotional deal of S$1 (78 US cents) per cup, served in just two minutes. In the first few months following its arrival, Chew saw sales at his independent cafe drop by 15 per cent.

But once the initial hype had died down and the promotions ended, Chew said regular patrons returned and coffee sales bounced back.

“We had to explain to customers that we offer something different. It’s the simple things, like knowing the baristas and coming back to the same places in the neighbourhood,” Chew said. “There’s a level of interaction and familiarity that becomes part of their routine, and that goes beyond the product itself.”

Chew, who opened Folk Yard in 2022, said that Chinese brands like Luckin worked because of their “incredible purchasing power and economies of scale”.

“I don’t think there’s a point where we can compete with them purely on price and convenience. What we can offer is individuality – something that is unique to us and can’t be replicated at the same scale,” Chew said.

Last month, Luckin announced it had hit its 100th-store milestone, just three years after making its overseas debut in the city state.

The chain now operates 103 outlets in Singapore, with up to six more reportedly planned by the end of the year. Its mobile app, which allows customers to order and pay in advance before picking up in-store, now has some 1.9 million users in the city state. Globally, the brand operates more than 36,000 stores across China, over 150 in Malaysia and more than 20 in New York.

Satish Kumar, a 40-year-old civil servant, said he became hooked after his first sip of Luckin’s coconut velvet latte two years ago.

While local coffee – affectionately known as kopi – is a cheaper alternative at S$1 to S$2 a cup, Kumar said Luckin had a different appeal.

“I got addicted after trying [it] because it tastes good to me, and I prefer lattes to kopi,” Kumar said. “They also now have a lot of different flavours and it’s so easy to order on the app.”

‘Like tech stores’

Singapore’s specialist coffee market was estimated to be worth about US$327 million last year, with Luckin capturing roughly 24 per cent of the market share. Starbucks, which entered Singapore in 1996, held about 34 per cent, according to Weihan Chen, insights lead at market intelligence consultancy Momentum Works.

Chen said the arrival of Chinese drink chains had raised the level of competition, particularly around convenience, product variety, pricing and the speed of new product roll-outs.

Yet Chen cautioned against framing Chinese chains as simply replacing local cafes, noting that consumers support very different drink formats, and these brands often compete for different occasions.

Nathanael Lim, Asia-Pacific insight manager for beverages at Euromonitor International, said Luckin’s rapid rise in Singapore reflected its ambitions beyond China.

“Unlike local brands, Luckin combines substantial financial backing with its playbook centred on digital ordering, frequent limited-edition product launches and strong app-based loyalty programmes,” Lim said, adding that Luckin’s scale gave it advantages in supply chain sourcing and operational efficiency.

Seshan Ramaswami, an associate professor of marketing education at Singapore Management University, pointed out that Luckin stores typically had limited seating, keeping overheads low while minimising staffing requirements.

App-based ordering also gives the brand a huge database to use for real-time customer analysis. Drawing from its experience in China, Luckin fine-tunes its customer relationship management to offer targeted discounts that drive repeat purchases.

“This sort of rapid expansion is not always successful, of course – so much depends on consumer loyalty as well as competitive reaction,” Ramaswami said. “But if the taste and the value perception at Luckin’s prices catch on, it could force other chains to change their product mix or even close some stores in the proximity of its outlet.”

Lawrence Loh, a professor of strategy and policy at the National University of Singapore Business School, noted that beyond menu options or marketing strategies, brands like Luckin used novel scaling models that rapidly expanded the number of physical stores to secure long-term market share, even at the expense of short-term profitability.

“Brands are often like tech stores at the shopfront, which not only reduces labour costs but adds a modern feel that appeals to customers, particularly the younger generations who are always on the move,” Loh said.

Deep-pocketed foreign players would often outbid competitors for retail space while constantly reinventing their products, he said, adding that the coffee experience they offered went beyond the menu to embrace culture, community, corporate social responsibility and the “cool” factor attached to being a patron.

“Of late, Chinese brands seem to be able to offer this totality in overseas markets even better than the incumbent brands,” Loh said.

But Denise Lum, co-owner of independent local cafe Maxi Coffee Bar, said she did not see Luckin as a competitor because it catered to a completely different consumer.

“Luckin probably attracts a distinct customer base – people who really care about convenience, price, efficiency, technology and all of that. We cannot compete in that space … All we can do is build on what we feel makes our shop special, which is the customer experience,” she said.

“For them, it’s a scale game. For us, it’s not a breadth but a depth game.”

Opening a new outlet for Maxi Coffee required careful consideration, Lum said, regardless of whether capital was readily available.

“Growth has to be intentional. It’s very much about the neighbourhood and less about just wanting to grow. It’s about identity and community building,” she said.

Folk Yard’s Chew agreed that Luckin customers appeared to want convenience and low prices, whereas his clientele were looking for something else entirely.

“Our customers are people who are looking to slow down,” he said. “They’re not just coming in for a coffee; they’re coming for the experience, the interaction and the sense of community.”

Looking ahead, Momentum Works’ Chen said Luckin would face challenges in maintaining its large network of stores.

“Opening stores quickly demonstrates that there is consumer demand, but sustaining a large network requires strong store-level economics, local management and supply chains,” Chen said.

“As they expand into more countries, the challenge becomes how much of the system developed in China can be replicated and how much needs to be localised.”

item.title: [SCMP] US search for missing airmen in China gains new attention after Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
For more than eight decades, the remains of US fighter pilot Morton Sher lay unrecovered in China. A photograph of a memorial to him in a Hunan village eventually helped investigators find where his plane crashed in 1943.

Sher was buried in his hometown of Greenville, South Carolina, in December 2025, a homecoming that offers a rare example of what US-China cooperation can achieve for families of missing servicemen.

That cooperation has now drawn fresh attention. After the recent summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, Beijing said that the two militaries had agreed to continue cooperating in the search for the remains of missing US servicemen in China.
item.content:encoded:
For more than eight decades, the remains of US fighter pilot Morton Sher lay unrecovered in China. A photograph of a memorial to him in a Hunan village eventually helped investigators find where his plane crashed in 1943.

Sher was buried in his hometown of Greenville, South Carolina, in December 2025, a homecoming that offers a rare example of what US-China cooperation can achieve for families of missing servicemen.

That cooperation has now drawn fresh attention. After the recent summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, Beijing said that the two militaries had agreed to continue cooperating in the search for the remains of missing US servicemen in China.

The account also said the militaries would seek to conclude a separate memorandum on military crisis communication and prevention “as soon as possible”, but it did not specify new recovery missions or arrangements for access to sites and records.

For American investigators, cooperation means permission to search crash sites and access to wartime records that could show where to look.

“All of our work starts with a historical study aspect,” said John Figuerres, a senior operations officer at the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA).

Records of battles, aircraft crashes and possible prisoners of war help investigators decide where to dig, and access to Chinese archives could help historians establish what happened to missing Americans.

“Both getting to sites and that exchange of information are important things with China,” Figuerres said.

China occupies a distinctive place in the agency’s work: it is the only country where DPAA has missing Americans associated with four conflicts, namely World War II, the Korean war, the Vietnam war and the Cold War. DPAA said just over 700 US personnel are missing in China across the four.

The work was already under way before the summit. Since 2024, DPAA has conducted two pre-deployment site surveys, three investigation missions and two recovery missions in China, the agency said.

This past August and September, two teams worked in southern China. A 12-member US recovery team excavated what is believed to be a World War II crash site and recovered possible human remains, while a nine-member investigative team surveyed multiple locations in Hunan and interviewed witnesses to prepare case proposals that could lead to future recovery missions.

Officials from the People’s Liberation Army and provincial and local governments assisted both teams, DPAA said.

US and Chinese scientists are due to hold a joint forensic review of the recovered evidence later this month, the agency said.

DPAA periodically communicates with the PLA Archives to share information on unresolved cases involving both countries, the agency said. The two sides are developing an archival exchange for the 2027 US financial year, which began on October 1.

For the US military, the search extends a battlefield commitment across generations. Figuerres called it part of the “warrior ethos”, the end point of never leaving a fallen comrade behind, and a “sacred obligation” to families waiting at home.

Sher’s case shows how such a search can unfold. He flew with the 23rd Fighter Group, which carried on the legacy of the Flying Tigers, the American volunteer pilots who fought for China against Japan.

Sher himself had crashed in China before: engine damage forced him down near a Chinese village in October 1942, according to a US military account, and residents welcomed him with a feast and helped him return to base.

The banquet, he told an Army newsletter, “turned out to be one of the biggest surprises of the trip”.

On August 20, 1943, the 22-year-old US Army Air Forces pilot was killed while intercepting a Japanese aircraft headed towards Hengyang. US forces located the crash site, but his remains were not recovered.

That changed in 2012, when a private citizen brought a photograph of the village memorial to the attention of the Joint POW/MIA Accounting Command, a predecessor of DPAA, prompting years of research.

During the 2024 excavation, the team found possible human remains and equipment. Anthropological analysis, other evidence and DNA testing led to Sher’s identification in June 2025.

Such identifications are painstaking. At DPAA’s laboratory in Hawaii, which the agency describes as the world’s largest skeletal identification laboratory, scientists may begin with fragments that are difficult to distinguish from animal bone or debris.

Dr Jennie Jin, a DPAA scientist, said anthropologists examine bones for clues such as age and healed injuries, then compare their findings with military files, dental records and DNA results. Anthropologists initially examine remains without knowing the case details, which helps guard against bias.

DNA can be a limited guide. Age and chemical treatment can damage it, Jin said, and a genetic match may narrow the search without establishing a single identity. She recalled a Korean war case in which DNA results narrowed the possibilities to five men.

An anthropologist spotted two old fractures, and in one serviceman’s file, Jin found a letter from his mother describing injuries to her son’s forearm and lower back.

“Ooh, I found him,” Jin remembered thinking. The man was identified and buried beside his mother.

But the work starts long before the laboratory, in China’s villages, and it depends on people who remember where an aircraft came down.

Figuerres said teams had met local residents who still remembered the US role in the second world war and had maintained tributes to fallen airmen.

Jin, who investigated three World War II crash sites in China in 2017, recalled a memorial residents had assembled for American personnel. Her team found no leads at those sites, she said, but residents and Chinese counterparts were helpful.

Historians from the two countries are also beginning to meet regularly, Figuerres said, and building those relationships is an important part of gaining information that could help resolve cases.

For Sher’s family, the search ended with a funeral. DPAA said his sister, who is 93, received his remains. His nephew, Bruce Fine, said that right before his last mission the pilot had turned down an opportunity to return home as an instructor.

On August 19, 1943, Sher wrote to his parents about his decision to stay in China: “I let another pilot take that instructing job, for I find things too exciting here to leave right now.”

He was killed the next day.

item.title: [SCMP] US defence experts to work inside Taiwan military HQ under reported pact
item.description:
A reported plan to station US defence personnel inside Taiwan’s military headquarters would take mutual cooperation into the heart of defence planning, potentially angering Beijing while raising questions over Taipei’s policymaking autonomy and military secrecy.

According to Taiwanese media reports at the weekend, the Pentagon plans to send one official from the Office of the Under Secretary of Defence for Policy and one expert from the Institute for Defence Analyses (IDA) to work on a long-term basis at the defence ministry’s headquarters in Taipei.

The two would aid policy coordination and combat capability assessments under an expanded “Taiwan-US Defence Ministry Joint Cooperation Assessment” programme that would run from this year to 2028, according to the reports.
item.content:encoded:
A reported plan to station US defence personnel inside Taiwan’s military headquarters would take mutual cooperation into the heart of defence planning, potentially angering Beijing while raising questions over Taipei’s policymaking autonomy and military secrecy.

According to Taiwanese media reports at the weekend, the Pentagon plans to send one official from the Office of the Under Secretary of Defence for Policy and one expert from the Institute for Defence Analyses (IDA) to work on a long-term basis at the defence ministry’s headquarters in Taipei.

The two would aid policy coordination and combat capability assessments under an expanded “Taiwan-US Defence Ministry Joint Cooperation Assessment” programme that would run from this year to 2028, according to the reports.

The programme has a total budget of more than NT$471 million (US$14.8 million), including NT$152.5 million this year for expenses such as US personnel and consultancy costs, travel, research equipment and data collection, and interpreting for classified-level meetings.

If confirmed, the arrangement would mark a significant change from the existing US military presence in Taiwan, where American personnel have generally worked as trainers or through the American Institute in Taiwan, Washington’s de facto embassy on the self-ruled island.

The reports said the US representatives could provide on-site advice on overall defence planning, war games for Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang exercises and assessments of major weapons procurement programmes.

Taiwan’s defence ministry did not confirm details of the reported arrangement. On Sunday, it said only that Taipei and Washington continued to deepen military exchanges to strengthen the armed forces’ overall defence capabilities and resilience.

It declined to elaborate on how the cooperation would be implemented.

On Monday afternoon, a representative for the US Department of Defence said it had no comment on the reports.

Wang Ting-yu, a legislator from Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party, has described the reported arrangement as a “major upgrade” in military cooperation.

He said on Monday that in addition to hundreds of US military instructors – sometimes referred to in Taiwan as “American English-language teachers” – helping to train Taiwanese forces, US representatives would now work directly inside the defence ministry.

“This means US personnel will directly enter the core of Taiwan’s defence policymaking establishment, assisting with policy coordination and assessments of combat capabilities,” Wang said, describing it as an upgrade of direct military cooperation “to the highest level”.

But Ma Wen-chun, a legislator of the main opposition party, the Kuomintang, questioned the sharp increase in spending on the cooperation programme, saying its annual budget had risen more than twelvefold compared with earlier years.

“Supporting Taiwan-US military exchanges and cooperation, and supporting national defence, does not mean the budget can be allowed to grow without restraint,” Ma said.

She questioned how many US personnel would come to Taiwan, how many meetings would be held and what concrete benefits the programme would deliver. The defence ministry had yet to provide specific answers, she said.

Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies in Taipei, said it had long been an “open secret” that serving and retired US military personnel were in Taiwan to provide training and advice and had taken part in Han Kuang exercises.

But stationing personnel directly inside the defence ministry would be considerably more sensitive.

“Beijing is certain to protest and could respond with measures such as expanded military exercises and intimidation,” he said, adding that this could explain Taipei’s reluctance to publicly confirm the arrangement.

He said he did not expect the US personnel to wear uniforms because that could be interpreted as a more formalised US-Taiwan military relationship and might further provoke Beijing.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any unilateral change to the cross-strait status quo by force and has been committed to supplying it with weapons.

Despite the closer cooperation, Zivon Wang said he did not believe US representatives would dictate Taiwan’s defence strategy.

“Many aspects of Taiwan’s military strategy are already closely linked with those of the United States,” he said. “Their main purpose in Taiwan would be communication and coordination rather than directly controlling Taiwan’s defence policy or strategy. Taiwan would retain the leading role.”

He acknowledged that US representatives were likely to gain access to at least some classified information, noting that the two sides already shared intelligence on People’s Liberation Army exercises and other activities.

However, he said it was less clear how sensitive the information available to them would be, which could depend partly on the broader US-China relationship.

James Yifan Chen, a Taipei-based international relations and strategic studies scholar, cautioned that embedding US personnel in the defence establishment could gradually increase Washington’s influence over Taiwanese decision making.

While the arrangement would represent “a significant upgrade in security ties”, Taiwan’s defence decisions could become increasingly influenced by US strategic planning and priorities, he said.

“If US national interests were ever to diverge from Taiwan’s interests, Taiwan could find itself facing an uncomfortable strategic dilemma, with limited flexibility to pursue an independent defence posture.”

Chen further argued that the asymmetrical nature of the relationship left Taipei with relatively little leverage and could make it difficult for the island to resist US policies that did not fully coincide with its interests.

Ho Jeng-sheng, vice-chairman of the Taiwan External Relations Research and Development Association, on Monday drew a distinction between benefiting from US expertise and becoming strategically dependent on Washington.

“The question is how far that cooperation should go before defence autonomy turns into outsourcing Taiwan’s defence,” he said.

US intelligence, technology, war-gaming models and strategic advice could help Taiwan improve its capabilities, Ho said, but decisions on defence policy, military command and force deployment ultimately had to remain in Taiwanese hands.

“The United States can have a seat at Taiwan’s defence conference table, but it cannot occupy the head of that table,” Ho said.

“Military cooperation between the two sides can be upgraded, but Taiwan’s defence autonomy cannot be downgraded.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia starts to rethink its AI data centre boom: ‘at what cost?’
item.description:
Southeast Asian governments are learning some hard truths about the data centre boom they spent years working to attract, analysts say – it promises jobs, digital infrastructure and a foothold in the AI economy, but the rapid buildout is also straining power grids, land and regulatory systems.

“There is this enthusiasm to attract investments, but now it raises the question: at what cost and at what speed?” said policy researcher Mark Manantan, a research fellow for the Centre for Global Security at La Trobe University.

At first, governments had good reason to aggressively compete for data centre investment, said political economist Alvin Camba, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Indo-Pacific Security Initiative.
item.content:encoded:
Southeast Asian governments are learning some hard truths about the data centre boom they spent years working to attract, analysts say – it promises jobs, digital infrastructure and a foothold in the AI economy, but the rapid buildout is also straining power grids, land and regulatory systems.

“There is this enthusiasm to attract investments, but now it raises the question: at what cost and at what speed?” said policy researcher Mark Manantan, a research fellow for the Centre for Global Security at La Trobe University.

At first, governments had good reason to aggressively compete for data centre investment, said political economist Alvin Camba, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Indo-Pacific Security Initiative.

“They bring in large investments, support cloud and AI infrastructure, and governments worry about being left behind,” said Camba, who is also director of research at US-based AI firm Lyvi.

“In that sense, not having enough capacity looked worse than having too much. The problem is that governments understood the upside much better than the downstream costs.”

That tension is now pushing governments across the region to take a closer look at data centre projects.

Last week, the governor of Indonesia’s West Java province ordered an immediate halt to construction at a site run by Singapore’s BDx Data Centres following an inspection, reportedly because key permits had yet to be issued, including the project’s environmental impact assessment.

BDx, which runs data centres for cloud companies and other enterprises across Asia, broke ground on the 640-megawatt AI data centre campus in Jatiluhur on September 22.

On September 4, Thailand paused work on 166 data centre projects – 49 of which were under construction and 117 awaiting approval – while government agencies drew up nationwide standards governing resource use, locations, safety and economic benefits.

“These are different levels of government responding to different regulatory gaps,” Manantan said. “The buildout outran the rule book.”

Stricter rules will not automatically make Southeast Asia less competitive, according to Camba, as investors do not necessarily need the most permissive regulatory environment.

“They need to know that they can actually secure power, water, permits and connectivity and continue operating predictably,” he said. “The countries with reliable infrastructure and predictable rules may actually be more competitive than the ones that simply approve everything.”

Singapore was one example of this, he said, with Johor also moving in the same direction as it continued to attract large investments.

“Investors can live with rules, but not with unpredictability,” Manantan said. “Competitiveness will depend less on how loose the rules are and more on how coordinated and predictable they are.”

Taking stock

The recent rethink also lent regional governments more bargaining power, Camba said. “If electricity and water are scarce, they can ask what exactly they are getting in return. That could mean local procurement, renewable power, technology transfer or more investment in domestic AI capacity.”

James Guild, an assistant professor of political economy at the Indonesian International Islamic University, said the regulatory interventions were a response to the rapid acceleration of data centre investment across the region.

“Investment is pouring in, there are lots of project approvals and applications, and this is possibly straining regulators’ ability to keep up,” he said. “A pause or slow-down gives them time to adjust and maybe seek to get more value out of these projects.”

Analysts say the same factors that make Southeast Asia attractive to data centre operators – cheap land, governments eager for investment and affordable power and water – are now becoming constraints.

“Once enough projects arrive, those resources stop being abundant,” Camba said.

He pointed to Malaysia’s Johor state as a clear example. “It initially attracted enormous investment precisely because those inputs were relatively cheap,” he said. “However, Malaysia is now becoming more selective because the data centre pipeline has grown large enough to pressure power and water resources.”

In other words, data centres not only consume scarce resources, they also change the economic realities of the areas that host them.

In July, a developer’s consultant withdrew an application to reassess the feasibility of a potential site in Kota Damansara, near the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur, after the local council received nearly 300 objections to its development.

At a public hearing in Iloilo province, the central Philippines, in August, residents and farmers protested against a proposed 50MW AI data centre so vociferously that its Norwegian investor withdrew the application days later.

Public protests

Although public backlash does not appear to be the primary driver of government decisions, analysts say addressing criticism is essential to mitigate the political cost of such projects.

“Another important question is whether the demand for data centre services will be sufficient to justify such massive investment outlays,” Guild said. “People are starting to question that assumption even in the US, and it’s worth considering in Southeast Asia as well where so much of economic activity is still informal sector work.”

Camba said the objections emerging around individual projects reflected a broader question about who would ultimately bear the costs of the AI data centre buildout.

“The pushback comes from the fact that governments competed for these projects before fully understanding what hosting them at scale would mean,” he said.

“They understood the investment figures and the strategic argument, as well as the fear of falling behind. What they understood less clearly was what happens when dozens of projects start competing for the same power, water and land.”

Public opposition mattered, “because it turns those abstract infrastructure costs into something politicians must respond to”, Camba added.

In Bangkok, for example, repeated odour complaints eventually forced the government to send inspectors to a data centre site last month, where they discovered more than 200,000 litres (53,000 gallons) of diesel being stored without a permit.

In the Philippines, the government’s US-backed Pax Silica hub – aimed at boosting the country’s AI and semiconductor capabilities while attracting infrastructure investment – has similarly caused the local costs and benefits to be put under the microscope.

“Governments sold these projects based on investment and technological competitiveness, but the public experiences them through land use, power demand, water use and local disruption,” Camba said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why the PLA’s Z-10 attack helicopter is taking a bigger role at sea
item.description:
Built to hunt tanks and support ground troops, the People’s Liberation Army’s main attack helicopter is increasingly being prepared for operations at sea.

Crews of the Z-10 are training to fly from ships – a shift that could give Beijing extra firepower in an amphibious assault on Taiwan.

Manufactured by AVIC subsidiary the Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation, the Z-10 entered service with the PLA Army in late 2010. It began documented shipboard trials in 2014, when Chinese navy imagery showed a Z-10 landing on the Baxianshan Type 072A tank landing ship.
item.content:encoded:
Built to hunt tanks and support ground troops, the People’s Liberation Army’s main attack helicopter is increasingly being prepared for operations at sea.

Crews of the Z-10 are training to fly from ships – a shift that could give Beijing extra firepower in an amphibious assault on Taiwan.

Manufactured by AVIC subsidiary the Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation, the Z-10 entered service with the PLA Army in late 2010. It began documented shipboard trials in 2014, when Chinese navy imagery showed a Z-10 landing on the Baxianshan Type 072A tank landing ship.

The attack helicopter’s maritime role has gradually expanded since then. In 2020, army helicopters practised landing, refuelling and rearming on a civilian semi-submersible.

The PLA has also operated Z-10s close to the Taiwan Strait. Defence intelligence publisher Janes said satellite imagery from December 2020 showed 12 of the aircraft at the Yuanqian helicopter base on the Fujian coast opposite Taiwan, while it was still under construction.

Four years later, images appeared to show eight Z-10s aboard another semi-submersible. And in November of the following year, state broadcaster CCTV said the Type 075 amphibious assault ship could carry the army-operated helicopter.

Together, the coastal presence and shipboard trials could allow the PLA to operate Z-10s closer to Taiwan, where they could escort troop-carrying helicopters, attack coastal positions and support troops ashore.

That could be important because Janes estimates the Z-10’s combat radius at 114km to 294km (70 to 182 miles), depending on the configuration. At the lower end, that is less than the roughly 130km width of the Taiwan Strait at its narrowest point.

That range limitation also helps explain the PLA’s interest in semi-submersibles. An analysis published in June by the US Army War College’s China Landpower Studies Centre said the PLA Army would likely rely on such ships and other flat-deck vessels as forward refuelling and rearming points in any attack on Taiwan.

The PLA has also tested how the Z-10 could be used against targets at sea. Footage aired by CCTV in 2023 showed Z-10s from the Eastern Theatre Command’s 73rd Group Army firing rockets at simulated maritime targets off Fujian.

Such training points to a possible role against small boats or other targets at sea, not just positions ashore.

Official footage released this February showed Z-10s, Z-20s and Mi-17s from a PLA Army brigade taking off from a land base and training together out at sea, illustrating how attack and multirole helicopters could be used together in maritime operations.

That broader maritime role is notable because the Z-10 was developed mainly for battlefields on land.

China’s first dedicated attack helicopter emerged from a programme that drew on foreign expertise. Kamov general designer Sergei Mikheyev said in 2013 that the Russian bureau had secretly designed the helicopter’s baseline configuration for China in 1995 – a preliminary design known as Project 941 – before further development continued under Chinese direction.

The first prototype flew in April 2003.

Pratt & Whitney Canada also supplied 10 engines for development aircraft in 2001 and 2002, while production versions later switched to Chinese power plants.

The tandem-seat helicopter carries a chin-mounted 23mm cannon and can be armed with anti-tank missiles, rockets and short-range air-to-air missiles, giving the PLA Army a purpose-built platform for anti-armour strikes, close air support and armed escort.

The Z-10 has also continued to evolve in PLA service. Upgraded versions have appeared with extra armour, upward-facing exhausts intended to reduce their infrared signature, a new identification system and a new BeiDou antenna.

The PLA is also testing how the helicopter can work with drones. Chinese reports citing CCTV said crews practised engaging a drone with the helicopter’s cannon in 2026, while another exercise paired Z-10s and Z-20T assault helicopters with a KVD-002 drone.

A separate analysis published by the China Landpower Studies Centre said the exercise showed coordination between helicopter crews and drone operators, but did not show that Z-10 crews themselves controlled the drone.

The IISS Military Balance 2026, published by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, lists about 200 Z-10s in service with the PLA Army and another eight Z-10Ks with the air force’s Airborne Corps.

China also adapted the Z-10 for the export market. The resulting Z-10ME made its public debut in 2018 at Airshow China in Zhuhai. Six years later, a demonstrator at the Singapore Airshow was shown with additional features including a mast-mounted millimetre-wave radar and directed infrared countermeasures.

Pakistan inducted the Z-10ME into army aviation service in August 2025, becoming its first and so far only confirmed foreign operator. The number of Z-10MEs acquired by Islamabad has not been publicly disclosed.

The Z-10 is considerably lighter than the US-made AH-64E Apache, which is also operated by the Taiwanese army. Janes puts its maximum take-off weight at an estimated 7 tonnes, about 3.4 tonnes less than the Apache’s maximum operating weight. While the figures are not strictly like-for-like, the gap reflects the Z-10’s smaller overall design, which gives it less scope to add fuel, armour, weapons and other equipment.

That helps explain why China is also looking at a larger attack helicopter. The country is now testing a new design commonly referred to as the Z-21, though the designation remains unofficial.

First seen in 2024, the tandem-seat aircraft is substantially larger than the Z-10. Separate test flights in 2026 have shown it carrying external fuel tanks and, on another occasion, a mast-mounted radar.

The June analysis said the fuel-tank tests pointed to an emphasis on longer-range missions and assessed that the new attack helicopter could enter PLA Army service by the end of 2027, though China has announced no service date. Its larger size could also provide more capacity for fuel, armour, sensors and weapons.

In an amphibious assault on Taiwan, the analysis said, the Z-21 could operate alongside Z-10s and Z-19s during beach landings or escort Z-20 transport helicopters in air-assault operations.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia is building a new research corridor across Asia to meet China’s rise: scientists
item.description:
When chemical engineer Ahmad Zuhairi Abdullah joined Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) 22 years ago, Western institutions dominated the field, from global research infrastructure and high-impact publications to the greatest breakthroughs.

Two decades later, the centre of gravity has moved eastward, says Zuhairi, now a professor with the USM school of chemical engineering in Penang.

“[Not much was known] about China at that time when I joined the university. I knew that they had quite a number of good universities and I was aware of their publications because some of them I referred to in my research work,” he said.
item.content:encoded:
When chemical engineer Ahmad Zuhairi Abdullah joined Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) 22 years ago, Western institutions dominated the field, from global research infrastructure and high-impact publications to the greatest breakthroughs.

Two decades later, the centre of gravity has moved eastward, says Zuhairi, now a professor with the USM school of chemical engineering in Penang.

“[Not much was known] about China at that time when I joined the university. I knew that they had quite a number of good universities and I was aware of their publications because some of them I referred to in my research work,” he said.

“But definitely nothing much was heard in terms of collaboration with Chinese counterparts. Now, you see a lot [of scientists and students] coming here,” for studies, research and fostering collaborations, Zuhairi added.

“Chinese scientists are very advanced in materials science,” he said, pointing to the high volume of publications and contributions to scientific journals.

As China rises as a scientific powerhouse and Malaysia diversifies its research networks to find collaborators closer to home, partnerships in critical domains – from semiconductors to sustainable energy materials – are increasingly shaping regional innovation.

“China is very aggressive and opening its doors to collaborations, which is shifting from probably 10 years back [when] it was quite close to their own things,” Zuhairi said.

He also observed that China was making an effort to include Southeast Asian partners in its research ecosystem, with some provincial funding programmes requiring Chinese scientists to work with researchers from the region.

At the Joint Laboratory of Biomass Chemical Engineering, inaugurated in January, researchers from USM and Huaqiao University in China’s southeastern coastal province of Fujian are working together to turn organic waste and plant material into useful products, as well as developing sustainable energy materials and low-carbon technologies.

According to Zuhairi, one of the common research interests between the two countries lies in combining Malaysia’s abundant agricultural waste with China’s advanced process engineering.

Malaysia’s massive palm oil sector generates vast quantities of biomass, including pressed fibre and kernel shells which contain lignin, a bonding agent in plants that was traditionally treated as a low-value by-product in the pulp and paper industry.

Zuhairi’s research aims to develop specialised catalysts to break down the lignin – the second most abundant biopolymer after cellulose – into smaller molecular fragments.

“Lignin is converted into phenolic substances, [which] will be a feedstock for the conversion into something more valuable,” he said.

These valuable renewable chemicals include adhesives and fuel additives to improve fuel performance and reduce emissions.

While chemical engineering lays the foundation for sustainable materials, advanced hardware and semiconductors are pushing the Malaysia-China corridor into critical hi-tech domains.

At USM’s Institute of Nano Optoelectronics Research and Technology (INOR), director Mohd Zamir Pakhuruddin is leading research into wide-bandgap semiconductors like gallium nitride, solar cells and nanophotonic devices.

The institute has broadened its international research partnerships over the past two years to work with scientists in China, Japan and Saudi Arabia, diversifying beyond its long-standing ties with research institutions in Germany and France.

It has established collaborations with leading Chinese institutions in semiconductor research, such as Chongqing University, Fudan University, Harbin Institute of Technology, Hunan Institute of Technology and Nanjing University.

For Zamir, an associate professor in advanced photovoltaic materials and devices, working across borders is a necessary step towards advancing technology, with the global supply and manufacturing chain for chips an example.

“To be able to realise high-end semiconductor devices, there is no one country that can do that alone. The same goes for the collaboration of the academy as well,” he said.

“We need our partners to be able to complement somewhere across the value chain of the fabrication.”

Malaysia aims to move beyond its back-end chip assembly and testing role towards integrated circuit design, high-end manufacturing and niche equipment, as outlined in its 10-year road map, the National Semiconductor Strategy released in 2024.

“The very goal of the national semiconductor strategy is to enhance the capacity of the nation to be stronger in the front end while leveraging the current strength in the back end,” Zamir said.

When asked about the growing trade friction and technological competition between Washington and Beijing, Zamir said that science and collaborations “should remain open”.

“Malaysia is in the neutral position politically because we do not favour sides. We do not choose sides anyway. The same goes for our academic collaboration. It is more of a diversification of our international partners that we have done in recent years,” he said.

Among INOR’s Chinese collaborators is the Harbin Institute of Technology (HIT), an institution subject to US sanctions and one of the “Seven Sons of National Defence” – universities directly under China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

In this partnership, the Malaysian and Chinese researchers are co-developing space solar cells with high radiation resilience for low Earth orbit satellite applications.

Asked about how the institute manages its partnership with HIT, Zamir said jointly agreed proposal terms defined the scope of their cooperation.

“In the areas that we agreed to collaborate, I believe these are the areas that are open for collaboration and we should leverage as long as the areas are open for exploration,” he said.

Zamir acknowledged that some fields were restricted but emphasised focusing on open avenues: “For the areas that are open for collaboration, we go by the first principle [that] science should be open and let’s leverage each other’s strengths to win together.”

Over his multiple trips to various Chinese cities in the past two years, Zamir said he observed that Western export controls and sanctions had accelerated China’s push towards domestic self-sufficiency.

“But in science, I think the bright side is it is pushing the capability of the nation to develop your very own technology – from science to technology, to eventually realising technology on the production floor,” he said.

At USM’s school of physics, deputy dean and associate professor Ahmad Fairuz Omar said that global cooperation endured as fundamental scientific inquiry continued to transcend borders.

“Science is very universal,” Fairuz said. “From our engagement with all different parts of the world, including China … everybody is passionate about knowledge.”

In May, the school hosted scientists from the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics’ College of Physics, who shared insights into using AI in research, nuclear physics and quantum-enabled space exploration technologies.

They also explored potential collaborations in fields such as cosmology and materials fabrication.

Fairuz pointed to his research using optical spectrometers to measure fruit quality metrics like sweetness, pH and firmness across different wavelengths as an area of potential for collaboration with China.

“The final intention is [to] find out several wavelengths that can specifically cater for the measurement of that particular quality of the fruit. That is what we are looking for. But the tricky situation is that fruits are really diversified.”

Looking to build “common understanding on this diversified world”, he said, “we can see that there are many researchers from China also working on visible near-infrared spectroscopy, particularly on agriculture”.

“[With] the growing number of people working in this area, hopefully that will be some sort of meeting point.”

Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

item.title: [SCMP] Japan’s tame answer to jobseeker sex harassment: name and shame
item.description:
Final-year students invited to recruiters’ apartments for help with their applications. Coffee dates with alumni who promise to explain how the company works. Inappropriate interview questions about boyfriends, marriage plans and sex lives.

For young women in Japan, looking for a job has long entailed submitting themselves to the skewed power dynamics of the recruitment process.

And before Thursday, no official legal safeguards existed to protect these jobseekers from such harassment.
item.content:encoded:
Final-year students invited to recruiters’ apartments for help with their applications. Coffee dates with alumni who promise to explain how the company works. Inappropriate interview questions about boyfriends, marriage plans and sex lives.

For young women in Japan, looking for a job has long entailed submitting themselves to the skewed power dynamics of the recruitment process.

And before Thursday, no official legal safeguards existed to protect these jobseekers from such harassment.

Campaigners and advocates have welcomed the change, but say it lacks teeth and came years too late, even as societal attitudes may have already moved ahead of it.

“It is good that this has happened, but it has taken five years of discussions to get to the point where it has become law,” said Chisato Kitanaka, an associate professor of sociology at Hiroshima University who advises the government on gender issues.

“Government measures against sexual harassment in Japan are very weak, including this kind of harassment.”

Amendments to the Equal Employment Opportunity Act that took effect last week address harassment in its many forms and settings, from misbehaviour in the office to verbal abuse and threats from customers in shops, taxis and elsewhere. One section deals specifically with what the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare terms “job-seeking sexual harassment”.

The ministry’s website lists examples: staff who make sexual jokes or tease applicants such that it causes distress, who pressure them into a sexual relationship, or who repeatedly invite them to one-to-one meals or drinks.

Employers are now legally required to take steps to stop their staff harassing applicants in this way, with corporate compliance enforced through the threat of publicly shaming offending companies and exposing them to the prospect of civil lawsuits and financial damages.

Kitanaka called the changes a “step in the right direction”, but said they did not go far enough.

“There is no formal punishment for companies that let this happen, with the only real sanction the ministry releasing the name of the company publicly,” she said.

She expects large companies and organisations to enforce the rules more stringently than smaller firms, even as part-time workers, freelancers and others in precarious jobs continue to have too few protections.

Sumie Kawakami, a lecturer at Yamanashi Gakuin University and author of a book on gender issues, agreed that reform was long overdue.

“This isn’t something that has only been happening in recent years and is now being addressed,” she said. “It has been going on for decades.”

One in three

A survey of 1,000 recent jobseekers conducted by Japan’s labour ministry in 2023 showed that 31.9 per cent of respondents – nearly one in three – reported being harassed.

Unnecessary physical contact and questions about sexual matters were each cited by over 25 per cent of the harassed respondents, while nearly 29 per cent said they were on the receiving end of sexual jokes and teasing.

One in four of the men and women who had these experiences reported feeling less motivated in their job search and more than one in three said they felt “anger, dissatisfaction or anxiety”.

For two dozen or so, the effect on their mental health was such that they required hospital treatment.

In the past, companies typically tried to hush up such incidents, but a number of court cases over the years have shone a spotlight on the issue.

In 2019, a male construction company employee was charged with indecent assault after allegedly convincing a university student to come to his flat on the pretext of helping her prepare for an interview.

His employer, Obayashi Corp, apologised and promised to “urgently review” its procedures, subsequently setting up a harassment prevention office and conducting “emergency training” for staff involved in recruitment.

Prosecutors ultimately dropped charges against the man without publicly providing a reason. Whether he kept his job is unknown.

That same year, a 24-year-old trading company employee was arrested and charged with sexual assault and theft after a student he met through a networking app accused him of getting her drunk and using a stolen key to molest her in her hotel room. His employer, Sumitomo Corp, issued a statement soon after his arrest, confirming his disciplinary dismissal.

One of the most serious cases involved Kenshiro Maruta, who was sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2023 for drugging and raping at least 10 female students who connected with him through apps designed to match jobseekers with university alumni and career counsellors.

His employer, Recruit Communications, fired Maruta following his arrest and launched an internal investigation, vowing to never allow such an outrage happen again.

“There have been many incidents in the past and gradually the government has changed its policies,” said Kitanaka, the sociologist. “Now, at last, they have changed the law.”

‘Not acceptable today’

Back in the 1980s, when gender studies lecturer Kawakami first joined Japan’s workforce, it was still dominated by men. Women had to work harder than their male counterparts just to be taken seriously or to advance, she said.

“Young women in the past did not feel that they could speak out when this happened to them because they wanted to get a good job and career,” she said of harassment.

Kawakami has watched attitudes shift in recent years, however, especially among the young women at her university preparing to start their careers.

“I think it has changed quite a lot,” she said. “There is far greater awareness among working people and companies about what constitutes unacceptable behaviour, and I believe employers are far less willing to tolerate sexual harassment.”

And while the threat of public naming and shaming a company might seem tame compared to criminal convictions, Kawakami says the threat “is a powerful one”.

“Companies are desperate to find capable and qualified staff nowadays, and negative publicity that would go with a sexual harassment accusation would be hugely damaging,” she said.

“Young women have lots of work options at the moment. Why would they go to a company that fails to act in a situation like this?”

One recent graduate, who declined to be named, told This Week in Asia that outlawing “clearly sexist” comments or actions by recruiters was a good idea, even if she did not believe that women of her generation would put up with such behaviour.

“If one of my friends were asked something inappropriate in an interview or were invited out for drinks, I’m certain that the man would be shouted at and his company would hear about it,” she said. “It’s just not acceptable today.”

item.title: [SCMP] Sinking city, rising rage: Bangkok’s floods fuel fury over government inaction
item.description:
As floodwaters surged from Bangkok’s drains, Fon’s car sank faster than her hopes of escaping the floods unscathed. She had bought it less than a month earlier.

“I woke up at 5am but it was too late,” the 24-year-old said, recalling her decision last weekend to wait until dawn to move her car to a nearby shopping centre. “My car was already submerged. I hadn’t even started making the payments and it’s gone.”

Relentless rain paralysed Thailand’s capital this September, dumping a month’s worth of precipitation on the city in just three days.
item.content:encoded:
As floodwaters surged from Bangkok’s drains, Fon’s car sank faster than her hopes of escaping the floods unscathed. She had bought it less than a month earlier.

“I woke up at 5am but it was too late,” the 24-year-old said, recalling her decision last weekend to wait until dawn to move her car to a nearby shopping centre. “My car was already submerged. I hadn’t even started making the payments and it’s gone.”

Relentless rain paralysed Thailand’s capital this September, dumping a month’s worth of precipitation on the city in just three days.

Bangkok, a city long plagued by a sinking feeling, went fully underwater. Not all of it, but enough of the city’s east and northeast to offer a terrifying teaser of what may lie ahead as this year’s “super” El Nino climate pattern intensifies into 2027.

In the Khlong Chan neighbourhood of Bangkok’s Bang Kapi district, Fon – whose full name is Siraprapha Sangseeluem – was still stranded in her block of flats five days after the deluge.

Her scathing assessment of the authorities’ handling of the floods? “I can say only one thing: the government is totally useless,” she said.

Some of her neighbours have been even less diplomatic. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul was met with a volley of abuse when he arrived to distribute relief to the flats last Sunday.

The reception was similar in several places Anutin visited last week with his cabinet ministers and the media, in a city that largely did not vote for him. His Bhumjaithai Party did not win any of Bangkok’s constituency seats in February’s general election.

Anger has boiled over in recent days at a government that seemed blindsided by a calamity meteorologists had warned was brewing, but which city and central authorities alike played down in the days before it struck.

Anutin’s own campaign boast that his party would make the country “so rich, you won’t know what to do with your money” has come back to haunt him. “I feel so rich”, chanted crowds of angry residents sarcastically as he arrived to distribute food and water.

I know we weren’t good enough, or prepared well enough

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Anutin acknowledged the backlash. “I know we weren’t good enough, or prepared well enough,” he said. “The fact that people scolded me, criticised me … rest assured that I’ve heard you and I’m not ignoring you.”

Critics are unconvinced, however. “If the measurement of the prime minister’s job is to manage the situation, to bring calm, a sense of trust … then he fails miserably,” said political commentator Voranai Vanijaka.

On September 25, as floods swallowed Bangkok’s roads, homes, shops and restaurants, residents struggled to find their bearings. Governor Chadchart Sittipunt, normally hypervigilant, appeared caught off guard by the speed and scale of the rising water. He apologised days later for delayed warnings and a slow start to the relief effort.

Anutin, who is also the interior minister, cut short a diplomatic visit to London to oversee the response. His initial absence was nonetheless felt in Thailand’s highly centralised, hierarchical political system, with key officials seeming reluctant to make snap decisions without him.

On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers blasted the government’s flood response, criticising everything from slow warnings to the sluggish relief effort.

Rain and floods are unpredictable and the lack of comprehensive flood defences of the kind found in Singapore, Shanghai or Amsterdam is the failing of successive Thai governments. But critics still say Anutin was caught flat-footed.

“As a leader, you are the man in charge, and you have to take control of the situation,” Voranai said.

“What he chose to do instead – hit the streets, pass out food, apparently pass out cash, walk through [flood]water with no shoes on – was political marketing. Political marketing is always part of politics … but he can’t forget to be the man in charge.”

Hotter, wetter, deadlier

As the planet heats to unprecedented and dangerous levels, extreme weather events are becoming ever more erratic and destructive, presenting governments everywhere with challenges many are ill prepared to meet.

As of Wednesday, Japan’s capital had logged 35 consecutive days of rain – its longest streak on record – while wildfires continue to rage in Indonesia’s Kalimantan region, sending toxic haze across borders to Singapore and Malaysia.

Thailand’s recent floods have cost at least 40 people their lives, with estimates of the damage running to hundreds of millions of US dollars.

In Bangkok, the floods were the worst in 15 years, filling drains and canals to capacity and affecting roughly one-tenth of the capital. The country’s southern provinces, where the rainy season typically peaks between November and January, are now bracing for a similar onslaught.

Bangkok’s misfortune has been decades in the making. The city’s ever-expanding urban sprawl is slowly sinking into the soft clay beneath it. Concrete has spread upwards and outwards far faster than investment in infrastructure, especially drainage – effectively turning the built-up city centre into a basin with few natural outlets or floodplains.

It floods easily in large storms and in the increasingly common “rain bombs” that dump vast quantities of water on the city in a matter of hours. In 2011, the worst floods in recent memory submerged the north of Bangkok, killing dozens and leaving parts of the capital up to two metres (6½ feet) under water for weeks on end.

This year’s floods, which may not be over yet, were the result of ceaseless rains overwhelming drains and inundating entire neighbourhoods, including affluent ones, with filthy, sludge-filled floodwater.

Drowning in delays

On Tuesday, Anutin’s cabinet approved a 160 billion baht (US$4.8 billion) plan to divert floodwaters away from the capital. It includes a new canal from Chai Nat province that aims to relieve pressure on the Chao Phraya River, which currently carries run-off from northern and central Thailand straight through Bangkok.

But that project is slated to take eight years to complete and critics say more needs to be done about the country’s sclerotic decision-making in the meantime.

Thailand’s hulking bureaucracy meant overlapping agencies were often left duplicating work as they deferred to one another, said Winyu “John” Wongsurawat, an actor turned political commentator and podcaster.

“When a crisis hits, they turn to the prime minister. Only then does the prime minister come in and say, ‘OK, do this.’ The crisis passes, and the water recedes before any real solution is reached,” he said.

“This isn’t limited to Bangkok. We can see it happening all over the country. Bangkok gets more attention because people there are louder, let’s be honest, it’s the capital.”

The central provinces of Ayutthaya and Ang Thong regularly endured weeks or months of flooding, Winyu said, “but just don’t make big news”.

A government that is prioritising growth and foreign investment now faces a conundrum. Most of Thailand’s data centres, and the supply chains for printed circuit boards and semiconductors that go with them, are being built in and around Bangkok, central Ayutthaya and the country’s eastern provinces.

All are low-lying and highly flood prone. The 2011 floods hammered the electronics and car industries of Thailand’s central provinces.

How a government with a sky-high ratio of debt to gross domestic product will pay for far-reaching flood resilience, public compensation and clean-up costs that climb each year remains unclear.

Other long-term economic risks are also emerging.
