“Repeated calamities from floods in Bangkok and other provinces pose challenges to Thailand’s attractiveness as a foreign investment destination,” said Pavida Pananond, a professor of international business at Thammasat Business School.

Companies pouring billions of US dollars into tech infrastructure “would be at a higher risk given Thailand’s frequent floods”, she said, adding that the latest deluge came just as the nation was trying to attract more foreign investment “in the era of global supply chain shifts”.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong vs Singapore in tackling bad behaviour
item.description:
Singapore is doing something about uncivilised behaviour on public buses. The city state has started enforcing new regulations that carry an immediate fine of up to S$500 (US$390) if you put your feet up on seats, play loud audio on your phone or make a nuisance of yourself in other ways such as eating, drinking and littering.

This aligns with existing rules governing passenger conduct on Singapore’s MRT railway system.

Did you know we have long had similar regulations for Hong Kong’s MTR network under its own by-laws? Probably not, because nobody cares, but they do exist.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore is doing something about uncivilised behaviour on public buses. The city state has started enforcing new regulations that carry an immediate fine of up to S$500 (US$390) if you put your feet up on seats, play loud audio on your phone or make a nuisance of yourself in other ways such as eating, drinking and littering.

This aligns with existing rules governing passenger conduct on Singapore’s MRT railway system.

Did you know we have long had similar regulations for Hong Kong’s MTR network under its own by-laws? Probably not, because nobody cares, but they do exist.

For instance, playing audio loudly on trains is punishable by a fine of up to HK$2,000 (US$250). The same penalty applies for uncouth behaviour such as placing your feet on seats and for ignoring eating or drinking bans.

Not only that, using profanity and language deemed offensive carries a fine of HK$5,000. If the MTR actually enforced this particular by-law, it would collect a revenue bonanza.

Rushing the train doors when they’re already closing, with the warning beeps going off, should earn you a penalty of HK$2,000 as well. It should but it won’t because the difference between Hong Kong and Singapore is that many of these rules are just there for lip service. Nobody bothers to follow or enforce them in one jurisdiction, while they are taken more seriously in the other.

You can resurrect the usual tropes about personal freedoms and repression in this comparison, in which we’re somehow supposed to take comfort in the assumption that at least it feels less controlling here than in Singapore. But if it’s about curtailing the freedom to behave badly in public and shared spaces, then bring on that Singaporean-style repression.

There is the concept of liberty, which is the freedom to act responsibly within an accepted legal and social framework without being a nuisance to others. Then there is licence, which is the entitlement to do whatever you want with zero regard for societal norms and the rights of others around you.

Millions of people in this city can’t be bothered with basic courtesy and social graces. These include holding the door open for someone right behind you, resisting the urge to furiously jab the “close door” button to deny someone entry into a lift even as you’re making eye contact, waiting for people to alight first before storming onto trains and many other daily acts of incivility and social ineptitude.

There is a lot of pent-up rage out there. This is reflected in a whole lot of honking in Hong Kong as rude and impatient drivers blast perceived irritants such as fellow motorists slowing down or getting stuck in front of them, children, cardboard-collecting grannies and even wheelchair users who fail to get out of their way in time.

Also in their way, as well as everyone else’s, are the mobile phone zombies. These people have their noses buried in their electronic pacifier while sauntering along the most crowded streets and walkways in the world with infuriating apathy and total disregard for the natural flow of human traffic.

The cocooned self-indulgence of these sidewalk narcissists and human roadblocks everywhere we go is as exhausting in its nonchalance as it is frustrating in its main-character syndrome. They expect the entire sea of humanity to conveniently part and warp around their immovable bodies like ignorable background noise.

This is not a problem unique to Hong Kong, but there is a difference that makes it all the more egregious here. While most of the world measures population density per square kilometre, Hong Kong’s 7.5 million residents are crammed into just 25 per cent of its total land area – the rest is uninhabitable or designated as protected areas and country parks.

That means when we talk in terms of volumetric hyper-density – how people actually fit into public space – we are in a different league. Vertical urbanism accommodates us, but when we pour out of our anthills to go about our daily business on the ground, the congestion is next-level.

On the streets of Mong Kok, for example, academic studies have shown that the population density can be up to 600,000 people per square kilometre, even though the figure for the wider district is 130,000 people, which is still one for the record books.

On an average footbridge or elevated walkway in Mong Kok, density can be up to 3.5 people per square metre. This is insane, and it is also why people who make it worse should not be dismissed as harmless manifestations of first-world problems. These miscreants with mobile phones are directly and constantly escalating stress levels in an already high-strung society.

Why can’t we have a law against it, just like we have one penalising the misuse of mobile phones while driving?

Should you feel the urge to pause in mid-stride to check your phone while walking elbow-to-elbow with 1,000 fellow humans at any given time, pull over to the side and get your dose of instant gratification without obstructing the rest of us.

If that sounds unrealistic, remember that people said something similar about banning smoking in public spaces some decades ago. Look how we pressed ahead with it and prospered.

Comparisons to Singapore bring to mind what the late Lee Kuan Yew said when he was accused of infringing on personal liberties by micromanaging public behaviour: “I say without the slightest remorse, that we wouldn’t be here, we would not have made economic progress, if we had not intervened on very personal matters – who your neighbour is, how you live, the noise you make, how you spit, or what language you use. We decide what is right. Never mind what people think.”

What a splendid man, unafraid and unapologetic about putting facts before feelings to get things done for the greater good. And what a pleasing thought, imagining what he would have done about the mobile phone menace if he were still around today.

Sure, pearls would be clutched and token noises sounded, but most of us would appreciate the net improvement in the quality of life. I’m not advocating the introduction of caning in Hong Kong, mind you, but perhaps a bit of a spanking is long overdue.

item.title: [SCMP] Wing Shya: photographer to Wong Kar-wai on working with the great and good of Hong Kong cinema
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Hong Kong in 1964. My parents came from Shandong province, in mainland China, arriving illegally, later legalised – a common story for that generation. I went to the all-boys Salesian School, in Chai Wan, and was not a good student. I spent all my time messing around with friends. Then, at 17 or 18, I watched a film called Boat People (1982) and there was a character holding a camera who looked cool. Something happened in me. “I want to be that,” I thought. Not the actor – the photographer. I saved every dollar I made from part-time jobs until I could buy a camera, then I started to photograph everything: friends, family, the street, skateboarders. I didn’t really have a plan. I just liked looking through that little window.

MY ENGLISH WAS so bad and I didn’t do well in my exams, so university in Hong Kong wasn’t possible. Art school was the only door open to me and, I’ll admit, a good excuse not to get a real job yet. I went to a technical college, the Lee Wai Lee Technical Institute (in Kowloon Tong), before I found the Emily Carr College of Art and Design, in Vancouver, Canada – the only overseas school I could afford, where tuition for international students was the same as for local students.

I WORKED THREE or four jobs at a time, sometimes illegally, as I was on a student visa. I delivered food for a Chinese restaurant, waited tables and even cleaned houses that were a two-hour drive from the city. On weekends, I would sell my drawings in Stanley Park.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in Hong Kong in 1964. My parents came from Shandong province, in mainland China, arriving illegally, later legalised – a common story for that generation. I went to the all-boys Salesian School, in Chai Wan, and was not a good student. I spent all my time messing around with friends. Then, at 17 or 18, I watched a film called Boat People (1982) and there was a character holding a camera who looked cool. Something happened in me. “I want to be that,” I thought. Not the actor – the photographer. I saved every dollar I made from part-time jobs until I could buy a camera, then I started to photograph everything: friends, family, the street, skateboarders. I didn’t really have a plan. I just liked looking through that little window.

MY ENGLISH WAS so bad and I didn’t do well in my exams, so university in Hong Kong wasn’t possible. Art school was the only door open to me and, I’ll admit, a good excuse not to get a real job yet. I went to a technical college, the Lee Wai Lee Technical Institute (in Kowloon Tong), before I found the Emily Carr College of Art and Design, in Vancouver, Canada – the only overseas school I could afford, where tuition for international students was the same as for local students.

I WORKED THREE or four jobs at a time, sometimes illegally, as I was on a student visa. I delivered food for a Chinese restaurant, waited tables and even cleaned houses that were a two-hour drive from the city. On weekends, I would sell my drawings in Stanley Park.

I DID A double major: graphic design and fine art. In the summer, I’d drive to San Francisco, or fly to New York on the cheapest ticket I could find. I could earn a few dollars drawing people in Washington Square Park, in Greenwich Village. I had so much energy then.

AFTER GRADUATING IN 1991, six classmates and I opened a graphic-design company in Vancouver. Eight months in, we were doing well. One afternoon at a restaurant in Chinatown, I picked up a Hong Kong gossip magazine and looked at the layout. I said to my friends, “I have to go back – this design is terrible. I want to do something in the city.” They tried to talk me out of it. But within a week, I’d sold my car and bought a ticket home, without telling my mother. I flew back and rang the doorbell. She opened it and said, “Why are you here? You’re not welcome. We have no space.” I slept on the sofa.

WORK WAS HARD to find, but in 1992, I won a biennial photography prize and gave the money to my mother – it’s the right order of things. In 1993, I got a job at J. Walter Thompson (JWT), the advertising agency, but only lasted about a year; I had too much ego and was always fighting clients. I ran into an old school friend, Jan Lamb Hoi-fung – a singer who DJ’d at Commercial Radio Hong Kong – on the street by chance and he got me hired as the creative director there. It was a tiny department, just two of us, responsible for everything – stage design, ads, CD covers, concerts. I worked hard and I loved it. I got to know the biggest Cantopop stars: Jacky Cheung Hok-yau, Andy Lau Tak-wah and Faye Wong – she was there all the time.

THROUGH A FRIEND, Eric Kot Man-fai, my portfolio landed in front of Wong Kar-wai, in 1996. He said I could shoot some promotional pictures. On a Japanese commercial he directed, I hid behind a sofa so the crew wouldn’t throw me out of the tiny set – and when the official photographer could not get enough pictures, my photos were the only ones that worked. Because of that, Wong Kar-wai sent me to Argentina a year later, for Happy Together, starring Tony Leung Chiu-wai and Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing.

I HAD NEVER done film stills professionally. I didn’t even own a sound blimp – the soundproof box for your camera so you can’t hear the shutter going off. Because of this, I mostly shot between takes. I captured the actors sitting, waiting, hanging out: Tony and Leslie just breathing, not performing. One afternoon, on a rooftop, the street noise was so loud that my shutter was no longer an issue and I could finally shoot freely. Most of my images that you know from that film came from that one afternoon.

THEN, THE COLOUR. I was shooting slide film. Wong Kar-wai demanded to see the images immediately, but there were no labs where we were in Argentina that could process slide film. We found a shop that only did negative film. Because slide film is positive film, they ran mine through the wrong chemicals, and that turned everything green. Argentina’s grey walls became luminous. In the end, Wong Kar-wai loved it. It became the visual language of the whole film. I can call it a mistake, or I can call it, “I had no choice. It ended up like this.” After that, I left the radio station and started my company, Shya-la-la Workshop.

ONE DAY, WE were shooting in a train station – it was too noisy for sound recording – so I could shoot freely. Leslie was annoyed at me for distracting him. My shutter was too loud, but I kept going. I explained to him, “I’m only scared of Wong Kar-wai, not you. Because he hired me, only he can fire me.” He looked at me for a long moment, then said, “I like your attitude. When we get back to Hong Kong, you’ll work for me.”

HE MEANT IT. From that day until he died, I shot almost every photograph of Leslie for his work, his concerts, behind the scenes, albums and tours. He was the most considerate person I’ve known in this industry. He remembered everyone’s habits, every name, if you took milk in your coffee. He looked after the whole crew, from driver to delivery boy. We travelled together for concerts, shot in countries I’d never been to. I still think about him.

FOR In the Mood for Love (2000), Wong Kar-wai gave me one instruction: the film is about red. He gave me some music to listen to, and that was it, initially. So, in 1999, I went to Tokyo, bought 40 or 50 different rolls of film, shot test after test and laid every print in front of him. He picked one: an old, obscure film – barely still in production, its colour deeply reddish. I called the manufacturer; they were closing the following month because nobody was buying their film any more. “How many rolls remained,” I asked. “Two hundred,” they said. I bought every single one.

THAT PHOTO FILM was made in the 1960s or 70s, and its dyes were slowly failing – that’s why my shots for In the Mood for Love look the way they do. After we finished the film, there was none left anywhere in the world.

THERE ARE PEOPLE who I learned almost everything from. One, of course, is Wong Kar-wai, who gave me access to everyone, all these famous faces. I learned how to crop a photograph by watching him on the monitor. But another one of my real teachers is William Chang Suk-ping – the famous production designer and art director. Even now, we work together regularly. Just the other day, I was on a shoot, with William beside me. I learned what makes a picture by watching what Wong Kar-wai and William chose to keep and what they threw away. I don’t think of my work as mine alone. It is a long conversation with two people I deeply respect.

IN 2010, FOX came to Hong Kong to make a Chinese film – my feature-film directorial debut, Hot Summer Days. Stars such as Jacky Cheung, Maggie Cheung Man-yuk, Nicholas Tse Ting-fung and Daniel Wu Yin-cho all appeared in it, for very little money, as a favour to me because we had 20 years of trust.

DIRECTING FELT LIKE another universe. You have to think about logistics, 80-people crews, egos, dangerous rigs, scenes and even the crew lunches! I’ve made more films since. I still shoot fashion campaigns, recently for Chanel and Bottega Veneta, and – fingers crossed – I am now writing a television drama.

MY FIRST BOOKS came about because cultural curator Shelly Verthime told me at a dinner many years ago that she wanted to make a book. One day, in 2015, she called from Hong Kong International Airport, so I put a hard drive with every photo I owned into a taxi and sent it to her, at the terminal. She spent a year and a half editing alone. An investor funded the printing and an exhibition in Shanghai, in 2017. My shows in Japan (in Tokyo and Kyoto), the books (Chaos [2020], Solace [2024], Is [2026] and more) – they happened all because someone pushed. I never start these things myself.

MY WORK HAS been in the Mori Art Museum, in Tokyo, and in the V&A, in London. I don’t think about it much. I’ve done it already, and the future is more exciting to me than the past. What I still love is being on set – the mess, the crew eating together, the gossip, the waiting. I think the universe already has a script written. My job is only to follow my heart and see what page it turns to next.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese art takes long march home from US museums
item.description:
Christie’s auctioneer Rupert Banner leans forward with practised showmanship as bidding stalls on a rare Yongzheng bowl near New York’s iconic Rockefeller Centre. He pauses as if willing offers from thin air, scanning dozens of in-person buyers and phone banks connecting with China, London, Texas.

It will be a bad look if the frenzy abates for this delicate peach-decorated bowl highlighted on Christie’s glossy Chinese sale catalogue and online advertising. But bidding soon resumes with a realised price of US$2.05 million, the sale’s top porcelain result.

The bowl is among over 100 items from the Art Institute of Chicago, part of a broader generational transition as rarefied relics amassed by 19th century American Gilded Age “robber barons” return to Chinese hands after gathering dust for more than a century in Western museums.
item.content:encoded:
Christie’s auctioneer Rupert Banner leans forward with practised showmanship as bidding stalls on a rare Yongzheng bowl near New York’s iconic Rockefeller Centre. He pauses as if willing offers from thin air, scanning dozens of in-person buyers and phone banks connecting with China, London, Texas.

It will be a bad look if the frenzy abates for this delicate peach-decorated bowl highlighted on Christie’s glossy Chinese sale catalogue and online advertising. But bidding soon resumes with a realised price of US$2.05 million, the sale’s top porcelain result.

The bowl is among over 100 items from the Art Institute of Chicago, part of a broader generational transition as rarefied relics amassed by 19th century American Gilded Age “robber barons” return to Chinese hands after gathering dust for more than a century in Western museums.

Then it is the turn of lot 1032, an archaistic zun-form vase once owned by finance magnate Charles Schwab. “They’re off and running,” says Banner, before a Chinese man snags it for US$40,960.

“China lost many relics to the West because of corrupt officials,” the new owner says. “We started losing our best relics to the West after the Song dynasty, lost on the Maritime Silk Road, with Guangzhou among the key ports. I want to bring this back to Guangzhou.”

The “wealthy farmer” from Jiangxi, who is in his 40s and dressed in black sportswear and trainers, does not give his name like many in the discreet art trade.

“The West is in decline, and it’s only fitting,” he says, adding that he will donate it to a Chinese museum. His next stop: France and Italy to repatriate more treasures.

Institute sales from the two-day event total US$17.3 million, led by a waistless Huanghuali daybed at US$3.2 million.

For Chinese art collectors, items from US museums hold special cachet, given their prestige and assurances against counterfeiting.

“The pieces that have museum provenance are absolutely the focus of any collector,” said Angela McAteer, Chinese works of art department head at rival auction house Sotheby’s. “In a category that’s plagued by not only fake pieces but fake provenance, fake catalogues, fake labels, you name it, a de-accession piece with that provenance is watertight.”

Provenance – ensuring items are not fake or stolen – and de-accession – essentially selling unneeded stuff from your attic – are among the rarefied art world’s special language, along with good title, burned art and white-glove sales.

US museum auctions also offer a recent workaround. After US President Donald Trump’s 2025 tariff bender, imported Chinese art faced up to 12.5 per cent taxes – and in some categories double – evidence that even art cannot avoid geopolitics, spurring US-sourced sales. A few months ago, after intense lobbying, the US Trade Representative agreed to exempt fine art.

Recent auctions include items from the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Brooklyn Museum, San Francisco Asian Art Museum and Honolulu Museum of Art.

“Every major museum in America has had to grapple with this. These American tycoons were buying all this Chinese art and donating thousands of objects,” said Vicki Paloympis, Christie’s Chinese department head, navigating half-opened crates ahead of the public viewing. “Insurance is high, storage is expensive, and they have all these pieces that are duplicates and triplets.”

Another factor, adds McAteer, is that museums display fewer objects these days, leaving more in storage.

Asian museums tend not to de-accession given strict heritage-protection laws, although private or corporate museums with underfunded endowments sometimes do. Japan’s Fujita Art Museum faced a cash crunch before its hugely successful 2017 US$262.8 million sale.

And last month’s heavily subscribed Okada Museum of Art Hong Kong auction of rare Chinese ceramics yielded HK$174.7 million (US$22.3 million) after its founder, pachinko magnate Kazuo Okada, faced a US$50 million legal dispute involving casino mogul Steve Wynn. Hong Kong faces fewer art-sale restrictions than mainland China.

But museum sales are hardly exempt from criticism.

“Some people were nationalistic. They wrote saying, look, American museums are getting rid of Chinese art because they don’t like Chinese culture,” said Tao Wang, the Chicago institute’s Chinese art curator, after months spent teeing up the sale. “But we made statements, and people realised what the de-accession purpose is, to upgrade and enhance.”

De-accession at accredited US museums follows exhaustive legal, ethical and curatorial standards, including restrictions on how proceeds can be spent after some early scandals.

“There are some people who dig in their heels and say museums shouldn’t sell their treasures, blah, blah,” said Eric Zetterquist, an artist and gallery owner. “I­t’s a much more natural process than people realise.”

Rising prices have given US museums further incentive to houseclean. The global Chinese fine art auction market rose from US$200-300 million in 1995 to US$5 billion in 2015 before settling at US$1.75 billion last year, according to industry estimates, with huge upside. A single Andy Warhol image of Brigitte Bardot sold in May for US$24.8 million, more than the entire Okada collection.

Long wary of the trade, Beijing has increasingly welcomed collecting while keeping a close eye on corruption, capital flight, tax evasion and political dissent.

“This is not a flashy Rolls-Royce, so Chinese people can still buy and not feel like the government’s going to come down on them,” said Zetterquist. “And the government wholly encourages people to buy Chinese masterpieces and bring them back to China.”

Wang’s career mirrors the dramatic arc of China’s art market.

Born in Yunnan in 1962, he lived through the 1966–1976 Cultural Revolution, watching art and books burned in the river and the anti-“Four Olds” campaigns that saw museums closed.

His early formal education was patchy. But he was a voracious reader, helped by an uncle who slipped him two “huge” Chinese literature books from a boarded-up library and by private calligraphy lessons.

“The artist was professional. But not like a professional painter. He drew cinema posters,” Wang said. “It was far from the capital, so artists had more freedom … There was no payment. You just had to know someone.”

Provincial universities reopened in 1977 and his clandestine reading helped him get into college at 16 alongside 30-something classmates.

Graduating from Yunnan Normal, he headed to Beijing for further studies and then to London in 1986 where he saw his first proper museum. After receiving an art history PhD in 1993, he taught at SOAS University of London and University College London before moving to Sotheby’s in 2012 and Chicago in 2015.

“At the bottom of my heart, I’m an academic,” he said, adding that he never imagined Chinese art would reach such heights.

In 2011, China’s Hurun Rich List listed 271 mainland US-dollar billionaires, though Wang says that 600 was probably more accurate. That year, Chinese art accounted for nearly half of global art auction revenues. Since then, curators say, Chinese collectors have become increasingly knowledgeable.

“The nouveau riche are now people who made their fortunes in the 80s and 90s and are sending their kids to Vassar,” said Zetterquist. “Their taste is much more sophisticated.”

Porcelain holds a particular fascination, especially items like the peach bowl made in imperial kilns. Chinese buyers last month pored over items in Christie’s pre-auction galleries, sometimes holding them for extended periods.

“Chinese people have a special relationship with ceramics because they in many ways invented them,” Wang said.

The rarity of top-end pieces and the centuries-long struggle to crack the recipe saw Westerners similarly fixated.

American shipping fortunes after 1800, some built on the illegal opium trade, spurred early interest. But demand exploded among Gilded Age steel, oil and banking magnates. The focus was initially on decorative Qing dynasty ceramics as political instability opened Chinese imperial collections and tomb excavations. Later decades saw their tastes refined towards older, rarer Song, Tang and Zhou dynasty items.

“These things were considered to be what aristocrats, old money, collected, and so that’s what the robber barons wanted,” Zetterquist said.

The original Morgans, Rockefellers and Fricks eventually died, leaving their collections to museums. More than a century later, some of those objects are passing to wealthy Chinese collectors.

But even timeless art weathers trends.

Chinese collectors tend to shun Tang dynasty horses and other funerary items favoured by Westerners.

“There’s the idea that the tomb has been invaded, so to speak, and the spirit of the deceased has been left without things that he or she needed,” said Robert Mowry, a senior consultant and Harvard Art Museums’ curator emeritus.

“The ironic thing is, a lot of other things that Chinese collectors are interested in, like ancient bronze vessels, like ancient jades from the Zhou dynasty, came out of tombs as well. But no one worries about that in terms of the spirit of the deceased seeking revenge.”

Chinese have also frequently sniffed at “export” Chinese art, often larger items in bold colours, some even adorned with lavish gold frames targeted at foreigners after the 16th century.

“People were just filling up crates and bringing them home,” said Zetterquist. “Think about the aesthetics of the Gilded Age. It was a lot of googly gook, shiny things with cachet.”

Of particular interest for new Chinese buyers are items associated with past emperors, especially Qianlong’s 1735–1796 reign.

“The nouveau riche collectors, it’s all about Qianlong. If Qianlong liked it, it must be good,” said Mowry, even though some imperial items were made in lots of 100,000.

“If somebody visits the White House, they’re going to leave with some kind of gift,” he added. “When it’s made for the palace, everyone thinks it’s made for the emperor. Well, not everything was.”

But imperial provenance provides a certain assurance, curators said.

“The brand new fakes can be very convincing,” said Mowry. “Qianlong? Come back tomorrow, we’ll have some more for you … There’s the idea: if we buy it in the US or Europe or wherever, and it’s been out of China for a long time, like 40 years, it’s probably OK.”

While patriotism may drive some Chinese bidders, others less so, he added. “They’re virtually all dealers,” said Mowry. “There’s nothing wrong with that. But to mask it all as repatriation is part of the truth, but not the whole truth.”

Wang said museums should treasure their collections as a mother does her children, even when they’re banished. “They’re going to a better home,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] US blast simulation targets China’s alleged secret nuclear testing
item.description:
The US has conducted a non-nuclear underground experiment to enhance its ability to detect low-yield nuclear explosions that it explicitly linked with a test that Washington suspects China carried out in 2020 – an accusation Beijing denies.

The US Department of Energy announced on Wednesday that the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) conducted a “subsurface, non-nuclear chemical high-explosive” experiment at the Nevada National Security Site, which it said aimed to “increase the United States’ ability to detect low-yield nuclear explosions”.

The experiment, which did not involve any nuclear explosions, collected data to validate scientific models and refine algorithms critical to US nuclear explosion detection capabilities.
item.content:encoded:
The US has conducted a non-nuclear underground experiment to enhance its ability to detect low-yield nuclear explosions that it explicitly linked with a test that Washington suspects China carried out in 2020 – an accusation Beijing denies.

The US Department of Energy announced on Wednesday that the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) conducted a “subsurface, non-nuclear chemical high-explosive” experiment at the Nevada National Security Site, which it said aimed to “increase the United States’ ability to detect low-yield nuclear explosions”.

The experiment, which did not involve any nuclear explosions, collected data to validate scientific models and refine algorithms critical to US nuclear explosion detection capabilities.

The Nevada test highlights the constraints of verifying suspected low-yield nuclear tests. Despite Washington’s allegation that Beijing has covertly conducted a nuclear test at the Lop Nur testing site in June 2020, Beijing denied the accusation, and the international nuclear-test monitoring body has said the available seismic data cannot establish the cause of the events with confidence.

The US Energy Department’s press release said that the experiment would enhance understanding of the signature produced by underground detonation and strengthen the “unmatched” capability to detect any foreign nuclear testing.

The department said that the experiment was especially focused on further enhancing the US capabilities to detect a “decoupled” explosion – a nuclear test where the warhead is detonated inside a large underground cavity instead of being in close contact with the surrounding rock, lowering the seismic signal that the nuclear detection sensors can detect.

The Trump administration accused China of covertly carrying out a low-yield nuclear test in June 2020 at the Lop Nur nuclear test site in northwest China, alleging that China had breached the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT).

US President Donald Trump has also ordered the resumption of US nuclear testing for the first time since 1992 on what he said was an “equal basis” in October 2025.

Beijing denies carrying out any covert nuclear testing

Beijing denied the accusation and contended that it continues to abide by the terms of the CTBT. China’s last officially acknowledged nuclear test is known to have taken place at the Lop Nur site in July 1996, only two months before it signed the CTBT.

Both the US and China signed the CTBT in 1996, but neither country has ratified the treaty, so it has not yet entered into force.

The South China Morning Post has asked the Chinese embassy in Washington for comment.

Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said that the NNSA experiment can “certainly enhance” US capabilities to detect “illicit” nuclear explosions that violate the CTBT, but detecting and actually deterring nuclear tests requires international cooperation.

He said that while the current Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organisation’s (CTBTO) International Monitoring System provides powerful nuclear test monitoring capabilities, very low-yield nuclear explosions may still escape detection.

“Indeed, the US has accused China of conducting a low-yield nuclear test in June 2020, but the available data from the CTBTO’s monitoring system and other civilian seismic networks about the seismic event on that date are inconclusive,” said Kimball.

“This is why it is so important for nuclear-armed states to engage in technical discussions to develop voluntary confidence-building measures to ensure ongoing and future activities at their former test sites are fully compliant with their obligations under the CTBT.”

The CTBTO has stated that its International Monitoring System did not detect any event consistent with a nuclear test explosion on June 22, 2020 – the date that Washington suspects China of conducting the test – though it also said that there were “two very small seismic events” spaced 12 seconds apart on that day.

Washington has ‘genuine concerns’ Russia, China conducted nuclear tests

Tong Zhao, senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that Washington has “genuine concerns” that Russia and China have conducted nuclear tests in violation of their commitments as signatories of the CTBT.

He said that the International Monitoring System established under the CTBT “may not reliably detect and distinguish very small nuclear tests”, where the NNSA experiment aims to enhance Washington’s own ability to “detect covert foreign nuclear tests”.

“Such a capability could strengthen deterrence by increasing concern among rival countries that prohibited nuclear testing could be detected despite efforts to hide it. It could also enable Washington to develop a better understanding of foreign nuclear-warhead modernisation programmes,” said Zhao.

“If China were indeed seeking to advance its nuclear-warhead designs through nuclear testing inconsistent with its CTBT commitment, improvements in US detection capabilities could complicate such efforts.”

China has recently accelerated its nuclear stockpile. The Pentagon’s China military power report published in December last year estimated that the People’s Liberation Army remains on track to have over 1,000 warheads by 2030.

According to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), China is estimated to have a nuclear stockpile of up to 620 warheads as of January 2026 and is expected to “keep growing over the coming decade”.

Robert Kelley, a former official at the US Energy Department and the director of nuclear inspections at the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), said that the focus of the experiment seems to be to detect very small nuclear tests that could be used to collect data about “how a larger bomb may work” or to examine a new technology aimed at disruption of electronic systems.

He said the experiment would help the US understand Chinese testing, and that the tests are part of a longer effort to detect “smaller and smaller underground tests since at least 1963”.

“China might be doing very advanced nuclear experiments, even what are called ‘subcritical tests’ to polish very high-end complex physics knowledge,” said Kelley, who now serves as the Distinguished Associate Fellow at SIPRI.

John Erath, senior policy director at the Centre for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation, said that the test was part of “long-standing efforts” by the US to identify any nuclear explosion.

“Such efforts are designed to detect nuclear tests, including those that would be contrary to the CTBT,” said Erath.

“The Nevada experiment is specifically designed to improve detection of decoupled nuclear explosions, such as allegedly occurred at Lop Nur in 2020. This would likely be a reason for linking the current [US Energy Department] experiment to activity at Lop Nur.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why a film about a dictator has South Korea at war with itself
item.description:
Like many films released during Chuseok, South Korea’s national mid-autumn harvest festival, The Assassin(s) shot right to the top, selling more than a million tickets in its first four days.

But the box-office success of the film about the 1974 assassination attempt on former president and military leader Park Chung-hee was quickly overshadowed by calls to halt screenings, as well as a police complaint against the film’s director and producers.

Park loyalists and conservative politicians are claiming the film, directed by acclaimed filmmaker Hur Jin-ho, distorts history and defames Park and his administration.
item.content:encoded:
Like many films released during Chuseok, South Korea’s national mid-autumn harvest festival, The Assassin(s) shot right to the top, selling more than a million tickets in its first four days.

But the box-office success of the film about the 1974 assassination attempt on former president and military leader Park Chung-hee was quickly overshadowed by calls to halt screenings, as well as a police complaint against the film’s director and producers.

Park loyalists and conservative politicians are claiming the film, directed by acclaimed filmmaker Hur Jin-ho, distorts history and defames Park and his administration.

Park, who came to power after a 1961 military coup, remains one of the most divisive figures in South Korean history. His authoritarian rule coincided with one of the world’s fastest periods of industrialisation, but his government was also marked by political repression and restrictions on civil liberties.

As the controversy spills beyond the cinema, several actors cancelled audience greetings. Global star Lee Min-ho, who plays a freedom-fighting journalist, abruptly called off a public appearance at next week’s Busan International Film Festival. Actors have faced a wave of online abuse, while calls to boycott the film and products advertised by its cast have circulated on social media.

The backlash has reignited a much older argument over how South Korea should remember the Park era, and whether unresolved political divisions are shaping how the public interprets its history.

Choosing a side

Sam Park is among those who have decided not to watch the film.

“People are pointing out that there are similarities between the film and North Korean propaganda films,” the 30-year-old brand designer said. The film’s cast and crew have been labelled “communists” and “North Korean sympathisers”, a common accusation directed at liberals by South Korea’s political right.

“Above all, this is a tragedy from relatively recent history, with surviving family members who are still alive today. The filmmakers should have been even more careful to distinguish between historical fact and creative interpretation, even while exercising their freedom of expression.”

The Assassin(s) centres on the incident during a ceremony marking the anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese rule. Mun Se-gwang, a Zainichi Korean living in Japan who was identified as a North Korean sympathiser, attempted to shoot Park but missed, killing then first lady Yuk Young-soo instead.

While the film does not identify accomplices, it raises the possibility that people within the presidential office or intelligence authorities may have been involved.

Park’s son, Park Ji-man, asked the President Park Chung Hee Memorial Foundation to demand that screenings be halted – as he did in 2005 over The President’s Last Bang, which depicted the night of Park’s assassination in 1979. The foundation issued a joint statement on Thursday calling for the film’s production company to formally apologise and take down the movie from theatres.

A former People Power Party city councillor on Tuesday filed a police complaint against Hur and the film’s producers, accusing them of defamation and spreading false information by implying that Park was involved in his wife’s assassination.

On Friday, the conservative civic group New Freedom Solidarity said it had submitted plans to the police to stage rallies outside the home of actor Yoo Hae-jin, who plays a police officer investigating the assassination in the film.

“We are asking the actor to also appear in right-wing movies so that there is a political balance,” Kim Sang-jin, the leader of the civic group, told Yonhap News Agency.

For Ellie Chung, who recently watched The Assassin(s), the controversy has brought renewed attention to an event she knew little about.

“I expected there to be controversy because the film deals with the authoritarian regime and the era of Park Chung-hee,” she said. “But the film is being used for political purposes due to its historical context, and I think it has gone too far.”

The production team denied having political intentions, saying the film used cinematic imagination rather than attempting to “prove a new historical conclusion”.

South Korean courts have previously grappled with similar disputes over films based on true stories.

In relation to the 2003 film Silmido, about a team recruited to take out North Korean assassins, relatives of those portrayed as criminals sought to halt screenings, but the court upheld the filmmakers’ freedom of expression. The President’s Last Bang was also given the go-ahead but with three scenes using documentary footage removed.

Unresolved history

The controversy is ultimately about how South Koreans interpret their past, according to Park Jong-rin, a professor of history education at Hannam University.

“It’s not really about facts, but the difference in interpreting the events that took place. This is the nature of looking at history,” he said. “When you look deeper into the different voices reacting to the movie, it’s really about how people have not come to a consensus on the legacy of the Park Chung-hee administration.”

Lee Taek-gwang, a philosophy and cultural studies professor at Kyung Hee University, said the dispute was rooted in South Korea’s democratisation struggle in the 1980s.

“Ultimately, this issue is connected to the forces that emerged in the 1980s – the democratisation movement that opposed military dictatorship and sought to establish a new political order and the authoritarian regimes of the earlier period that brought on a generation of economic development,” he said.

Films such as The Man Standing Next, another dramatisation of Park’s assassination, and 12.12: The Day had sought to reinterpret modern Korean history, Lee said, contrasting with efforts, particularly from conservatives, to normalise Park’s legacy.

The use of popular culture to establish a political identity and world view was a distinctive feature of South Korean society, which went through several periods of civil democratic movements, he added.

“South Korea is still a country where these historical arguments remain unresolved,” Lee said. “A decade ago, people assumed neoliberal forces would simply continue to dominate influence, but we are now seeing the rise of far-right movements.”

The film’s critics, however, say their objections are not simply political.

Park Hye-eun, chief editor of The Screen movie media publication, said audiences had every right to criticise a film they found inaccurate or objectionable.

“What concerns me is that the head of a major political party singled out a particular film and called on people not to watch it, while also filing criminal complaints against the filmmakers and bringing the film into the political arena,” she said.

“That seems less like the exercise of an audience member’s right to criticise and more like political power intervening in the cultural sphere.”

Park said the controversy had ultimately led her to view the film through a different lens.

“The film is actually trying to say that we should live in a society where anyone can ask questions and anyone can try to provide answers to those questions,” she said.

“Perhaps the film is ultimately asking what a mature society should look like. Maybe it’s a society where anyone is free to ask questions, and where people are mature enough to listen to and consider the answers.”

item.title: [SCMP] As Saudi Arabia steps up war against Yemen’s Houthis, Pakistan set to play support role
item.description:
Pakistani troops are expected to take over various defensive functions for Saudi Arabia to enable the Middle East country to fight an all-out war aimed at defeating Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

According to defence analysts, Pakistani troops are not expected to participate directly in ground offensives against the Houthis being planned by Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s squabbling government factions.

Instead, their primary objective would be to free up Saudi forces to focus on what is likely to be a sustained conflict involving hundreds of thousands of Yemeni fighters on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
Pakistani troops are expected to take over various defensive functions for Saudi Arabia to enable the Middle East country to fight an all-out war aimed at defeating Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

According to defence analysts, Pakistani troops are not expected to participate directly in ground offensives against the Houthis being planned by Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s squabbling government factions.

Instead, their primary objective would be to free up Saudi forces to focus on what is likely to be a sustained conflict involving hundreds of thousands of Yemeni fighters on both sides.

“Saudi Arabia needs Pakistan to help defend Saudi Arabia so that Saudi forces have greater freedom to operate against the Houthis,” said Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London.

That means air and missile defence personnel, radar and early warning, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, counter-drone capabilities, electronic warfare, intelligence fusion and command-and-control support.

Pakistan can also provide maintenance, munitions support, training, operational planning and potentially additional aircraft and unmanned systems for defensive patrols and surveillance.

Riyadh would value Pakistani surveillance, intelligence and potentially naval support around the Red Sea and Saudi approaches, Krieg said, particularly as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which straddles Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea in Africa, had become increasingly contested.

Dave Des Roches, a retired Pentagon official and senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said the Saudis wanted the Pakistanis to deploy across the “full range of military operations”.

The Pakistanis would likely not agree to such a comprehensive role, while the scope of the functions to be assumed by Pakistani forces and their area of duty would be under intense negotiation between both sides, he added.

According to Saudi political scientist Nawaf Obaid, some specialist Pakistani military units may already be providing intelligence and command-and-control support.

Writing for Al Jazeera English on September 26, Obaid claimed Saudi and Pakistani joint terminal attack controller (JTAC) teams were already “embedded” with major Yemeni government formations in the north of the country.

They are being pitted against Iranian military advisers, whom Western intelligence agencies reported as having played a critical role in the Houthi seizure of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month.

Obaid said the Saudi-Pakistani JTAC teams were “restoring an authenticated link” between government forces on the ground and the Saudi-led joint forces command strike system, following its disruption last month by Revolutionary Guards advisers who were supporting Houthi military communications.

The system reportedly operated by the Saudi and Pakistani JTAC teams was far more advanced than its Iranian counterpart, he wrote. Its deployment has enabled Saudi warplanes and drones to mount a sustained aerial counteroffensive against the Houthi command structure and massing ground forces.

According to Yemeni military spokesmen, several Revolutionary Guards advisers have been killed in “government” air strikes.

Security officials in Islamabad remain tight-lipped about the specifics of Pakistan’s role in the Saudi-Houthi conflict while privately telling journalists that their silence should not be misconstrued as a sign of inaction.

In April, Pakistan deployed some 8,000 troops, a squadron of JF-17 fighters co-developed with China, and Chinese-built HQ-9 long-range air defence systems to Saudi Arabia under their mutual defence pact signed in September 2025.

At the same time, political and military leaders have ratcheted up rhetoric about the extent of Pakistan’s commitment to the defence of Saudi Arabia.

“We are bound by this arrangement to defend Saudi Arabia. That means whatever means that are available at our disposal, they’ll be available to Saudi Arabia also,” Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif told Al Jazeera on Wednesday.

To rally public support among their mostly Muslim populations, the Saudi and Pakistani governments have cloaked preparations for the decisive conflict in religious garb.

Riyadh has accused the Houthis of carrying out drone strikes against Islam’s two holiest shrines in Mecca and Medina in recent weeks, allegations that the Yemeni militia has dismissed as propaganda.

Echoing the Saudi narrative at the United Nations General Assembly on September 26, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the first alleged drone attack on Mecca last month had “provoked the anger of Muslims throughout the world”.

Any threat to the security and sanctity of the two holy mosques “constitutes a red line that must not be crossed under any circumstances”, Sharif warned.

Des Roches saw the alleged Mecca attack as a “requirement” for Pakistani public opinion to support any enhanced military action against the Houthis, given some suspicion about the motives for defending Saudi Arabia.

“Pakistanis in particular know how things work in the Gulf, and they are extremely proud of their armed forces,” Des Roches said.

“Defending Mecca and Medina could meet the requirement.”

Sharif’s declaration at the UN coincided with three other significant developments on the same day.

The grand mufti of Saudi Arabia Saleh bin Fawzan bin Abdullah al-Fawzan issued an edict validating the actions of Saudi-led coalition forces against the Houthis.

“Preserving this great entity, defending its borders, repelling aggression against it, and punishing anyone who seeks to encroach upon even an inch of it, are among the greatest duties and the best acts of devotion, for which lives and souls are sacrificed in pursuit of God’s pleasure,” Fawzan declared in a written statement.

The military commanders of the Mecca Defence Alliance – comprising Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey – also met in Riyadh for the first time to “explore measures supporting” the Saudis under the pact signed in August.

In addition, the leader of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashid al-Alimi issued a call for general mobilisation with the unprecedented goal of comprehensively defeating the Houthis.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reiterated this goal in his annual address to the kingdom’s consultative assembly on Wednesday.

Krieg expected Pakistan to be cautious about the distinction between defending Saudi territory and conducting offensive operations inside Yemen.

“That distinction is politically useful to everybody,” he said.

Britain and France are adopting “essentially the same principle” but in different ways to enhance Saudi Arabia’s resilience, according to Krieg.

If Pakistan helps protect Saudi airspace, France protects oil infrastructure to enable oil exports via the Red Sea port of Yanbu, and British air force tankers keep Saudi aircraft airborne for longer, Riyadh can focus more on its operations in Yemen.

“The interesting consequence is that all these defensive contributions can indirectly enable a more offensive Saudi posture,” Krieg said.

“Defensive burden-sharing can therefore become an offensive force multiplier without any of those partners formally joining the war.”

item.title: [SCMP] If young US people accept Xi’s invitation to China, what will Beijing show them?
item.description:
China is ramping up its efforts to bring young Americans to China, and ready to be seen as a country concerned with environmental protection, lifting people out of poverty, protecting minority cultures and building the technology of the future.

During his trip to the United States last week, Chinese President Xi Jinping said his country aimed to welcome 100,000 young Americans on exchange or study trips over the next five years.

That builds on an earlier target announced in 2023 that set the goal of bringing 50,000 US youth people to China by 2028, which the authorities said they had reached ahead of schedule.
item.content:encoded:
China is ramping up its efforts to bring young Americans to China, and ready to be seen as a country concerned with environmental protection, lifting people out of poverty, protecting minority cultures and building the technology of the future.

During his trip to the United States last week, Chinese President Xi Jinping said his country aimed to welcome 100,000 young Americans on exchange or study trips over the next five years.

That builds on an earlier target announced in 2023 that set the goal of bringing 50,000 US youth people to China by 2028, which the authorities said they had reached ahead of schedule.

The Young Envoys Scholarship (YES) initiative was launched to support this target. It is run by the China Education Association for International Exchange, a non-profit organisation under the Ministry of Education.

The YES initiative coordinates with Chinese institutions, mostly universities, which create itineraries and curricula, and manage the visitors on the ground. Universities set varying admissions criteria for their programmes, but in general, the YES initiative is open to non-Chinese citizens between the ages of 18 and 45.

Marine conservation

For one group of students, their China trip began at sea.

Starting in March, a group of 20 Chinese and US students spent 10 days travelling up the Chinese coast from Hong Kong to the eastern cities of Ningbo and Shanghai. The three stops are all coastal cities with links to marine research and the ocean economy.

The trip was organised by two Chinese state-linked non-profit organisations and the Ray Dalio-backed OceanX, with support from China’s Second Institute of Oceanography, the Ministry of Education and the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

The programme included marine exploration, visits to research facilities and laboratories and discussions about international cooperation in ocean science, according to the organisers.

In one activity, the students collected marine biological samples and identified species including the Calanus sinicus crustacean, which has been studied by Chinese scientists for decades.

“I am delighted to know that the students from both countries have embarked on an unforgettable friendship voyage aboard the China-US Youth Friendship vessel,” Xi said in a letter to the programme in May, state news agency Xinhua reported.

China has emphasised marine science in recent years, with its latest five-year plan – which runs from this year through to 2030 – calling for more research, expanded deep-sea exploration and deepened international cooperation.

The US and China are the two biggest contributors to oceanographic research in the Pacific, with the US first in terms of the share of publications and China second between 1992 and 2021, according to a study published in the Ocean Sustainability journal.

The two countries have also cooperated on marine research under the broader US-China Science and Technology Agreement, first signed in 1979 and extended for another five years in 2024.

Under the agreement, a protocol on cooperation in marine and fishery science and technology provides a framework for collaboration between China and the US.

Minority culture

A programme organised by Shanghai’s Donghua University took US students into ethnic minority communities in southwestern China’s Guizhou province, with field studies focused on the intangible cultural heritage of the Bouyei, Miao, Shui and Dong peoples.

The initiative aimed to “promote the global dissemination of outstanding traditional Chinese culture and enhance the international influence of intangible cultural heritage”, according to the university.

In the city of Kaili, students attended a workshop on batik dyeing techniques and later wore traditional costumes to take part in a “village runway” event with residents.

Guizhou has used its ethnic minority culture to drive tourism as part of its poverty alleviation and rural development efforts, with tourism projects helping nearly 900,000 people increase their incomes between 2017 and 2019, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism.

China’s rural revitalisation plan for 2024 to 2027 calls for stronger protection and use of traditional villages and intangible cultural heritage.

China’s latest five-year plan for intangible cultural heritage also seeks to promote Chinese intangible cultural heritage overseas as part of efforts to strengthen the global influence of Chinese culture and promote cultural exchanges.

Poverty alleviation

Peking University said it organised a trip through Ningxia, Sichuan and Chongqing focused on “poverty alleviation, regional development and urban renewal”.

In Ningxia, students visited Minning, a town established over two decades ago that is touted as an example of China’s east-west cooperation in poverty alleviation.

The town has developed industries including wine, goji berry cultivation and photovoltaic agriculture supported by investment and technical aid from the wealthier coastal province of Fujian.

Minning’s per capita disposable monthly income rose from about 500 yuan (US$74.50) in 1997 to 20,292 yuan last year, according to the local authorities.

The five-year plan calls for an institutionalised system of support for underdeveloped areas, including measures to consolidate poverty alleviation gains and strengthen industrial and employment support. It also calls for improving east-west cooperation and other forms of regional assistance.

In Sichuan and Chongqing, the trip’s focus shifted towards agricultural modernisation and urban development.

Cutting-edge technology

The Suzhou-Hangzhou-Shanghai itinerary, also organised by Peking University, offered a very different picture from the previous two: an image of how China is seemingly building the future.

The trip took students through three cities in the prosperous Yangtze River Delta and focused on advanced manufacturing, robotics and the digital economy.

The group visited Unitree Robotics and carmaker Geely, two companies working in sectors that have become increasingly important to China’s push up the value chain.

This has intensified competition between China and the US, with advanced chips, artificial intelligence and other strategic technologies at the centre of the rivalry.

The five-year plan calls for the faster development of strategic, emerging and future industries while encouraging technological innovation and the upgrading of traditional manufacturing.

Lasting impression

“You cannot truly understand another country from books. You have to experience it first-hand,” said Anoushka Soni, a University of California, Berkeley student who visited China this year, according to a Peking University social media account.

The university quoted her as saying that the stories she encountered “cannot be found in textbooks and cannot be presented simply by searching the word ‘China’ online”.

Saanvi Bhatia, a Stanford University fourth-year student from Pennsylvania who took part in Tsinghua University’s summer fellowship last year, said she also made unexpected discoveries.

“I did not know how involved China was in climate stuff and how much they cared about making it non-toxic to us,” Bhatia said.

During her visit to Guizhou, Bhatia and other students were shown how waste was incinerated and treated so that only water vapour was released into the environment.

“I feel like a lot of the perspective of China and the US is seen [through] rivalry. We’re both kind of competing, and so then to be on the other person’s land and knowing what they are interested in was very cool,” Bhatia said.

Additional reporting by Tim Yuen Lingk

item.title: [SCMP] Name and shame: Japan’s tame answer to jobseeker sex harassment
item.description:
Final-year students invited to recruiters’ apartments for help with their applications. Coffee dates with alumni who promise to explain how the company works. Inappropriate interview questions about boyfriends, marriage plans and sex lives.

For young women in Japan, looking for a job has long entailed submitting themselves to the skewed power dynamics of the recruitment process.

And before Thursday, no official legal safeguards existed to protect these jobseekers from such harassment.
item.content:encoded:
Final-year students invited to recruiters’ apartments for help with their applications. Coffee dates with alumni who promise to explain how the company works. Inappropriate interview questions about boyfriends, marriage plans and sex lives.

For young women in Japan, looking for a job has long entailed submitting themselves to the skewed power dynamics of the recruitment process.

And before Thursday, no official legal safeguards existed to protect these jobseekers from such harassment.

Campaigners and advocates have welcomed the change, but say it lacks teeth and came years too late, even as societal attitudes may have already moved ahead of it.

“It is good that this has happened, but it has taken five years of discussions to get to the point where it has become law,” said Chisato Kitanaka, an associate professor of sociology at Hiroshima University who advises the government on gender issues.

“Government measures against sexual harassment in Japan are very weak, including this kind of harassment.”

Amendments to the Equal Employment Opportunity Act that took effect last week address harassment in its many forms and settings, from misbehaviour in the office to verbal abuse and threats from customers in shops, taxis and elsewhere. One section deals specifically with what the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare terms “job-seeking sexual harassment”.

The ministry’s website lists examples: staff who make sexual jokes or tease applicants such that it causes distress, who pressure them into a sexual relationship, or who repeatedly invite them to one-to-one meals or drinks.

Employers are now legally required to take steps to stop their staff harassing applicants in this way, with corporate compliance enforced through the threat of publicly shaming offending companies and exposing them to the prospect of civil lawsuits and financial damages.

Kitanaka called the changes a “step in the right direction”, but said they did not go far enough.

“There is no formal punishment for companies that let this happen, with the only real sanction the ministry releasing the name of the company publicly,” she said.

She expects large companies and organisations to enforce the rules more stringently than smaller firms, even as part-time workers, freelancers and others in precarious jobs continue to have too few protections.

Sumie Kawakami, a lecturer at Yamanashi Gakuin University and author of a book on gender issues, agreed that reform was long overdue.

“This isn’t something that has only been happening in recent years and is now being addressed,” she said. “It has been going on for decades.”

One in three

A survey of 1,000 recent jobseekers conducted by Japan’s labour ministry in 2023 showed that 31.9 per cent of respondents – nearly one in three – reported being harassed.

Unnecessary physical contact and questions about sexual matters were each cited by over 25 per cent of the harassed respondents, while nearly 29 per cent said they were on the receiving end of sexual jokes and teasing.

One in four of the men and women who had these experiences reported feeling less motivated in their job search and more than one in three said they felt “anger, dissatisfaction or anxiety”.

For two dozen or so, the effect on their mental health was such that they required hospital treatment.

In the past, companies typically tried to hush up such incidents, but a number of court cases over the years have shone a spotlight on the issue.

In 2019, a male construction company employee was charged with indecent assault after allegedly convincing a university student to come to his flat on the pretext of helping her prepare for an interview.

His employer, Obayashi Corp, apologised and promised to “urgently review” its procedures, subsequently setting up a harassment prevention office and conducting “emergency training” for staff involved in recruitment.

Prosecutors ultimately dropped charges against the man without publicly providing a reason. Whether he kept his job is unknown.

That same year, a 24-year-old trading company employee was arrested and charged with sexual assault and theft after a student he met through a networking app accused him of getting her drunk and using a stolen key to molest her in her hotel room. His employer, Sumitomo Corp, issued a statement soon after his arrest, confirming his disciplinary dismissal.

One of the most serious cases involved Kenshiro Maruta, who was sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2023 for drugging and raping at least 10 female students who connected with him through apps designed to match jobseekers with university alumni and career counsellors.

His employer, Recruit Communications, fired Maruta following his arrest and launched an internal investigation, vowing to never allow such an outrage happen again.

“There have been many incidents in the past and gradually the government has changed its policies,” said Kitanaka, the sociologist. “Now, at last, they have changed the law.”

‘Not acceptable today’

Back in the 1980s, when gender studies lecturer Kawakami first joined Japan’s workforce, it was still dominated by men. Women had to work harder than their male counterparts just to be taken seriously or to advance, she said.

“Young women in the past did not feel that they could speak out when this happened to them because they wanted to get a good job and career,” she said of harassment.

Kawakami has watched attitudes shift in recent years, however, especially among the young women at her university preparing to start their careers.

“I think it has changed quite a lot,” she said. “There is far greater awareness among working people and companies about what constitutes unacceptable behaviour, and I believe employers are far less willing to tolerate sexual harassment.”

And while the threat of public naming and shaming a company might seem tame compared to criminal convictions, Kawakami says the threat “is a powerful one”.

“Companies are desperate to find capable and qualified staff nowadays, and negative publicity that would go with a sexual harassment accusation would be hugely damaging,” she said.

“Young women have lots of work options at the moment. Why would they go to a company that fails to act in a situation like this?”

One recent graduate, who declined to be named, told This Week in Asia that outlawing “clearly sexist” comments or actions by recruiters was a good idea, even if she did not believe that women of her generation would put up with such behaviour.

“If one of my friends were asked something inappropriate in an interview or were invited out for drinks, I’m certain that the man would be shouted at and his company would hear about it,” she said. “It’s just not acceptable today.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why Sabah has Malaysia watching South China Sea tensions more closely
item.description:
Malaysia’s long-standing strategy of non-alignment amid US-China rivalry in the South China Sea could soon be tested, with the eastern state of Sabah sitting near a potential flashpoint involving Philippine territory.

Observers pointed to comments by Malaysian Defence Minister Khaled Nordin, who last week voiced concern that a conflict or “unexpected incident” in the maritime region could spill over into Malaysia.

Khaled, who singled out Sabah, added that Malaysia was looking to strengthen its national defence as a precautionary measure.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s long-standing strategy of non-alignment amid US-China rivalry in the South China Sea could soon be tested, with the eastern state of Sabah sitting near a potential flashpoint involving Philippine territory.

Observers pointed to comments by Malaysian Defence Minister Khaled Nordin, who last week voiced concern that a conflict or “unexpected incident” in the maritime region could spill over into Malaysia.

Khaled, who singled out Sabah, added that Malaysia was looking to strengthen its national defence as a precautionary measure.

“We know the challenges in the South China Sea and the rivalry between major powers. If something happens in that geographically small area, it could also affect our country,” local media quoted Khaled as saying on Saturday.

The Philippines and the US have deepened defence cooperation since 2014, including by expanding American military access to Philippine facilities under the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) as tensions with China have mounted.

Two of the nine EDCA sites accessible to US forces are in Palawan, an island province north of Sabah. They include Antonio Bautista Air Base in Puerto Princesa and Naval Station Narciso Del Rosario on Balabac Island. The sites remain under Philippine control and while they do not function as permanent US bases, the agreement allows American forces rotational access.

Balabac, the southernmost EDCA site and closest to Sabah, is being developed to include a 3km (1.86 mile) military runway.

About 50km (31 miles) away lies Banggi Island, the northernmost part of Sabah state that sits at the southern end of the so-called first island chain – a Cold War-era American defence concept describing an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines and Malaysia that act as a strategic bottleneck for China’s navy.

Hoo Chiew-Ping, a senior fellow at the East Asian International Relations Caucus, said this proximity meant Malaysia could no longer ignore the possibility of a conflict spreading southwards even as it sought to remain non-aligned.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim raised concerns over Balabac in August, pledging to strengthen Malaysia’s defences in response to the growing US-backed Philippine military presence on the nearby island.

“As a neighbouring country closely affected by claims over Sabah, we are somewhat concerned with the tension, even though our bilateral relations with the Philippines remain very good,” Anwar said on August 18.

Malaysia could not match the scale of military facilities being developed on Balabac, he said, noting a need to strengthen basic defensive capabilities as the regional security environment became increasingly shaped by US-China competition.

Hoo said Malaysian defence and security strategists had yet to fully recognise this reality despite long-term defence cooperation with the US, including extensive joint military exercises in these areas.

“The assumption that a US-China military confrontation could occur near Borneo stems from concerns over a Taiwan Strait contingency, where the Philippines would become the immediate frontline,” Hoo said. “If the conflict is about Taiwan, strategic space will become extremely narrow.”

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

While a major conflict would inevitably add pressure on countries to choose sides, Hoo said Malaysia would make every effort to stay out of it, prioritising protecting and evacuating its citizens instead.

She argued that Malaysia’s existing defence relationship with Washington gave both countries established channels to discuss concerns over US deployments and regional escalation, rather than addressing them through public political statements that could reflect “limited substantive bilateral dialogue”.

Over the years, Malaysia has maintained close defence ties with both Washington and Beijing.

Malaysia has taken part in joint drills with the US for more than three decades, including maritime exercises such as Cooperation Afloat Readiness and Training.

This July, nearly 2,850 Malaysian, US and Australian personnel took part in Exercise Keris Strike in Kota Belud, Sabah, involving tactical and live-fire drills aimed at strengthening interoperability.

In October 2025, Malaysian and Chinese forces held the Aman Youyi exercise in the Strait of Malacca, including maritime interdictions, search-and-rescue and surveillance drills between the Malaysian and Chinese navies.

Innocent passage?

Distancing itself from any conflict would require Malaysia to enforce its neutrality consistently against both sides, said Mohd Hazmi Mohd Rusli, a maritime law expert at the Islamic Science University of Malaysia.

Hazmi said Malaysia should also make its position clear in advance so both Washington and Beijing understood the limits of what it would allow.

“If a US-China conflict spills over near Sabah, Malaysia … should not allow its territory, territorial sea or airspace to be used by either side to conduct hostile military operations,” he said.

But Malaysia’s exclusive economic zone would present a different challenge, Hazmi said, as other states retained freedom of navigation and overflight under international law.

Foreign warships could still pass through Malaysia’s territorial waters during an armed conflict provided that their passage remained “innocent”, he added, referring to Article 19 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia, said the conundrum for Southeast Asian states would revolve around requests by rival powers for logistical support or access to facilities in the event of a conflict.

“Their acquiescence or refusal will be seen by either big power as alternately friendly or hostile,” Oh said.

Andrea Passeri, a programme director for international relations at Taylor’s University in Malaysia, said there was a “breaking point” where maintaining non-alignment would become difficult if the rivalry escalated into open conflict.

“Non-alignment would not vanish as a principle, but it would become much harder for Malaysia and many Southeast Asian states to sustain in practice,” Passeri said, adding that even states seeking autonomy could find their waters and airspace increasingly important for military access and surveillance.

The pressure could also expose internal fault lines within Asean, he said, with the Philippines pulled directly towards Washington while other members faced pressure to clarify positions they had deliberately kept ambiguous.

“Consensus becomes harder precisely when collective diplomacy is most needed,” Passeri added.

Such pressures could also deepen existing divisions within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, whose 11 member states maintain vastly different relationships with Washington and Beijing.

“There are already Asean member states which are viewed as either very pro-US or very pro-China,” Oh said. “Their vastly different positions are likely to deepen should a conflict break out between the two big powers.”

This Week in Asia has contacted Malaysian Defence Minister Khaled Nordin for comment.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea hits back at Trump’s investment claims in ‘tit-for-tat move’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement of a “colossal” South Korean investment package has prompted Seoul to clarify that the deal is far from finalised, laying bare stark differences between the allies over the terms of their trade agreement, observers have said.

On Wednesday, Trump announced that South Korea would invest in the construction of a natural gas-fired power plant in Texas, eight large-scale nuclear power plants across the United States and a liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska.

Hours later, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung issued a clarification that effectively pushed back against Washington’s portrayal of the investment package as a done deal, making clear that further negotiations were still necessary.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement of a “colossal” South Korean investment package has prompted Seoul to clarify that the deal is far from finalised, laying bare stark differences between the allies over the terms of their trade agreement, observers have said.

On Wednesday, Trump announced that South Korea would invest in the construction of a natural gas-fired power plant in Texas, eight large-scale nuclear power plants across the United States and a liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska.

Hours later, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung issued a clarification that effectively pushed back against Washington’s portrayal of the investment package as a done deal, making clear that further negotiations were still necessary.

Trump’s announcement comes just weeks before the highly competitive November midterm elections, apparently aiming to bolster the Republican Party’s economic record and support vulnerable candidates, including Alaska Senator Dan Sullivan.

It followed protracted negotiations over the implementation of Seoul’s commitment to invest US$350 billion in the US – US$150 billion in the shipbuilding sector and US$200 billion in strategic industries – in return for Washington lowering tariffs on South Korean goods.

Trump touted the three projects as a “colossal package” that marked a “major step towards securing our critical energy supply chain, ensuring American energy dominance and making our partnership with South Korea and the entire Pacific region stronger than ever before”.
