He said Seoul would invest up to US$200 billion in US energy infrastructure, including US$22.3 billion for a 6-gigawatt power generation facility in Texas and US$120 billion for the eight nuclear power plants.

“And at long last, the Alaska liquefied natural gas pipeline. That’s a big one,” he added.

US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also said the investment in the Alaska LNG project would exceed US$50 billion, and the eight nuclear reactors would be built in Ohio, Tennessee, South Carolina and Kentucky.

Seoul’s position is that only the Texas project has been finalised, while the commercially contentious Alaska LNG project and the eight nuclear power plants remain subject to further discussions.

On Thursday, Lee reiterated that “commercial viability” must be a prerequisite for South Korean investment in the US.

“Among the investment projects in the United States announced by the US, we have agreed to begin ‘working’ on the Alaska LNG project on the condition that its commercial viability is confirmed and that it complies with South Korea’s legal procedures,” he said on social media.

Lee’s emphasis on “working” appeared intended to underscore that both sides had yet to bridge their differences over the project’s commercial feasibility and the conditions for Seoul’s participation.

A joint statement issued by the two governments appeared to support Lee’s interpretation concerning where Seoul’s investment would be made.

The statement said both sides had “agreed to commence working” on the Alaska LNG project, subject to “meeting commercial reasonableness and all applicable domestic legal requirements”.

South Korea’s Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said last week that the Alaska project remained under review. “We will review the Alaska LNG project under the clear principle that we will proceed only if its commercial viability is established,” Kim said.

The joint statement also said both sides “have agreed to a comprehensive cooperation framework” for constructing eight large-scale nuclear power plants.

Lee has stressed that the commercial viability of each nuclear power plant must be assessed individually, apparently contrasting with Washington’s position that the investment should be evaluated as an overall package.

His clarification comes despite reports that both countries agreed on the operating arrangements for a US$200 billion umbrella investment vehicle to govern the investment component of Seoul’s commitment.

Under the reported mechanism, revenues from individual projects would be consolidated, allowing profits from commercially successful ventures to offset losses incurred by others.

Both sides would initially share profits equally, with a 50-50 split maintained until South Korea recovered its principal investment and interest from each project. Only then would the profit-sharing ratio shift to 10 per cent for Seoul and 90 per cent for Washington.

Even after the recovery of principal and interest, however, the 50-50 arrangement would continue across the entire portfolio, including projects whose individual investments had already been recouped, Lee said.

He added that the arrangement was designed to minimise investment losses and ensure South Korea recovered its overall investment.

Observers say the arrangement suggests that both countries still need to resolve important details concerning the investment mechanism, including how commercial risks and returns will be assessed and distributed across the portfolio.

“This is a tit-for-tat move by President Lee in response to Washington’s unilateral action,” Hur Jung, a professor in the economics department at Sogang University, told This Week in Asia.

Trump’s announcement was designed to appeal to voters ahead of the midterm elections, while Lee, facing declining approval ratings and domestic criticism over his handling of negotiations with Washington, also needed to send a strong message to South Korean audiences, Hur said.

“President Lee’s remarks, however, are throwing up new obstacles in negotiations with Washington. He is doubling down on his stance as part of his negotiation tactics, but there is little possibility of the talks breaking down,” Hur said, citing the strategic importance of the two allies to each other.

Kim Jae-chun, a political-science professor at Sogang University, said Lee was “staking out his firm position” to secure South Korean interests in the negotiations, but warned that “it would be very difficult for Seoul to withstand Washington’s pressure” given that Trump’s term runs until January 2029.

The conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), meanwhile, accused the government of deceiving the public, arguing that it had already agreed on specific investment amounts with Washington but concealed the details from the National Assembly.

It described Trump’s announcement as a “serious diplomatic disaster” for South Korea.

The PPP urged the government to disclose whether it had agreed to invest in the Alaska LNG project, release detailed plans and the criteria for determining commercial viability and seek parliamentary approval for the investment.

Lee and Trump reached the trade deal last year, under which Washington agreed to lower its so-called reciprocal tariffs on South Korean goods to 15 per cent from 25 per cent in return for Seoul’s US$350 billion investment commitment.

Both sides have since engaged in difficult negotiations over the selection and implementation of investment projects, with Seoul seeking to ensure its commitments are commercially viable and do not expose South Korean taxpayers and public finances to excessive risks.

item.title: [SCMP] JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon on how growth can untangle US-China strife, thorny global issues
item.description:
Jamie Dimon’s recent whirlwind visit to Hong Kong followed a similar script: a schedule packed with meetings involving the entrepreneurs and business leaders connecting China with global markets.

But it was his increasingly visible stance on global issues that appeared to extend his career beyond market strategy and financial industry leadership as CEO of JPMorgan Chase.

His preoccupation with economic growth and world affairs drew particular attention in Hong Kong last week, shortly before boarding a private plane and jetting back to Washington for a state dinner at the White House to welcome President Xi Jinping.
item.content:encoded:
Jamie Dimon’s recent whirlwind visit to Hong Kong followed a similar script: a schedule packed with meetings involving the entrepreneurs and business leaders connecting China with global markets.

But it was his increasingly visible stance on global issues that appeared to extend his career beyond market strategy and financial industry leadership as CEO of JPMorgan Chase.

His preoccupation with economic growth and world affairs drew particular attention in Hong Kong last week, shortly before boarding a private plane and jetting back to Washington for a state dinner at the White House to welcome President Xi Jinping.

“My biggest concern is geopolitics – world peace,” Dimon, the longest-serving CEO of a major Wall Street bank, told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday.

His emphasis on global economic growth also echoed US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s views and the decades-old philosophy of China’s leaders, including Xi, that “development is of overriding importance”, laying the groundwork for China-US trade talks that were recently held at the bank’s New York headquarters.

Markets: prepared, not scared

Global markets have endured repeated panics this year, driven by surging oil prices, rising US Treasury yields, the Federal Reserve’s interest rate increase to fight inflation, and soaring debt – factors that have fuelled concerns about another major financial crisis.

The world economy and global markets are also grappling with geopolitical conflicts – including the Ukraine war that began in February 2022 and the US-Israeli war on Iran that just crossed the seven-month mark – as well as persistent trade tensions between China and the United States, and increasingly louder warnings about artificial intelligence.

You always need to be prepared. Because if you look at economic history, the market isn’t always right

Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase

Dimon, whose signature financial strategy – a combination of low debt-to-equity ratios, high liquidity and large cash reserves known as the “fortress balance sheet” – often resurfaces in times of crisis, expressed concerns about “sticky inflation” in the US that has persistently hovered above 2 per cent for more than five years.

“If you are in business, you should be thinking about whether you can handle higher rates, higher credit spreads,” Dimon said, speaking from the JPMorgan office in Central district, the bustling financial centre of Hong Kong. “Just as a normal course, how do you manage risk?

“You always need to be prepared. Because if you look at economic history, the market isn’t always right.”

However, Dimon noted that current conditions were “different” from the 2008 crisis, driven by excessive speculation on financial instruments backed by mortgage loans. Banks, the backbone of the financial system, are currently not overleveraged and have much more liquidity, while American corporations and consumers are not overleveraged either, he observed.

“The highest debt is sovereign debt. So, governments need to be financially responsible. And hopefully, they will be before a crisis forces the issue.”

Government data shows that US sovereign debt has doubled in a decade, topping US$40 trillion last month. The cost of capital is jumping as oil, grain and other shocks resonate, with the yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury bills at 5.234 per cent as of Monday afternoon, the highest in over 20 years.

Although Dimon maintains that the US remains a permanent investment destination, and that its economy is still “hugely powerful”, talk of diversification and de-dollarisation has accelerated. This is accompanied by Beijing’s growing efforts to lure international investors and push for global use of the yuan.

Many central banks and institutional investors also altered their strategies since March, reducing US bill holdings, purchasing gold, and diversifying away from the US dollar. Even Japan, an American ally, trimmed a total of US$135.4 billion in US Treasuries from March to July – a 10.9 per cent drop.

While acknowledging that stock prices were quite high and credit spreads were quite low, Dimon said people should never be surprised about market fluctuations.

“The markets aren’t always right,” he said. “Things are very good today, and there’s reason for some happiness.”

China-US: growth is the antidote

In the days preceding Dimon’s Hong Kong visit, JPMorgan Chase’s New York headquarters hosted a round of trade talks between Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US negotiators, including Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

Underpinning these discussions was Dimon’s notion of government-business collaboration and a shared focus on growth, which he mentioned repeatedly in his interview, considering them vital to tackling many global problems.

“Secretary Bessent mentioned the other day – which is dead right – growth is the best antidote,” Dimon said. “So, countries should be thinking about what policies will maximise growth.

“You see a lot of politicians always speaking about raising taxes or cuts. Before you do that, why don’t we all fix the things that are inhibiting growth? Growth is good for all the citizens, not just good for business. When you have growth, you have more employment, more wages.”

Such thoughts are strikingly similar to Beijing’s stance, which views economic growth as the foundation for well-being, social stability and debt resolution.

“My view is: engagement is the best thing – at multiple levels and consistently,” Dimon said of bilateral relations, highlighting the importance of high-level meetings. “I’m glad that they are meeting and engaging. I think it’s important to hear each other out.”

The latest talks yielded some results – Beijing and Washington agreed to extend a nearly year-long trade truce for two more months, until January 10. And for the first time, the two sides discussed AI, according to their official statements.

Ahead of Thursday’s state dinner, in their speeches to officials and top American business executives – including Dimon – presidents Xi and Trump praised past friendships and downplayed current rivalries.

While competition persists over AI, biotech and many other sectors, Dimon identified potential areas for cooperation between the two superpowers, such as working towards world peace, nuclear non-proliferation and counterterrorism.

“We should keep reminding ourselves that China wants to lift up its people, America wants to lift up its people,” he noted.

On AI: roll up your sleeves

Despite market debate over the rapid deployment of AI, Dimon argued that the progression of the technology would move from machine learning to large language models and then, eventually, artificial general intelligence – thinking that matches or surpasses human cognitive ability.

Dimon said the technology would transform lives and industries. “AI is real. We’ve been doing it for 13 years,” he said, citing its customer-oriented use to prevent fraud and to facilitate marketing, prospecting, design and call centres.

“It’ll save lives, prevent car accidents and develop drugs and composite materials. If you have kids, they may live to 100. We may not have some of the diseases we were all afflicted with. So, yeah, you should applaud that.”

As any technology carries potential downsides, he called for broad government actions to redeploy or retrain workers, but remained broadly positive on the technology’s future gains.

“I think AI’s productivity benefits are still some way down the road. We don’t yet know exactly when they’ll be fully realised, but I believe it will be a huge plus.”

It does create real vulnerabilities and drives the need for increased spending on cyber protection, Dimon said, mentioning possible threats through open-source code and internet access.

“Again, my attitude is: roll up your sleeves, get to work,” he said. “It’s not like we’re ignoring it.

“It may cause some disruption. But I don’t spend much time debating it. My job is to do a better job for my customers. We use computers, we use technology, and we’ll use AI the same way. The north star is serving customers better. AI is just another tool to help us do that.”

If you make it ideological – Democrats against Republicans – and make moral statements about what works, then you lose sight of the facts

Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase

The next chapter

After spending more than two decades at the helm of one of the world’s most valuable banks, Dimon still maintains a sharp sense of global market risks and business deals. Increasingly, however, the 70-year-old multibillionaire has set his sights beyond bank profits and personal wealth towards some of the “big issues” facing the world.

“You know, the war in Ukraine is terrible, and it’s causing a lot of issues in Europe now,” he said. “And it’s getting worse. Obviously, that affects oil and grain prices. And now you have the war in the Middle East – Iran – and that’s also affecting oil.”

He is also keen on advising younger generations to develop critical-thinking skills and a strong work ethic.

“You can’t have critical thinking without deep curiosity and an open mind and asking yourself, ‘Does this really work that way?’” he said, adding: “And learn, learn, learn, learn, learn.”

When asked about any personal goals he may have, Dimon, who is already a business icon respected across Wall Street and Washington, started laughing. “It’s getting a little late for me to have personal-development goals,” he quipped, before quickly adding: “I want to be smarter and better and help people, and help lift up the world.”

At a JPMorgan town hall meeting immediately before the interview, the CEO touched on global chaos. Later, with the SCMP, he expressed pride in the “vibrant, healthy, innovative” US economy while also flagging some of his home country’s shortcomings.

“In America, there are things we have done really badly,” Dimon said. “And whether it’s Democrat or Republican policies, we’ve done a bad job for inner cities; our schools aren’t graduating enough kids. The only way you fix that is to acknowledge it, and then you can attack it.

“But, if you make it ideological – Democrats against Republicans – and make moral statements about what works, then you lose sight of the facts. Sometimes our policies don’t work, and we have to be willing to say they don’t work.”

Regarding questions about how he would help change the situation, Dimon shied away from personal pursuits, focusing instead on his company’s strategy.

“I tell people that at JPMorgan, we hope we help cities, states, schools, hospitals, companies, governments,” he said. “We bank all the development banks, we bank the United States government.

“And that’s what we’re there for.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia faces a false binary in US-China mineral trade
item.description:
Critical minerals have become a recurring source of friction in international diplomacy, with China’s dominance in the sector and US efforts to build alternative supply chains raising concerns that Southeast Asian countries may be forced to choose between the two powers.

But this is a false choice. As important exporters of rare earth elements, Southeast Asian countries have leverage of their own and can use intensifying competition to diversify partnerships and capture more of the value chain at home.

The recent meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in the United States ended with a chairman’s declaration rather than a joint statement, underscoring the lack of unanimity. China objected to, among other things, calls to eliminate “non‑market policies” and ensure smooth global supply chains for vital goods, including critical minerals.
item.content:encoded:
Critical minerals have become a recurring source of friction in international diplomacy, with China’s dominance in the sector and US efforts to build alternative supply chains raising concerns that Southeast Asian countries may be forced to choose between the two powers.

But this is a false choice. As important exporters of rare earth elements, Southeast Asian countries have leverage of their own and can use intensifying competition to diversify partnerships and capture more of the value chain at home.

The recent meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in the United States ended with a chairman’s declaration rather than a joint statement, underscoring the lack of unanimity. China objected to, among other things, calls to eliminate “non‑market policies” and ensure smooth global supply chains for vital goods, including critical minerals.

The disagreement comes amid China’s tightening controls over rare earth elements (REEs), first introduced in April 2025 in retaliation for US tariffs and export controls. In October it went further, extending licensing requirements to certain foreign-made products containing at least 0.1 per cent Chinese-origin controlled REEs or using specified Chinese rare earth technologies. These measures were subsequently suspended until November this year, while the April 2025 controls remain.

Although Beijing has sought to reassure non-US importers that normal commercial trade will continue, such controls inevitably increase costs and uncertainty for firms dependent on Chinese rare earths, processing and magnets.

At the same time, a number of East Asian economies have joined Pax Silica and other US-supported efforts to build more resilient critical-mineral and technology supply chains. Has this increased pressure on them to choose between China-centred and US-backed supply chains? Given the region’s economic geography and dense webs of trade, few can afford such a binary choice.

In the case of critical minerals, however, such concerns about being forced to choose need to be put into context.

First of all, China’s present dominance in REEs stems from a long process of industrial development, not a strategy originally conceived to give Beijing a geopolitical weapon. The industry dates to the late 1950s. As applications expanded across metallurgy, petrochemicals, glass and ceramics, agriculture and equipment manufacturing, REEs were incorporated into national research and development programmes in 1986. In January 1991, the State Council issued a circular to curb rampant illegal mining under a national licensing regime, strengthen regulation and consolidate a fragmented industry.

REEs were thus initially treated as industrial resources for domestic use and export; they were not designed to be used as geopolitical instruments. Yet decades of investment and capability-building have given China considerable leverage within global REE supply chains. Amid intensifying Sino-US competition, these accumulated advantages have acquired strategic significance – hence the observation by Belgian political scientist Victor de Decker that, over REEs and other minerals deemed critical by the US, “Beijing is now mirroring Washington’s own semiconductor export control regime almost to the letter”.

For Beijing and Washington, the legitimacy of their export controls relies partly on the military applications of dual‑use materials and technologies, but their effectiveness is also limited. Curbing supply incentivises investment in alternatives, eroding the restricting country’s credibility and long‑term competitiveness as a supplier. Neither side can fully control an interdependent supply chain – midstream producers rely on downstream consumers abroad, while end users can reduce dependence through alternative sourcing, substitution and recycling.

This interdependence is particularly relevant to Southeast Asia. Despite its dominance of REE extraction and processing, China is a net importer of raw REEs, including substantial supplies from the region. In 2024, Myanmar supplied 34.3 per cent of China’s REE imports, Malaysia contributed 10.6 per cent and Laos 8.3 per cent. Together, they accounted for over half of China’s total imports.

Southeast Asia will not remain a mere supplier of raw materials, however. Malaysia already hosts the most commercially significant rare earth separation facility outside China, with much of its feedstock supplied from Lynas’s Mount Weld mine in Western Australia. The facility’s outputs are used in products ranging from lamps to semiconductors, a sector where Malaysia has decades of experience. It is only a matter of time before other regional ore exporters move into separation and other downstream applications.

Indonesia is another case in point. In recent years, it has banned the export of unprocessed minerals like nickel, requiring producers to invest in processing facilities to add value before export. While this builds on earlier practices, its character also aligns with the industrial policies adopted by China, the US and others at comparable stages of technological development.

As such, the proverbial choice between aligning with China or joining the US‑led Pax Silica is largely rhetorical for Southeast Asia. Both countries are interested in accessing Southeast Asian supplies of raw REEs on the basis of cost, not for the lack of material availability elsewhere, including within their own countries.

The more consequential question for Southeast Asian exporters is how competition over critical minerals can help them diversify into more higher-value activities. The real measure of competing partnerships should therefore be what China, the US and other partners contribute to Southeast Asian efforts to move up the value chain. This includes investments in processing and refining, technology and skills transfer, and stronger linkages to downstream manufacturing.

Seen in this context, the emerging competition is not just over who secures Southeast Asia’s minerals, but over who offers a more credible pathway from resource supplier to higher-value producer. To address societal concerns that REE refining is detrimental to the environment, the challenge is committing to importing the most environmentally-friendly processing technologies and rigorously enforcing standards on foreign corporate practices.

In the final analysis, access to critical minerals is likely to remain high on the regional agenda. But this is also the area in which Southeast Asian REE exporters can exercise a certain level of agency.

China’s dominance of REE processing gives it considerable leverage, but this should also not be overstated. Excessive restrictions incentivise alternative sourcing, substitution and recycling. Between China and the US, the likely outcome is a shifting balance between interdependence and diversification, not a full decoupling.

For Southeast Asia, the perceived binary choice between the two powers is a false one: all countries face the same task of adjusting their policies within a shared set of mineral‑industry dynamics among producers, processors and consumers.

Zha Daojiong is a Visiting Senior Fellow with ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is also Professor of International Political Economy at the School of International Studies, Peking University. This article was first published by the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg

item.title: [SCMP] How Zara Chui aims to find early-warning solutions for fatty liver disease
item.description:
Young minds, big ideas: meet five laureates of the AIA Scholarships programme, which was founded on the belief that education can open doors not only for individuals, but for the communities they will one day serve. See our other features, on King Chan Kai-man, Selina Wong Yuen-shan, Wilson Cheng Wui-sum and Atta Yu Yee-ting

Fatty liver disease, Zara Chui Siu-wa will tell you, has a strict definition: when more than 5 per cent of liver cells contain fat. But while defining the cause is straightforward, the hard part is identifying it. In most cases, there are no symptoms until the condition becomes severe. “It is a relatively silent disease,” she says, “but it is also the driver of other diseases.”

item.content:encoded:
Young minds, big ideas: meet five laureates of the AIA Scholarships programme, which was founded on the belief that education can open doors not only for individuals, but for the communities they will one day serve. See our other features, on King Chan Kai-man, Selina Wong Yuen-shan, Wilson Cheng Wui-sum and Atta Yu Yee-ting

Fatty liver disease, Zara Chui Siu-wa will tell you, has a strict definition: when more than 5 per cent of liver cells contain fat. But while defining the cause is straightforward, the hard part is identifying it. In most cases, there are no symptoms until the condition becomes severe. “It is a relatively silent disease,” she says, “but it is also the driver of other diseases.”

Chui, 24, is a second-year PhD student in medicine at the University of Hong Kong, specialising in endocrinology and metabolism. Her research area is fatty liver disease, also known as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD.

“Many people have fatty liver disease without knowing it,” she says. According to a recent study published in the Singapore Medical Journal, the prevalence of fatty liver disease in Asian adults has increased significantly, rising from 25.3 per cent in 1999 to 2005 to 33.9 per cent in 2012 to 2017 – roughly one in three people – underlining the importance of the topic.

Fatty liver disease’s “invisibility” is what makes it dangerous. It is mistakenly associated only with visible body fat, alcohol use or obvious ill health, but someone can appear slim, or have a low body-fat percentage, and still have liver dysfunction. As fat accumulates in the liver, it becomes a stressor: liver function deteriorates, inflammation builds and, over time, the cycle can contribute to fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver cancer and other metabolic conditions.

For this AIA Scholar, the liver’s complexity begins with a paradox: it is one of the body’s most regenerative organs, able to heal itself in ways many others cannot, and that regenerative potential was what first drew Chui in. But the deeper question – the one that continues to fascinate her – is why that ability disappears at a certain point.

Because the liver is famous for healing itself, many assume that early-stage fatty liver disease is harmless. Chui wants to challenge that idea. Once fibrosis or cirrhosis develops and the liver stiffens, its regenerative capacity is blunted. Even if the organ retains its normal size, it can no longer heal itself or function as it once did.

Her research is aimed at finding solutions to spot the warning signs of the condition early enough to reverse the damage. Instead of relying mainly on liver biopsies, which are invasive, or ultrasounds, which can be costly and are better at reflecting later-stage stiffness, Chui is investigating how to maximise the use of a far simpler indicator to detect the existence of fatty liver: blood. So far, blood tests have not been definitive enough to signal the disease on their own, meaning other, more surgical, or more expensive assessments are usually required. She wants to change that.

Using AI-assisted systems, she analyses liver-tissue slides to identify features such as lipid droplets and immune cells – small visual clues that may point towards larger disease patterns – which are then cross-referenced with protein levels in blood, in the hope of recognising biomarkers that can support earlier diagnoses, more personalised treatment plans and, eventually, new drug targets for a disease with limited medication options.

Her work matters particularly for non-Western patients, as existing tools do not always reflect biological differences between populations. “Many AI algorithms and non-invasive panels are developed using predominantly Caucasian population data. But the progression pattern of liver disease in Asians is very different,” says Chui.

She believes AI algorithms for fatty liver disease should recognise biological and genetic differences. MASLD research on non-Western populations is still relatively limited, she says. However, with the kind of resources her pharmaceutical biotechnology lab team at HKU can access – unique biobank clinical data, including blood and tissue biopsy samples from 1,200 obese patients of Chinese ethnicity, collected by the Hong Kong Cardiovascular Risk Factor Prevalence Study – more can be done to make good use of available information.

Despite studies showing its strong performance, Chui remains cautious about AI. A diagnostic platform, she believes, should assist clinicians, not replace them. AI can provide data and hints, but the final diagnosis still needs human judgment and clinical context.

Her path to the lab began in secondary school, when she learned about iGEM, an international competition specialising in synthetic biology. It offered her a rare opportunity to glimpse the inner workings of the research world, through presentations led by various universities. Later, during her time as an undergraduate in biomedical sciences at HKU, she interned at a biotech start-up at Hong Kong Science Park, working on metal 3D printing for orthopaedic implants and surgical guides – an early lesson in how raw lab discoveries can turn into real-world medical care.

In her third year, she travelled to Switzerland with the company as it explored overseas growth, where she saw research from a different perspective: not only as experiments and prototypes, but as factories, hospitals, banks, tax incentives, talent schemes and market strategy. It was an eye-opening experience that showed her how scientific ideas can be translated into products, but it also clarified her path forward: to stay in academia.

What the AIA Scholarships gave her was time. With the programme’s funds covering the tuition fees for her undergraduate degree, Chui gained time that she would have otherwise lost to chasing hourly wages through part-time jobs. “It’s how I was able to do so many lab and industry internships,” she says, adding that the support helped her “discover what I wanted to do next”.

But even with her mind set on her goal, research is anything but glamorous. Much of her work happens behind the scenes: cleaning data, repeating experiments, studying inconsistent results, annotating images and testing biomarkers. Failure is a daily occurrence.

In textbooks, experiments seem foolproof: follow the protocol and expect the result. In real life, even the same steps can produce different outcomes. Wrestling with unexpected results is exhausting, Chui admits, but it is also when the real breakthroughs happen.

After her PhD, Chui hopes to continue researching fatty liver disease and explore whether her biomarker candidates can be translated into drug development. One day down the line, she plans to teach and pass on knowledge and curiosity to a new generation.

For Chui, doing good means breaking the silence around a quiet disease, raising awareness of an underestimated health risk and taking action before the organ loses its chance to heal.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ jeepney drivers ‘stuck between a rock and a hard place’ despite fare increase
item.description:
Reggie Manlapig, 46, has been driving jeepneys for nearly 25 years and has weathered rising fuel prices – but with costs spiking amid the global energy crunch, he is now wrestling bigger demons.

“The impact has been huge. Before, in a 16-hour shift of driving, I could take home 400 to 500 pesos [US$6.30 to US$8] – now there’s a big cut to that income,” said Manlapig, who plies a two-hour daily round route from Malolos in Bulacan, north of Manila, to San Fernando, Pampanga.

“Doing the full route five times straight in a day really pushes you. Before, three round trips alone would already give you decent earnings – especially on days with no classes, holidays, or student holiday periods; those are especially hard.”
item.content:encoded:
Reggie Manlapig, 46, has been driving jeepneys for nearly 25 years and has weathered rising fuel prices – but with costs spiking amid the global energy crunch, he is now wrestling bigger demons.

“The impact has been huge. Before, in a 16-hour shift of driving, I could take home 400 to 500 pesos [US$6.30 to US$8] – now there’s a big cut to that income,” said Manlapig, who plies a two-hour daily round route from Malolos in Bulacan, north of Manila, to San Fernando, Pampanga.

“Doing the full route five times straight in a day really pushes you. Before, three round trips alone would already give you decent earnings – especially on days with no classes, holidays, or student holiday periods; those are especially hard.”

His sentiments reflect the broader grievances of jeepney drivers and other public transport operators in the Philippines, who continue to bear the brunt of soaring fuel prices from the gridlocked Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war.

On Monday, increased prices finally implemented by the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr took effect, raising jeepney fares by 1 peso – a long-overdue move that was first suspended in March.

“We’re grateful for it, but it’s a very small help – very small for us. What good is a one-peso fare increase if fuel prices keep rising one after another – 10 pesos, 8 pesos at a time? How is that one peso supposed to keep up? It barely makes a dent,” Manlapig said.

The high costs had forced drivers off the road, leading to longer wait times for commuters and crowded vehicles, Julius Dalay, founder of the concern group Commuters of the Philippines, told This Week in Asia.

Diesel prices rolled back by 7.57 pesos this week after reaching nearly 100 pesos per litre in some areas in the Philippines.

Yet for the country’s transport sector, the latest adjustments are insufficient to make up for the massive loss of livelihoods as prices continue to rise.

Transport group Piston held a two-day strike on Tuesday, demanding the removal of excise and value-added taxes on petroleum. It also urged authorities to restore diesel costs to 55 pesos per litre – its last price the week before the Iran war began – and repeal a 28-year-old oil deregulation law that leaves the discretion of price caps to private companies.

“With every price increase, income shrinks, and the cost of basic goods rises faster than workers’ small incomes and wages can keep up,” Mody Floranda, leader of Piston, told This Week in Asia.

Floranda said the group first petitioned for fare increases in February when diesel prices rose following the Gulf conflict.

“It took six months for the [government] to finally grant it, timed right as we announced the strike. So we consider the increase a win from people’s mobilisation – but small as it is, it’s no longer enough for our drivers’ needs,” Floranda said.

The extra 1 peso was “nowhere near the scale of what our drivers are losing”, he lamented. He noted that many drivers, unable to keep up with the rising transport costs due to mounting debts and repair expenses, had moved to other jobs such as construction work or farming in the provinces.

Nanoy Rafael, convenor of the PARA-Commuters Network, told This Week in Asia his group had estimated a 10 to 20 per cent reduction in public transport vehicles before August.

Data from the transport ministry in August reflected the group’s predictions, Rafael said. The figures showed 18,000 traditional jeepneys had stopped plying the roads year on year, down from 128,000 units in August last year, he said, while only 8,000 electric jeepneys remained operational.

“So that was really the first effect: we have nothing to ride,” Rafael said, adding that in March and April, cities such as Baguio in northern Philippines nearly ground to a halt.

His group supported the fare increase despite the cost of goods outpacing wages “because there’s nothing else. We’re stuck between a rock and a hard place”.

The persistent price shocks in the Philippines highlight the country’s differences in preparation and supply compared with Southeast Asian neighbours that may be better equipped to cushion the blow, according to Jaideep Singh, an analyst at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies in Malaysia.

“For Southeast Asia, the conflict in West Asia, including periodic closures of the Strait of Hormuz, manifests primarily as a supply chain and energy shock. However, the first-order economic effects of the crisis depend on the trade and energy profiles of Asean countries, particularly their exposure to fuel imports from the Gulf region,” Singh said.

Among the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the Philippines remained the most vulnerable as over 97 per cent of its crude petroleum imports were sourced from the Gulf, mainly Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, Singh said.

These pipelines were prone to supply-side disruptions beyond Hormuz, such as Houthi attacks, he noted. “What exacerbates the situation for the Philippines is its negligible domestic production and structural challenges in diversifying imports.”

By contrast, other major oil importers in Asean such as Thailand and Singapore have sufficient stockpiles of crude petroleum and considerable refining capabilities that help cushion the direct impact on fuel prices.

Malaysia has diversified its oil imports and continues to have sizeable oil reserves, remaining a net exporter of liquefied natural gas, a critical commodity for electricity production.

Malaysia and Indonesia also expanded their use of palm-based biodiesel to reduce reliance on conventional diesel.

“While the Philippines has mandated a 10 per cent bioethanol blend into all petrol sold nationwide, there is inadequate domestic supply of ethanol to satisfy rising demand,” Singh warned.

He also pointed to differing fiscal policy responses on how authorities passed the buck to consumers through pump prices.

Malaysia has a fuel subsidy scheme for citizens that keeps petrol prices stable, subject to an adjustable quota, though fiscal resources are increasingly under strain.

Vietnam manages domestic fuel prices through a hybrid mechanism that encompasses a maximum retail price, alongside a petroleum price stabilisation fund.

“In the Philippines meanwhile, given its very high exposure and limited manoeuvrability, pump prices are largely market-driven, with efforts geared towards providing cash assistance to the most price-sensitive consumers,” Singh said.

The Philippines offers few, if any, subsidies for consumers to manage pump prices, while public transport drivers and operators have lamented the uneven and inconsistent implementation of these subsidies.

“When it comes to the government subsidy, there’s favouritism involved – not all drivers and operators actually receive it,” Manlapig said, noting that only certain petrol stations allowed the subsidy to be claimed.

Floranda urged the government to remove the excise and value-added taxes on petrol to ease citizens’ burden.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Xi Jinping skipped the UN after his Trump summit
item.description:
Han Zheng, China’s vice-president, called on “major countries” to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations and bring about a two-state solution for the “Palestinian question” on Saturday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in an implicit dig at the US and Israel.

This came as some analysts questioned why Chinese President Xi Jinping opted not to address the global body given his three-day summit in Washington with US President Donald Trump this week – despite the short distance between New York and Washington, Beijing’s long-standing assertions on the UN’s importance and active campaign to build soft power and promote its global initiatives.

“Many months ago, Chinese officials said that Xi wouldn’t go to the UN unless it was to mark a major anniversary,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “Seems like a missed opportunity.”
item.content:encoded:
Han Zheng, China’s vice-president, called on “major countries” to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations and bring about a two-state solution for the “Palestinian question” on Saturday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in an implicit dig at the US and Israel.

This came as some analysts questioned why Chinese President Xi Jinping opted not to address the global body given his three-day summit in Washington with US President Donald Trump this week – despite the short distance between New York and Washington, Beijing’s long-standing assertions on the UN’s importance and active campaign to build soft power and promote its global initiatives.

“Many months ago, Chinese officials said that Xi wouldn’t go to the UN unless it was to mark a major anniversary,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “Seems like a missed opportunity.”

Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has addressed the annual General Assembly gathering once in person, in 2015 for the 70th anniversary. He appeared by video in 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic but missed the 80th anniversary last year when Premier Li Qiang spoke. In other years, China has generally been represented by other senior officials, including Han and Foreign Minister Wang Yi.

China has also placed significantly more importance on Washington relations than on multilateral issues, analysts said.

This week’s summit mirrored its counterpart hosted by China for Trump in May – limited to 48 hours with no side trips or multilateral events – to underscore the geopolitical parity Beijing sees as its due.

“He’s not giving America any more honour than Trump gave to the Chinese,” said Jeffrey Moon, principal at China Moon Strategies, a former US consul general in Chengdu. “In the Chinese psyche, that was more important than attending UNGA. Somebody else can do the speech.”

“Protocol-wise, [Xi’s appearance] would get slightly more benefit. But not appearing to be anything less than equal to the US would be probably more important.”

Among the initiatives China has promoted at the UN in recent years, touted by Han on Saturday, are its vaguely worded global development, security, civilisation and governance initiatives aimed at promoting prosperity, stability, mutual trust and procedural justice.

These dovetail with China’s growing global reputation.

A Pew Research Centre survey released this month found that US favourability across 20 countries was 36 per cent in 2026, down from 58 per cent in 2023, while China’s rose to 46 from 32 during the same period.

A Global Soft Power Index released in January saw the US maintain its No 1 ranking with a score of 74.9 out of 100 but it recorded the largest decline among the 193 countries ranked, while China strengthened its No 2 position modestly with a score of 73.5.

“It is difficult not to make a connection between some of the ‘America first’ policies and the negative turn of the US perceptions internationally,” the survey said, adding that China’s “soft power gains are underpinned by a long-term policy-led programme”.

Some wonder how much of the change is due to China’s actions, however, and how much to Trump’s deeply unpopular foreign policy, damaging tariffs, military adventurism and threats against long-standing allies.

While it has strongly supported multilateralism and the UN Charter, China has not always walked the walk, some argue.

“To fill the lane that America’s retreat has opened … China will need to put forward resources, not just rhetoric,” said Ryan Hass, a director at the Brookings Institution and former US National Security Council official. “Beijing clearly has ambition. I’m not clear that they’ll be able to realise it.”

Analysts say China attributes the Soviet Union’s demise and what it sees as America’s inexorable decline to being overstretched, including the US actions in the Middle East.

“Historically, global leaders have spent pretty generously to realise their vision of revising the international system. Beijing has not,” added Hass, a former US diplomat in Beijing, citing reduced Belt and Road Initiative largesse, perhaps given economic weakness and high youth unemployment at home.

While nations welcome Chinese infrastructure projects and preferential lending, few appear keen to follow its governance model, Hass said.

“They’ve been very tight-fisted,” he added. “It is striking how little progress Beijing is making in attracting followers to its vision. It reflects the limits in Beijing’s ability to attract support.”

Others said it may be unrealistic to expect China to fill the US void.

“The US has burned so many bridges and China has taken over so completely,” said Marc Limon, executive director of Universal Rights Group, a civic group based in Geneva. “They’re very good at coalition building with countries of the Global South. They have a huge number of friends. They really do try to help.”

Han’s speech on Saturday comes as the Iran war started by Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nears its seventh month. Earlier in the week, in a fiery exchange, Netanyahu accused UN diplomats of “mind-blowing hypocrisy” over protests as he addressed the assembly on Thursday.

Envoys booed loudly and many walked out during his speech, prompting him to accuse those leaving the cavernous hall of being “moral cowards”, claiming that many of their same nations had “privately thanked us for taking out Iran’s nukes”.

Relations between Trump and Netanyahu have also grown notably cooler recently. Trump chose not to meet Netanyahu earlier this week when they overlapped in New York.

The death toll now exceeds 73,600 Palestinians in Gaza since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel that killed some 1,200 people and saw 251 others taken hostage, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, as Netanyahu revs up campaigning for his late October re-election bid.

Han on Saturday called on the international community to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations.

At a thinly attended Saturday morning session, Han called on the international community to “reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation”.

“We should settle differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation, and oppose unilateral military actions that violate the UN Charter and circumvent Security Council authorisation.”

He also called for efforts to safeguard peace, rebuild trust and reject unilateralism at the expense of multilateralism, echoing themes voiced this week by Wang.

China’s vice-president did not join Xi during the Washington summit that saw Trump meet Xi on the tarmac when he arrived Wednesday evening. The Chinese president did not bestow the same honour on Trump when he landed in Beijing in May, a role he delegated to Han.
